### [1] [Revisiting Classic Thought Experiments to Measure Consciousness for Artificial Intelligence Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00001)
*Peter David Fagan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper revisits classic philosophy of mind arguments through a computational framework, showing that systems can achieve similar task performance while differing in how efficiently their internal structure supports that behavior, with implications for AI safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to reframe classic philosophical disputes about understanding and consciousness (Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, Searle's Chinese Room) by developing a formal framework that separates outward behavioral performance from the internal organization that sustains it.

Method: The authors use the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework to formalize a toy symbolic setting. They define two metrics: task performance (W_causal,T) measures successful behavior, while operational consciousness (κ_T) measures the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behavior. They compare two system types: uncompressed lookup systems and compact generative systems.

Result: Both system types can achieve comparable behavioral success on tasks, but diverge sharply in operational consciousness (κ_T). Uncompressed lookup systems rely on expanding stores of unreused mappings, while compact generative systems reuse compact internal structure more efficiently.

Conclusion: The paper provides a formal framework to separate outward performance from internal organization, reframing classic philosophy of mind debates and suggesting this distinction may be important for future AI safety analysis.

Abstract: This research note revisits Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, and Searle's Chinese Room through the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework. It formalises a toy symbolic setting in which successful behaviour is measured by task performance ($W_{causal,T}$), while the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behaviour is measured by operational consciousness ($κ_T$). Within this setup, an uncompressed lookup system and a compact generative system can in principle achieve comparable behavioural success, yet diverge sharply in $κ_T$: the former relies on an expanding standing store of unreused mappings, whereas the latter reuses compact internal structure. The note therefore reframes classic disputes about understanding by separating outward performance from the organisation that sustains it, and motivates why this distinction may matter for later AI-safety analysis.

</details>


### [2] [AutoFOAM: The Self-Refining Autonomous OpenFOAM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00003)
*Arun Govind Neelan,A Seshaditya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoFOAM is a self-evolving LLM agent that automatically creates, runs, and evolves OpenFOAM CFD simulations from natural language instructions, reducing the expertise and setup time required for open-source fluid dynamics simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-source CFD solvers like OpenFOAM require substantial expertise and time-consuming configuration, creating barriers to adoption. There's a need to democratize advanced CFD workflows and accelerate rapid prototyping.

Method: AutoFOAM uses a pre-trained Qwen-coder 2.5-14B model fine-tuned on 252 text prompts covering 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 mesh templates, and y plus-aware numerical policies. The system employs a 7-stage evolution loop with three anti-collapse mechanisms: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing to prevent model degeneration during self-training.

Result: The paper demonstrates that AutoFOAM successfully bridges generative AI with rigorous fluid simulations, enabling automated CFD workflow generation and evolution based on natural language instructions.

Conclusion: AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows by reducing the expertise barrier through its self-evolving LLM agent approach, effectively connecting generative AI with computational fluid dynamics.

Abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays an important role in modern engineering, but using open-source solvers such as OpenFOAM requires considerable knowledge and skills, as well as time-consuming configuration file setup. To reduce this burden, we propose AutoFOAM - a self-evolving large language model (LLM) agent that creates, evaluates, runs, and evolves its own OpenFOAM simulations based solely on natural-language instructions. Our model is pre-trained on the Qwen-coder 2.5-14B, which is then fine-tuned on 252 text prompts targeting 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parametrized mesh templates, and a y plus-aware numerical policy. The crucial element of the algorithm is a sophisticated evolution loop composed of 7 stages. To prevent model degeneration under repeated self-training, the agent employs three complementary anti-collapse streams: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing. By bridging generative artificial intelligence with rigorous fluid simulations, AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows.

</details>


### [3] [Enhancing LLMs with Context-Specific Knowledge for Mitigating Misinformation in SMEs: A RAG-based Modeling and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00006)
*Md. Samiul Islam,Iqbal H. Sarker,Chadni Islam,Ahmad Mohsin,Ahmed Ibrahim,Helge Janicke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAG-enhanced LLMs (VectorRAG and GraphRAG) significantly improve response quality and reduce hallucinations/misinformation in SME question-answering systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used by SMEs for question-answering and decision-making, but hallucinations in LLM outputs create misinformation risks and reduce user confidence in their reliability and trustworthiness.

Method: Proposed VectorRAG and GraphRAG modeling approaches that incorporate external knowledge sources to mitigate hallucinations. Experimental evaluation on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) assessing useful response generation, hallucination risk, contextual relevance, and human interpretation.

Result: RAG-enhanced LLMs significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, supporting more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments.

Conclusion: RAG approaches (VectorRAG and GraphRAG) are effective solutions for mitigating LLM hallucinations and misinformation risks in SME applications, enhancing the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-powered decision support systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), a part of artificial intelligence (AI), are increasingly being adopted by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to enhance question-answering capabilities and support business decision-making processes. However, hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs can serve as a source of misinformation, reducing user confidence in their reliability and trustworthiness within SMEs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge by incorporating external knowledge sources into the modeling process. In this paper, we present VectorRAG and GraphRAG modeling approaches to mitigate hallucinations and misinformation risks and evaluate their effectiveness in SME environments. Our experimental evaluation is conducted on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, to assess performance in terms of useful response generation, risk of hallucination, contextual relevance, as well as human-interpretation. The results demonstrate that RAG-enhanced LLMs can significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, thereby supporting more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments.

</details>


### [4] [Energy Efficiency of Locally Deployed LLMs: A Preliminary Quantitative GPU Power Benchmark on Consumer Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00008)
*Philipp M. Zähl,Anika Hennig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B-7B parameters) on consumer GPU reveals that model architecture and quantization, not just parameter count, determine energy efficiency, with Gemma3:1b and Llama3.2:1b being most efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local deployment of LLMs is increasing for privacy and on-premise inference, but energy costs on consumer hardware are poorly characterized as most benchmarks focus only on accuracy, not energy efficiency.

Method: Reproducible hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) on RTX 4060Ti 16GB GPU using Ollama inference engine, sampling GPU power draw at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across fixed prompt set. Measured mean/peak power, total energy per prompt, energy per output token, and throughput.

Result: Gemma3:1b and Llama3.2:1b achieve lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and highest throughput (>170 tok/s). 7B-Mistral consumes up to 4.4x more energy per token than most efficient model. Qwen3.5:2b shows anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning. Model architecture and quantization strategy drive efficiency more than raw parameter count.

Conclusion: Energy efficiency in LLM deployment depends on factors beyond parameter count, particularly model architecture and quantization. Future energy benchmarks should distinguish between different token generation modes (e.g., internal reasoning vs. standard generation) for more accurate efficiency assessment.

Abstract: The local deployment of large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction due to privacy concerns and the desire for on-premise inference. However, the energy costs on consumer hardware remain poorly characterized, as most benchmarks focus solely on accuracy. This paper presents a reproducible, hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti 16GB). Using the Ollama inference engine, GPU power draw was sampled at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. We evaluate mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s). Our findings suggest that factors beyond raw parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy, drive energy efficiency. Specifically, gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieve the lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and the highest throughput (>170 tok/s). In contrast, the 7B-Mistral model consumes up to 4.4x more energy per token than the most efficient model. Notably, qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, highlighting the need to distinguish between token generation modes in efficiency metrics.

</details>


### [5] [CoT-Core: Accelerating LLM Evaluation via CoT-Aware Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00014)
*Qihua Pan,Zhenheng Tang,Peijie Dong,Xiang Liu,Huacan Wang,Bo Li,Xiaowen Chu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT-Core is a training-free framework that uses Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories to select core evaluation questions for LLMs, reducing computational costs while maintaining accurate score estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation methods incur prohibitive computational costs. Existing coreset selection approaches have limitations: they either require massive historical logs (cold start problem) or exhibit lexical biases that miss the underlying reasoning structure of tasks.

Method: CoT-Core prompts LLMs to generate zero-shot Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories for questions. These reasoning paths are projected into a latent space to cluster questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than superficial text similarity, enabling efficient question selection without training.

Result: Extensive experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA show CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation. The method reveals that reasoning-aware pruning efficacy is intrinsically gated by task complexity.

Conclusion: CoT-Core provides an effective training-free framework for efficient LLM evaluation by leveraging reasoning trajectories to identify logically equivalent questions, overcoming both cold start and lexical bias problems in existing methods.

Abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) incurs prohibitive computational overhead during continuous development processes. While coreset selection accelerates evaluation, existing methods either suffer from a severe ``cold start'' bottleneck requiring massive historical logs (e.g., Item Response Theory) or exhibit a surface lexical bias that misses the underlying reasoning manifold of tasks. We propose CoT-Core, a novel training-free core question selection framework. Recognizing that lexically disparate questions can share equivalent underlying logic, CoT-Core prompts LLMs to unroll zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trajectories. Projecting these paths into a latent space effectively clusters questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than superficial text similarity. Extensive experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA demonstrate that CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation, and delineate the boundary conditions of reasoning-aware pruning, revealing that its efficacy is intrinsically gated by task complexity.

</details>


### [6] [Optimization and Constraint Modeling using LLMs with a Retrieval Augmented Generation Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00015)
*Prateek Roy,Akash Singirikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAG pipeline with synthetic datasets improves LLM optimization modeling accuracy from 40% to 72% without costly fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, especially in combinatorial settings, limiting their practical use in domains like logistics, healthcare, and supply chain management despite the importance of optimization modeling.

Method: Created a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline using: 1) 500 synthetic optimization problems generated from Text2Zinc seed descriptions with professional personas via LLM, 2) JSON encoding with validated Python solver scripts, 3) Chroma vector database for storage, 4) Semantic retrieval of similar problems as contextual guidance for LangChain LLM agent, evaluated with Qwen 3 30B Instruct model on three benchmark testbeds.

Result: Accuracy improvements: 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The pipeline significantly enhances both solution accuracy and structural consistency.

Conclusion: Synthetic dataset generation combined with retrieval augmentation offers an effective alternative to fine-tuning, providing a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

Abstract: Both optimization modeling and constraint modeling are non-trivial problems requiring deep domain expertise and proficiency in modeling formalism languages. Despite their importance across logistics, healthcare, and supply chain management, current large language models regularly produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, particularly in combinatorial settings. This paper evaluates whether a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline built on a curated synthetic dataset can meaningfully improve LLM optimization modeling performance. A total of 500 optimization problems were synthesized using seed descriptions from the Text2Zinc dataset and professional personas created using an LLM, specified in JSON and associated with validated Python solver scripts. These problems were encoded in a Chroma vector database. For each inference problem, semantically similar problems were retrieved and used as contextual guidance for a LangChain LLM agent. Three benchmark testbeds were used to evaluate the proposed pipeline under the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model. Accuracy rose from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The use of semantically validated synthetic examples greatly improves both solution accuracy and structure. The combination of synthetic dataset generation with retrieval augmentation provides an effective alternative to fine-tuning, suggesting that domain-specific synthetic corpora paired with retrieval augmentation can serve as a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

</details>


### [7] [Memory Reward Inflation in Self-Improving LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00017)
*Mohammad Asadolahi,Amir Amini,Samira Talebi,Amirfarhad Farhadi,Azadeh Zamanifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-improving LLM agents that learn from experience without weight updates can develop a failure mode called the "Echo Gap" where incorrect episodes receive inflated rewards from the LLM's own assessments, leading to compounding errors as agents preferentially reuse their most confident mistakes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly learn from experience by storing episodes in external memory with scores, then retrieving them for similar future tasks. However, in deployment without ground-truth labels, the stored rewards come from LLM assessments rather than true labels, creating a potential failure mode where the agent's own biased assessments compound errors through memory retrieval.

Method: The authors formalize the Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) as a necessary condition for correcting reward inflation, showing that usable signals must track truth AND decorrelate error from memory bias. They analyze how inflation compounds not only with score-based retrieval but also similarity-based retrieval. They propose an answer-free de-inflation algorithm called LUCID.

Result: LUCID delivers consistent end-to-end gains on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark, raising execution accuracy to 56.9%, outperforming both a Memento-style self-graded agent (54.0%, +2.9-point mean gain) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture (52.4%).

Conclusion: The Echo Gap represents a fundamental challenge for memory-based self-improving agents when using LLM-assessed rewards without ground truth. The Error-Independence Assumption is necessary for correcting reward inflation, and the proposed LUCID algorithm demonstrates practical effectiveness in mitigating this issue, providing a framework for more reliable self-improving agents.

Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly learn from experience without updating any weights. Each episode is stored in an external memory, scored, and retrieved for similar future tasks to shape later behavior. Viewed through a reward lens, the stored score is a proxy reward for an implicit, non-parametric policy. Each retrieved episode then becomes a policy-improvement step whose reliability hinges on how that score is produced. In deployment, ground-truth labels are unavailable, so the stored reward is at best an LLM assessment. This substitution creates a failure mode, the *Echo Gap*, across the memory-based self-improving agents and model families studied. Incorrect episodes receive inflated rewards; thus, the agent preferentially reuses the very mistakes it has most confident in. Because the error compounds through memory rather than averaging out and the confirming judge's errors remain correlated with the original self-grading bias, so it cannot identify which memories are overvalued. The missing property is formalized as the *Error-Independence Assumption* (EIA), which we prove is a *necessary* condition for correcting the inflation, not merely a description of a good verifier: a usable signal must track truth *and* decorrelate its error from the memory bias, and the recoverable payoff is a closed-form function of exactly those two quantities. We further show the inflation compounds not only when retrieval ranks by the stored score but also under plain similarity retrieval which is the regime the deployed agent uses. Finally, the answer-free de-inflation algorithm LUCID delivers a consistent end-to-end gain on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark. It raises execution accuracy to $56.9\%$, above both a Memento-style self-graded agent ($54.0\%$, a $+2.9$-point mean gain across seeds) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture ($52.4\%$).

</details>


### [8] [Can LLM Agents Price Competitively? A Dynamic Multi-Attribute Auction Benchmark for Agentic Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00102)
*Shimaa Ahmed,Yiwei Cai,Mohsen Minaei,Rahul Rachuri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs show emerging but limited competency in dynamic pricing for agentic commerce, with performance varying across metrics and conditions, revealing substantial room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic commerce is becoming real with infrastructure deployment, but it's unclear if LLMs can effectively price in real market conditions with hidden preferences, competitor adaptation, and demand shifts.

Method: Introduces Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auctions that tests LLMs in realistic market conditions while maintaining closed-form customer utilities for exact evaluation.

Result: Across 11 frontier LLMs, performance rankings shift between metrics: agents excelling at customer acquisition (Gemini 3.1 Pro) differ from profit leaders (Opus 4.6). Under demand shocks, fastest learners pre-shock adapt slowest afterwards, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest. Even top agents capture less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit.

Conclusion: Current LLMs are making progress in agentic commerce but have substantial headroom for improvement, with no single agent dominating all performance dimensions and significant challenges in dynamic market adaptation.

Abstract: Agentic commerce is moving from concept to deployed infrastructure: payment networks, retailers, and AI platforms are setting the stage for agents to transact on behalf of merchants and consumers. Yet whether the LLMs behind these agents can price competently in real markets, where customer preferences are hidden, competitors adapt in real time, and demand can shift without warning, has not been systematically tested. We introduce Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auction under these conditions. Despite its dynamics, the benchmark is grounded in closed-form customer utilities, enabling exact evaluation. Across 11 frontier LLMs from four providers, the leading agents on customer acquisition (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro) are often not the leading agents on profit (e.g. Opus 4.6). The ranking shifts again under demand shocks: agents that learned fastest pre-shock are typically the slowest to revise their beliefs afterwards, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest despite not leading on profit. However, even the strongest agent captures less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit, suggesting current LLMs are progressing in agentic commerce but leave substantial headroom.

</details>


### [9] [Request-Level Energy Attribution for Batched LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00026)
*Qi Luo,Kunlin Li,Ziwen Wang,Dongsheng Wang,Yun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JouleShare is a framework for fair request-level energy attribution in batched LLM serving, using measured Shapley values as ground truth and learning to predict them from cheap features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Batched LLM serving improves throughput but makes energy accounting complex. Current methods use aggregate GPU power telemetry or approximate metrics (token-proportional, model/phase-level energy), but lack measured request-level ground truth for fair energy attribution needed for sustainability reporting, chargeback, and workload analysis.

Method: Two-component framework: 1) Offline harness establishes ground truth by replaying request subsets under vLLM with reproducible protocol, integrating GPU power telemetry, and computing exact Shapley energy for each request. 2) JCalib, a lightweight calibration model that learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for serving-time use.

Result: Token-proportional attribution deviates significantly from exact Shapley values (0.440-0.458 normalized L1 error). JCalib reduces error to 0.116-0.177, below standalone-measurement baseline, while preserving batch-energy efficiency. The gap persists across larger group sizes and different GPUs.

Conclusion: Token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution. Measured Shapley ground truth can effectively calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer energy attribution in practical LLM serving scenarios.

Abstract: Batched LLM serving improves throughput but complicates energy accounting. GPU power telemetry is aggregate, whereas sustainability reporting, chargeback, and workload analysis often require request-level energy charges. Existing inference-energy benchmarks report model-, phase-, or token-level energy, and recent carbon-accounting work motivates Shapley fairness conceptually. Neither provides measured request-level ground truth, so how far the accounting rules used in practice deviate from a fair allocation has remained unknown. We present JouleShare, an attribution framework with two components. An offline harness establishes this ground truth by replaying request subsets under vLLM with a reproducible protocol, integrating GPU power telemetry, and computing exact Shapley energy for each request. A lightweight calibration model, JCalib, then learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for use at serving time. Across 16 model/workload runs, token-proportional attribution differs from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 on average under static batching and by 0.458 under continuous batching, a gap that reproduces across three data-center GPUs. JCalib reduces this error to 0.116 under static batching and 0.177 under continuous batching, below even a standalone-measurement baseline that is unavailable online, while preserving exact batch-energy efficiency. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes, where the gap persists and a single offline calibration remains the most accurate deployable rule. The results show that token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution, and that measured Shapley ground truth can calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer attribution.

</details>


### [10] [Motif-Mamba: network motif improved mamba for long-range sequence modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00027)
*Chonghe Hao,Yue Sun,Jian Zhang,Yansong Wang,Wangzi Yao,Yunjie Yao,Tielin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Motif-Mamba enhances Mamba's selective state space model by adding a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway to enable better cross-dimensional state interactions while maintaining linear-time efficiency for long-sequence modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-attention in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length, making long-sequence modeling inefficient. Mamba offers linear-time alternative but its predominantly diagonal state transitions limit explicit interactions among state dimensions, restricting cross-dimensional communication.

Method: Augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway inspired by three-node network motifs. Projects hidden states into compact dynamical subspace, imposes motif-guided interactions, then maps dynamics back to original state space while preserving linear-time recurrent structure.

Result: Experiments show consistent improvements over Mamba backbones on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain-computer interface decoding tasks. Demonstrates better performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Motif-guided low-rank dynamics provide an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling, enhancing cross-dimensional communication in state space models while preserving their linear-time efficiency advantages over attention-based approaches.

Abstract: Efficient long-sequence modeling remains a central challenge for large language models, as self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length. Mamba offers a linear-time alternative through selective state space recurrence, but its predominantly diagonal state transitions restrict explicit interactions among state dimensions. We propose Motif-Mamba, a structured state space model that augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway. Inspired by the dynamics of three-node network motifs, the proposed pathway projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, imposes motif-guided interactions, and maps the resulting dynamics back to the original state space. This design enhances cross-dimensional communication while preserving the linear-time recurrent structure of Mamba. Experiments on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain--computer interface decoding show consistent improvements over Mamba backbones, suggesting that motif-guided low-rank dynamics provide an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling.

</details>


### [11] [HetGPS: Scalable Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Physics-Anchored Adaptive Safety for EV Charging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00679)
*Xiangwei Wang,Nanduni Nimalsiri,Yu Xia,Peng Wang,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HetGPS is a hybrid graph-control framework for EV charging coordination that separates intervention magnitude from corrective direction, using learned graph risk for authority scheduling and physics models for corrective direction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints (like voltage limits in EV charging) without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions, requiring scalable approaches that can coordinate across different network topologies.

Method: Proposes HetGPS: a hybrid framework combining learned graph risk (action-conditioned graph residual model schedules state-dependent intervention authority) with physics-anchored correction (physics model determines corrective direction). Uses parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic policy enabling topology-aware coordination with model size independent of fleet size.

Result: Reduces bus-step voltage violations from 3.93-7.74% to 0.52-3.44% across five distribution networks with 200-3,218 EVs, while maintaining 99.06-100% departure success. Improves mean reward on all five networks vs fixed authority approach. Model scales efficiently (383,702 parameters vs ~170× larger for centralized approach). Policy transfers zero-shot to larger systems with 0.57-0.75% violations and ≥99.99% success.

Conclusion: Learned graph risk can effectively allocate intervention authority at scale while feeder physics anchors corrective action, enabling safe coordination of large EV fleets with model size independent of fleet scale and good transfer capability across different network topologies.

Abstract: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions. We present HetGPS, a hybrid graph-control framework synergizing learned graph risk with physics-anchored correction by separating intervention magnitude from corrective direction. An action-conditioned graph residual model schedules state-dependent intervention authority, while a physics model determines its direction. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, we couple this filter with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic policy, enabling topology-aware coordination with a learned model size independent of fleet size. Across five nested distribution networks with 200--3,218 EVs and 100 evaluation days, Adaptive Authority reduces bus--step voltage violations from 3.93--7.74\% without filtering to 0.52--3.44\%, while maintaining 99.06--100\% departure success. Relative to the same physics-directed projection with fixed authority, it improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers the mean safety score on four. The deployed policy-and-risk model contains 383,702 learned parameters at every scale; at 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is about $170\times$ larger. A policy trained on the eight-transformer system transfers zero-shot to the 16- and 32-transformer systems, attaining 0.57--0.75\% violation rates and at least 99.99\% departure success. These results show that learned graph risk can allocate intervention authority at scale while feeder physics anchors corrective action.

</details>


### [12] [Nova: An End-to-End MLIR Compiler for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00029)
*Adwaid Suresh,Aparna A,Harshini V M,Jona Delcy C A,Killi Uma Maheswara Rao,Ram Charan Golla,Surendra Vendra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Nova is an automated JIT compiler that achieves fine-grained hardware control for deep learning by performing whole-graph optimizations, eliminating search time for execution schedules, and reducing memory footprint to enable larger models on consumer GPUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current high-level tensor frameworks with eager execution lack whole-graph visibility and granular hardware/memory control, preventing optimal physical hardware utilization. There's a need to bridge the gap between flexible model design abstractions and efficient hardware mapping.

Method: Nova captures eager executions and unifies forward/backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect for whole-graph optimizations. It uses an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity (zero search time). A structural hashing runtime synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from computation structure.

Result: On RTX 3060, Nova matches/exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls with <5e-4 relative error. Achieves up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% greater than XLA on 42M parameter model. Reduces memory footprint by up to 29% relative to PyTorch, enabling training of 144M parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch OOMs on same 12GB GPU.

Conclusion: Nova successfully bridges the gap between high-level abstractions and hardware efficiency by providing absolute hardware mapping control through automated whole-graph optimization and memory reduction, enabling larger models to run on consumer-grade hardware without compromising numerical fidelity.

Abstract: The performance of deep learning models at scale relies heavily on how effectively high-level mathematical operations are mapped to underlying physical hardware. While high-level tensor frameworks provide flexible abstractions for model design, their eager execution models inherently lack the whole-graph visibility and granular control over hardware and memory required to maximize physical hardware utilization natively. To bridge this gap, we designed Nova, an automated end-to-end JIT compiler whose defining purpose is to achieve absolute control over this hardware mapping: fusing operations across operation boundaries, optimizing complex memory hierarchies, and tuning execution down to the register level. By capturing eager executions and unifying forward and backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect, Nova unlocks aggressive whole-graph optimizations. It then utilizes an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, dropping search time to zero. Backed by a structural hashing runtime, Nova synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from the computation's structure. In our evaluations on an RTX 3060, Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls on most shapes, maintaining a stringent < 5e-4 relative error. At the model level, Nova achieves up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% greater than XLA on a 42-million parameter model, without compromising on numerical fidelity. Crucially, by reducing the memory footprint by up to 29% relative to PyTorch, Nova successfully trains a 144-million parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch encounters Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures on the same 12 GB consumer GPU.

</details>


### [13] [Co-evolution of social reward and punishment under institutional interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01183)
*Van An Nguyen,Vuong Khang Huynh,Hoai Thuong Nguyen,Duc Tin Duong,An Nguyen Gia,Tat Kien Nguyen,Huu Loi Bui,My Nguyen Tra,Ho Nam Duong,Ba Thanh Phan,Thanh Vo,Dinh Anh Trung Hoang,Adeela Bashir,Zhao Song,Manh Hong Duong,Le Hong Trang,The Anh Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study shows peer punishment best promotes cooperation while peer reward maximizes welfare; institutional support for peer incentives boosts both, but punishing peer incentives harms cooperation and welfare, revealing tensions between cooperation and social welfare objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how peer and institutional incentives jointly shape cooperation evolution, social welfare, and enforcement efficiency in social dilemmas, particularly examining tensions between cooperation promotion and welfare maximization.

Method: Analyze four-strategy Prisoner's Dilemma (C, D, SP, SR) with simultaneous peer and institutional incentives; use replicator dynamics for infinite well-mixed populations and agent-based simulations on square lattices for structured populations.

Result: Peer punishment promotes cooperation most strongly; peer reward maximizes social welfare. Institutional reward for peer incentive strategies improves both cooperation and welfare. Institutional punishment of defectors works, but punishing peer incentives dismantles decentralized systems, reducing cooperation and welfare.

Conclusion: Institutions should balance cooperation promotion with welfare maximization by supporting peer incentive strategies, avoiding policies that undermine decentralized enforcement, as maximizing cooperation doesn't necessarily optimize overall societal benefit.

Abstract: We investigate how peer and institutional incentives jointly shape the evolution of cooperation, social welfare, and enforcement efficiency in social dilemmas. In a Prisoners Dilemma with four strategies, unconditional cooperators (C), defectors (D), social punishers (SP), and social rewarders (SR), we allow decentralised peer incentives and centralised institutional incentives to act simultaneously, with the institution able to reward or punish any subset of strategies. In infinite well-mixed populations, we analyse the resulting four-strategy replicator dynamics, and in structured populations we use agent-based simulations on square lattices to study spatial effects and network reciprocity. Intervention schemes are evaluated by equilibrium states and evolutionary flow for infinite well-mixed populations, by cooperation levels and social welfare for structured populations, defined as aggregate population payoff net of institutional cost. We find that peer punishment most strongly promotes cooperation, whereas peer reward is more beneficial for social welfare. Institutionally rewarding peer incentive strategies substantially improves both cooperation and welfare, while subsidising unconditional cooperators has little impact. Under institutional punishment, directly penalising defectors is the only consistently effective policy; punishing peer incentive strategies dismantles decentralised incentives, reduces cooperation, and harms social welfare, showing that maximising cooperation does not necessarily optimise overall societal benefit. Our findings provide design principles for institutions seeking to balance cooperation promotion with welfare maximisation.

</details>


### [14] [SIRIN: A Unified Toolkit for Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented and Memory-Grounded LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00033)
*Julia Belikova,Rauf Parchiev,Mikhail Filimonov,Konstantin Polev,Andrey Savchenko,Maksim Makarenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIRIN is a unified toolkit and web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations in LLM systems, integrating multiple detection paradigms and query answerability assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for comprehensive tools to detect contextual hallucinations (fluent but unsupported responses) in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems, which current approaches lack unified solutions for.

Method: Developed SIRIN toolkit unifying three detector paradigms: representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification, plus pre-generation query answerability. Features web UI for live analysis, supports both white-box and black-box settings, response- and span-level inspection, and plug-in architecture for new detectors.

Result: SIRIN successfully demonstrates capabilities in hallucination detection, query answerability assessment, and serving as a faithfulness gate in long-term memory systems, with publicly available source code.

Conclusion: SIRIN provides a comprehensive, unified solution for contextual hallucination detection in modern LLM systems, offering practical tools for researchers and developers through its toolkit architecture, web interface, and extensible design.

Abstract: SIRIN (Semantic Inconsistency Recognition and Inspection Nexus) is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations (fluent, plausible responses unsupported by the provided evidence) in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems. SIRIN unifies three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) and the complementary task of pre-generation query answerability under one interface, configuration system, and evaluation pipeline, supporting response- and span-level inspection in both white-box and black-box settings. The web UI enables live analysis of user-supplied context-query-answer triples through hallucination scores, unsupported-span highlighting, and side-by-side detector comparison, with a lightweight plug-in design for adding new detectors. We demonstrate SIRIN on hallucination detection, query answerability, and as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems.
  The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sb-ai-lab/SIRIN.

</details>


### [15] [Humans Are More Diverse: Frontier LLMs Show Extreme Policies in Idealised AI Development Races](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01193)
*Phu Hoa Pham,Duy Minh Dao Sy,Trung Kiet Huynh,Phu Quy Nguyen Lam,Chi Nguyen Tran,Minh Trung Le,Phong Hao Le,Dinh Nam Nguyen,Thien Ky Nguyen Dong,Elias Fernandez Domingos,Le Hong Trang,The Anh Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents in multi-agent AI development races show strategic safety behavior, but audit reveals that strong rule recall coexists with weak state tracking and payoff calculation, highlighting the need for validity checks before interpreting actions as strategic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need to validate whether AI agents truly understand strategic games in AI safety races. There's a concern that LLM actions might not reflect genuine strategic understanding, requiring audit mechanisms to distinguish between valid actions and actual comprehension of game dynamics.

Method: The study creates a repeated game simulating AI development races with 2-5 players. They implement an audit gate with multiple validation steps: verifying the game engine, testing rule recall, state tracking, payoff calculation, and stability across equivalent task descriptions. They compare LLM action sequences with evolutionary game theory benchmarks and human data, examining differences across models, risk conditions, personas, and player counts.

Result: Audit reveals that strong rule recall can coexist with weak state tracking and expected-payoff calculation. Providing verified arithmetic and changing response representations can alter later actions despite fixed game rules. Across seven model endpoints, aggregate rates mask significant differences in action sequences, responses to opponents, and responses to race position. Patterns in 3-5 player races are model-specific rather than showing a consistent effect of adding competitors.

Conclusion: Multi-agent AI-race simulations require comprehensive validity checks and trajectory-level analysis before outputs can be described as strategic, human-like, or safety-aware. The exploratory findings are specific to the tested models, prompts, and decoding settings, emphasizing the need for careful interpretation of LLM behavior in strategic contexts.

Abstract: An AI development race creates a multi-agent safety dilemma. Each company can develop slowly and safely, or move faster while taking a risk that may remove its final reward. We use this repeated game to study strategic safety behaviour among large language model (LLM) agents in races with two to five players. However, a valid action does not show that an agent understands the game. We therefore place an audit gate before behavioural interpretation. We first verify the game engine, then test rule recall, state tracking, payoff calculation, and stability under different but equivalent task descriptions. We then compare LLM action sequences with an evolutionary game-theory benchmark and published human data, and explore differences across models, risk conditions, personas, and two- to five-player races. The audit shows that strong rule recall can coexist with weak state tracking and expected-payoff calculation. Providing verified arithmetic and changing the response representation can also change later actions, even when the game rules stay fixed. Across seven tested model endpoints, aggregate rates hide large differences in action sequences, responses to opponents, and responses to race position. Patterns across the tested three- to five-player races are also model-specific rather than a single effect of adding competitors. These results show why multi-agent AI-race simulations need validity checks and trajectory-level analysis before their outputs are described as strategic, human-like, or safety-aware. Our findings are exploratory and apply only to the tested models, prompts, and decoding settings.

</details>


### [16] [Linguistic Context Recodes Visual Representations in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00035)
*Brian Song,Michael A. Lepori,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vision-language models dynamically recode visual representations based on goal-directed language prompts, rather than treating visual representations as static.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how vision-language models dynamically adjust their visual representations in response to goal-directed language prompts, rather than treating visual representations as static repositories of information.

Method: Identified abstract reference representations denoting goal-relevant objects via contrastive steering vectors; demonstrated language-induced attribute modulation in later layers that amplify goal-relevant attributes; performed causal interventions to test the role of these mechanisms.

Result: Found concrete evidence for language-induced recoding: (1) abstract reference representations generalize across objects, task contexts, and synthetic/natural images; (2) later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes; (3) causal interventions show attribute modulation mediates VLM response distributions.

Conclusion: Vision-language models employ dynamic cross-modality processing where visual representations are actively modulated to support goal-directed language queries, challenging the view of visual tokens as static information repositories.

Abstract: Goal-directed visual processing is a hallmark of human visual intelligence, resulting in representations that support downstream tasks such as categorization or search. Though vision-language models (VLMs) are often faced with these same tasks, their ability to recode visual representations when presented with goal-directed language remains poorly characterized. Indeed, prior work largely treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories of visual information that are manipulated by language representations. In the present work, we provide evidence for two concrete instances of language-induced recoding of visual representations. First, we identify an abstract reference representation that denotes which objects are goal-relevant under a natural language prompt. We extract contrastive steering vectors corresponding to this reference representation and demonstrate that they are causally implicated in model predictions. These reference representations are abstract in that they generalize to different objects, different task contexts, and even from synthetic to naturalistic images. Second, we demonstrate language-induced attribute modulation: later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes in visual representations of objects. We demonstrate this phenomenon across a range of different prompts. Finally, we provide a causal intervention that demonstrates that attribute modulation mediates a VLM's response distribution. Together, our results support a more dynamic account of cross-modality processing in VLMs -- rather than vision tokens serving as static repositories of information, they are modulated to support queries articulated in language.

</details>


### [17] [CRAFTS: Collaborative Role-Adaptive Fine-Tuning of LLM Agents for Chemical Process Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01369)
*Ziyun Zhang,Yuxin Lin,Eldin Wee Chuan Lim,Xinghao Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAFTS is an automated system that constructs chemical process models from natural language requests using a staged workflow with 7 specialized LLM roles, achieving 91.5% success rate on validation and execution contracts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constructing executable chemical-process models is manually intensive and error-prone, requiring chemical engineers to translate underspecified requests into numerous coupled decisions about unit operations, thermodynamics, streams, and solver configurations.

Method: Decomposes simulation building into bounded subtasks assigned to 7 specialized roles (Input Understanding, Intent, Visual, Topology, Specification, Debug, Optimization) with deterministic IDAES/Pyomo gates between stages. Fine-tunes 3 critical roles (visual, topology, specification) while using untuned Qwen for others. Uses typed intermediate representations (VisualGraphIR, TopologyIR, SpecIR) and engineering gates to validate decisions before attaching constructors.

Result: On OpenIDAES-450 dataset's 82-case held-out split, CRAFTS completes prescribed validation and execution contracts for 91.5% of cases, achieving unit F1=0.815, stream F1=0.791, and directed-connection F1=0.782. Successfully demonstrates reliable automated process-model construction.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of role specialization, typed intermediate representations, and deterministic engineering gates for reliable automated chemical process-model construction, addressing the traditionally manual and error-prone nature of this task.

Abstract: Constructing an executable chemical-process model remains manually intensive. Chemical engineers translate underspecified requests into coupled decisions about unit operations, thermodynamics, streams, specifications, degrees of freedom (DoF), initialization, solver repair, and optimization; one error can invalidate the model. CRAFTS mirrors the staged workflow of chemical engineers by decomposing simulation building into bounded subtasks assigned to seven bounded roles, with deterministic IDAES/Pyomo gates between stages. Given a natural-language request, process flowsheet diagram (PFD) evidence, and curated chemical-engineering knowledge, Input Understanding and Intent recover requirements, constraints, and process semantics; visual, topology, and specification specialists translate them into typed simulator contracts; and Debug and Optimization support bounded repair and eligible optimization. Fine-tuning is applied to the three schema-critical visual, topology, and specification roles, while the remaining roles use untuned Qwen. The resulting VisualGraphIR, TopologyIR, SpecIR, BuildPlan, and SolveReport expose unit, port, thermodynamic, numerical, and execution decisions. Compatible constructors, property packages, and runners are attached only after semantic artifacts pass engineering gates. We introduce OpenIDAES-450, a 450-case IDAES process- simulation dataset, and evaluate the complete seven-role LangChain/LangGraph workflow through solve and eligible optimization on its frozen 82-case held-out split. CRAFTS completes the prescribed validation and execution contract for for 91.5% of cases and achieves unit, stream, and directed-connection F1 scores of 0.815, 0.791, and 0.782. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of role specialization, typed intermediate representations, and deterministic engineering gates for reliable automated process-model construction.

</details>


### [18] [RAG-TESTER: Automated End-to-End Testing of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00054)
*Ange Maiztegi,Jon Ayerdi,Miren Illarramendi,Aitor Arrieta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RagTester is an automated end-to-end testing framework for RAG systems that generates tests targeting complex passages, unsupported queries, and document coverage, detecting 21,633 failures across 72,000 test executions and outperforming baseline approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems combine multiple components (generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, prompt construction), making reliability dependent on complex interactions between these components. There's a need for automated testing approaches to expose failures before deployment.

Method: RagTester is an automated end-to-end testing approach that generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs, then executes tests and evaluates answers using an LLM as a judge. The test-generation strategy specifically targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria.

Result: Evaluated with eight LLMs and six embedding models (24 configurations) across 72,000 test executions. RagTester detected 21,633 failures (6.6% more than baseline) and outperformed the baseline in 20 of 24 configurations. Detected failures included inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete context usage, and difficulties with complex passages.

Conclusion: Coverage-oriented test generation effectively exposes failures caused by interaction between retrieval and generation components, supporting assessment of RAG configurations before deployment. RagTester provides a systematic approach to improve RAG system reliability.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to use external and domain-specific knowledge, but its reliability depends on the interaction between the generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, and prompt construction strategy. We present RagTester, an automated end-to-end testing approach for RAG systems. RagTester generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs; executes the tests; and evaluates the resulting answers using an LLM as a judge. Its test-generation strategy targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria. We evaluate RagTester using eight LLMs and six embedding models, yielding 24 compatible configurations, and compare it with a baseline test-input generator. Across 72,000 test executions, RagTester detected 21,633 failures, 6.6% more than the baseline, and outperformed it in 20 of the 24 configurations. The detected failures include inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete use of retrieved context, and difficulties interpreting complex passages. These results show that coverage-oriented test generation can effectively expose failures caused by the interaction between retrieval and generation components and support the assessment of RAG configurations before deployment.

</details>


### [19] [Where Reasoning Diverges: Localized Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01463)
*Weijun Gao,Xiang Ding,Tiancheng Xing,Haoyang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LMAD improves multi-agent debate by localizing conflicts to specific reasoning segments instead of exchanging complete traces, boosting accuracy on multi-hop QA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-agent debate protocols inefficiently exchange complete reasoning traces even when disagreements only concern a few intermediate claims, leading to unnecessary overhead and inefficiency.

Method: LMAD represents agent traces as typed nodes, locates earliest conflicts, and restricts debate to corresponding local segments. Uses guarded resolution to extend shared committed state so later conflicts can be addressed without reopening accepted steps.

Result: Evaluated on four multi-hop QA benchmarks using ten backbones from four model families. Achieved highest macro-averaged judge accuracy across all ten backbones, outperforming strongest conventional baseline by up to 7.20 percentage points.

Conclusion: Localized multi-agent debate (LMAD) provides a more efficient and effective protocol for multi-agent reasoning by focusing debate on specific conflict points rather than complete traces, leading to significant accuracy improvements.

Abstract: Multi-agent debate commonly exchanges complete reasoning traces even when disagreements concern only a few intermediate claims. We introduce Localized Multi-Agent Debate (LMAD), an inference-time protocol that represents agent traces as typed nodes, locates their earliest conflict, and restricts debate to the corresponding local segments. Guarded resolution extends a shared committed state so that later conflicts can be addressed without reopening accepted steps. We evaluate a single fixed LMAD configuration on four multi-hop question-answering benchmarks using ten backbones from four model families. Our method achieves the highest macro-averaged judge accuracy across all ten backbones, outperforming the strongest conventional baseline by up to 7.20 percentage points.

</details>


### [20] [H+ Embedding: Harmonizing Global and Token-Level Retrieval with Context-Dependent Phrases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00065)
*Shusen Zhang,Junyi Hu,Ye Feng,Ziteng Wang,Zhaoyuan Pan,Guosheng Dong,Xiaojun Yuan,Jiangshou Hong,Xiangzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: H+ Embedding introduces a unified multi-granularity retriever that uses context-dependent phrases as intermediate retrieval units between global vectors and tokens, improving efficiency while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval representations have limitations: single-vector retrievers over-compress local relevance signals, while token-level late interaction is computationally expensive. There's a need for an intermediate retrieval unit between these extremes that can handle terminology-intensive retrieval in domains like medicine.

Method: H+ Embedding predicts variable-length phrase partitions, preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction. It creates a unified multi-granularity retriever that operates at different levels of granularity.

Result: Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks, the phrase retrieval branch outperforms global retrieval by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It nearly matches Token-level performance while using 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets.

Conclusion: Context-dependent phrase interaction provides an effective intermediate quality-cost point between global compression and token-level interaction, making it practical for terminology-intensive retrieval systems.

Abstract: Terminology-intensive retrieval, especially in medical settings, depends on preserving multi-word entities, abbreviations, numerical constraints, and compositional concepts. However, existing representations lie at two extremes: single-vector retrievers often over-compress local relevance signals, while token-level late interaction retains every tokenizer subword at substantial indexing, storage, and scoring cost. This mismatch raises a natural question: can context-dependent phrases provide a useful retrieval unit between global vectors and tokens? We introduce H+ Embedding, a unified multi-granularity retriever that predicts variable-length phrase partitions, preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction. Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks, its phrase retrieval branch exceeds the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It also nearly matches Token while using 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets. Context-dependent phrase interaction therefore provides an intermediate quality-cost point between global compression and token-level interaction for practical retrieval systems.

</details>


### [21] [Securing Agentic AI: From Per-Action Checks to Trajectory Assurance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01558)
*Alireza Lotfi,Subangkar Karmaker Shanto,Imtiaz Karim,Elisa Bertino*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based autonomous agents face complex security challenges across the entire agentic stack, from single-agent vulnerabilities to multi-agent coordination and behavioral containment, requiring security to become a verifiable property of system architectures rather than optional guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based autonomous agents become more autonomous and delegate tasks across organizational boundaries for executing consequential tasks, their safety depends not on individual action correctness but on maintaining consistency with system rules and invariants.

Method: The paper analyzes the security landscape systematically across the entire agentic stack, examining challenges at single-agent level (untrusted inputs), multi-agent settings (delegation, communication), behavioral containment, and broader systemic issues (supply-chain, accountability).

Result: Identifies a broad interconnected security landscape with key challenges including: attack surfaces through prompts/memory/tools; multi-agent identity/trust/capability issues; model routing vulnerabilities; behavioral containment problems; and systemic issues of provenance and observability.

Conclusion: Security must become a verifiable property of the architectures, protocols, and runtimes that govern agent behavior rather than optional guidance, and charting these challenges provides a roadmap toward trustworthy autonomous agent deployment.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly used to execute consequential tasks in environments governed by operational constraints, organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and technical standards. Their safety is therefore determined not by the correctness of individual actions, but by whether their overall behavior remains consistent with the rules and invariants of the systems in which they operate. As large language model (LLM)-based agents become more autonomous and increasingly delegate tasks across organizational boundaries, securing them evolves from a single challenge into a broad and interconnected landscape spanning the entire agentic stack. At the single-agent level, untrusted inputs through prompts, memory, retrieved knowledge, and tool interfaces create attack surfaces. In multi-agent settings, delegation and communication introduce challenges related to identity, trust, capability control, and decision transparency, while the underlying model routing and execution control plane remains vulnerable to manipulation and to unverified model provenance. Perhaps the most fundamental challenge is behavioral containment: sequences of individually permissible actions may collectively violate system-level constraints and safety invariants. At the broader level, supply-chain integrity, provenance, accountability, and end-to-end observability remain largely open problems. A common principle unifies these directions: security must become a verifiable property of the architectures, protocols, and runtimes that govern agent behavior, rather than an optional layer of guidance. Charting these challenges provides a roadmap toward trustworthy autonomous agent deployment.

</details>


### [22] [Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00101)
*Banruo Liu,Haoran Qiu,Íñigo Goiri,Rodrigo Fonseca,Ricardo Bianchini,Esha Choukse*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents the first production-scale characterization of AI coding agent workloads using GitHub Copilot data, revealing distinctive properties with significant systems implications including high KV cache hit rates within turns but poor reuse across turns, and proposing an idle-time predictor for efficient resource orchestration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex create workloads that are fundamentally different from chatbots due to their interleaving of multi-step LLM inference with tool execution. There is a lack of production-scale characterization of this emerging workload, which has important implications for LLM-serving system design and resource efficiency.

Method: The researchers analyzed sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising a massive dataset of 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens. They characterized the workload properties through empirical analysis of agentic coding sessions, examining patterns of LLM calls, tool execution, KV cache behavior, token consumption, and user idle periods.

Result: The analysis revealed that coding agent sessions consist of sparse user-initiated turns that unfold into autonomous agent loops with nearly-always coupled LLM calls and tool execution. This structure yields high KV cache hit rates (90%) within turns but poor reuse across turns (55%) due to events like model switches or context compaction. The researchers identified diverse workflows with variable, long-tailed token consumption and designed a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90% of total idle time for proactive resource orchestration.

Conclusion: The findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems and provide an empirical foundation for designing agent-native infrastructure. The distinctive properties of AI coding agent workloads necessitate specialized system optimizations, particularly around KV cache management and idle-time resource orchestration for improved efficiency.

Abstract: AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of this workload using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens.
  Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with important systems implications. For example, agentic coding sessions consist of sparse user-initiated turns, each unfolding into an autonomous agent loop of LLM calls almost always coupled with tool execution. This structure yields KV cache hit rates averaging 90% within a turn, but falling to 55\% across turn boundaries and drastically invalidated after events like model switches or context compaction. Diverse workflows and user behaviors are observed with variable and long-tailed token consumption, time span, and tool calls. We highlight the difference between quick agentic turnaround times and the minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries, and design a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90\% of total idle time, enabling proactive decisions for efficient resource orchestration. These findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems and provide an empirical foundation for agent-native infrastructure.

</details>


### [23] [Shared Organizational Memory for Enterprise Coding Agents: System Design and Deployment Snapshot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00122)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A deployed organizational memory system for enterprise coding agents that captures task-adjacent experience during coding workflows, curates it into reusable QA memories with security/privacy gating, and retrieves them for future agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise knowledge (internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, tacit workflows) often remains outside public training data and formal documentation. Existing knowledge interfaces require agents to explicitly recognize and record lessons, disconnecting capture from coding workflow and causing repeated rediscovery of development experience.

Method: Deployed a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates into reusable question-answer memories, gates security/privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents.

Result: The paper describes an ongoing production deployment and operational snapshot of this system. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation (still being studied).

Conclusion: The system represents an approach to embedding knowledge capture directly into the coding workflow to prevent repeated rediscovery of enterprise-specific development experience, though full impact assessment is ongoing.

Abstract: Enterprise coding agents rely on tools and retrieval, yet enterprise knowledge often remains outside public training data and formal documentation: internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, and tacit workflows. Existing knowledge interfaces expose stored resources but still depend on agents recognizing and explicitly recording lessons worth reusing, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and leaving development experience repeatedly rediscovered. We report an ongoing production deployment of a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: it collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates it into reusable question-answer memories, gates obvious security and privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents. This short paper describes the deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation.

</details>


### [24] [AgentStream: How Well Do Self-Evolving LLM Agents Perform Under Streaming Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00155)
*Dong Yan,Jian Liang,Dapeng Hu,Ran He,Nicholas Jing Yuan,Qi Zhang,Tieniu Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentStream is a framework for evaluating self-evolving LLM agents under realistic streaming scenarios, showing that no single method dominates across models and scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing studies on self-evolving LLM agents use independent evaluation, failing to capture how they perform in realistic streaming settings with diverse and complex task streams.

Method: Introduced AgentStream framework that organizes agentic benchmarks into configurable task streams, instantiated three streaming scenarios (Isolated, Sequential, Interleaved), and combinatorially evaluated five self-evolving methods across three frontier foundation models.

Result: Self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios; benefits are gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength; no single method dominates across models and scenarios; concrete guidance provided for method selection.

Conclusion: Self-evolving agents should be evaluated under realistic task streams rather than isolated single-task settings, as streaming scenarios significantly impact performance and method selection.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve by continually improving from their own accumulated experience. However, existing studies predominantly adopt independent evaluation. Consequently, the behavior of self-evolving agents in realistic streaming settings, where agents adapt to diverse and complex task streams, remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce AgentStream, a unified framework that evaluates self-evolving agents spanning diverse evolution components by organizing agentic benchmarks into a configurable task stream and instantiating the \texttt{Isolated}, \texttt{Sequential}, and \texttt{Interleaved} streaming scenarios at test time, which progressively vary the scope and domain composition of the stream. Over these scenarios, we combinatorially evaluate five representative self-evolving methods across three frontier foundation models, disentangling how model capability, method architecture, and streaming scenario jointly shape self-evolution. Our results show that self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios, the benefit of self-evolution is gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength, and no single method dominates across models and scenarios. These findings offer concrete guidance for selecting self-evolving methods across models and streaming scenarios. Overall, we advocate that self-evolving agents should be evaluated under realistic task streams rather than isolated single-task settings.

</details>


### [25] [TRACE-TS: Attribution-Grounded and Traceable Sensor-Language Reasoning for Human Activity Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00200)
*Sparsh Rastogi,Tanmay Kumar,Baiyu Chen,Jatin Bedi,Zechen Li,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE-TS is a framework for generating structured, signal-grounded reasoning traces for wearable sensor data, using attribution-guided evidence and training compact language models to produce verifiable explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing wearable sensor analysis methods reduce rich motion signals to simple activity labels, while recent LM-based approaches generate unverifiable natural language explanations that lack grounding in the underlying sensor signals.

Method: Uses expert classifier attribution to identify salient sensor regions, constructs DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, trains compact language models via gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens, and generates joint activity prediction + reasoning traces at inference without needing teacher guidance.

Result: Achieves best average accuracy (84.43%) and F1 (81.24%) across seven wearable benchmarks, outperforms best LLM baseline by 17.96% F1, with proposed Semantic Node Match metric showing superior reasoning fidelity assessment.

Conclusion: TRACE-TS enables structured, verifiable reasoning over wearable time series data through signal-grounded evidence chains, addressing limitations of both traditional activity labeling and LLM-based hallucination-prone explanations.

Abstract: Wearable sensors capture fine-grained motion patterns that support rich behavioral understanding, yet most existing methods reduce these signals to activity labels. Recent LM-based approaches generate natural-language explanations for sensor data, but their reasoning is weakly grounded in the underlying signal, leading to fluent yet unverifiable explanations. We introduce TRACE-TS (Traceable Reasoning with Attribution-Grounded Evidence), a framework for structured and signal-grounded reasoning over wearable time series. TRACE-TS uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify salient spatio-temporal sensor regions, uses them to construct DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, and trains a compact language model to generate these traces through gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens. At inference, the adapted model jointly outputs the activity prediction and its reasoning trace, without requiring attribution computation or teacher guidance. We introduce Semantic Node Match(SNM), an LLM-as-judge metric that diagnoses reasoning fidelity at the observation, inference, and synthesis levels, localizing hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard NLG metrics. Across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieves the best average accuracy and F1 among all evaluated methods (84.43%/81.24%), and outperforms the best LLM-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. Our code is available at https://github.com/SparshRastogi/TRACE-TS.

</details>


### [26] [Personalizing Large Language Model Agents with Small Policy Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00215)
*Dian Jin,Zhi Zhang,Huichao Li,Yihe Pan,Rundong Huang,Doudou Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FABLE (Factorized Adaptive Bandit Layer for Execution) is a lightweight policy layer for personalizing frozen LLM agents by learning per-user execution policies from scalar feedback without modifying the core model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalizing LLM agent execution decisions (like memory retrieval, tool calling, question asking) to individual users is challenging. Fine-tuning is costly/impossible for proprietary systems, while existing approaches primarily expose user info rather than adapt execution based on feedback.

Method: FABLE is a lightweight policy layer outside potentially black-box host agents. It factorizes execution decisions (memory, information-acquisition, response), filters actions through feasible sets before exploration, and learns user-specific residual preferences relative to fixed default-cost scores using Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling.

Result: FABLE improves preference-sensitive behaviors across personalized-reasoning, controlled-feedback, and executable tool-use evaluations while remaining competitive on end-to-end task performance. Theoretical analysis provides regret bounds against best feasible actions and addresses preference identifiability.

Conclusion: FABLE provides an effective framework for personalizing frozen LLM agents through lightweight policy learning from user feedback, balancing preference adaptation with task performance, offering theoretical guarantees, and addressing real-world feasibility constraints.
