Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve memory, call tools, ask clarifying questions, and vary response style, yet adapting these execution decisions to an individual user remains difficult. Fine-tuning a separate LLM is costly or impossible for proprietary systems, while prompts and memory primarily expose user information to the agent rather than adapt its execution decisions from feedback. We formulate personalization of a frozen agent as online learning of a per-user execution policy from scalar feedback observed only for the executed action. We propose FABLE (Factorized Adaptive Bandit Layer for Execution), a lightweight policy layer outside a potentially black-box host agent. FABLE factorizes memory, information-acquisition, and response decisions so feedback updates related choices; filters actions through an externally specified feasible set before exploration; and learns user-specific residual preferences relative to a fixed default-and-cost score via Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling. Under a linear residual-reward model, a calibrated variant inherits an expected-regret bound against the best feasible action. We also characterize preferences unidentifiable under persistent feasibility constraints and provide anytime-valid false-promotion control. Across personalized-reasoning, controlled-feedback, and executable tool-use evaluations, FABLE improves several preference-sensitive behaviors relative to rule-only control while remaining competitive on end-to-end task performance.

</details>


### [27] [More Debate, Same Evidence: Structural Limits of Homogeneous Multi-Agent Groundedness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00243)
*Yuelyu Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM multi-agent panels for groundedness verification show mixed results: some datasets show accuracy gains, others show losses, and some are inconclusive compared to single-agent baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether multi-agent LLM panels with critique exchange actually improve judgment quality over single-agent systems for groundedness verification tasks, testing a common assumption in LLM judge design.

Method: The authors evaluate a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public fact-verification and hallucination-detection benchmarks, comparing it against a fixed single-agent reference system.

Result: Results show mixed performance: system-level accuracy differences range from +8.5 to -4.4 percentage points. Two datasets show reliable gains, one shows reliable loss, and three are statistically inconclusive. The study cannot isolate debate effects due to different model variants used.

Conclusion: The assumption that multi-agent panels with critique exchange improve judgment quality for groundedness verification is not universally supported - performance varies by dataset, and systematic benefits over single-agent systems are not guaranteed.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly organized as multi-agent panels under the assumption that exchanging critiques improves judgment quality. We test this assumption for \emph{groundedness verification}, where a judge must determine whether a claim is supported by the supplied evidence. We evaluate a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public fact-verification and hallucination-detection benchmarks. Relative to a fixed single-agent reference, the panel's system-level accuracy difference ranges from $+8.5$ to $-4.4$ percentage points: two datasets show reliable gains, one shows a reliable loss, and three are statistically inconclusive. Because the reference and panel use different model variants, these differences characterize the complete systems rather than isolate a causal debate effect.

</details>


### [28] [Geometric Self-Supervised Pre-training for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00270)
*David Aguado,Daniel Fuertes,Carlos R. del-Blanco,Fernando Jaureguizar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A geometric self-supervised pre-training framework for Neural Combinatorial Optimization that improves generalization to large-scale routing problems by capturing spatial invariance and relative distance distributions through isometric transformations, achieving 7.23% better tour lengths and up to 100x speedups over exact solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models for routing problems like TSP suffer from poor generalization when scaling to high-dimensional instances. While self-supervised pre-training has succeeded in computer vision and NLP, applying it to routing graphs with simple 2D spatial coordinates remains challenging due to lack of complex topological attributes.

Method: Proposes a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework that captures spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. The method applies isometric transformations (rotations and axial reflections) to help models learn robust structural representations before the policy optimization phase, specifically designed for routing graph structures.

Result: The pre-training strategy consistently outperforms baseline models trained from scratch, achieving 7.23% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation on TSP1,000. The model also shows remarkable computational efficiency with speedups of up to two orders of magnitude (100x) over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.

Conclusion: Geometric self-supervised pre-training effectively addresses generalization issues in Neural Combinatorial Optimization for routing problems. The approach successfully transfers robust structural learning to downstream routing tasks, demonstrating significant performance improvements and computational efficiency gains over both baseline NCO models and traditional exact solvers.

Abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) techniques have emerged as a highly efficient alternative to traditional exact algorithms for solving routing problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, the generalization capabilities of these Reinforcement Learning-based models are severely hindered when scaling to high-dimensional instances. This issue has been mitigated in other domains, like computer vision and natural language processing, by adopting a self-supervised pre-training strategy. Nevertheless, its application to routing graphs, which lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates, remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework specifically designed to capture spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. By applying isometric transformations, such as rotations and axial reflections, the model learns robust structural representations prior to the policy optimization phase. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy consistently outperforms models trained from scratch (baselines), achieving a 7.23\% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation scenarios (TSP1,000). Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, delivering speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.
  The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/davidaguadocosano/TSP-GeoPretrain.git.

</details>


### [29] [RF-HOI: Recognize Human-Object Interaction with Radio Frequency Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00289)
*Lihao Wang,Linlu Gao,Jiacan Yu,Yanyu Lin,Yifan Yin,Jianxin Wang,Tianmin Shu,Renjie Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RF-HOI is the first framework using only radio frequency signals for human-object interaction recognition, combining mmWave radar and RFID through novel modality fusion and synthetic data generation to overcome training data limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based HOI recognition faces privacy concerns and poor lighting limitations. RF sensing offers a privacy-preserving alternative that works in various lighting conditions, but single-modality RF is insufficient for recognizing both actions and objects simultaneously.

Method: RF-HOI combines mmWave radar and RFID through novel modality fusion for simultaneous action recognition and target identification. To address limited training data, they developed a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, enabling fine-tuning with minimal real-world data.

Result: RF-HOI outperforms all baselines and approaches vision model performance. The diverse synthetic training data significantly boosts system performance on real-world scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of the RF data synthesis approach.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust, privacy-preserving HOI recognition and validates the effectiveness of synthetic RF data generation for overcoming training data limitations across diverse setups.

Abstract: Recognizing Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is essential for intelligent systems, underpinning applications in virtual and augmented reality, embodied AI, and assistive robotics. However, vision-based HOI methods face challenges in privacy concerns and poor light conditions. In this work, we introduce RF-HOI, the first framework that only uses radio frequency (RF) signals for HOI recognition. A key challenge of RF-HOI is that single-modality RF sensing is insufficient to recognize both actions and the objects being interacted with. RF-HOI addresses this through a novel modality fusion that combines mmWave radar and RFID, enabling simultaneous action recognition and target identification. Another challenge is limited training data across diverse setups, which impairs the generalizability of the recognition model. To overcome this, we develop a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing us to fine-tune with only a small amount of real-world data. Experiment results show that RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance, and that our diverse synthetic training data can significantly boost our system's performance on real-world scenarios. These results highlight the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust and privacy-preserving HOI recognition as well as the effectiveness of our RF data synthesis.

</details>


### [30] [WM-Cov: Test Adequacy for Interactive World-Model-Style Autonomous Driving Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00298)
*Jianxun Cui,Ping Wu,Stanisa Peric,Marko Milojkovic,Vladan Devedzic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WM-Cov is an evaluation layer for world-model-based autonomous driving testing that measures testing adequacy through coverage growth, valid failures, and evidence convergence rather than just counting generated failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models enable interactive testing of autonomous driving systems by generating counterfactual scenarios, but there's a need to determine what constitutes valid evidence to support testing decisions and stopping criteria.

Method: WM-Cov is introduced as a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw world model outputs into quantified evidence metrics including coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision.

Result: Testing showed dangerous-looking events often include valid failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. In DriveArena evaluations, 304 of 360 ego-route requests became fully realized evidence while 56 remained partial. A separate 80-request check yielded 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts.

Conclusion: World-model-style testing should be evaluated by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget constraints, not by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone. WM-Cov provides the framework to assess testing adequacy through evidence quality metrics.

Abstract: World models and generative simulators are emerging as interactive testing infrastructure for autonomous driving because they can react to the ego planner and produce counterfactual, rare, and safety-critical rollouts. This changes a test scenario from a fixed replayed trajectory into an interactive scenario family whose realized evolution depends on the planner under test. The unresolved question is therefore not only whether dangerous rollouts can be generated, but what valid closed-loop evidence is enough to support a specified testing intent and stopping decision. This paper formulates interactive world-model-style testing adequacy and introduces WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw provider outputs into requested, realized, and valid evidence. WM-Cov reports adequacy through coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Studies on executed TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a real DriveArena TrafficManager--WorldDreamer matrix show that dangerous-looking events can include valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. The DriveArena matrix evaluates two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, and 360 ego-route requests; 304 attempts become fully realized evidence and 56 remain partial. A disjoint 80-request route-slice check yields 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts. The results support evaluating world-model-style testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget, rather than by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.

</details>


### [31] [CrystalMem: Elastic Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Knowledge Crystallization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00303)
*Beining Wu,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrystalMem is an elastic memory system for LLM agents that uses four fidelity states and crystallization scheduling to minimize performance loss when memory budgets fluctuate, achieving higher restored capability than baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent memory systems assume memory budgets only grow, but cloud platforms dynamically adjust memory quotas based on load and cost. When memory is squeezed and then recovered, agents don't return to their pre-squeeze capability levels - this gap is called "memory hysteresis." The problem is structural: deletion and one-way compression discard material needed for later rebuilding.

Method: CrystalMem is proposed as an elastic memory sidecar with four fidelity states for memory entries. It uses a crystallization-energy schedule for demoting entries, orders demotions by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling, and recovers capability through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps.

Result: Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six LLM backbones, with multi-tenant serving and physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting and closes the hysteresis loop. From a 50% byte budget, it matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision; at equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 percentage points on average.

Conclusion: Memory hysteresis is a fundamental problem in LLM agents when memory budgets fluctuate, and CrystalMem's approach of maintaining memory entries across fidelity states with crystallization scheduling effectively mitigates this issue, providing superior capability restoration compared to existing memory management methods.

Abstract: Memory for self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents is often provisioned as if its byte budget only grows. Cloud platforms, however, adjust quotas with load and cost, and we show that capability does not follow the budget back up: after a squeeze-and-recover cycle, the agent settles below its pre-squeeze level, a gap we call memory hysteresis. The cause is structural. Deletion and one-way compression discard the material needed for later rebuilding, and we prove that any policy that only keeps or drops entries carries a residual-deficit floor. We propose CrystalMem (Crystallized Memory), an elastic memory sidecar that demotes entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule, orders demotions by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling, and recovers capability through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps. Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six backbones, with multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting and closes the loop left open by every baseline. From a 50% byte budget, CrystalMem matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision on every environment; at equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 pp on average.

</details>


### [32] [Trust and Its Betrayal under Three Representational Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00321)
*Mihnea C. Moldoveanu,Joel A. C. Baum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trust is analyzed as a subjunctive epistemic state with three representations: lexicographic assumptions, ordinal closeness, and strong belief, exploring how common trust differs from common belief and how betrayal affects each representation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a formal analysis of trust as a distinctive propositional attitude that differs from mere prediction, and to examine how common trust behaves compared to common belief, particularly in light of the Brandenburger-Keisler impossibility result when rationality is replaced by trustworthiness.

Method: Develop three mathematical representations of trust as a subjunctive epistemic state: 1) as lexicographic assumption, 2) as ordinal closeness in a Lewis-Stalnaker sphere system, and 3) as strong belief in a conditional probability system. Examine whether the Brandenburger-Keisler impossibility survives when replacing rationality with trustworthiness.

Result: All three representations agree that finite depths of common trust are realizable while the completed common-trust fixed point presents difficulties. However, they differ significantly in how betrayal affects each representation: betrayal refutes level ordering in lexicographic representation, contaminates closeness ordering proportionally to deliberateness in ordinal representation, and merely shifts conditioning hypothesis while maintaining coherent belief structure in strong-belief representation.

Conclusion: Trust is fundamentally different from prediction, with betrayal representing a qualitative disappointment. The choice of representation for modeling trust significantly impacts how we understand the resilience of trust structures after betrayal, with strong-belief representation showing the greatest robustness to betrayal while maintaining coherent belief systems.

Abstract: Trust is a propositional attitude of a distinctive kind: to trust is to rely on another under conditions where reliance could be disappointed, and the disappointment of trust---betrayal---differs qualitatively from the disappointment of a prediction. We treat trust as a \emph{subjunctive} epistemic state: $A$ trusts $B$'s competence when $A$ believes that \emph{were $P$ true, $B$ would know it}, and $B$'s integrity when $A$ believes that \emph{were $B$ to know $P$, he would disclose it to $A$}. We develop three representations of this state---as lexicographic \emph{assumption} as \emph{ordinal closeness} in a Lewis--Stalnaker sphere system , and as \emph{strong belief} in a conditional probability system and for each we ask whether the Brandenburger--Keisler impossibility on common belief survives when the assumption of rationality is replaced by an assumption of trustworthiness. The three representations agree that every \emph{finite} depth of common trust is realizable while the \emph{completed} common-trust fixed point is the locus of difficulty, but they differ sharply in \emph{how} the difficulty manifests, and---our organizing finding---in how each survives a concrete betrayal. W show that the same betrayal refutes an agent's \emph{level ordering} under the lexicographic representation, contaminates her \emph{closeness ordering} in proportion to the betrayer's deliberateness under the ordinal representation, and merely \emph{shifts her operative conditioning hypothesis} while leaving her belief structure coherent under the strong-belief representation.

</details>


### [33] [Learning to Coordinate Symbolic Tools: LLM Agents for Verified Sum-of-Squares Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00326)
*Bohan Chen,Shivam N. Patel,Richard Hoffmann,Sam Looi,Tony Yue Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based agent combines algebraic training, symbolic tools, and verifier feedback to find weighted sum-of-squares decompositions for proving polynomial inequalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool calling enables LLMs to perform external computation, useful for mathematical problem solving. Weighted sum-of-squares decomposition provides a machine-checkable way to prove polynomial nonnegativity and inequalities, but finding such decompositions requires complex symbolic transformations and coordination.

Method: 1) Create 1.35M synthetic examples covering 8 supporting polynomial tasks plus weighted-SOS decomposition. 2) Use supervised fine-tuning on algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces. 3) Apply Group Relative Policy Optimization with task-specific symbolic rewards. 4) At evaluation, use native SymPy calls for symbolic operations. 5) Verify every final SOS answer by exact expansion and coefficient comparison.

Result: Full SFT+GRPO+tools system achieves 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS problems (vs 44.73% for base model with same tools). Also achieves 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks on held-out synthetic problems.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates combining domain-specific skill training, executable tools, and verifier feedback for mathematical problem solving. This approach provides a case study for designing tool-calling agents in domains with exactly checkable outputs.

Abstract: Tool calling allows large language models (LLMs) to invoke external computation during problem solving, a useful capability in various fields including AI for mathematics. We study this setting through weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decomposition, a machine-checkable route to proving polynomial nonnegativity and hence polynomial inequalities. A candidate decomposition can be checked exactly, but finding one requires choosing among non-unique regroupings and coordinating multiple symbolic transformations. We develop an agent that combines algebraic task training, symbolic tools, and verifier-grounded optimization for this task. Rather than training only on the composite SOS task, we construct 1.35 million synthetic examples covering eight supporting polynomial tasks together with weighted-SOS decomposition. We first apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, and then use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. The SFT corpus contains no native tool-calling messages; at evaluation, the agent uses native SymPy calls for expansion, collection, reordering, and factorization. Every final SOS answer is checked by exact expansion and coefficient comparison. On held-out, same-generator synthetic problems, the full SFT+GRPO+tools system is the strongest of four evaluated configurations, reaching 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS, compared with 44.73% for the base model with the same tools, and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks. Within this controlled setting, our work provides a case study of combining domain-specific skill training, executable tools, and verifier feedback, and may inform the design of tool-calling agents in other domains with exactly checkable outputs.

</details>


### [34] [RMSWeb: Reflection, Failure-Mode Mining, and Salvage-DS for Web Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00335)
*Chengbo Liu,Lifang Zhou,Ruijie Yan,Pei Tan,Ao Sun,Haojun Huang,Guichun Hua,Sining Wei,Yining Chen,Yingying He,Yutao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RMSWeb is a three-part training method for compact web agents that improves efficiency through reflection-conditioned retries for better data collection, failure-mode mining for focused RL, and Salvage-DS for improved reward design, achieving better performance with fewer action steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training compact web agents is challenging due to expensive trajectory collection (which often contains inefficient detours) and problems with post-SFT reinforcement learning where routine states dominate corpora and poorly designed action-level rewards can mislead learning.

Method: RMSWeb has three components: 1) Reflection-conditioned retries that increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories, 2) Failure-mode mining that concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by SFT policy, and 3) Salvage-DS which combines action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and action-only anchor for rejected groups.

Result: RMSWeb-trained policies use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, it improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. The 8B model achieves strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models and leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench.

Conclusion: RMSWeb addresses key challenges in training compact web agents through improved data collection, focused RL training on critical states, and better reward design, enabling more efficient web agents with better performance-cost trade-offs.

Abstract: Compact web agents can reduce deployment cost, but training them poses challenges in both data collection and post-SFT reinforcement learning (RL). Successful trajectories are expensive to collect and often contain inefficient detours. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states; moreover, when group-relative RL is applied to web actions, inadequately designed action-level rewards can yield weak or misleading relative updates, while groups rejected as unsuitable for such updates receive no fallback learning signal. We present RMSWeb, a three-part recipe for Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B. Reflection-conditioned retries increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; failure-mode mining concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; and Salvage-DS combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups. Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. Our 8B model also achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models in our comparison and a leading reported accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

</details>


### [35] [Bayesian and Motivated Reasoning in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00339)
*Eddie Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents' conclusions are strongly influenced by prior beliefs when analyzing identical numerical data in different substantive framings, creating hidden risks in high-stakes decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks where their conclusions guide consequential decisions, but there's concern that their decision-making may be influenced by factors not specified in the task.

Method: Researchers conducted experiments holding numerical evidence constant while changing the substantive framing/scenario in which evidence appears across three high-stakes domains: medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting.

Result: Across 12 agent-domain comparisons, agents' conclusions were strongly influenced by prior beliefs. They were more likely to reach affirmative conclusions when framed around propositions they already considered likely, and the reverse when framing conflicted with priors. Framing also changed how agents worked (search behavior, analytical choices, evidence evaluation).

Conclusion: This identifies a particular risk in delegating decision-making to AI agents, as their decisions may depend on prior beliefs that are neither specified in the task nor visible in decision records, creating hidden biases.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly perform open-ended tasks in settings where their conclusions can guide consequential decisions. We provide evidence that AI agents draw different conclusions from identical numerical data when the substantive framing changes. We demonstrate this behavior in high-stakes domains in medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting by holding the evidence fixed while changing the scenario in which the evidence appears. Across twelve agent-domain comparisons, agents' conclusions are strongly influenced by their prior beliefs. They are more likely to reach an affirmative conclusion when it is framed around a proposition they already regard as likely, while the reverse holds when the framing conflicts with their prior. The framing also changes how some agents work: they search more extensively, choose different analytical specifications, and evaluate the same evidence differently. These results identify a particular risk of delegating decision-making to AI agents, as their decisions may depend on prior beliefs that are neither specified in the task nor visible in the decision record.

</details>


### [36] [Gene Ontology-Guided Hierarchical Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00405)
*Zhiwen Xu,Xiaoming Yan,Chengkun Wu,Juan Chen,Haoang Chi,Liyang Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSGR uses Gene Ontology hierarchy as a structural prior to improve spatial gene expression prediction from histopathology images by organizing genes into functional groups and refining predictions through multi-scale residual corrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat gene prediction as flat, unstructured vector decoding, ignoring important biological dependencies between genes that arise from shared pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies from limited data, constraining prediction quality.

Method: MSGR organizes target genes into a four-level Gene Ontology (GO) tree hierarchy and uses a GO-guided decoder that progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections with scale-weighted supervision. The decoder operates solely on the gene side as a plug-in replacement for existing architectures.

Result: Extensive experiments on nine datasets from HEST-1k benchmark show: 1) GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against state-of-the-art generative baselines; 2) The improvement is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than just hierarchical decomposition, as shown by a +0.027 margin over structurally equivalent random hierarchies.

Conclusion: Incorporating curated biological knowledge (Gene Ontology) as an explicit structural prior significantly improves spatial gene expression prediction from histopathology images. The GO-guided decoder serves as an effective plug-in module that enhances existing architectures without requiring image-side modifications.

Abstract: Predicting spatial gene expression from histopathology images enables large-scale transcriptomic profiling without the cost of direct measurement. Existing methods decode the target gene set as a flat, unstructured vector, ignoring the inter-gene dependencies arising from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality. We propose MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner), which bridges this gap by incorporating the Gene Ontology (GO), a curated functional hierarchy of genes, as an explicit structural prior. MSGR organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree. Its GO-guided decoder then progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. Operating solely on the gene side, the GO-guided decoder serves as a seamless plug-in replacement that consistently improves existing architectures without requiring any image-side modifications. Extensive experiments on nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark provide empirical evidence for two central claims: GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against a state-of-the-art generative baseline, and the gain is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, as confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.

</details>


### [37] [Where did the ambiguity go? Examining how multimodal models interpret polysemous words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00410)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Raja Marjieh,Thomas L. Griffiths*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multimodal foundation models show a significant gap in how they express polysemous words across modalities, with text generation being more diverse than image generation, and both being less varied than human imagination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human language is highly polysemous, and while LLMs have been shown to understand multiple meanings, little is known about how polysemy surfaces in other modalities like images. The paper aims to study how foundation models express polysemous meanings across different modalities.

Method: The study examined 17 text-to-image and 15 text-generation models by providing each with polysemous words without context to fix meaning. Researchers measured which senses were produced over many samples and compared normalized entropy scores across modalities. They also asked models to predict how often they would generate outputs for each possible meaning.

Result: Found a clear multimodal gap: generated images settle on far fewer senses than generated sentences (normalized entropy 0.10 vs. 0.25), and both are far less varied than human imagination (normalized entropy 0.47). However, when models predict distributions of possible outputs, they anticipate more diversity than their actual outputs produce.

Conclusion: There is a multimodal gap in how foundation models express meaning, and their understanding may not transfer faithfully nor equally across modalities. The study reveals limitations in how current models handle polysemy across different output formats.

Abstract: Human language is highly polysemous. Many common words (e.g., 'bank' or 'palm') carry several distinct meanings that shape what humans communicate and imagine. Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to understand this multiplicity of meaning, but much less is known about how polysemy surfaces in other modalities such as images. We study this across 17 text-to-image and 15 text-generation models by giving each a polysemous word with no context to fix its meaning and measuring which senses are produced over many samples. We find a clear multimodal gap, where within every model family, generated images settle on far fewer senses than generated sentences (normalized entropy 0.10 vs. 0.25), and both are far less varied than what people imagine for the same words (normalized entropy 0.47). However, when we instead ask a model to list how often it would generate outputs corresponding to each possible meaning of a word, it predicts distributions that are more diverse than the actual space of outputs. These results reveal a multimodal gap in how foundation models express meaning, and how their understanding may not transfer faithfully nor equally across modalities.

</details>


### [38] [SymboUQ: Symbolic Uncertainty Quantification for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00417)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SymboUQ is a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates the reliability of LLM answers in spatial reasoning by distinguishing between whether claims can be formally represented and whether they yield definite semantic verdicts, achieving better performance than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often produce fluent spatial reasoning traces where intermediate relations may not support the final conclusion, making token-level confidence insufficient for reliability estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence but have partial applicability because not all parsed claims yield definite semantic verdicts.

Method: SymboUQ distinguishes symbolizability (whether a claim can be represented in the verifier's formal language) from semantic determinacy (whether execution yields an entailed or contradicted verdict rather than unknown). It consists of three components: (1) Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (2) label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage; and (3) Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability.

Result: Extensive experiments on five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones show that SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: SymboUQ effectively addresses the limitations of existing methods by distinguishing symbolizability from semantic determinacy, providing a more reliable framework for estimating final-answer reliability in LLM spatial reasoning tasks, with demonstrated improvements across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent spatial reasoning traces, their intermediate relations may fail to support the final conclusion, making token-level confidence insufficient for final-answer reliability estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence, but their applicability is partial: a parsed claim need not yield a definite semantic verdict. To address this issue, we introduce SymboUQ, a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates final-answer reliability from reasoning traces by distinguishing symbolizability, whether a claim can be represented in the verifier's formal language, from semantic determinacy, whether its execution yields an entailed or contradicted verdict rather than an unknown or not-evaluable outcome. SymboUQ comprises (i) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability. Extensive experiments on five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones show that SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [39] [Mask-Based Priors Are More Persistent than Query-Key Initializations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00418)
*Mingze Ma,Hemanth Saratchandran,Cameron Gordon,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Transformers fail to extrapolate correctly on Boolean tasks due to systematic inductive bias; mask-based initialization (rather than QK initialization) enables near-perfect extrapolation by embedding persistent structural priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers exhibit systematic failure in extrapolation on Boolean tasks, defaulting to simpler minimum-degree interpolators rather than learning true target functions. Existing structured-initialization methods that manipulate query-key projections are inadequate as they get overwritten during training, failing to correct Transformer inductive bias.

Method: Proposes initializing additive attention masks directly from task-level interaction structure, creating finite learnable attention-logit biases. Unlike hard masks for causality/locality, these mask-based priors separate structural bias from content-dependent attention scores, allowing persistence throughout optimization.

Result: Mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation on Boolean reasoning tasks where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers fail. The approach also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision/language benchmarks, demonstrating persistent inductive bias encoding.

Conclusion: Attention masks can serve not just as architectural constraints but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers, effectively correcting systematic extrapolation failures and enabling better generalization beyond training distributions.

Abstract: Transformers do not merely lack data on some Boolean extrapolation tasks; they generalize in a systematically wrong way. Recent work on generalization on the unseen has shown that, despite fitting the observed domain, Transformers often extrapolate according to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. These Boolean tasks are not practical applications, but controlled stress tests for understanding Transformer inductive bias. We ask whether this failure mode can be corrected by injecting explicit structural priors into attention. Existing structured-initialization methods alter Transformer inductive bias indirectly, by choosing query and key projections whose similarity scores approximate a desired attention pattern. However, we find that when applied to Boolean extrapolation, these QK-based priors can be rapidly overwritten during training and fail to change the learned extrapolation rule. We propose a simpler alternative: initialize the additive attention mask directly. Unlike standard hard masks used for causality or locality attention, our mask is a finite, learnable attention-logit bias initialized from task-level interaction structure. This separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization. On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by the default inductive bias. The same mechanism also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks. These results show that attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints, but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers.

</details>


### [40] [TrAC: Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00422)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrAC is a novel uncertainty quantification method for LLMs that combines active and passive signals from a single reasoning trace to better predict answer correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often generate fluent but incorrect reasoning traces, making uncertainty estimation crucial. Existing methods either use passive single-trace signals, sampling-based approaches with high cost, or active prefix-based methods, but none actively re-elicits answers from completed reasoning traces to measure consistency.

Method: TrAC has two components: 1) Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE) that re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace, measuring consistency and token-level support; 2) Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP) that summarizes token-level uncertainty evolution during original generation. A lightweight head integrates both representations into a response-correctness score.

Result: Across five math reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% vs eight-sample self-consistency, using only one complete trace and short cached answer probe. With eight samples, augmenting with re-elicitation further improves AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%.

Conclusion: TrAC effectively combines active and passive uncertainty signals from single reasoning traces, providing better correctness prediction than existing methods while being computationally efficient and scalable to existing sample sets.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent reasoning traces that nevertheless lead to incorrect answers, making response-level uncertainty estimation important for abstention, human review, and adaptive compute allocation. Existing approaches generally fall into three categories: passive single-trace methods use token-level confidence signals, sampling-based methods compare multiple complete traces at higher generation cost, and active prefix-based methods probe partial traces to study answer stabilization or preference transitions. However, none actively re-elicits an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure its consistency with and support for the original answer. To address this gap, we introduce Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency (TrAC), a correctness-supervised uncertainty quantification framework that combines active and passive signals anchored to one completed reasoning trace. Its active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace and represents both its consistency with the original answer and its token-level probabilistic support. Its passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), summarizes how token-level uncertainty evolves throughout the original generation without additional decoding. A lightweight head then integrates the two representations into a response-correctness score. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using one complete reasoning trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting sample consensus with re-elicitation further improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%, without additional full-trace generation.

</details>


### [41] [Diagnose Before You Compress: Prediction-Independent Bottleneck Witness Refinement for LLM Serving Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00423)
*Liming Liu,Chao Hu,Mingfei Lu,Cong Tan,Yiwei Ge,Chijin Zhou,Yongjun Xie,Runzhe Wang,Xiaohai Shi,Heyuan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BPW is a framework for creating compact LLM serving replay suites that preserve bottleneck-revealing workloads rather than just representative ones, enabling more reliable performance diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trace reduction methods for LLM serving mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Current approaches cannot transfer evidence between components and create circular evaluation when using predicted bottlenecks as target truth.

Method: BPW has three stages: 1) Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and source-side measurements to identify potential bottleneck-exposing workloads; 2) Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction organizing multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges prioritizing weak/uncovered dimensions; 3) Bottleneck Truth Verification deriving prediction-independent labels from direct target-system measurements.

Result: Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show BPW reaches verified gate with compact workload sets, outperforming 16 policies with 2.3% improvement in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and 16.3% improvement in WBRC-AUC. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm contributions and stability of each stage.

Conclusion: BPW provides a quality-constrained framework for creating diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites that preserve evidence for every bottleneck component, moving beyond workload representativeness alone to enable more accurate performance diagnosis.

Abstract: Production LLM serving generates millions of diverse requests, making full-trace replay across serving configurations increasingly expensive. Existing trace reduction methods mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Moreover, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, while using predicted bottlenecks as target truth creates circular evaluation. These limitations make it necessary to preserve evidence for every bottleneck component rather than rely on workload representativeness alone. We propose Bottleneck-Preserving Witnessing (BPW), a quality-constrained framework for compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW first performs Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements. This stage identifies workloads that may expose scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks. Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction then organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak and uncovered dimensions. Finally, Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements. The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component. Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show that BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set and outperforms 16 policies, achieving relative improvements of 2.3% and 16.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC, respectively. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm the distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llmllmllm/BPW

</details>


### [42] [Ekova: A Personality-Support Agent for Self-Discovery Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00478)
*Yuyan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Personality Support (PS) as a new paradigm distinct from traditional Emotional Support, focusing on cognitive clarity and self-articulation rather than emotional distress relief. It presents DSD dataset, DeepSupport system with OrthoTune framework, and Ekova agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current emotional support systems primarily focus on alleviating immediate emotional distress. The authors argue there's a complementary need for helping users gain cognitive clarity and self-understanding, which defines a distinct Personality Support paradigm that is not clinical intervention but focuses on self-discovery and articulation.

Method: Three-layer approach: 1) DSD - a Chinese self-discovery dataset of 8,590 samples collected through real longitudinal interactions across five minimal units (Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, Gonzo). 2) DeepSupport - a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, a PS-tailored framework with style-specific adapters and style-consistency regularizer. 3) Ekova - a persistent personality-support agent that unifies the five personas with cross-session memory layer supporting adaptive routing and user-customized persona selection.

Result: OrthoTune-trained models outperform all baselines with an average relative gain of 16.3% across all metrics over the strongest prompt-based baseline. The system successfully instantiates the Personality Support paradigm through both technical architecture and experimental validation.

Conclusion: The paper successfully establishes Personality Support as a distinct paradigm from traditional Emotional Support, provides a concrete instantiation through dataset, framework, and system, and demonstrates effectiveness through experimental results. The work opens new directions for AI systems focused on cognitive clarity and self-understanding rather than just emotional relief.

Abstract: Emotional Support (ES) systems have long optimized a single objective: alleviating the user's emotional distress in the moment. We argue that a complementary need, helping users see themselves more clearly, defines a distinct paradigm we call Personality Support (PS). PS is not counseling or clinical intervention: it targets cognitive clarity and self-articulation, not symptom relief or diagnosis. We instantiate this paradigm in three layers. First, we present DSD, a Chinese self-discovery PS Dataset of 8,590 samples collected through real longitudinal interaction across five minimal units, Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, and Gonzo. Second, we build DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, a PS-tailored framework with style-specific adapters and a style-consistency regularizer. Third, we unify the five DeepSupport personas into Ekova, a persistent personality-support agent with a unified cross-session memory layer, supporting both adaptive routing and user-customized persona selection. Experiments show that OrthoTune-trained models outperform all baselines with an average relative gain of 16.3% across all metrics over the strongest prompt-based baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Yukyin/Ekova.

</details>


### [43] [F-WANDA: Fisher-Reweighted Post-Training Pruning for Sustainable Deployment of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00481)
*Himanshu Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: F-WANDA improves one-shot post-training LLM pruning by using Fisher information to reallocate pruning budgets, achieving better quality than WANDA and faster computation than SPARSEGPT with minimal overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing one-shot post-training pruning methods for LLMs either sacrifice quality (WANDA) or require high compute cost (SPARSEGPT). There's a need for a method that achieves better quality-efficiency trade-offs without extra calibration data or fine-tuning.

Method: F-WANDA modifies WANDA by reallocating per-row pruning budgets across output neurons using empirical Fisher information of pre-activations. The Fisher signal is collected in one additional backward pass over the same calibration data WANDA uses, without updating any weights.

Result: On LLAMA-2-7B at 50% unstructured sparsity: achieves WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA's fluency, improves 5-shot MMLU by +1.6 percentage points over WANDA and +1.1 pp over SPARSEGPT, with only one-third of SPARSEGPT's pruning wall-clock time and energy consumption.

Conclusion: F-WANDA achieves superior quality-compute trade-offs for sustainable LLM compression, placing it on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost without requiring extra calibration data or fine-tuning.

Abstract: One-shot post-training pruning is the most energy-frugal compression strategy for largelanguage models (LLMs), yet existing approaches trade either quality (WANDA) or compute cost (SPARSEGPT). We introduce F-WANDA, a drop-in modification of WANDA that reallocates the per-row keep budget across output neurons in proportion to the empirical Fisher information of the pre-activation. The Fisher signal is collected in a single additional backward pass over the same calibration corpus WANDA already uses; no weights are updated. On LLAMA-2-7B at 50 % unstructured sparsity, F-WANDA attains WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA fluency, and improves 5-shot MMLU by +1.6 pp over WANDA and +1.1 pp over SPARSEGPT, while incurring only one-third of SPARSEGPT pruning wall-clock and energy. The headline trade-off is achieved without extra calibration data or fine-tuning, placing F-WANDA on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost for sustainable LLM compression.

</details>


### [44] [The Bayesian Reflex: A Predictive Coding Engine for Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00492)
*Sourabh Bhattacharya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Bayesian reflex, a computational framework that implements predictive coding through hierarchical generative models, Bayesian updating, and active inference, enabling scalable brain-inspired AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive coding offers a powerful theory of cortical computation, but scalable algorithmic implementations for artificial intelligence have remained elusive. There's a need for mathematically principled, brain-inspired frameworks for continual learning, perception, and decision-making.

Method: Introduces Bayesian reflex framework with three pillars: 1) belief maintenance via hierarchical generative models, 2) sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and 3) uncertainty-driven action via active inference. Combines recent breakthroughs: ellipsoidal decomposition for exact i.i.d. sampling, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization.

Result: The framework enables mathematically principled, scalable, and brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making. It's demonstrated through diverse applications including climate model evaluation and prime number discovery, showing versatility across domains.

Conclusion: Bayesian reflex offers a blueprint for truly adaptive artificial intelligence by directly instantiating predictive coding theory into practical, scalable algorithmic implementations, bridging neuroscience insights with AI applications.

Abstract: Predictive coding offers a powerful theory of cortical computation, but corresponding scalable algorithmic implementations for artificial intelligence have remained elusive. This paper introduces the Bayesian reflex, a computational framework that directly instantiates predictive coding through three pillars: belief maintenance via hierarchical generative models, sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and uncertainty-driven action via active inference. We show that recent breakthroughs---ellipsoidal decomposition for exact $i.i.d.$ sampling, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization---provide the missing algorithmic ingredients. The resulting framework enables mathematically principled, scalable, and brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making. We illustrate its versatility through applications ranging from climate model evaluation to prime number discovery, offering a blueprint for truly adaptive artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [45] [TaPR: Test-Aware Policy Refinement for Feedback-Conditioned Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00494)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TaPR is a framework that transforms execution feedback into dense per-turn test-pass-ratio rewards for multi-turn code agents, improving their self-repair capabilities by better aligning training with multi-turn interaction dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard reinforcement learning for code agents uses single-shot outcome rewards, which conflates initial code generation with feedback-driven refinement, discards granular execution signals across intermediate turns, and fails to properly evaluate self-repair capabilities.

Method: Test-aware Policy Refinement (TaPR) transforms execution feedback into dense per-turn test-pass-ratio rewards under a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol, providing more granular feedback throughout the refinement process.

Result: TaPR improves pooled three-turn success rate (Pass@3) by 2.44 percentage points across six models on 219 LiveCodeBench problems. In the 7B/8B high-headroom slice, accuracy increased from 30.25% to 33.56% (+3.31 pp) with 42 improvements vs 13 regressions. The dense reward provides nonzero feedback in all first ten steps and achieves higher Hard-subset peak than outcome-only GRPO.

Conclusion: The primary contribution is a reward-decomposition framework and turn-aware evaluation protocol that decouple first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence, providing better alignment between training objectives and multi-turn agent behavior.

Abstract: Multi-turn code agents rely on execution feedback to repair incorrect programs, yet standard reinforcement learning paradigms optimize and evaluate policy performance primarily using single-shot outcome rewards. This misalignment conflates initial code generation with feedback-driven refinement, discards granular execution signals across intermediate turns, and fails to evaluate whether the policy actually acquires self-repair capabilities. We propose Test-aware Policy Refinement (TaPR), a framework that transforms execution feedback into a dense per-turn test-pass-ratio reward under a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol. Across six models on 219 code-generation problems from LiveCodeBench, TaPR improves the pooled three-turn success rate (Pass@3) by 2.44 percentage points. In the predefined 7B/8B high-headroom slice, pooled accuracy increases from 30.25% to 33.56% (+3.31 pp), with 42 improvements and 13 regressions in paired trials. On a matched Qwen3-8B ablation, the dense reward supplies nonzero feedback in all of the first ten steps and reaches a higher Hard-subset peak than outcome-only GRPO within the tested budget, although GRPO nearly matches pooled Pass@3 by step 300. Our primary contribution is a reward-decomposition framework and a turn-aware evaluation protocol that decouple first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence.

</details>


### [46] [BayesSeg: A Bayesian Optimization Framework for State Segmentation of Electricity Consumption Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00513)
*Zhenya Zhang,Wendi Zhu,Ping Wang,Hongmei Cheng,Shuguang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BayesSeg is a unified NILM framework combining adaptive time-series segmentation, multi-dimensional evaluation, and Bayesian optimization for automated parameter tuning, achieving 5700x speedup over grid search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NILM segmentation methods suffer from heuristic parameter tuning, boundary sensitivity, and metric saturation problems, requiring an automated and robust solution.

Method: Three-layer framework: 1) Segmentation using dual steady-state criterion and sequential extraction/complement-set parsing; 2) Evaluation via composite metric of event-level F1 score and NMI; 3) Optimization using Bayesian optimization with TPE surrogate model.

Result: Achieves 0.7149 composite score and 0.9340 event_F1 on SustDataED2 dataset; reduces optimization from ~5300 seconds to <1 second (5700x speedup); finds optimal parameters with only ~100 evaluations (within 0.35% of grid-search optimum).

Conclusion: BayesSeg provides an automated, scalable, and efficient segmentation framework for NILM that overcomes key limitations of existing methods and enables practical deployment.

Abstract: In Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), adaptive segmentation of electricity consumption time series is critical for appliance recognition. However, prevailing methods face challenges including heuristic parameter tuning, boundary sensitivity, and metric saturation. This paper proposes BayesSeg, a unified framework integrating time-series segmentation, multidimensional evaluation, and automatic parameter optimization. The segmentation layer employs a dual steady-state criterion based on the tail value and mean of preceding subsequences, combined with a sequential extraction and complement-set parsing strategy, to achieve precise unsupervised partitioning of steady-state and transition-state segments. The evaluation layer maps segmentation results to binary state sequences and formulates a composite metric integrating an event-level F1 score (event_F1) with Normalized Mutual Information (NMI). The event_F1 quantifies switching-event precision and recall via tolerance matching, while NMI captures global structural consistency, jointly overcoming the boundary sensitivity and limited discriminability of point-wise metrics. In the optimization layer, the composite score serves as the objective function for Bayesian optimization, which constructs a TPE surrogate model for efficient global parameter-space exploration. Experiments on the SustDataED2 dataset demonstrate that Bayesian optimization requires only ~100 objective evaluations to locate a parameter region within 0.35% deviation of the exhaustive grid-search optimum. The framework achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and an event_F1 of 0.9340 while reducing optimization latency from ~5300 seconds to under 1 second, a speedup exceeding 5700x. BayesSeg automates segmentation configuration and provides a scalable, efficient solution for time-series analysis in NILM and related domains.

</details>


### [47] [CURE: Local Uncertainty Repair for Block-Parallel Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00531)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CURE introduces a budget-aware dynamic repair tree that identifies and repairs errors at high-uncertainty tokens in speculative decoding, improving accepted draft length and achieving 2.66-3.49× speedup over baseline decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parallel drafting in speculative decoding suffers from rapid accuracy degradation over long horizons, leading to high rejection rates and suboptimal speedups. Drafting errors stem from localized high-uncertainty tokens that destabilize downstream generation trajectories.

Method: CURE uses predictive confidence margins to dynamically locate candidate error tokens within block-parallel drafts, expands bounded repair paths only at these fragile nodes, and employs a novel repair resynchronization mechanism to realign draft states post-verification. It's a plug-and-play repair module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks.

Result: On code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench-lite) and mathematical reasoning benchmark (GSM8K), CURE increases average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines without repair, achieving 2.66-3.49× end-to-end speedup over target-only decoding.

Conclusion: CURE effectively addresses the error accumulation problem in speculative decoding by targeted repair at uncertainty focal points, balancing draft compute and verification efficiency while maintaining compatibility with existing parallel drafting frameworks.

Abstract: Speculative decoding mitigates the latency of sequential generation in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by interleaving draft generation with target verification. However, existing parallel drafting backends often suffer from rapid accuracy degradation over long horizons, leading to high rejection rates during verification and suboptimal wall-clock speedups. We observe that drafting errors are not uniformly distributed but typically stem from localized high-uncertainty tokens that destabilize downstream generation trajectories. Motivated by this token error pattern, we propose CURE, a budget-aware dynamic repair tree designed to repair errors at uncertainty focal points without incurring prohibitive tree-verification overheads. Specifically, our method uses predictive confidence margins to dynamically locate candidate error tokens within a block-parallel draft, expands bounded repair paths only at these fragile nodes, and employs a novel repair resynchronization mechanism to realign draft states post-verification. Evaluations on code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench-lite) and mathematical reasoning benchmark (GSM8K) demonstrate that CURE increases the average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines without repair, translating to an end-to-end speedup of $2.66-3.49\times$ over target-only decoding. Furthermore, we provide a plug-and-play repair module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks. We also characterize the trade-off between draft compute and verification efficiency.

</details>


### [48] [Through the LENS: Local Geometric Decomposition of Vision-Language Model Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00561)
*Shalom Kachko,Raz Lapid,Margarita Vald,Almog Dubin,Moshe Sipper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LENS method discovers local geometric neighborhoods in vision-language models, revealing distinct fusion patterns and enabling effective multimodal steering and retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current interpretability methods for vision-language models focus on global linear directions, which may miss representations that are globally high-dimensional but locally low-dimensional. The local geometry of how image and text modalities interact remains poorly understood.

Method: LENS (Local Explanation of Neighborhood Subspaces) decomposes VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods using a Mixture of Factor Analyzers. The method includes an automated multimodal labeling pipeline to assign semantic descriptions to neighborhoods. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B models.

Result: Revealed distinct depth-dependent fusion trajectories: LLaVA progressively mixes modalities at later layers, while Qwen3-VL mixes early, partially re-segregates, and recombines near output. MFA steering outperforms baselines in most conditions (5.7x VL-SAE score in one setting). Human evaluation shows competitive with prompting. Improved Qwen3-VL image-to-text retrieval from 14.9% to 48.6% R@1 at deepest layer. Findings are stable across component counts and thresholds.

Conclusion: Local geometric neighborhoods serve as useful interpretable and causal units for analyzing cross-modal representations in vision-language models, offering better understanding of modality fusion patterns and enabling effective intervention capabilities.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process image patches and text tokens in a shared residual stream, but the local geometry through which the two modalities interact remains poorly understood. Most interpretability methods identify global linear directions, which may miss representations that are globally high-dimensional but locally low-dimensional. We introduce LENS (Local Explanation of Neighborhood Subspaces), a method that decomposes VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods using a Mixture of Factor Analyzers. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, LENS reveals distinct depth-dependent fusion trajectories consistent with each model's fusion mechanism: LLaVA progressively mixes modalities at later layers, whereas Qwen3-VL mixes them early, partially re-segregates them, and recombines them near the output. An automated multimodal labeling pipeline assigns concise semantic descriptions to these neighborhoods. Interpolating activations toward neighborhood centroids causally redirects generation within and across modalities and outperforms difference-in-means and VL-SAE in most evaluated conditions; in one LLaVA vision-to-vision setting, MFA achieves 5.7 times the VL-SAE score. Human evaluation finds MFA steering competitive with prompting and substantially stronger than the other intervention baselines. Finally, the MFA coefficient space improves Qwen3-VL image-to-rendered-text retrieval at the deepest evaluated layer from 14.9% to 48.6% R@1. Ablations show that the reported fusion trajectories are stable across component counts, local ranks, and modality-purity thresholds. These results support local geometric neighborhoods as useful interpretable and causal units for analyzing cross-modal representations in the evaluated VLMs.

</details>


### [49] [Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00591)
*Yibin Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ClosurePairs is a novel evaluation protocol that distinguishes between state aliasing and true process noise in stochastic world models by using interventional data pairs, addressing a decision-relevant ambiguity that standard forecasting metrics cannot identify.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard evaluation of stochastic world models focuses on prediction accuracy and calibration, but these metrics fail to distinguish whether uncertainty stems from state aliasing (observations conflating different physical states) or true process noise (randomness even with full state knowledge). This attribution is crucial for decision-making but is not identifiable from ordinary transition data alone.

Method: The authors introduce ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that crosses compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances. The method uses a two-way variance decomposition to separate state aliasing, process noise, and their nonlinear interaction. An independent-repeat variant handles cases where disturbances cannot be reused. The approach provides paired supervision to distinguish these sources of uncertainty.

Result: ClosurePairs significantly outperforms standard evaluation methods: reduces alias-fraction error 15.96-fold in Gaussian systems, cuts attribution MAE from 0.372 to 0.051 in nonlinear Langevin conditions, improves sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003, reduces alias-fraction MAE from 0.584 to 0.130 in distribution for pixel-conditioned models, and achieves near-perfect 99.99% accuracy in REFINE/BRANCH tests compared to 66.48% for variance-based methods.

Conclusion: ClosurePairs successfully identifies why futures branch in stochastic world models, providing crucial decision-relevant information that proper forecast scores alone cannot capture. The method effectively separates state aliasing from process noise, enabling better understanding and potentially improved model design for decision-making applications.

Abstract: Stochastic world models are usually evaluated by the accuracy and calibration of their predicted futures. These criteria leave a decision-relevant ambiguity: the same conditional future distribution can arise because an observation aliases different physical states, or because the dynamics remain random after the declared full state is fixed. We prove that this attribution is not identifiable from ordinary transition data, even with an optimal probabilistic predictor. We introduce ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that crosses compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances. A two-way variance decomposition identifies state aliasing, process noise, and their nonlinear interaction; an independent-repeat variant applies when disturbances cannot be reused. On likelihood-equivalent Gaussian systems, paired supervision reduces alias-fraction error 15.96-fold at identical test NLL. Across 18 nonlinear Langevin conditions, it reduces attribution MAE from 0.372 to 0.051 and sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003 without changing NLL. On a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, a frozen shared-state probe reduces alias-fraction MAE against a deep ensemble from 0.584 to 0.130 in distribution and from 0.630 to 0.170 out of distribution over ten seeds. Finally, in a matched-total-variance REFINE/BRANCH test, a total-variance router reaches 66.48 percent plus or minus 1.06 percent accuracy, whereas ClosurePairs reaches 99.99 percent plus or minus 0.02 percent and improves selected NLL from -2.087 to -2.717 over five seeds. ClosurePairs therefore measures why futures branch, information that proper forecast scores cannot identify.

</details>


### [50] [Escaping Confidence Trap: Evolutionary Decoding for Mathematical Reasoning in Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00605)
*Zhenhong Sun,Hanqing Zhao,Yatao Bian,Rongcheng Tu,Liuyue Xie,Xu Zhang,Jue Wang,Davide Modolo,Daoyi Dong,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Diffusion LLMs struggle with mathematical reasoning due to confidence traps; Evolutionary Decoding improves reliability through evolutionary selection and mutation during decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) show strong general-purpose performance but fail to reliably handle mathematical reasoning, where correctness depends on coherent numerical-symbolic reasoning trajectories. The authors identify a "diffusion confidence trap" where local token confidence becomes misaligned with global reasoning correctness during progressive block decoding.

Method: The authors analyze decoding trajectories of LLaDA 2.0 and propose Evolutionary Decoding, a training-free test-time scaling framework. This framework treats diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states, combining step-wise selection (to preserve useful numerical-symbolic signals and suppress repetitive patterns) with block-wise mutation (to introduce structured alternatives and escape incorrect high-confidence basins).

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Evolutionary Decoding improves LLaDA 2.0 over confidence-based decoding, leading to more reliable mathematical reasoning. The framework addresses two failure regimes identified: sampling-sensitive failures (correct paths exist but unstable) and sampling-consistent failures (repeated sampling converges to repetitive high-confidence but incorrect continuations).

Conclusion: Evolutionary Decoding effectively mitigates the diffusion confidence trap in mathematical reasoning tasks by applying evolutionary principles to diffusion decoding, resulting in more reliable reasoning performance without requiring additional training.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, offering efficient generation through block-wise progressive unmasking. However, their strong general-purpose performance does not necessarily translate into reliable mathematical reasoning, where correctness depends on preserving coherent numerical-symbolic reasoning trajectories. In this work, we analyze the decoding trajectories of LLaDA 2.0 and identify a recurring diffusion confidence trap: local token confidence can become misaligned with global reasoning correctness during progressive block decoding. Our analysis reveals two representative failure regimes: sampling-sensitive failures, where correct paths exist but are unstable, and sampling-consistent failures, where repeated sampling converges to repetitive high-confidence but incorrect continuations.
