Motivated by this observation, we propose Evolutionary Decoding, a training-free test-time scaling framework that views diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states. The framework combines step-wise selection, which preserves useful numerical-symbolic signals and suppresses repetitive patterns, with block-wise mutation, which introduces structured alternatives to escape incorrect high-confidence basins. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Evolutionary Decoding improves LLaDA 2.0 over confidence-based decoding, leading to more reliable mathematical reasoning.

</details>


### [51] [Slides2MindMap: Reconstructing Cognitively Efficient Knowledge Hierarchies from Lecture Slides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00610)
*Yuzhi Wang,Rongjun Ye,Shengyuan Chen,Huachi Zhou,Jiaqi Bai,Chuang Zhou,Zhicong Hong,Xiao Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoMindMap: An agentic framework that automatically generates mind maps from lecture slides using global-local knowledge balancing and iterative refinement, with S2M-Bench as a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating mind maps from lecture slides can help learners assimilate fragmented knowledge efficiently, benefiting intelligent education. However, dedicated automatic generation and evaluation frameworks are underexplored and challenging due to needing to balance global-local knowledge focus and handling large-scale, heterogeneous slides.

Method: Proposes AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by Structure Building Framework. It comprises three components: 1) Skeleton Laying for global scaffold anchoring, 2) Iterative Knowledge Integration augmented by context-aware summarization, and 3) Dual-Stage Refinement with local-global decoupling mechanism. Also introduces S2M-Bench benchmark (12,774 slide pages with expert-annotated mind maps across 24 courses) with cognitive-science-grounded evaluation framework.

Result: Experiments on S2M-Bench demonstrate that AutoMindMap outperforms baselines and achieves superior robustness across different models and scenarios, highlighting its pedagogical application value.

Conclusion: The proposed AutoMindMap framework successfully addresses the Slides2MindMap task by reconciling local knowledge faithfulness with global coherence, adapting to slide-specific features, and showing strong performance on the comprehensive S2M-Bench benchmark.

Abstract: Generating mind maps from lecture slides can help learners efficiently assimilate fragmented knowledge, promising substantial benefits for intelligent education. However, dedicated automatic generation and evaluation frameworks remain underexplored and challenging, requiring a global-local knowledge focus balance and handling large-scale, heterogeneous slides. We formulate the Slides2MindMap task, which aims to reconstruct cognitively efficient knowledge hierarchies from a course's slide deck collection. For systematic evaluation, we introduce S2M-Bench, a benchmark comprising 12,774 slide pages with expert-annotated mind maps spanning 24 university courses. S2M-Bench includes a cognitive-science-grounded evaluation framework that integrates ground-truth-based comparison, structure conformity analysis, and VLM-as-a-Judge. To address this task, we propose AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by the Structure Building Framework. AutoMindMap comprises Skeleton Laying for global scaffold anchoring, Iterative Knowledge Integration augmented by context-aware summarization, and Dual-Stage Refinement with a local-global decoupling mechanism. The framework reconciles local knowledge faithfulness with global coherence, and adapts to slide-specific features. Experiments on S2M-Bench demonstrate that AutoMindMap outperforms baselines and achieves superior robustness across different models and scenarios, underscoring its pedagogical application value.

</details>


### [52] [DASH: Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate - Acquisition Harness for Automated Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00641)
*Changquan Zhao,Yuxiang Sun,Ruihao Zhu,Cheng Hua,Yulian He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH is a decoupled AutoBO framework that independently selects surrogate models based on predictive reliability and acquisition functions using a two-stage controller with LLM delegation, achieving significant performance gains in chemical optimization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AutoBO methods have limitations: they either adapt only one component (creating mismatches), or jointly select surrogate-acquisition pairs using a shared criterion that overlooks their distinct roles. Surrogate selection should focus on predictive reliability, while acquisition adaptation should respond to campaign context.

Method: DASH decouples surrogate and acquisition adaptation. It selects surrogates based on predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency. The two-stage acquisition controller periodically reallocates quotas across acquisition functions, builds a BO shortlist, and delegates final selection to an LLM. Includes knowledge-guided warm start and structured memory for domain grounding.

Result: Across four chemical optimization tasks, DASH outperforms the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. Results remain strong across LLM backbones, with ablations verifying complementary contributions of all components. No evidence of benchmark memorization or source-cell leakage.

Conclusion: DASH successfully addresses the limitations of existing AutoBO methods by decoupling surrogate and acquisition adaptation while leveraging LLM capabilities, demonstrating superior performance in real-world optimization tasks through its comprehensive approach to component adaptation.

Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) relies on a surrogate model and an acquisition function, yet the most suitable choices vary across tasks and optimization stages. Automated Bayesian optimization (AutoBO) addresses this variability by adapting BO components online. However, existing AutoBO methods either adapt one component, leaving the other mismatched and creating a bottleneck, or jointly select surrogate--acquisition pairs under a shared criterion, overlooking their distinct roles: surrogate selection depends on predictive reliability, whereas acquisition adaptation should respond to campaign context.In this paper, we propose DASH, a Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate--Acquisition Harness for large-language- model (LLM)-enhanced AutoBO. DASH selects surrogates by predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency; its two-stage acquisition controller periodically reallocates quotas across acquisition functions, builds a BO shortlist accordingly, and delegates final selection to an LLM. DASH also incorporates an integrated harness, consisting of knowledge-guided warm start and structured memory, to ground optimization in domain knowledge and accumulated feedback. Across four chemical optimization tasks, DASH outperforms the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. Results remain strong across LLM backbones, and ablations verify the complementary contributions of all components. Full-table and behavioral contamination checks find no detectable evidence that direct benchmark memorization or source-cell leakage explains these gains.

</details>


### [53] [Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC): A Theoretical Framework for Process-Oriented Cognitive Evaluation of Text-Based AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00680)
*Abdalla Doleh,Ratna Babu Chinnam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAAC is a framework that shifts AI evaluation from outcome-based benchmarks to cognitive process assessment, defining nine dimensions grounded in cognitive science theories to understand how AI systems think rather than just what they produce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI evaluation relies heavily on outcome-based benchmarks (accuracy, robustness, fairness) which provide limited diagnostic insight into the underlying cognitive processes. These benchmarks don't answer critical questions about how AI systems reason, integrate memory, manage complexity, or avoid generating false information.

Method: The paper introduces the Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC) framework with nine cognitively motivated dimensions: Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, and Process-Outcome Alignment. The framework is grounded in established cognitive science theories (Marr's tri-level hypothesis, Baddeley's working memory model, Sweller's cognitive load theory, unified theories of cognition). Five theoretical analyses are conducted: dimension-to-theory mapping, coverage matrix assessing breadth/non-redundancy, formal gap analysis, worked diagnostic illustration, and interdependency predictions for future testing.

Result: MAAC provides a theoretically grounded framework for principled process-level cognitive assessment of text-based AI systems. It complements existing outcome-based benchmarks with cognitively grounded, multi-dimensional evaluation. The framework demonstrates coherence and empirical testability through the five theoretical analyses.

Conclusion: MAAC represents a significant shift in AI evaluation methodology from focusing solely on what AI systems produce to understanding how they think. This cognitive process assessment framework addresses critical gaps in current evaluation practices and enables deeper diagnostic insights into AI reasoning and cognitive capabilities.

Abstract: Evaluating artificial intelligence systems has historically relied on outcome-based benchmarks that measure task accuracy, robustness, or fairness. While indispensable, these benchmarks provide limited diagnostic insight into the underlying cognitive processes that generate performance-leaving critical questions unanswered about how AI systems reason, integrate memory, manage complexity, or avoid generating false information. This paper introduces the Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC), a theoretically grounded framework for shifting evaluation from what text-based AI systems produce to how they think. MAAC defines nine cognitively motivated dimensions: Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, and Process-Outcome Alignment. Each dimension is grounded in established cognitive science theory-drawing on Marr's tri-level hypothesis, Baddeley's working memory model, Sweller's cognitive load theory, and unified theories of cognition. Five theoretical analyses provide initial support for the framework's coherence and empirical testability: dimension-to-theory mapping; a coverage matrix assessing breadth and non-redundancy; a formal gap analysis relative to current evaluation practice; a worked diagnostic illustration; and a set of a priori interdependency predictions for future empirical testing. MAAC provides a theoretical and operational framework for principled process-level cognitive assessment of text-based AI systems, complementing existing outcome-based benchmarks with cognitively grounded, multi-dimensional evaluation.

</details>


### [54] [When Does LLM Orchestration Pay Off? A Controlled Evaluation of Accuracy, Cost, and Task Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00685)
*Nicolas Leins,Nico Pelleriti,Jana Gonnermann-Müller,Sebastian Pokutta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM orchestration methods (Self-Refine, Best-of-N, Debate) show modest accuracy gains (4-5 percentage points) but require 2-4x more tokens than task-only inference, with effectiveness heavily dependent on the underlying model rather than task difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM orchestration evaluations often overlook differences in optimization effort and fail to isolate the true value of orchestration itself, making it difficult to determine whether the performance gains justify the increased computational costs.

Method: Controlled evaluation of three orchestration methods (Self-Refine, Best-of-N, Debate) against task-only and chain-of-thought baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains (competitive programming, chess puzzles, mathematics). All methods were optimized with GEPA under the same optimization budget and evaluated on the same difficulty-stratified benchmark items.

Result: Orchestration yields moderate, benchmark-dependent gains (largest improvement: 4.6 pp over optimized CoT, 4.5 pp over task-only), requiring 2-4x mean total tokens of task-only inference. Human difficulty correlates with lower accuracy, but orchestration effects don't increase with difficulty. Strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model show effectiveness is highly model-specific.

Conclusion: Orchestration decisions should be model-specific and consider whether moderate accuracy gains justify additional inference costs. LLM orchestration evaluations should control optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy-cost trade-offs rather than assuming additional inference-time structure is uniformly beneficial.

Abstract: LLM orchestration is often assumed to improve reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation, yet its gains may not justify its cost. Existing comparisons also frequently overlook differences in optimization effort, making it difficult to isolate the value of orchestration itself. We conduct a controlled evaluation of Self-Refine, Best-of-$N$, and Debate against task-only and chain-of-thought (CoT) single-call baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains: competitive programming, chess puzzles, and mathematics. For comparability, we optimize each method with GEPA under the same optimization budget and evaluate all methods on the same difficulty-stratified benchmark items. Orchestration yields moderate but benchmark-dependent gains: averaged across backbones within each benchmark, the largest improvement is 4.6 percentage points over optimized CoT inference and 4.5 points over task-only inference, while requiring approximately 2 to 4 times the mean total tokens of task-only inference. Human-derived difficulty is associated with lower absolute accuracy in all three benchmarks, but within-benchmark analyses do not indicate that orchestration effects increase with task difficulty. By contrast, exploratory mixed-effects analyses reveal strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model across all three benchmarks, showing that orchestration effectiveness depends substantially on the underlying model. Our results suggest that orchestration decisions should be model-specific and account for whether moderate accuracy gains justify the additional inference cost. More broadly, evaluations of LLM orchestrations should control optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than treating additional inference-time structure as uniformly beneficial.

</details>


### [55] [Evolutionary Curriculum Learning Improves Biological Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00697)
*Richard Zhu,Kento Nishi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL) improves VAE training for biological sequences by progressively exposing models to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance, boosting performance on protein variant prediction and RNA generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure that organizes homologous sequences from evolutionarily close to highly divergent. This misses important evolutionary information that could improve model performance.

Method: Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL) exploits evolutionary structure by progressively exposing VAE models to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from sampled anchors, following a power-law expansion schedule. This creates a curriculum where the model learns from close evolutionary neighbors first before more distant ones.

Result: ECL improves downstream task performance across two biological domains: protein variant effect prediction (EVE model) and RNA family sequence generation (RfamGen). For p53, mean ClinVar classification AUROC rose from 0.981 to 0.989; for PTEN, ECL attained 1.000 AUROC in every seed while baseline was unstable (mean 0.905, dropping as low as 0.54). For RNA, ECL raised mean covariance-model bit scores and exceeded baseline in 12 of 15 training runs.

Conclusion: Evolutionary distance is a useful inductive bias for ordering the training curriculum in biological sequence modeling. Progressively expanding the sampled sequences by evolutionary distance outperforms both fixed-size neighborhood sampling and uniform random sampling.

Abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) have emerged as powerful generative models for biological sequences, with applications ranging from disease variant prediction to functional RNA design. However, standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure that organizes homologous sequences from evolutionarily close to highly divergent. We propose Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a training strategy that exploits this structure by progressively exposing the model to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from sampled anchors, following a power-law expansion schedule. Applied to two architecturally distinct VAE models and two biological domains--protein variant effect prediction with EVE and RNA family sequence generation with RfamGen--ECL improves downstream task performance across five random seeds per configuration. Mean ClinVar classification AUROC rises from 0.981 to 0.989 for p53; for PTEN, ECL attains 1.000 in every seed whereas the baseline is unstable (mean 0.905, falling as low as 0.54). For RNA, ECL raises mean covariance-model bit scores on all three families tested and exceeds its seed-matched baseline in 12 of 15 training runs, though with only three families the effect cannot be established as significant at the family level. Ablation experiments show that progressively expanding the sampled sequences by evolutionary distance outperforms fixed-size neighborhood sampling in addition to uniform random sampling. Evolutionary distance is therefore a useful inductive bias for ordering the training curriculum in biological sequence modeling.

</details>


### [56] [DGA$_2$D: Directed Graph-Guided Automated Algorithm Design with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00700)
*Jiale Zhao,Zimu Chen,Sirui Mao,Wentao Yang,Yuxiang Bai,Liyuanjun Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A directed graph framework (DGA2D) for automated algorithm design that represents program space as a directed graph with functional operators, using path-dependent credit assignment to improve combinatorial optimization solver generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-driven automated heuristic design methods are limited to rigid solver templates with isolated module tuning, lacking fully autonomous system-level algorithm design due to issues with operator reliability, large search spaces, and ineffective credit assignment.

Method: DGA2D structures program space as a directed graph where nodes are functional operators with multiple candidate code implementations, and directed walks form complete algorithmic pipelines. It uses first-order path-dependent credit assignment to evaluate code variations based on their topological context.

Result: Extensive experiments across 12 distinct combinatorial optimization problems (scheduling to routing) show DGA2D reduces average normalized gap by up to 10.96 percentage points compared to state-of-the-art LLM baselines.

Conclusion: The DGA2D framework successfully addresses limitations of existing LLM-driven automated heuristic design methods by enabling fully autonomous system-level algorithm design through directed graph representation and context-aware credit assignment.

Abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened new avenues for Automated Heuristic Design (AHD) for solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems (COPs). However, existing LLM-driven AHD methods are largely confined to rigid solver templates, relegating the search process to isolated module tuning. Transitioning to fully autonomous, system-level algorithm design is essential but fraught with low reliability of generated operators, extremely large search spaces, and ineffective credit assignment. To overcome these drawbacks, this paper proposes a Directed Graph-Guided Automated Algorithm Design framework, termed DGA$_2$D. It structures the open-ended program space as a directed graph, where each node represents a functional operator that can be instantiated using one of multiple candidate code implementations, while directed walks constitute complete algorithmic pipelines. A first-order path-dependent credit assignment mechanism is introduced to evaluate code variations strictly based on their topological context. Extensive experiments across 12 distinct COPs, ranging from complex scheduling to routing, demonstrate the consistent empirical advantages of DGA$_2$D. It reduces the average normalized gap by up to 10.96 percentage points compared to state-of-the-art LLM baselines.

</details>


### [57] [Tracing the Cascade: A Topology-Aware Evaluation Framework for Scientific Agent Hallucinations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00711)
*Xinshun Feng,Ziqi Miao,Lijun Li,Jing Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCHEMA is a new framework for evaluating hallucinations in scientific LLM agents that considers knowledge topology rather than treating facts in isolation, revealing that hallucinations cluster at knowledge hubs and terminal accuracy doesn't reflect reasoning reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hallucination benchmarks treat facts in isolation with uniform accuracy metrics, ignoring the interconnected nature of scientific knowledge where a single error can propagate through multi-step reasoning and corrupt entire reasoning trajectories.

Method: SCHEMA automatically constructs scientific concept graphs from benchmark seeds and literature evidence, creates graph-grounded tasks (claim verification, multi-hop reasoning, open-ended explanation, code generation), and uses two diagnostics: 1) trajectory hallucination pipeline with topology-weighted severity scores, and 2) multi-agent counterfactual attribution module to pinpoint causal mechanisms of failures.

Result: Hallucinations concentrate at a small set of highly connected knowledge hubs, and final-answer accuracy decouples from trajectory honesty - models often reach correct conclusions through structurally flawed reasoning.

Conclusion: For high-stakes scientific applications, terminal accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating agent reliability, motivating mechanism-level evaluation grounded in knowledge topology.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in scientific research, where reliability is critical and the underlying knowledge is densely interconnected. In such settings, hallucinations are particularly damaging: a single erroneous claim on a foundational concept can propagate through multi-step reasoning and corrupt entire trajectories. Existing hallucination benchmarks largely operate at the surface level, treating facts in isolation and relying on uniform accuracy metrics that ignore this topological structure. We address this gap with SCHEMA, the first evidence-grounded, topology-aware evaluation framework for hallucinations in scientific agents. SCHEMA automatically constructs scientific concept graphs from benchmark seeds and literature evidence, synthesizes graph-grounded tasks spanning claim verification, multi-hop reasoning, open-ended explanation, and experimental code generation, and evaluates agents with two complementary diagnostics. A trajectory hallucination pipeline audits intermediate reasoning at scale via a topology-weighted severity score, while a multi-agent counterfactual attribution module pinpoints the causal mechanism behind selected failures. SCHEMA reveals that hallucinations concentrate at a small set of highly connected knowledge hubs, and that final-answer accuracy decouples from trajectory honesty; models often reach correct conclusions through structurally flawed reasoning. These results indicate that for high-stakes scientific applications, terminal accuracy alone is an insufficient signal of agent reliability, motivating mechanism-level evaluation grounded in knowledge topology. Code is available at https://github.com/circles-post/SCHEMA.

</details>


### [58] [AI-Based Thesis Assessment: An Empirical Study of Human Evaluation Priorities and Their Impact on Automated Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00717)
*Garv Vikram Gursahaney,Baskhad Idrisov,Thorsten Fröhlich,Tim Schlippe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study examines how thesis supervisors prioritize assessment criteria, compares their weights to default AI system weights, and finds that using supervisor-derived weights doesn't significantly improve AI-human assessment alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a gap in empirical evidence about how thesis supervisors actually prioritize evaluation criteria, while AI assessment systems use expert-defined weights. Understanding supervisor-derived weights could improve AI assessment accuracy and alignment with human evaluation.

Method: Surveyed 84 thesis supervisors across four academic disciplines to collect weighting data for 35 assessment criteria. Compared supervisor-derived weights to default AI system weights (RubiSCoT), then integrated supervisor weights into multiple calibration configurations and evaluated them on 80 German-language theses.

Result: Found substantial divergences between supervisor-derived and default AI system weights. The best calibration reduced mean relative deviation between AI and supervisor assessments from 11.18% to 10.85%, but the improvement wasn't statistically significant. Human supervisors showed much stronger agreement (4.44% mean inter-supervisor deviation).

Conclusion: Criterion-weight calibration alone doesn't substantially improve alignment between AI-generated and human assessments. The study highlights that supervisor-derived weights differ from default AI weights, but incorporating them doesn't lead to significant improvements in assessment accuracy.

Abstract: Rubric-based AI systems for thesis assessment use criterion weights to assign different levels of importance to evaluation criteria. These weights are typically defined through expert judgment, although little empirical evidence exists regarding how thesis supervisors actually prioritize evaluation criteria. Consequently, this study investigates supervisor-derived criterion weights in thesis assessment and evaluates their impact on AI-based assessment. We surveyed 84 thesis supervisors across four academic disciplines and collected weighting data for 35 thesis assessment criteria. Comparison with the default criterion weights of the AI assessment system RubiSCoT [1] revealed substantial divergences between supervisor-derived and default criterion weights. To evaluate the practical implications of these differences, the supervisor-derived weights were integrated into multiple calibration configurations and evaluated on a corpus of 80 German-language theses. The best-performing configuration reduced the mean relative deviation between AI-generated and supervisor-assigned evaluations from 11.18% to 10.85%, although the improvement was not statistically significant. Human supervisors showed substantially stronger agreement with each other, exhibiting a mean inter-supervisor relative deviation of 4.44%. The findings indicate that criterion-weight calibration alone does not substantially improve alignment between AI-generated and human assessments.

</details>


### [59] [Behavioral Grammar: Detecting Adaptive Malware via Tiny Language Model Priors and Second-Order Temporal Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00745)
*Zihan Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Behavioral Grammar detection uses a compact 0.88M-parameter Transformer to model host behavior as structured language, achieving 93% detection against adaptive threats with bounded false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional endpoint detection faces tension: signature-based approaches are easily evaded by polymorphic threats, while deep learning models lack auditability and scalability. There's a need for a system that combines detection power with deployability and auditability.

Method: 1) Treat host runtime behavior as structured language; 2) Learn grammar with compact 0.88M-parameter causal Transformer; 3) Discretize system events into 8-token representation; 4) Self-supervised learning of normal behavior distribution; 5) Anomaly detection via negative log-likelihood statistics; 6) Enhanced with prototype learning, temporal analysis, pattern extraction, and 5-network fusion.

Result: Achieves 93% detection against Adaptive Adversarial Agent threats at 3.84% false positive rate. Key finding: strongest signal is coefficient of variation of inter-event intervals (CV=0.310 for attacks vs 9.786 for benign, 30x separation).

Conclusion: Behavioral grammar detection shifts evasion cost from cheap rule circumvention to expensive distribution matching, creating structural asymmetry favoring defenders. The approach successfully balances detection power, auditability, and deployment scalability.

Abstract: Modern endpoint detection systems face a fundamental tension: signature-based approaches are trivially evaded by polymorphic or adaptive threats, while heavy deep-learning models resist auditability and deployment at scale. This paper presents Behavioral Grammar, a detection architecture that treats host runtime behavior as a structured language and learns its grammar with a compact 0.88M-parameter causal Transformer (TinyGPT). Each system event is discretized into an 8-token representation spanning event type, process, argument skeleton, path category, parent process, user, destination, and inter-event timing. The model learns the conditional distribution of normal behavior in a purely self-supervised manner, and anomaly scores are derived from per-slot negative log-likelihood (NLL) statistics, yielding a mathematically bounded false-positive rate. We augment this prior with prototype learning for known-attack attribution, second-order temporal analysis for cadence-based detection, self-learning pattern extraction, and a five-network fusion pipeline. Against an Adaptive Adversarial Agent (AAA)--a threat that learns survival strategies under defensive pressure, performs behavioral mimicry, and matches host event rates--our system achieves 93% detection at 3.84% onboarding false-positive rate. The strongest discriminative signal arises not from any single event but from the coefficient of variation of inter-event intervals: the AAA stepping cadence exhibits CV=0.310 versus 9.786 for benign sleep intervals, a 30x separation reflecting a fundamental stealth-functionality trade-off. We frame these findings within a coevolutionary economics model, arguing that behavior-grammar detection shifts the evasion cost from rule circumvention (cheap) to distribution matching (expensive), establishing a structural asymmetry favoring the defender.

</details>


### [60] [FinDeepIndicator: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents in End-to-End Financial Indicator Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00764)
*Chaoqun Yang,Fengbin Zhu,Xinyu Lin,Long Bai,Xiaoluan Liu,Ke-Wei Huang,Roger Zimmermann,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinDeepIndicator is the first benchmark for evaluating Deep Research agents in end-to-end financial indicator construction, covering formula specification, data collection, calculation, and answer generation across 3,350 QA pairs, showing that while LLMs perform well on formulas, they struggle with data retrieval and numerical execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial benchmarks focus primarily on answer-level accuracy and assume relevant data is already provided, leaving the intermediate process of indicator construction underexplored. There's a gap in evaluating the complete workflow of financial indicator construction from raw data to interpretable measures.

Method: The authors create FinDeepIndicator, a benchmark evaluating Deep Research agents across four stages of indicator construction: formula specification, data collection, indicator calculation, and answer generation. The benchmark covers fundamental, technical, and macroeconomic indicators organized into 21 sub-categories, with 3,350 QA pairs derived from US and Chinese markets, 10 years of historical data, and 800 listed companies.

Result: Experiments show that while LLMs generally perform well in formula specification, their accuracy drops substantially during data retrieval and numerical execution. Deep Research agents consistently outperform search-equipped LLMs but remain unreliable in realistic financial analysis settings.

Conclusion: The FinDeepIndicator benchmark provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating financial indicator construction, revealing limitations in current LLMs and DR agents, and offering insights for developing more capable and trustworthy Deep Research agents in finance.

Abstract: Financial indicators are essential tools for transforming raw financial data into interpretable measures for various downstream tasks, such as valuation, risk assessment, and economic analysis. However, existing financial benchmarks largely focus on answer-level accuracy and often assume that relevant data are already provided, leaving the assessment of the intermediate process of indicator construction underexplored. In this work, we propose FinDeepIndicator, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating Deep Research (DR) agents in end-to-end financial indicator construction. Specifically, FinDeepIndicator evaluates DR agents across four stages in indicator construction: formula specification, data collection, indicator calculation, and answer generation, and covers fundamental, technical, and macroeconomic indicators organized into 21 fine-grained sub-categories. It contains 3,350 curated question-answer (QA) pairs derived from both U.S. and Chinese markets, 10 years of historical financial data, and 800 listed companies. Extensive experiments on search-equipped Large Language Models (LLMs) and DR agents show that, while LLMs generally perform well in formula specification, their accuracy drops substantially during data retrieval and numerical execution. DR agents consistently outperform search-equipped LLMs, yet remain unreliable in realistic financial analysis settings. These findings provide insights for developing more capable and trustworthy DR agents in finance.

</details>


### [61] [Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00794)
*William Caban*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI evaluation benchmarks have compounding reliability problems: LM-generated tasks have validity flaws, LLM simulators are poorly calibrated, and proper inter-rater reliability metrics are often missing, making scores far less trustworthy than assumed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to expose the systematic unreliability of automated benchmarks used to evaluate agentic AI systems. These benchmarks are critical for deployment decisions, safety certifications, and regulatory compliance, but current practice overlooks compounding validity issues that make scores less trustworthy than acknowledged.

Method: The authors conducted a multi-layered empirical analysis: 1) Audited 10 popular benchmarks for validity flaws in LM-generated tasks, 2) Calibration studies of LLM simulators showing high variance and miscalibration, especially for non-Standard American English, and 3) Structured survey of 55 papers examining inter-rater reliability practices. They formalized the compounding error problem mathematically.

Result: The analysis revealed severe reliability problems: 7/10 benchmarks had validity flaws, LLM simulators showed up to 9 percentage point variance and systematic miscalibration, and ~82% of papers used mismatched/incomplete/absent IRR metrics. These errors compound multiplicatively, reducing validity to as low as 22-54% of intended construct measurement.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that current evaluation practices are systematically flawed and propose eight psychometric prescriptions including simulation calibration floors, domain-stratified reliability thresholds, structured IRR selection rules, and mandatory IRR reporting. The measurement tools exist but need proper application.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems are evaluated using automated benchmarks whose scores justify deployment decisions, safety certifications, and regulatory compliance claims. We present an empirical analysis demonstrating that these scores are systematically less trustworthy than current practice acknowledges.
  The problem operates at three compounding layers. First, tasks are increasingly generated by language models: audits of ten popular benchmarks found validity flaws in seven and reporting gaps in all ten. Second, human users are replaced by LLM simulators, but calibration studies document inter-simulator variance up to 9 percentage points and systematic directional miscalibration, particularly for non-Standard American English speakers. Third, our structured survey of 55 papers finds that approximately 82% apply structurally mismatched, incomplete, or absent inter-rater reliability (IRR) metrics.
  These failures compound multiplicatively rather than additively. Under independence, a pipeline retaining 70% of valid signal at task generation, 80% at simulation, and 65% at judgment is at most 36% valid against the intended construct; the bound spans 0.22--0.54 across the empirical estimate range. We formalize this as $V_{\text{total}} \leq V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3$ and show it tightens further under correlated failures when the same model family operates across all three layers.
  We derive eight prescriptions grounded in psychometric science: a simulation calibration floor of $\text{ICC}(A,1) \geq 0.70$; domain-stratified reliability thresholds ($α\geq 0.67$ / $0.70$ / $0.80$ by consequence level); structured IRR metric selection rules based on pipeline design; and IRR as a mandatory reporting field. The measurement tools exist; the field's task is to apply them.

</details>


### [62] [AgentSLABench: Evaluating and Benchmarking Agentic Systems Under Resource Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00805)
*Meher Bhaskar Madiraju,Meher Sai Preetam Madiraju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentSLABench is a resource-aware evaluation framework for AI agents that measures both correctness and resource consumption (latency, cost, compute, memory, network) under declared budgets, providing multi-dimensional profiling like systems profilers but for AI task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard benchmarks only report accuracy without considering resource consumption, but real-world production deployments require agents to operate efficiently within resource constraints. Current evaluation lacks comprehensive measurement of correctness alongside computational costs and resource usage.

Method: The framework includes 16 task environments across 6 categories in isolated Docker containers with declared CPU/memory/time/network budgets. It uses sealed test sets with SHA256 hashes and standardized profiling protocol to measure both task correctness and resource consumption. Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate (EASR) weights success by resource consumption relative to budgets.

Result: Specialized agents achieved 100% success on 3/5 core tasks and 66.7-83.3% on retail and code generation tasks, while general baselines failed entirely on 4/5 domain tasks. EASR reveals that high accuracy at unbounded cost is not production-viable, providing more realistic performance assessment.

Conclusion: AgentSLABench enables reproducible, resource-aware agent evaluation by measuring both correctness and resource efficiency. The framework addresses the gap between lab accuracy and production viability, with full infrastructure and sealed test sets released to standardize resource-conscious AI agent benchmarking.

Abstract: We present AgentSLABench, a resource-aware evaluation framework for autonomous AI agents that measures correctness alongside latency, cost, compute, memory, and network usage under declared resource budgets. Unlike standard benchmarks that report only accuracy, AgentSLABench produces a multi-dimensional profile per agent per task - the same way systems profilers (perf, pprof, cProfile) measure resource consumption of code, but extended with task correctness as a first-class dimension. AgentSLABench provides 16 task environments across 6 categories (5 core: multi-hop QA, retail substitution, code generation, web shopping, travel planning; 11 extended) with isolated Docker containers, declared CPU/memory/time/network budgets, sealed test sets with SHA256 hashes, and a standardized profiling protocol. We profile 5 general-purpose baseline agents (ReAct, PlanAndSolve, Reflexion, CoT, Random) plus 4 task-specialized agents, finding that specialized agents achieve 100% success on 3/5 core tasks (fact_qa, web_shopping, travel_planning) and 66.7-83.3% on retail and code_gen, while general baselines fail entirely on 4/5 domain tasks. Crucially, we report the Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate (EASR) - success weighted by resource consumption relative to declared budgets - revealing that high accuracy at unbounded cost is not production-viable. We release the full infrastructure, sealed test sets, and profiling results to enable reproducible, resource-aware agent evaluation.

</details>


### [63] [Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00817)
*Tirtha Chanda,Christoph Wies,Franziska Schramm,Carina Nogueira Garcia,Nicolas B. Merl,Martin J. Hetz,Jochen S. Utikal,Phillip Tschandl,Cristian Navarrete-Dechent,Alexander Thiem,Jakob N. Kather,Consortium,Titus J. Brinker*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Source-linked LLM assistance (CORA) improves physician accuracy but creates asymmetry: citations strongly increase adoption of correct advice while dangerously reducing resistance to incorrect answers when they appear citation-supported.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate how source-linked evidence affects physician decision-making in clinical support systems, specifically whether displayed evidence guides or distorts physician reliance on LLM recommendations.

Method: Developed CORA, an agentic retrieval-augmented LLM system, and tested it in a study with 46 physicians, comparing unaided decisions vs. CORA-assisted decisions, analyzing the impact of supporting citations on answer adoption.

Result: Physician accuracy increased from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. Citations predicted correct answers (87.7% vs 65.5%). However, citations created dangerous asymmetry: when correct answers had citations, adoption increased from 34% to 76.9%, but when incorrect answers had citations, resistance dropped from 92% to 34.8%.

Conclusion: Source-linked LLM assistance can improve physician accuracy while introducing a grounding-dependent safety risk - citations powerfully influence physician trust but can dangerously reduce skepticism toward incorrect advice when it appears citation-supported.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) promise source-linked clinical support, but their value depends on whether displayed evidence guides rather than distorts physician reliance. We developed CORA, an agentic retrieval-augmented LLM, to investigate how source-linked assistance affects physician decision-making. CORA maintained benchmark performance and achieved larger gains on cases published after the models' training-data cutoffs. In a study of 46 physicians, accuracy increased from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. Supporting citations predicted correct answers (87.7% vs 65.5%), but citations created an important asymmetry: perceived support increased adoption of correct advice from 34% to 76.9% but when an incorrect LLM answer appeared citation-supported, physician resistance to it fell from 92% to 34.8%. These findings show that source-linked LLM assistance can improve physician accuracy while introducing a grounding-dependent safety risk.

</details>


### [64] [The Scaling Paradox in Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00818)
*Anyan Qi,Mengxin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI scaling benefits don't automatically translate to better human-AI system performance; accurate human perception of AI capabilities is crucial, with misperception potentially creating scaling paradoxes where better AI reduces overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While AI scaling laws show predictable capability improvements with scale, real-world AI typically operates in human-AI collaborative settings. The paper aims to understand whether and when AI scaling benefits translate to improved human-AI system performance, addressing the gap between isolated AI scaling and practical collaborative applications.

Method: Developed an analytical model to examine how AI scaling affects human-AI joint system performance. The model considers scenarios where humans have accurate perception of AI capabilities versus cases of over-perception and under-perception. Analyzed firm-level operational policies including cost internalization and perception alignment strategies.

Result: Human-AI system performance scales positively with AI scaling only when humans accurately perceive AI capabilities. Over-perception creates a scaling paradox where better AI reduces overall system performance and amplifies profit losses. Under-perception still allows performance improvement but at slower rates. Firms can mitigate distortions through operational policies, with effectiveness depending on deployment economics and misperception direction.

Conclusion: Organizations should prioritize managing human-AI interfaces over simply investing in larger AI systems. AI scaling should be viewed as both a technological and behavioral/operational challenge. The value of AI scaling depends on how increased AI capabilities shape human beliefs and collaborative efforts, not just technical capabilities alone.

Abstract: The discovery of scaling laws has highlighted the extraordinary potential of AI systems with a striking empirical pattern: as AI systems scale, their capabilities tend to improve predictably. Yet, in real-world applications, AI rarely operates in isolation; instead, it often works alongside humans, raising the question of whether these gains persist in human-AI collaboration. In this work, we develop an analytical model to examine when the empirical scaling benefits of AI translate into improved human-AI joint system performance. We demonstrate that the performance of a human-AI system can scale positively as the AI scales up-provided that humans have an accurate perception of the AI's capabilities. Human misperception, however, can fundamentally alter this relationship: i) when humans over-perceive the AI's capabilities, a scaling paradox may arise, in which greater AI scale reduces overall system performance and amplifies firm-level profit losses, and (ii) when humans under-perceive the AI's capabilities, performance still improves with scale but at a substantially slower rate. We further show that firms can actively manage these distortions through operational policies such as cost internalization and perception alignment, whose effectiveness depends on the economics of AI deployment and the direction of human misperception. These findings suggest that organizations may benefit more from managing the human-AI interface than from simply investing in larger, more expensive AI systems. More broadly, our results suggest that AI scaling should be viewed not only as a technological challenge, but also as a behavioral and operational one, and caution against the view that larger AI systems will automatically lead to better operational outcomes. Whether AI scaling creates value ultimately depends on how increased AI capabilities shape human beliefs and collaborative efforts.

</details>


### [65] [Isotropy Cliffs: The Geometric Signature of Decision-Making in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00828)
*Okan S. Coskun,Florian Rottach,Carsten Eickhoff,William Rudman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Analysis of decision-making in MCQA models reveals a critical transition layer where isotropy shifts, coinciding with representational changes and emergence of task-relevant clusters, strongly correlating with model accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the geometry of decision-making in Multiple Choice Question Answering models through the lens of isotropy, investigating how model representations evolve during decision processes.

Method: Analyzed five open-weight models across diverse datasets to identify decision-critical transition layers characterized by isotropy shifts, correlating these geometric behaviors with downstream accuracy metrics.

Result: Found synchronized geometric behavior strongly correlated with downstream accuracy (r≈0.84), showing decision-critical transition layers with isotropy shifts coinciding with major representational changes and emergence of task-relevant clusters. This transition is robust to prompt variations.

Conclusion: The isotropy shift in decision-critical transition layers represents a general mechanism of model behavior that strongly correlates with successful decision-making in MCQA tasks, suggesting geometric analysis provides valuable insights into model decision processes.

Abstract: We investigate the geometry of decision-making in Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA) through the lens of isotropy. Analyzing five open-weight models across diverse datasets, we identify decision-critical transition layers characterized by a shift in isotropy, coinciding with a major representational change and the emergence of task-relevant clusters. We demonstrate that this synchronized geometric behavior is strongly correlated with downstream accuracy ($r\approx0.84$), displaying its relevance for successful decision-making. Furthermore, we show that this transition is robust to prompt variations, suggesting that it reflects a general mechanism of model behavior.

</details>


### [66] [Similarity Weighted Aggregation with Global Differential Privacy for Federated Brain Lesion Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00872)
*Muhammad Irfan Khan,Eero Lehtonen,Joni Obradovic,Elina Kontio,Esa Alhoniemi,Suleiman A. Khan,Mojtaba Jafaritadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DP-SimAgg: Privacy-preserving federated learning framework combining similarity-weighted aggregation with differential privacy for brain tumor segmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FL enables collaborative training without sharing sensitive medical data, but faces challenges with heterogeneous data distributions across institutions and potential information leakage through model updates that need addressing.

Method: Integrates similarity-weighted aggregation with server-side differential privacy: applies L2 clipping to bound updates, computes similarity-based aggregation weights for non-IID data, and injects calibrated Gaussian noise at the central server for per-round privacy guarantees.

Result: Achieves Dice scores of 0.6357 (ET), 0.5305 (TC), 0.5274 (WT) with strict privacy budget (ε=1); approaches non-private baseline performance with relaxed budget (ε=10) while maintaining privacy protection.

Conclusion: DP-SimAgg demonstrates potential for enabling privacy-preserving collaborative learning in medical imaging by maintaining competitive segmentation performance while providing differential privacy guarantees.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across multiple institutions without sharing sensitive data, making it particularly suitable for medical imaging applications. However, heterogeneous data distributions across institutions and potential information leakage through model updates remain important challenges. In this work, we propose DP-SimAgg, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework that integrates similarity-weighted aggregation with a server-side differential privacy mechanism. The proposed method applies L2 clipping to bound collaborator updates, computes similarity-based aggregation weights to mitigate the effects of non-IID data distributions, and injects calibrated Gaussian noise at the central server, providing per-round privacy guarantees under the assumed sensitivity bound. The framework is implemented using Intel's OpenFL platform and evaluated on the FeTS 2022 dataset consisting of 1251 multi-modal MRI scans for brain tumor segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-SimAgg maintains competitive segmentation performance while providing privacy protection. Under a strict per-round privacy budget (epsilon = 1, cumulative epsilon_total = 20 over 20 rounds), the method achieves Dice scores of 0.6357, 0.5305, and 0.5274 for the enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), and whole tumor (WT) regions, respectively. With a more relaxed per-round budget (epsilon = 10, cumulative epsilon_total = 200), performance approaches that of the non-private baseline while incorporating a central Gaussian mechanism with per-round (epsilon, delta)-DP accounting under the assumed sensitivity bound. These results highlight the potential of DP-SimAgg for enabling privacy-preserving collaborative learning in medical imaging applications.

</details>


### [67] [Assuming You Knew: Fixing an Epistemic Semantics for Flow Policies Using Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00882)
*David A. Naumann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A corrected formalization of epistemic semantics for expressive flow policies was machine-checked using Rocq proof assistant with AI assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-level security requirements about information flow are difficult to formalize due to selective downgrading needs. Existing epistemic logic approaches lack robust general frameworks.

Method: Used Rocq proof assistant with AI coding assistance to correct and formally verify the epistemic semantics framework originally presented at CSF 2018.

Result: Successfully achieved a machine-checked corrected formalization of the unifying framework for relational annotations in expressive flow policies.

Conclusion: The corrected framework provides a simple, general approach that may help compare different policy specification styles and enable enforcement using existing techniques.

Abstract: Many high-level security requirements are about the allowed flow of information in programs and are difficult to make precise because they involve selective downgrading. Notions from epistemic logic have emerged as a good approach to policy semantics but a robust general framework remains elusive. A paper appearing in CSF 2018, entitled ``Assuming You Know: Epistemic Semantics of Relational Annotations for Expressive Flow Policies'', attempted to provide a unifying framework---but the formalization was sketchy and a correction was announced during the conference presentation. With aid from an agentic AI coding assistant, a corrected formalization has been machine checked in the Rocq proof assistant. The simplicity and generality of the framework may help compare different policy specification styles and enforce them by leveraging existing techniques.

</details>


### [68] [Neuro-Evolved Heuristics for Variable Gapped Common Subsequence Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00888)
*Marko Djukanović,Christian Blum,Aleksandar Kartelj,Saso Dzeroski,Ziga Zebec*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neuro-evolutionary approach learns data-driven heuristics to guide beam search for solving the multi-sequence Variable Gapped Longest Common Subsequence Problem, outperforming existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The multi-sequence Variable Gapped Longest Common Subsequence Problem (VGLCSP) is typically solved with beam search-based heuristics, but these hand-crafted designs lack robustness and effectiveness. There's a need for more robust, data-driven heuristics that can automatically adapt to problem characteristics.

Method: A learning-based approach where a neural network represents heuristics, with weights optimized by a genetic algorithm in a neuro-evolutionary framework. The learning alternates between weight optimization and evaluation within an iterative multi-source beam search procedure. The neural network learns to guide the search rather than constructing solutions directly. An ensemble heuristic combines learned scores with the best-performing hand-crafted heuristic.

Result: The proposed hybrid approach outperforms existing methods on both synthetic benchmark instances and newly introduced real-world instances with data-driven gap constraints. The integration into iterative multi-source beam search framework yields superior performance.

Conclusion: Learning-based heuristics for VGLCSP can effectively overcome limitations of hand-crafted designs, with neuro-evolutionary approaches providing robust, data-driven solutions that enhance search guidance and outperform existing methods across diverse instance types.

Abstract: This study addresses the Variable Gapped Longest Common Subsequence Problem (VGLCSP), a variant of the classical longest common subsequence problem with additional gap constraints and applications in sequence alignment and time-series analysis. While the two-sequence version has been widely studied using dynamic programming, the generalized multi-sequence form is usually solved with beam search-based heuristics, whose hand-crafted designs often lack robustness.
  To overcome this limitation, we propose a learning-based approach for automatically designing more effective data-driven heuristics. The heuristics are represented by a neural network with predefined architecture, whose weights are optimized by a genetic algorithm within a neuro-evolutionary framework. The learning process alternates between weight optimization and evaluation within an iterative multi-source beam search procedure, a state-of-the-art method for the problem. Rather than constructing solutions directly, the neural network learns to guide the search process, producing a neuro-evolved heuristic. We further introduce an ensemble heuristic that combines the scores of learned and the best-performing hand-crafted heuristic. Integrated into the iterative multi-source beam search framework, the resulting hybrid approach outperforms existing methods on both synthetic benchmark instances and newly introduced real-world instances with data-driven gap constraints.

</details>


### [69] [CADIR: A Cross-Backend Editable Intermediate Representation for Agentic CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00891)
*Yu Liu,Jingzhe Ni,Yiming Chen,Junqi Huang,Ruofeng Tong,Min Tang,Peng Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CADIR is an agent-friendly intermediate representation for CAD that enables cross-backend editing by recording construction history and using geometric signature matching for reliable topology identification across different CAD systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAD generation methods produce backend-specific sequential scripts or static geometry that don't preserve construction history, stable topological references, and feature-level editability across different CAD systems.

Method: CADIR builds on OCCT geometry kernel via OCP, providing explicit compositional modeling operations and fine-grained execution diagnostics. It records operations, dependencies, constraints, and topology selections in a construction graph. Geometric Signature Matching identifies corresponding edges/faces despite parameter changes and backend differences. Also introduces construction-graph retrieval for text/image queries.

Result: Extensive experiments show CADIR achieves higher geometric fidelity and execution reliability than existing CAD representations. Construction-graph retrieval improves model generation quality. Cross-backend editing enables reliable model reconstruction and post-reconstruction editing across FreeCAD, SolidWorks, and Fusion 360.

Conclusion: CADIR provides an effective intermediate representation that addresses key limitations in cross-CAD compatibility, enabling both generation and editing of CAD models while preserving construction history and editability across different CAD systems.

Abstract: Large language models have made it possible to generate executable computer-aided design (CAD) programs from natural-language descriptions or images. However, existing methods represent modeling processes as backend-specific sequential scripts with implicit dependencies or as static geometry, making it difficult to simultaneously preserve construction history, stable topological references, and feature-level editability across different CAD systems. We present CADIR, an agent-friendly executable intermediate representation for CAD generation and cross-backend editing. Built on the OCCT geometry kernel via OCP, CADIR provides explicit, compositional modeling operations and fine-grained execution diagnostics. During program execution, CADIR records modeling operations, parameter dependencies, constraints, and topology selections in a construction graph. To enable reliable cross-backend reconstruction, we introduce Geometric Signature Matching, which identifies corresponding edges and faces despite parameter changes and backend differences, allowing adapters to reconstruct native editable feature histories in FreeCAD, SolidWorks, and Fusion 360. Building on this representation, we further propose a construction-graph retrieval method for text and image queries that supports both full-graph and subgraph retrieval, enabling agents to leverage complete models and modeling substructures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CADIR achieves higher geometric fidelity and execution reliability than existing CAD representations, that construction-graph retrieval further improves model generation quality, and that cross-backend editing enables reliable model reconstruction and post-reconstruction editing across multiple CAD environments.

</details>


### [70] [Modeling Social Dynamics with an LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00929)
*Lynnette Hui Xian Ng,Kathleen M. Carley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents AuraSight, a large-scale social simulation using the GhostField LAND model to study how network interactions among 314K+ agents produce collective influence and coordination dynamics in a fictional song contest scenario.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how individual network and discourse interactions aggregate into collective influence, narrative dominance, and coordinated behavior in social systems.

Method: Used GhostField architecture (hybrid LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic model) to create AuraSight scenario with 314,244 heterogeneous cyber social agents and human actors exchanging 529,327 messages over 30 days about a fictional international song-writing contest.

Result: Simulations produce social dynamics where coordination and influence emerge not from individual agents but from recursive interactions between network topology and narrative exchange. Results analyzed across four layers: ego-network topology, semantic network evolution, coordination dynamics, and influence dynamics.

Conclusion: Social dynamics (including coordination and influence) emerge from the complex interplay between network structure and narrative exchange rather than from individual agent characteristics, demonstrating the value of large-scale hybrid simulations for studying collective social phenomena.

Abstract: Social dynamics encode the process in which individual network and discourse interactions aggregate into collective influence, narrative dominance and coordinate behavior. This paper uses the the GhostField architecture, a hybrid LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) model as a social simulation framework to build the AuraSight scenario. In the AuraSight scenario, 314,244 heterogeneous cyber social agents and human actors exchange 529,327 messages over 30 days surrounding a fictional international song-writing contest. We methodologically examine emergent social dynamics across four analytical layers: ego-network topology, semantic network evolution, coordination dynamics and influence dynamics. Our results show how generated social simulations do also produce social dynamics, and how the dynamics of coordination and influence emerge not from individual agents but from the recursive interaction between network topology and narrative exchange.

</details>


### [71] [PMMC: Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation for Long-Term LVLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00962)
*Jingyu Sun,Yan Lin,Yuyang Xue,Yifan Wang,Zhengtao Yao,Rui Qian,Zefeng Xu,Jiachen Li,Xianyang Liu,Jiancheng Pan,Jingyuan Sun,Syed Murtuza Baker,Hongpeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation: A framework that shifts memory reasoning from query time to consolidation time by predicting future questions, planning multimodal memory programs, and verifying evidence paths to create efficient question banks for long-term multimodal agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LVLM agent memory systems are inefficient and brittle - they reduce visual experiences to textual summaries or use static retrieve-then-reason pipelines that fail at image-text binding, temporal updates, and preserving visual details during long multimodal interactions.

Method: 1) Questioner predicts future question candidates from accumulated multimodal interactions. 2) Planner compiles question-conditioned multimodal memory programs. 3) Doubter verifies whether planned evidence paths can support predicted answers. Verified question-program pairs form a structured question bank for efficient query-time routing and evidence retrieval.

Result: Experiments on multimodal long-term memory benchmarks show improved answer quality and visual evidence recall while reducing query-time token and latency costs. Ablation studies analyze effects of self-feedback, dynamic planning, raw-image access, and question bank coverage.

Conclusion: Prospective memory compilation is effective for long-term multimodal agents, shifting reasoning to consolidation time improves efficiency and robustness, and the structured question bank approach outperforms traditional memory systems in both performance and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for LVLM agents to maintain consistency and integrate information across extended multimodal interactions. Existing agent memory systems, however, often reduce visual experiences into textual summaries or rely on static retrieve-then-reason pipelines, which are inefficient at query time and brittle when questions require image-text binding, temporal updates, or visual details. We propose Prospective Multimodal Memory Compilation, a framework that shifts part of the memory reasoning process from query time to memory consolidation time. Given accumulated multimodal interactions, a Questioner predicts future question candidates, a Planner compiles question-conditioned multimodal memory programs, and a Doubter verifies whether the planned evidence path can support the predicted answer. The verified question-program pairs form a structured question bank for efficient query-time routing and evidence retrieval. Experiments on multimodal long-term memory benchmarks show that our method improves answer quality and visual evidence recall while reducing query-time token and latency costs. Extensive ablations analyze the effects of self-feedback, dynamic planning, raw-image access, and question bank coverage.

</details>


### [72] [TrajWiki: Source-Grounded Memory Trajectories for Long-Horizon Dialogue Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00967)
*Jingyu Sun,Yuyang Xue,Mingyang Li,Zhengtao Yao,Jiachen Li,Yang Cui,Wenhao Cai,Haozhe Liu,Fangying Wang,Magdalene Katharina Montgomery,Syed Murtuza Baker,Hongpeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrajWiki is a trajectory-based memory framework for long-horizon conversational agents that represents memory as source-grounded evolution trajectories with immutable snapshots and operations, plus a Memory Wiki layer for structured compilation, improving dialogue performance and interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents lack robust external memory for long-horizon dialogue that is traceable, updatable, and diagnostically transparent. Existing memory-augmented agents store memories as isolated records or overwritable states, making it difficult to preserve how information originates, evolves, conflicts, or becomes obsolete over time.

Method: TrajWiki represents each memory as a source-grounded evolution trajectory with immutable episodic snapshots and claim-level operations (ADD, REVISE, DEPRECATE). It introduces Memory Wiki, a persistent intermediate layer that incrementally compiles dialogue history into structured, interlinked wiki pages capturing entities, events, quantities, topics, and conflicts. At inference, queries are routed hierarchically from relevant wiki pages to memory trajectories, then to source snapshots for evidence-grounded answer synthesis.

Result: Experiments on LoCoMo and MedMT datasets show TrajWiki improves long-horizon dialogue performance across both open-source and closed-source LLM backbones, while providing greater interpretability and diagnostic visibility into memory evolution, retrieval failures, and answer generation.

Conclusion: TrajWiki addresses key limitations in current memory-augmented agents by providing a trajectory-based memory framework that maintains information provenance and evolution while enabling structured retrieval, leading to better long-horizon dialogue performance and enhanced diagnostic transparency.

Abstract: Large language model agents have shown strong capabilities in generating coherent and contextually appropriate responses, yet robust long-horizon dialogue remains limited by the lack of external memory that is traceable, updatable, and diagnostically transparent. Existing memory-augmented agents often store memories as isolated records or overwritable states, making it difficult to preserve how information originates, evolves, conflicts, or becomes obsolete over time. We propose TrajWiki, a trajectory-based memory framework for long-horizon conversational agents. Instead of treating memory as static entries, TrajWiki represents each memory as a source-grounded evolution trajectory, maintained through immutable episodic snapshots and claim-level operations such as ADD, REVISE, and DEPRECATE. To reduce fragmentation and retrieval cost, TrajWiki further introduces Memory Wiki, a persistent intermediate layer that incrementally compiles dialogue history into structured and interlinked wiki pages capturing salient entities, events, quantities, topics, and conflicts. At inference time, queries are routed hierarchically from relevant wiki pages to linked memory trajectories, then to corresponding snapshots and source messages for evidence-grounded answer synthesis. Experiments on LoCoMo and MedMT show that TrajWiki improves long-horizon dialogue performance across both open-source and closed-source LLM backbones, while providing greater interpretability and diagnostic visibility into memory evolution, retrieval failures, and answer generation.

</details>


### [73] [PROGRESS: Coverage-guided RL to Train Search-augmented LLM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00969)
*Sudipta Paul,Vijay Srinivasan,Vivek Kulkarni,Aounon Kumar,Yashas Malur Saidutta,Wenbo Li,Srinivas Chappidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PROGRESS is a method that uses teacher-guided coverage rewards to explicitly supervise the decomposition of complex queries in search-augmented LLM agents, improving search behavior through lightweight RL training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-trained search-augmented LLM agents rely primarily on outcome-level rewards, which provide little supervision over search behavior and overlook the agent's ability to properly decompose complex queries into essential search queries.

Method: PROGRESS uses frozen teacher models to decompose complex queries into essential search queries, then utilizes these as teacher-guided coverage rewards to shape the policy model's query decomposition. This is integrated into an RL-style training framework to provide lightweight guidance without dense process-level supervision.

Result: Experiments show that coverage-guided RL improves overall task performance, demonstrating the importance of explicitly supervising search strategies in agentic LLMs.

Conclusion: Explicit supervision of search strategies through teacher-guided coverage rewards is crucial for improving the query decomposition capabilities of search-augmented LLM agents, and PROGRESS provides an effective lightweight approach to achieve this.

Abstract: Existing search-augmented LLM agents are trained using Reinforcement Learning to boost its reasoning capabilities. However, these approaches primarily rely on outcome-level rewards, which provide little supervision over search behavior and overlook agent's ability to decompose complex queries properly. To mitigate this issue, we propose PROGRESS which utilizes teacher-guided coverage reward to explicitly shape decomposed query generation of the policy model. During training, frozen teacher models are used to decompose complex queries into essential search queries. These essential search queries are utilized to guide the search behavior of the policy model. Integrated into an R1-style training framework, our approach provides lightweight guidance over query decomposition decisions without dense process-level supervision. Experiments show that coverage-guided RL improves overall task performance, highlighting the importance of explicitly supervising search strategies in agentic LLMs.

</details>


### [74] [Search-GRT: Guided Retrieval Training of Search Agents to Optimize for Complex Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00974)
*Aounon Kumar,Sudipta Paul,Vivek Kulkarni,Vijay Srinivasan,Srinivas Chappidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRT is a reinforcement learning method that uses ground truth information to guide retrieval during training, improving LLM search capabilities for multi-hop QA tasks by reducing sparse reward problems and enhancing learning signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with effective search engine use in complex multi-hop QA tasks, where poor early-stage retrieval causes cascading errors. Reinforcement learning helps but suffers from sparse rewards during training, limiting effective learning.

Method: Guided Retrieval Training (GRT) restricts the retrieval process during RL training using ground truth information, focusing on relevant documents to provide stronger learning signals and mitigate sparse reward problems.

Result: GRT achieves consistent improvements over existing methods like Search-R1 across QA tasks, with over 40% improvement in MHQA tasks. It also enhances training efficiency by achieving better performance with fewer training steps.

Conclusion: GRT effectively addresses the sparse reward problem in RL for LLM search agents by leveraging ground truth guidance during training, resulting in significant performance gains and improved efficiency for multi-hop question answering tasks.

Abstract: The effective use of search engines by large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge, particularly in complex, multi-hop question-answering (MHQA) tasks. These tasks require the model to decompose questions into subqueries, retrieve relevant information, and synthesize answers from multiple sources, often leading to cascading errors due to poor retrieval in early stages. Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in improving LLMs' search capabilities, but it often suffers from sparse rewards during training, hindering the model's ability to learn effectively. To address these challenges, we introduce Guided Retrieval Training (GRT), a novel method that improves the performance of a search agent by restricting the retrieval process during RL training using ground truth information. By focusing on a curated set of relevant documents, GRT provides the model with a stronger learning signal, mitigating the problem of sparse rewards and improving its ability to generate accurate subqueries and synthesize correct answers. Our experimental results demonstrate that GRT achieves consistent performance improvements over existing methods, such as Search-R1, across a wide range of question-answering (QA) tasks. Notably, GRT excels in MHQA tasks, achieving over 40% improvements in performance. Additionally, GRT enhances training efficiency by achieving better QA performance with fewer training steps.

</details>


### [75] [Passing Coarse Marginal Checks Can Be Cheap: Persona Mixtures and Imprecise Treatment-Response Estimates in an LLM Persona Panel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00979)
*Yohei Nakajima*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPT-4.1 personas were tested in repeated strategic games, meeting most preregistered criteria. Treatment effects showed modest continuation probability increases but wide confidence intervals. Prompt variations significantly influenced results, and some findings were compromised by statistical issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether lightweight persona-conditioned GPT-4.1 configurations can serve as synthetic research participants by evaluating their responses in repeated strategic games against human data benchmarks and examining how prompt variations affect behavior.

Method: Used a fixed panel of sixteen persona-conditioned GPT-4.1 configurations in repeated strategic games with preregistered criteria. Applied prompt-indexed variations and conducted sensitivity analyses with different uncertainty assumptions (Jeffreys alpha=0.5 and alpha=1). Tested wording-and-position operations and performed external review/reanalysis.
