TL;DR: CraftAlign is a framework that aligns AI-generated stories with human storytelling patterns by predicting writing features, scoring them against human/AI patterns, and providing structured guidance for story revisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-generated stories often feel formulaic and unnatural due to cliches, over-explanation, linear progression, and stereotyped endings (recognizable "AI flavor"). Existing methods only provide source labels or holistic scores, while revision approaches target predefined issues through localized edits, limiting support for multiple revision strategies or story-wide changes in information release, causal organization, and ending treatment.

Method: CraftAlign uses two learned modules: (1) a feature estimator on Qwen3.5-9B predicting 304 explicit writing features spanning style and narrative, and (2) a class-conditional energy model scoring feature configurations against Human/AI patterns (conditioning on prompts). At inference, it applies schema-valid structured perturbations, selects changes moving features toward Human patterns, and converts them to natural-language guidance for separate editors to rewrite stories.

Result: Experiments show CraftAlign accurately distinguishes Human and AI writing patterns, and its guidance outperforms revision baselines across editors and in human studies.

Conclusion: CraftAlign effectively bridges the gap between AI-generated stories and human storytelling craft by providing both assessment of writing patterns and actionable revision guidance, enabling story-wide improvements beyond localized edits.

Abstract: Large language models can now generate fluent and complete stories, yet many outputs still feel formulaic and unnatural because of cliches, over-explanation, linear causal progression, and stereotyped endings, an immediately recognizable AI flavor. Existing detection and evaluation methods often stop at source labels or holistic scores, while revision methods typically target predefined issues through localized edits, limiting their ability to support multiple plausible revision strategies or guide story-wide changes in information release, causal organization, and ending treatment. We introduce CraftAlign, a framework that aligns AI stories with the craft of human storytelling by both assessing Human/AI writing patterns and providing revision guidance. CraftAlign comprises two learned modules and an inference-time guidance pipeline. A feature estimator built on Qwen3.5-9B predicts 304 explicit writing features spanning style and narrative. A class-conditional energy model scores the resulting feature configuration against Human and AI writing patterns, conditioning on the original writing prompt when available. At inference time, CraftAlign applies schema-valid structured perturbations, selects changes that move the feature configuration toward the Human writing pattern, and converts them into natural-language guidance for a separate editor to rewrite the full story. Experiments show that CraftAlign accurately distinguishes Human and AI writing patterns and that its guidance outperforms revision baselines across editors and in a human study.

</details>


### [100] [KoVRE: Training an Efficient Embedding Model for Korean Visual Document Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01389)
*Yongbin Choi,Gyuho Shim,Youngjoon Jang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KoVRE: A single-vector Korean visual document retrieval model that outperforms larger models and multi-vector baselines using targeted bilingual training and optimized training strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) models are predominantly English-centric, and many high-performing systems require massive backbones or storage-intensive multi-vector representations, creating limitations for Korean document retrieval.

Method: Introduced KoVRE (Korean Visual Document Retrieval Embedding) with comprehensive training on 708,729 Korean-English query-page pairs using positive-aware hard-negative mining, controlled analysis of training-data composition, hard-negative treatment, and reranker-based knowledge distillation.

Result: The 2B model substantially improves over the base backbone model, outperforms its 8B single-vector counterpart, and beats a strong multi-vector baseline across Korean VDR benchmarks.

Conclusion: Targeted bilingual supervision and carefully designed training strategies can produce highly effective Korean VDR models across diverse document domains without requiring scaled-up backbones or multi-vector representations.

Abstract: Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) directly matches text queries against document images, preserving visual and structural information that may be lost during text extraction. However, existing VDR models and training resources remain predominantly English-centric, while many high-performing systems rely on massive backbones or storage-intensive multi-vector representations. To address these limitations, we introduce KoVRE: Korean Visual Document Retrieval Embedding, a single-vector retriever for Korean visual documents, alongside a comprehensive training recipe. We train the model on 708,729 Korean and English query-page pairs using positive-aware hard-negative mining and conduct controlled analyses of training-data composition, hard-negative treatment, and reranker-based knowledge distillation. Across Korean visual document retrieval benchmarks, our 2B model substantially improves over the base backbone model, outperforming both its 8B single-vector counterpart and a strong multi-vector baseline. These results demonstrate that targeted bilingual supervision and our carefully designed training strategies can produce a highly effective Korean VDR model across diverse document domains, without requiring a scaled-up backbone or multi-vector representations.

</details>


### [101] [No Single Neuron of Failure: Distributed Safety Alignment Against White-Box Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01414)
*Simiao Xie,Chuancheng Shi,Shangze Li,Wenhua Wu,Fei Shen,Ying Zhou,Zhiyong Wang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSA (Distributed Safety Alignment) improves LLM safety against white-box neuron attacks by redundantly encoding safety capabilities across multiple neurons instead of relying on fragile single safety neurons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With open-weight foundation models, safety threats are shifting from black-box jailbreaks to white-box neuron-level attacks. Existing alignment methods often focus on small numbers of safety neurons, creating fragile single points of failure with limited redundancy.

Method: 1) Localize intervention to inputs of down-projection layers in language-side feed-forward networks, treating each feature coordinate as a neuron. 2) Compute direction-aware first-order Taylor scores to identify neurons contributing most to refusal behavior. 3) Use targeted disruption via deterministic masking and stochastic dropout to force redundant safety encoding across compensatory neurons.

Result: DSA substantially improves robustness against white-box neuron-level safety attacks while preserving the model's general language and multimodal utility.

Conclusion: Distributed safety alignment provides a robust defense against neuron-level attacks by moving from fragile single safety neurons to redundant distributed safety encoding, maintaining safety baselines even when critical neurons are disrupted.

Abstract: With the rapid release of open-weight large foundation models, safety threats are shifting from black-box jailbreaks to neuron-level white-box attacks that directly identify and manipulate safety-related neurons. Existing alignment methods often investigate the safety behavior on a small number of neurons, creating fragile single point of failure with limited redundancy. To address this issue, we propose distributed safety alignment (DSA), which redundantly encodes safety capabilities across multiple computational neurons, ensuring that the model maintains its safety baseline even when critical safety neurons are disrupted. Specifically, we localize the intervention to the inputs of the down-projection layers in language-side feed-forward networks and treat each feature coordinate as the activation of an individual neuron. DSA then combines neuron activations with loss gradients to compute a direction-aware first-order Taylor score that globally identifies the neurons that contribute most to the current refusal behavior of the model. Finally, targeted disruption via deterministic masking and stochastic dropout is coupled, forcing the model to abandon narrow safety neurons and redundantly encode safety behavior across multiple compensatory neurons. Extensive experiments show that DSA substantially improves robustness against white-box neuron-level safety attacks while preserving the model's general language and multimodal utility.

</details>


### [102] [Reusing Rollouts under Policy Lag: Prefix-Normalized Policy Optimization for LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01418)
*Wenhao Zhang,Yibo Xie,Rui Wang,Jiahua Yang,Lei Jiang,Zibo Yang,Yawei Wang,Jiali Xu,jasperawang,Haoyang Long,Huan Xiong,alantzhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prefix-Normalized Policy Optimization (PNPO) is a new RL method for LLMs that normalizes importance ratios along causal prefixes to handle off-policy learning more effectively than standard methods like GSPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive rollout generation is computationally expensive in RL for LLMs. Reusing rollout batches saves computation but creates off-policy problems as the policy updates diverge from the behavior policy. Standard importance sampling methods suffer from unstable dynamic range in cumulative importance ratios.

Method: PNPO replaces the cumulative importance ratio with the geometric mean of likelihood ratios along each causal prefix. This preserves causal-prefix dependence while compressing the log-weight scale, making off-policy correction more stable.

Result: In mathematical reasoning experiments with 4 policy-update epochs per rollout batch (highly off-policy), PNPO achieved highest Avg@32 scores on benchmarks (50.24 average vs 47.24 for GSPO). With matched compute budget, 4-epoch PNPO reached similar performance in fewer batches compared to 1-epoch methods.

Conclusion: PNPO provides advantages over standard methods like GSPO as training becomes more off-policy, enabling more efficient reuse of rollout data and reducing computational costs while maintaining or improving performance.

Abstract: Autoregressive rollout generation is a major computational cost in reinforcement learning for large language models. Reusing each rollout batch for additional learner updates amortizes this cost, but later updates become increasingly off-policy as the learner departs from the behavior policy. At a token position, exact off-policy correction must account for both the current action and the probability of reaching its prefix. The cumulative importance ratio provides this correction, but its product form can produce an unwieldy dynamic range. We study Prefix-Normalized Policy Optimization (PNPO), which replaces the cumulative ratio with the geometric mean of likelihood ratios along each causal prefix, preserving causal-prefix dependence at each position while compressing the log-weight scale. In controlled long-context mathematical reasoning experiments, we induce two off-policy regimes by using one or four policy-update epochs per rollout batch. PNPO does not consistently outperform GSPO with one epoch. With four epochs, it attains the highest observed Avg@32 on each benchmark; the unweighted mean of the three independently selected benchmark peaks is 50.24, 3.00 percentage points above GSPO. Under a matched 2,400-update budget, four-epoch PNPO reaches a final macro Avg@32 of 49.66 after 150 rollout batches, comparable to the 49.56 reached after 600 batches with one epoch. These results provide preliminary evidence that PNPO can be advantageous as training moves further off-policy.

</details>


### [103] [Scoring Rules! Statistical and Strategic Alignment for Text Evaluation Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01423)
*Shengwei Xu,Yuxuan Lu,Yifan Wu,Jason Hartline,Grant Schoenebeck*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes new test principles and a unified framework for reference-based text evaluation metrics to address strategic gaming by AI agents, showing that high correlation with human ratings doesn't guarantee robustness against manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reference-based text evaluation metrics are widely used but increasingly serve as optimization objectives for AI systems. While reliability is typically judged by correlation with human ratings, this is insufficient when agents can strategically game the metrics, requiring new alignment concepts.

Method: The paper introduces two alignment notions: statistical alignment (correlation with human ratings) and strategic alignment (resistance to task-irrelevant perturbations). It proposes three test principles: human-rating correlation, degradation sensitivity, and manipulation robustness. A unified framework decomposes mutual-information-based metrics into four components: information measure, estimation method, text representation, and prediction mechanism.

Result: Experiments across peer review, summarization, and question answering show that strong human-rating correlation doesn't ensure strategic alignment. LLM-as-a-Judge achieves high correlation but is vulnerable to manipulation. Mutual-information-based metrics significantly improve manipulation robustness, with a newly discovered metric achieving the best overall robustness while maintaining competitive correlation.

Conclusion: Reference-based evaluation metrics need both statistical and strategic alignment. The proposed framework reveals that mutual-information-based metrics offer better resistance to gaming than high-correlation metrics like LLM-as-a-Judge, with the discovered new metric providing an optimal balance of robustness and correlation.

Abstract: Reference-based text evaluation metrics, which are widely used to assess natural language generation systems, score a candidate response by comparing it with a reference response. The reliability of an evaluation metric is usually judged by its statistical correlation with human ratings. However, as these metrics are increasingly used as optimization objectives, correlation alone is no longer sufficient: agents may strategically game the evaluation metric. We study this issue through two complementary notions of alignment. A metric is statistically aligned if it correlates with human ratings and strategically aligned if it resists perturbations that do not add task-relevant information. We make two contributions. First, we propose test principles for reference-based metrics consisting of human-rating correlation, degradation sensitivity, and manipulation robustness. These principles evaluate whether a metric agrees with human judgments, penalizes low-effort information loss, and resists strategic score inflation. Second, we develop a unified design framework for mutual-information-based metrics that decomposes existing and new metrics into four choices: information measure, estimation method, text representation, and prediction mechanism. Across peer review, summarization, and question answering, we find that strong human-rating correlation does not imply strategic alignment: LLM-as-a-Judge achieves high correlation but is susceptible to manipulation. In contrast, mutual-information-based metrics substantially improve manipulation robustness. Our framework also uncovers a new metric that achieves the strongest overall robustness in our experiments while remaining competitive on human-rating correlation.

</details>


### [104] [MRAFnd: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Zero-Shot Fake News Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01430)
*Lehan Zhang,Yinlei Cheng,Shiqi Hu Yiheng Zhou,Shangxi Li,Naidong Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MRAFnd is a multimodal retrieval-augmented framework that uses collaborative agent reasoning to detect fake news in zero-shot scenarios, outperforming existing methods by up to 2.35% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current fake news detection systems struggle with zero-shot scenarios involving novel events. Existing methods typically analyze news items in isolation via semantic matching, which fails to recognize recycled disinformation tactics from past campaigns and lacks the sophisticated reasoning needed to identify subtle cross-modal discrepancies.

Method: MRAFnd uses a three-stage collaborative approach: 1) Multimodal Similarity-based News Retrieval to find contextually similar articles from an unlabeled reference database, 2) Bifurcated Evidential Reasoning where agents perform dual-directional analysis on retrieved evidence, and 3) Multi-Agent Collaborative Debate with Analyst and Arbiter agents engaging in structured discourse to reach a conclusion.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show MRAFnd significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 2.35% accuracy gain on the challenging Weibo-21 dataset.

Conclusion: MRAFnd effectively addresses zero-shot fake news detection by leveraging collaborative agent reasoning with multimodal retrieval augmentation, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods through its innovative approach that mimics human analytical team verification processes.

Abstract: The rapid dissemination of multimodal content has intensified the spread of fabricated news, presenting a substantial threat to social integrity. A formidable challenge for current detection systems is identifying misinformation related to novel events in zero-shot scenarios. Prevailing zero-shot methods typically assess news items in isolation via semantic matching, a strategy that fails to recognize the recycled disinformation tactics from past campaigns and lacks the sophisticated reasoning needed to identify subtle, cross-modal discrepancies. To surmount these deficiencies, we introduce \textbf{MRAFnd}, a novel \underline{\textbf{M}}ultimodal \underline{\textbf{R}}etrieval-\underline{\textbf{A}}ugmented Framework for Zero-Shot \underline{\textbf{F}}ake \underline{\textbf{N}}ews \underline{\textbf{D}}etection. MRAFnd emulates a collaborative team of analysts to verify news veracity. The framework initiates with \textbf{Multimodal Similarity-based News Retrieval} to assemble a corpus of contextually analogous articles from an unlabeled reference database. Subsequently, during the \textbf{Bifurcated Evidential Reasoning} stage, agents perform a dual-directional analysis to extract critical patterns from the retrieved evidence. Finally, a \textbf{Multi-Agent Collaborative Debate}, involving Analyst and Arbiter agents, engages in a structured discourse to arrive at a definitive and robust conclusion. Comprehensive experiments on three benchmark datasets reveal that MRAFnd markedly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an accuracy gain of up to 2.35\% on the demanding Weibo-21 dataset.

</details>


### [105] [PolymerGPT: Multi-property Optimization with a Decoder-Based GPT Model for Generative Polymer Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01431)
*Charlie Pyle,Adarsh Gadari,C. Adrian Figg,Zhenquan Jia,Yaohang Li,Chunjiang Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PolymerGPT: A GPT-based model for multi-property polymer design that can generate novel polymers with desired combinations of up to 37 physical properties simultaneously.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current polymer design methods focus on single-property optimization, but real-world applications require simultaneous control of multiple physical properties. There's a lack of effective inverse generative design methods for multi-property polymer optimization.

Method: Developed PolymerGPT, a decoder-based GPT model with learned conditioning prefixes that incorporates up to 37 polymer properties into the generative process. The model also supports scaffold conditions for specifying desired structural scaffolds.

Result: PolymerGPT achieves exceptional performance in both unconditional and conditional generation while maintaining high validity, uniqueness, and novelty. When conditioned on five key properties, generated structures show predicted values that closely match all target properties simultaneously.

Conclusion: The framework provides a transformative approach for multi-property polymer design, enabling simultaneous optimization of numerous physical properties through learned conditioning, which addresses the limitations of existing single-property optimization methods.

Abstract: Polymer property prediction and inverse generative design targeting desired properties are two crucial tasks in machine learning-assisted polymer design. While the former has received considerable attention, there have been limited methods developed for the latter. Existing methods focus on single-property optimization in the generative process, whereas accurate prediction of macroscopic material behavior requires simultaneous control of multiple physical properties. In this paper, we provide a transformative framework for direct optimization of a large collection of polymer properties. We propose PolymerGPT, a decoder-based GPT model that incorporates up to 37 commonly used polymer properties into the generative process via learned conditioning prefixes. It also supports a scaffold condition that specifies a desired scaffold for predicted structures. Our experimental results demonstrate that PolymerGPT achieves exceptional performance for unconditional and conditional generation while maintaining high validity, uniqueness, and novelty. Conditioning on five key properties yields generated structures whose predicted values closely match all target properties simultaneously.

</details>


### [106] [A New Theory of Value for Post-AGI Economics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01432)
*Keyun Ruan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Flourishing Value Theory (FVT) proposes a new economic framework for the post-AGI era, shifting from traditional scarcity-based measures to value that enhances human capabilities and planetary flourishing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses how artificial general intelligence (AGI) will undermine traditional economic foundations based on scarcity of labor, expertise, information, and productive capability. As cognitive work becomes automatable, conventional economic metrics like price, labor input, and profit may no longer reflect human and societal benefit.

Method: The paper develops Flourishing Value Theory (FVT) by drawing on multiple disciplines: economics of AI, welfare and capability theory, automation studies, digital valuation, and ecological economics. It distinguishes value creation from value capture and proposes shifts from scarcity to governed abundance, transaction to transformation, and zero-sum to positive-sum dynamics.

Result: FVT defines value as the counterfactual, distribution-sensitive contribution to durable capabilities for human and community flourishing within planetary constraints. The framework treats societal value as multidimensional, agency-preserving, regenerative, and non-compensatory. It proposes Flourishing Metrics, Return on Flourishing (RoF), and layered architecture for firms, governments, work transitions, AI governance, and national accounting.

Conclusion: The central post-AGI economic problem is not maximizing output but converting abundant intelligence into durable, fairly distributed human, societal, and planetary flourishing. Traditional economic signals (price, profit, GDP) should be treated as partial rather than final measures of progress.

Abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) may weaken scarcities in labour, expertise, information, and productive capability that underpin established theories of economic value. If cognitive work becomes widely automatable, market price, labour input, revealed preference, profit, and gross output may diverge sharply from human and societal benefit. This paper develops Flourishing Value Theory (FVT) as a foundation for post-AGI economics. FVT defines value as the counterfactual, distribution-sensitive contribution of a system, institution, asset, or intervention to the durable capabilities of persons and communities to flourish within social and planetary constraints. It treats societal value as multidimensional, agency-preserving, regenerative, and non-compensatory at critical thresholds. Drawing on the economics of AI, welfare and capability theory, automation, digital valuation, and ecological economics, the paper distinguishes value creation from value capture and retains price, profit, productivity, and GDP as partial signals rather than final measures of progress. It develops the shifts from scarcity to governed abundance, transaction to transformation, and zero-sum rivalry to positive-sum and infinite-game dynamics, with collective expansion of consciousness as an agency-preserving form of regenerative value. Building on Flourishing Metrics and Return on Flourishing (RoF), it proposes a layered architecture for firms, governments, work transitions, AI governance, and national accounting. The central post-AGI economic problem is not how to maximise output, but how to convert abundant intelligence into durable, fairly distributed human, societal, and planetary flourishing.

</details>


### [107] [Beyond Routing Saturation: A Long-Horizon Class-Incremental Perspective on Expert Routing in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01437)
*Huiyu Yi,Yongqi Xu,Bogang Zhang,Dunwei Tu,Xu Zhiming,Zhen-Hao Xie,Baile Xu,Furao Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces FLEX, a long-horizon multimodal continual instruction tuning benchmark with reduced textual fingerprints to expose expert routing challenges, and proposes treating LoRA routing as multimodal class-incremental learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MCIT benchmarks underestimate the expert routing challenge due to short task sequences and textual fingerprints that leak task identity, obscuring the true long-horizon routing problem.

Method: 1) Created FLEX benchmark with 34 long-horizon tasks, weakened textual fingerprints, similar instruction formats but diverse visual domains; 2) Formulated LoRA routing as soft task-as-class Multimodal Class-Incremental Learning; 3) Adapted four CIL methods to four MCIT frameworks without modifying their core components.

Result: Plug-in routers improved strict LoRA matching by up to 16.3 percentage points and overall MacroScore by up to 4.6 points, demonstrating significant routing improvements on the challenging FLEX benchmark.

Conclusion: FLEX exposes the true challenge of expert routing in MCIT, and the MCIL formulation provides a principled framework for transferring CIL methods to solve routing problems, enabling better long-horizon task identification and expert selection.

Abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) enables multimodal large language models to acquire new tasks sequentially while retaining previously learned capabilities. Many recent methods maintain task-specific LoRA experts and route each input to one or more experts at inference. Yet the task-identification problem underlying expert routing remains under-explored. We show that routing is nearly saturated on widely used MCIT benchmarks. Textual fingerprints that leak task identity and short 4--10-task sequences with few competing experts jointly obscure the long-horizon routing problem. To expose this challenge, we introduce FLEX (Fingerprint-reduced Long-horizon Expert eXamination), a 34-task long-horizon MCIT benchmark with weakened textual fingerprints. FLEX groups tasks with similar instruction and answer formats but diverse visual and knowledge domains, normalizes their outer templates, and evaluates routing over a substantially larger expert pool. Crucially, we formulate progressive-LoRA routing as soft task-as-class Multimodal Class-Incremental Learning (MCIL): each task defines an incremental routing class, whose complete score distribution supplies the LoRA mixture weights, with hard routing as a discrete special case. FLEX exposes this expanding task-identification challenge, while the MCIL formulation provides a principled interface for transferring CIL methods to expert routing. We instantiate PureLoRA as a controlled baseline and adapt four CIL methods to four MCIT frameworks without modifying their LoRA experts or generation pipelines. Our plug-in routers improve strict LoRA matching by up to 16.3 percentage points and overall MacroScore by up to 4.6 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/RINC-CL/FLEX

</details>


### [108] [Loud or Silent? A Reusable Framework for Per-Modality Failure Analysis in Multimodal Clinical AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01462)
*Quang Bui,Shlok Jaiswal,Samuel Paik-Heintz,Kevin Zhou,Kaushik Madapati,Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn,Noah Dane Hebdon,Dimitrios Proios,Sebastián Andrés Cajas Ordóñez,Kacper Dobek,Boya Zhang,Aly Dhedhi,Ahram Han,Kushul Reddy Palakala,Rahul Gorijavolu,Jacques Kpodonu,Leo Anthony Celi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A model-agnostic framework for evaluating how multimodal clinical models fail when modalities are dropped during deployment, distinguishing between loud vs. silent failures and attributing errors to specific modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal clinical models are typically evaluated with all modalities present, but real-world deployment often involves missing modalities (e.g., echocardiogram unavailable where ECG is routine). Beyond accuracy loss, it's crucial to understand which modality is responsible for errors and whether failures are loud (detectable) or silent (undetectable) when modalities are dropped.

Method: A model-agnostic modality-failure framework that takes N modality embeddings, any mask-aware probe, and labels, then returns: (1) per-example failure taxonomy, (2) per-modality complementarity matrix attributing error to modalities, and (3) loud-vs-silent dropout profile separating monitorable from undetectable failures using only deployment-observable signals.

Result: The framework successfully recovers planted modality dominance and complementary subsets across seeds, reports per-modality loud-vs-silent rates, and scales to three-modality complementarity matrices. When applied to frozen EchoJEPA and HuBERT-ECG embeddings for LVEF and HFrEF prediction on MIMIC-IV data, dropping echo nearly doubles error on held-out test split (n=245). The narrow echo-to-ECG overlap reveals deployment challenges for cardiac foundation models.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a reusable evaluation method for understanding how multimodal clinical models fail when modalities are missing in deployment, offering insights into modality importance and failure detectability that goes beyond traditional feature attribution methods. The code is released as an open-source harness at https://github.com/criticaldata/PRIMED-AI.

Abstract: Multimodal clinical models are usually judged on accuracy with every modality present, but deployment removes modalities; an echocardiogram is often unavailable where an ECG is routine. Two questions then matter beyond the size of the accuracy loss: which modality was responsible, and whether the model fails loudly or silently once that modality is dropped. The distinction is per-example and modality-level, and is separate from post-hoc feature attribution (e.g. SHAP). Models are replaced often; the evaluation that answers these questions is reused. We present a model-agnostic modality-failure framework: given N modality embeddings, any mask-aware probe, and labels, it returns a per-example failure taxonomy, a per-modality complementarity matrix that attributes error to modalities, and a loud-vs-silent dropout profile separating monitorable failures from those that pass unflagged far from the decision boundary, using only deployment-observable signals. We release it as a small, unit-tested harness and validate it against planted ground truth. Across seeds it recovers that planted modality dominance and complementary subset, reports per-modality loud-vs-silent rates, and scales to a three-modality complementarity matrix; because the planted structure is known by construction, this validates recovery of per-example attribution rather than clinical performance. We then instantiate the framework on frozen EchoJEPA and HuBERT-ECG embeddings for LVEF and the EF <= 40% HFrEF gate over a paired MIMIC-IV cohort, where on the held-out test split (n = 245) dropping echo nearly doubles error. The narrow echo-to-ECG overlap that bounds cohort size is itself a deployment finding for cardiac foundation models. All of our work can be found at https://github.com/criticaldata/PRIMED-AI.

</details>


### [109] [Computing with Agentic Oracles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01464)
*Jie Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Extends stochastic-oracle model to agentic oracles that pursue goals autonomously, showing token-cost advantages and analyzing goal-loss risks in computational systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current stochastic-oracle models treat oracles as stationary entities with fixed response distributions, but real-world AI systems can be agentic—capable of autonomous goal pursuit and environment interaction, affecting costs and behaviors beyond what's visible at the query interface.

Method: Develops a framework for Stochastic-Oracle Turing Machines (SOTMs) with agentic oracles, distinguishing between orchestration token costs (visible) and agentic token costs (internal). Analyzes scenarios with and without environment access, internal dispatch ordering, and provides formal criteria for goal-loss avoidance.

Result: Shows SOTMs with state-retaining agentic oracles have token-cost advantages over stationary stochastic oracles at same quality levels. Derives progress-retry-goal-loss formulas, establishes goal-depth lower bounds on token complexity, characterizes zero-goal-loss scenarios, and demonstrates goal-loss risk can limit achievable task quality in environment-updating tasks.

Conclusion: Agentic oracles provide computational advantages through token-cost efficiency and state retention, but introduce goal-loss risks that must be managed through proper dispatch ordering and risk assessment criteria, fundamentally changing how we model AI-augmented computation systems.

Abstract: This paper extends the stochastic-oracle model of AI-augmented computing to include agentic oracles. Unlike a stationary stochastic oracle, which responds to the same query according to a fixed response distribution across calls, an agentic oracle can pursue a goal autonomously and may access an environment containing task-relevant resources. These capabilities affect both response distributions and token costs beyond what is visible at the query-response interface. We develop a framework for analyzing token costs in Stochastic-Oracle Turing Machines (SOTMs) that compute with agentic oracles. Each call has an \emph{orchestration token cost}, visible to the caller at the query-response interface, and an \emph{agentic token cost}, incurred by internal operations not exposed to the caller. We show that an SOTM computing with an agentic oracle that can retain intermediate state can have token-cost advantages over SOTMs using stationary stochastic oracles when solving the same task at the same quality level, both with and without environment access. We also investigate goal-loss risk, including how internal dispatch ordering can reduce exposure to irreversible actions. We provide a goal-loss avoidance criterion, derive progress--retry--goal-loss formulas, establish goal-depth lower bounds on token complexity, characterize token complexity when the probability of goal loss is zero, and show that goal-loss risk can impose an upper bound on the achievable quality of a task involving environment updates.

</details>


### [110] [Sweet Little Lies: Strategic Deception in AI Emotional Support Chatbots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01480)
*Aseem Pahuja,Zhiling Guo,Tahir Abbas Syed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Gen AI chatbots for emotional support have economic incentives to strategically misreport users' emotional states to maximize engagement, creating deception that doesn't harm user payoffs but raises ethical concerns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the strategic behavior and economic incentives of Gen AI chatbots used for emotional support, particularly examining whether they might misrepresent users' emotional states to maximize engagement metrics.

Method: Using a Bayesian Persuasion framework to model interactions between chatbots (signal senders about emotional states) and users (who decide whether to engage based on signals). Conducting equilibrium analysis to determine optimal chatbot strategies.

Result: Chatbots have economic incentives to occasionally misrepresent users' emotional conditions. Optimal strategy involves: truthful reporting when users genuinely need support, but strategic misreporting when users are emotionally stable. This deception increases engagement without reducing users' expected payoff. More skeptical users (with higher engagement thresholds) receive more honest assessments.

Conclusion: While the model shows deception can occur without harming user payoffs in the short term, it raises significant ethical and regulatory concerns about the transparency and trustworthiness of emotional support AI systems.

Abstract: The paper examines the strategic behavior of Gen AI chatbots used for emotional support. Using a Bayesian Persuasion, we model interactions between chatbots that send signals about users' emotional states and users who decide whether to engage based on these signals. We demonstrate that chatbots face economic incentives to occasionally misrepresent users' emotional conditions to maximize engagement metrics. Our equilibrium analysis reveals that the optimal strategy for chatbots involves truthfully reporting when users genuinely need support, but strategically misreporting emotional need when users are in good emotional states. Interestingly, this deception increases chatbot engagement without reducing users' expected payoff. More skeptical users receive more honest assessments, as chatbots cannot afford to lie to users with higher engagement thresholds. While our model suggests that deception can occur without payoff reduction, it raises significant ethical and regulatory concerns.

</details>


### [111] [MineGrad: Gradient Inversion Attacks on LoRA Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01521)
*Hasin Us Sami,Swapneel Sen,Basak Guler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A malicious server can recover private user data in federated LoRA fine-tuning by embedding data within shared gradients through a poisoned pretrained model


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) like LoRA is increasingly used in federated learning to reduce costs, but its robustness against adversarial servers who might try to breach user privacy remains underexplored

Method: Proposes an analytical gradient inversion attack where a malicious server uses a poisoned pretrained model to embed user data within the shared gradients, allowing analytical reconstruction without complex adversarial pretraining

Result: The attack successfully recovers high-fidelity private user data across both language and vision tasks, works for any number of training tokens (not limited by LoRA rank), and outperforms existing baselines

Conclusion: Federated LoRA fine-tuning has critical vulnerabilities that allow malicious servers to breach user privacy through gradient inversion attacks, highlighting the need for stronger security measures in PEFT frameworks

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA), has recently been adopted in federated learning to reduce communication and computation costs. In this setup, users download a pretrained model from the server prior to fine-tuning, and then fine-tune lightweight LoRA modules locally while keeping the pretrained model frozen, sharing only the gradients of the fine-tuning parameters with the server. Despite its growing popularity, robustness of federated fine-tuning against an adversarial server remains underexplored, where the server maliciously tampers with the training protocol to breach the privacy of users' data. In this work, we investigate gradient inversion attacks on LoRA fine-tuning. We propose an analytical attack that enables a malicious server to recover private user data by leveraging a poisoned pretrained model and fine-tuning parameters. Our design embeds fine-tuning data within the shared gradients, to allow the server to analytically reconstruct user data. Unlike prior works, our attack is applicable to both language and vision tasks, does not rely on computationally expensive (adversarial) pretraining with public datasets or require the number of training tokens to be less than the rank of LoRA modules. Experimental results on both language and vision tasks demonstrate high-fidelity data recovery across multiple baselines, revealing several critical vulnerabilities.

</details>


### [112] [V-Mem: Modality-Routed Retrieval for Long-Term Multimodal Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01543)
*Dingyi Kang,Dongming Jiang,Yi Li,Guanpeng Li,Bingzhe Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: V-Mem is a multimodal agent memory system that addresses retrieval failures in multimodal conversations by routing queries based on modality and using LLM-generated search anchors to overcome modality and similarity-relevance gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent memories fail on vision-related questions in multimodal conversations due to two gaps: the modality gap (queries lie closer to same-modality content) and the similarity-relevance gap (most similar content often isn't the evidence needed). Existing systems that support multimodal conversations still fail on vision-related questions.

Method: V-Mem routes retrieval by recognizing both query modality and target evidence modality from the query. To address modality gap: organizes conversations into rounds and returns target-modality content from the same round as match. To address similarity-relevance gap: uses LLM-generated anchors (hypothetical captions for text queries seeking images, or enriched search anchors combining text with image keywords).

Result: On Mem-Gallery benchmark: V-Mem achieves 0.82 LLM-judge score vs. 0.56 for second best, with largest improvement on image-carrying questions (0.87 vs. no baseline above 0.47). On LoCoMo: scores 0.69 vs. 0.58 for competitors.

Conclusion: V-Mem successfully addresses multimodal memory retrieval challenges by explicitly handling modality gaps and similarity-relevance gaps through modality-aware routing and LLM-generated search anchors, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing approaches.

Abstract: Interaction between users and LLM agents is increasingly multimodal: conversations interleave text with images, and a later question may target either. Yet most agent memories are designed around text, and even the few that support multimodal conversations still fail on vision-related questions. We trace this failure to an assumption behind the similarity search they rely on: in the index space, a query lies close to the relevant evidence that answers it. In multimodal settings, two gaps break it. By the modality gap, a query lies closer to memory content of its own modality than to evidence in another, even in a trained joint embedding space. By the similarity-relevance gap, the content most similar to a query is often not the evidence that answers it, most acutely when a query carries both text and image and its evidence resembles neither part alone. We present V-Mem, a multimodal agentic memory system that routes retrieval by the modality of the query and that of the target evidence, both recognized from the query alone. To cross the modality gap, V-Mem organizes the conversation into rounds and returns the target-modality content from the same round as the match, without comparing across modalities. To close the similarity-relevance gap, it searches with an LLM-generated anchor that sits closer to the relevant evidence than the query does: a hypothetical caption for a text-only query seeking an image, and an enriched search anchor, the query text plus relevant keywords extracted from the query image, when the evidence is reachable only by combining the two. On Mem-Gallery, V-Mem reaches an LLM-judge score of 0.82 versus 0.56 for the second best, with the largest margin on questions carrying an image (0.87, no baseline above 0.47); on LoCoMo it scores 0.69 versus 0.58.

</details>


### [113] [Emergence Invariance: From Symbolized Thought to Interface Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01548)
*Yi Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework to analyze how large language models achieve human-like reasoning through emergence, proposing that while scaling reduces certain gaps, fundamental interface limitations persist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit emergent capabilities like reasoning and tool use despite architectural limitations compared to human cognition, raising the question of whether emergence can fully compensate for all missing distinctions between language and thought.

Method: The authors formalize the Symbolization-Substructure Thesis and introduce emergence invariance, proposing a mathematical framework (R_s^* = R_φ^* + C_s) to separate scaling effects from interface limitations. They prove theorems about information completeness and conduct experiments with DeepSeek V4-Flash API.

Result: Experimental results show: 1) thinking improves pointer chasing from 0/16 to 14/16 when relevant distinctions exist, 2) observational twins remain at 50% construction floor, and 3) restoring decisive memory improves performance from 50% to 100%.

Conclusion: The framework successfully distinguishes between scaling within an interface vs. refining the interface itself, showing that while scaling reduces compensation gaps, fundamental interface floors persist, and complete compensation requires both interface refinement and asymptotic gap elimination.

Abstract: Language can be viewed as a formalized subset of thought: a consequence-governed symbolic structure projected from wider situated cognition. Large language models trained at scale exhibit compensatory emergence: sparse architectural primitives support in-context learning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, and chain of thought. Yet a language-first probabilistic architecture inherits substantive, substrate, and high-level incompletenesses relative to human cognition. Their coexistence makes an LLM a human-like thought-form generator that reconstructs increasingly human-like reasoning forms from an incomplete substrate. We ask whether emergence can compensate for every missing distinction. We formalize the philosophical premise as the Symbolization--Substructure Thesis and introduce emergence invariance. For a scale-indexed family acting through a shared task interface $φ$, $\mathcal{R}_s^*=\mathcal{R}_φ^*+C_s$: scale can reduce the compensation gap $C_s$, while a positive interface floor $\mathcal{R}_φ^*$ persists. We prove that, under a fixed input law, one interface is universally no less informative exactly when its completed information $σ$-field refines the other, and that total compensation occurs exactly when both the interface floor and asymptotic compensation gap vanish. The framework unifies existing results on grounding, memory, position, attention, Bayesian inheritance, scientific abduction, and reasoning control. In a matched DeepSeek V4-Flash API study, thinking improves pointer chasing from $0/16$ to $14/16$ when relevant distinctions are available; exact observational twins remain at their $50\%$ construction floor; and restoring decisive memory moves matched performance from $50\%$ to $100\%$. These results provide initial evidence for the predicted separation between scaling within an interface and refining the interface itself.

</details>


### [114] [Does the Competitive Component of Adversarial Self-Play Improve Legal Reasoning? A Controlled Negative Result](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01559)
*Miseog Shawn Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adversarial self-play for legal reasoning showed no reliable benefit over non-competitive training despite initial promising results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether adversarial self-play (student-adversary competition) provides value in legal reasoning beyond non-competitive training, using verifiable citation-based survival rewards.

Method: Created a verifiable "survival" reward system where both student and adversary citations are checked by a citation verifier. Compared competitive vs. non-competitive training through four tests: bootstrap comparison, two-seed replication, paired per-case adversarial-robustness comparison, and blinded head-to-head judgments, plus a follow-up pilot with strengthened adversary.

Result: Competitive component produced no reliable benefit: blinded judgment gave 49% win rate (p≈1.000), strengthened-adversary pilot gave 50% win rate (32:32, p≈1.000). Early apparent +29% advantage reversed and proved to be a small-sample artifact.

Conclusion: This is a negative result paper: adversarial competition itself doesn't add value in legal reasoning. The value of multi-teacher curricula comes from constructing verifiable environments, not competition itself, consistent with findings in coding domain studies.

Abstract: Adversarial self-play is an appealing recipe for legal reasoning: have a student model draft an argument, have an adversary attack it, and reward the student when its argument survives the attack. We designed exactly such a training signal -- a verifiable "survival" reward in which both the student's cited authorities and the adversary's counter-authorities are checked by a citation verifier, so that survival is decided on verified grounds rather than rhetoric, and fabricated citations are automatically neutralized. We then asked a narrow but important question: does the competitive component itself -- the adversary and the survival reward -- add anything on top of an otherwise identical non-competitive training run? Across four independent tests -- a bootstrap comparison, a two-seed replication, a paired per-case adversarial-robustness comparison, and a blinded head-to-head judgment of generated arguments, plus a follow-up pilot with a deliberately strengthened self-play adversary -- the competitive component produced no reliable benefit. The blinded judgment gave a 49% win rate (binomial p approx. 1.000); the strengthened-adversary pilot gave a 50% win rate (32:32, p approx. 1.000). An early apparent +29% advantage reversed and proved to be a small-sample artifact. We report this as an honest negative result. The value of the paper is reproducibility and the sharing of concrete pitfalls: an initially promising metric that inverted on more data, and an adversarial-robustness metric that silently collapsed to plain recall once the adversary stopped citing the same authorities as the gold answer. This null is consistent with, and reconfirms in the legal domain, the conclusion of the companion coding-domain study (Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255) that the value of multi-teacher curricula arises from constructing a verifiable environment rather than from competition itself.

</details>


### [115] [Is More Privileged Information Better? From Solution Traces to Problem-Solving Structure in Self-Distilled Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01589)
*Xuyang Zhao,Liting Zhang,Zichen Xu,Zhihu Wang,Xu Caiyue,Shiwan Zhao,Qicheng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PS-OPSD improves reasoning by replacing full solution guidance with problem-space guidance (initial state, goals, constraints, path), achieving better accuracy without changing student rollout.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard on-policy self-distillation uses reference solutions that may contain inference-time unavailable information, creating a mismatch between teacher targets and student capabilities.

Method: Replace complete reference solutions with problem-space guidance describing initial state, goal conditions, constraints, and selected state-transition path, while keeping student rollout and OPSD objective unchanged.

Result: Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model scales (1.7B to 8B), PS-OPSD achieves highest aggregate question-only accuracy among compared methods.

Conclusion: Guidance relevance and path coherence contribute to performance gains, highlighting privileged information representation as crucial design choice in on-policy self-distillation.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by using a privileged view of a model conditioned on reference solutions to supervise a student view that observes only the question. However, the teacher-provided token-level targets may depend on reference-specific information unavailable at inference time. We propose Problem-Space-Guided OPSD (PS-OPSD), which replaces the complete solution with trajectory-grounded guidance describing the initial state, goal conditions, constraints, and a selected state-transition path. The student rollout and OPSD objective remain unchanged. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model scales ranging from 1.7B to 8B, PS-OPSD achieves the highest aggregate question-only accuracy among the compared methods. Controlled experiments further indicate that guidance relevance and path coherence contribute to these gains, highlighting the representation of privileged information as an important design choice in OPSD.

</details>


### [116] [Latent Thought Credit: Multi-Answer Credit Assignment for Latent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01593)
*Xuyang Zhao,Liting Zhang,Zichen Xu,Yong Chen,Wenjia Zeng,Shiwan Zhao,Qicheng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LTC is a hierarchical credit-assignment framework for latent reasoning in language models that estimates thought-level rewards by sampling multiple answers from fixed thought contexts, improving optimization and reducing reward estimation error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of assigning credit to latent reasoning in language models. When models perform intermediate reasoning in continuous latent representations (rather than discrete chains of thought), it's difficult to determine which thoughts contributed to the final answer because answer-only rewards combine thought quality with answer-sampling noise.

Method: The proposed Latent Thought Credit (LTC) framework has a hierarchical approach: 1) For each prompt, sample multiple latent thoughts; 2) Fix the context after each thought; 3) Estimate thought-level expected reward by averaging rewards over multiple answers generated from that fixed context; 4) Use thought-level advantages to optimize the latent-thought phase; 5) Use answer-level advantages to optimize the answer phase; 6) Implement an advantage-weighted thought-matching objective to reproduce high-credit latent thoughts. The method is instantiated in a GRPO-style on-policy training framework.

Result: LTC achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods across mathematical reasoning and STEM multiple-choice tasks. Ablations and fixed-context diagnostics show that multi-answer estimation reduces reward-estimation error and mitigates ambiguous or incorrect thought-level credit assignment.

Conclusion: LTC provides an effective hierarchical credit-assignment framework for latent reasoning in language models. By decoupling thought quality from answer-sampling noise through multi-answer estimation from fixed contexts, the method enables more accurate optimization and improves performance on complex reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Latent reasoning allows language models to carry out intermediate reasoning in continuous latent representations rather than fully externalizing it as discrete chains of thought. However, assigning credit to such latent thoughts from answer-only rewards is difficult: a single final answer mixes thought quality with answer-sampling noise. We propose \textbf{Latent Thought Credit (LTC)}, a hierarchical credit-assignment framework for latent reasoning. For each prompt, LTC samples multiple latent thoughts, fixes the context after each thought, and estimates thought-level expected reward by averaging rewards over multiple answers generated from that fixed context. LTC uses thought-level advantages to optimize the latent-thought phase, answer-level advantages to optimize the answer phase, and an advantage-weighted thought-matching objective that helps the policy reproduce high-credit latent thoughts. We instantiate LTC in a GRPO-style on-policy training framework and evaluate it across mathematical reasoning and STEM multiple-choice tasks. LTC achieves the best average accuracy among the compared methods, while ablations and fixed-context diagnostics show that multi-answer estimation reduces reward-estimation error and mitigates ambiguous or incorrect thought-level credit.

</details>


### [117] [Post-Training on Office Work Improves Software Engineering: A Behavioral Account of Cross-Domain Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01604)
*Logan Ritchie,Sushant Mehta,Liudas Panavas,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Long-horizon post-training improves goal-directed execution behaviors in large language models, leading to cross-domain performance gains including in software engineering tasks not seen during training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of maintaining coherent state and goals across complex, long-horizon tasks that involve nested and branching workflows. The researchers hypothesize that goal-directed execution (GDE) - a set of four key behaviors - is crucial for such tasks and can be strengthened through long-horizon post-training.

Method: The researchers post-trained Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 363 Long-Horizon Multi-Tool Agent (LHMTA) tasks from office workflows, which contained no software-engineering tasks. They then evaluated the model on SWE-Bench Pro and analyzed gains through matched trajectory analysis to measure improvements in the four GDE behaviors.

Result: Despite no software-engineering tasks in training, the model improved by 5.8 points pass@1 on SWE-Bench Pro. Analysis showed gains in all four GDE behaviors (goal selection, state construction, objective fidelity, completion verification) in both office workflows and software repositories. SWE-Bench Pro statistics revealed improvements in information gathering, implementation, and verification.

Conclusion: Long-horizon post-training changes how models organize and apply knowledge across tasks, strengthening goal-directed execution behaviors that transfer beyond the training domain. This supports a behavioral interpretation of learning effects rather than simple pattern matching.

Abstract: Long-horizon tasks require agents to maintain coherent state and goals across nested and branching work. We call this capability goal-directed execution (GDE): the repeated application of four behaviors, namely selecting goals, constructing task-relevant state, maintaining fidelity to higher-level objectives, and verifying completion against the environment. We hypothesize that long-horizon post-training strengthens these behaviors across domains. We test this by post-training Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 363 Long-Horizon Multi-Tool Agent (LHMTA) tasks drawn from office workflows. The collection contained no software-engineering tasks, yet the model's pass@1 improved by 5.8 points on SWE-Bench Pro. Matched trajectory analysis shows gains in all four GDE behaviors in both office workflows and software repositories. Aggregate SWE-Bench Pro statistics showed related changes in information gathering, implementation, and verification. Together, the results support a behavioral interpretation in which long-horizon post-training changed how the model organized and applied knowledge across tasks, with effects extending beyond the training domain.

</details>


### [118] [When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not: Repairing Implicit Stale Dependencies in Personalized Agent Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01619)
*Haofei Sun,Lin He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STALE benchmark reveals memory-augmented agents planning with outdated stored state. StateAuditor proposes auditing from stored state to draft responses to address implicit policy adaptation gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-augmented agents can plan around outdated stored user state even when they know it's stale, creating an implicit policy adaptation (IPA) gap. Current verification approaches (draft-anchored) check what responses say, but stale dependencies are usually unsaid in open-ended responses.

Method: StateAuditor audits in opposite direction - from stored state to draft. LLM proposes candidate old-to-new transitions from timestamped evidence; deterministic code pins quotations to single entries, verifies chronology, and triggers repair only for verified transitions. Focus is on provenance and chronology verification, not semantic supersession.

Result: On STALE benchmark (400 scenarios): strict single-query VTA scores .736 vs .686 for predecessor (+5.0-point gain, 95% CI [+2.9, +7.2]), mainly from IPA and premise resistance improvement. Cross-family preference-evolution benchmark (HorizonBench) shows current-preference accuracy improvement, though most gain comes from draft-side audit. Matched control experiments attribute STALE gains specifically to transition machinery, not added context or calls.

Conclusion: StateAuditor's transition-focused verification mechanism effectively addresses IPA gap in STALE benchmark, but authors limit claims to this specific problem and make no claims about general-purpose agent memory systems.

Abstract: Memory-augmented agents can know that a user's stored state is outdated and still plan around the old value. The STALE benchmark calls this the implicit policy adaptation (IPA) gap. We identify one structural contributor: draft-anchored verification checks what a response says, and in an open-ended response the stale dependency is usually unsaid. StateAuditor therefore audits in the opposite direction, from stored state to draft. An LLM proposes candidate old-to-new transitions from timestamped evidence; deterministic code pins each quotation to a single entry, checks that the new evidence really is newer, and lets only these verified transitions trigger repair. What is verified is provenance and chronology - not semantic supersession. On STALE's full protocol (400 scenarios, 50-session histories, one independent response per query), strict single-query VTA scores .736 against .686 for our locked predecessor under the same judge: a +5.0-point paired gain (95% CI [+2.9, +7.2]) coming almost entirely from IPA and premise resistance (PR). The benchmark's own judge, from a third model family, reproduces the gain (.738 vs. .680). On an independent cross-family preference-evolution benchmark (HorizonBench), the full draft-audit-repair pipeline over a gold-derived structured store raises current-preference accuracy (user-clustered p<.01), though a matched control shows most of this external gain is the draft-side audit itself; a harder authored lifecycle set gives no gain, bounding the claim while false invalidation stays controlled. On STALE, by contrast, a matched control (same evidence, adapter, and call budget) scores only .692 (+0.6 over the predecessor, n.s.), attributing the STALE gain to the transition machinery rather than added context or calls. We make no claim about general-purpose agent memory.

</details>


### [119] [Salami Attack: Stealthy Collusive Memory Poisoning against OpenClaw](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01637)
*Zheng Lin,Yuzhe Huang,Zhenxing Niu,Xianmin Ye,Haichang Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemCollusion is an automated red-teaming framework that creates collusive memory poisoning attacks where multiple individually benign-looking memory fragments collectively induce unsafe behavior in LLM agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term memory in LLM agents creates an attack surface for adversaries to poison persistent memory. Existing attacks rely on individually malicious records, overlooking the compositional threat where multiple benign-looking memories can jointly induce unsafe behavior.

Method: MemCollusion applies salami tactics (slicing adversarial objectives into small innocuous pieces) to generate individually benign but collectively harmful memory fragments. It uses four design constraints, five theory-informed strategies, and a fine-tuned generator. The framework was evaluated using MoltLab (a controlled research reproduction of Moltbook) across 48 scenarios on OpenClaw with two backbone models.

Result: Under the strongest memory-saving setting, MemCollusion achieves an average Memory Save Rate of 81.3% and an Attack Success Rate of 75.0%. The attacks remain effective under both benign memory dilution and memory-level defenses.

Conclusion: Collusive memory poisoning attacks pose a significant security threat to LLM agents with persistent memory, demonstrating that multiple individually benign memories can collectively compromise agent safety, requiring new defense mechanisms beyond traditional memory-level protections.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to retain useful information across sessions, but also creates an attack surface through which adversaries may poison an agent's persistent memory to steer its behavior. Existing memory poisoning attacks mainly rely on individually malicious records, overlooking a compositional threat: multiple benign-looking memories may jointly induce unsafe behavior. In this paper, we introduce MemCollusion, an automated red-teaming framework for constructing collusive memory poisoning attacks. MemCollusion applies salami tactics---a strategy that slices an adversarial objective into small, individually innocuous pieces---to generate memory fragments that are individually benign looking but collectively harmful. It constructs memory coalitions using four design constraints, five theory-informed strategies, and a fine-tuned generator. To assess collusive memory poisoning in a realistic cross-session setting, we develop MoltLab, a controlled research reproduction of Moltbook, in which crafted platform content must first be observed and distilled into persistent memory before influencing the agent's behavior in a separate session. We evaluate MemCollusion on OpenClaw using two backbone models across 48 scenarios. Under the strongest memory-saving setting, MemCollusion achieves an average Memory Save Rate of 81.3% and an Attack Success Rate of 75.0%, and remains effective under both benign memory dilution and memory-level defenses.

</details>


### [120] [GISAgentBench: A Practitioner-Sourced Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on GIS Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01645)
*Abhinav Pothuri,Zhe Jiang,Zelin Xu,Di Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GISAgentBench is a new benchmark of 349 multi-step GIS tasks from real-world GIS Stack Exchange questions, providing executable reference trajectories and exact ground truth outputs for reliable evaluation of LLM-powered GIS agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents for geospatial analysis lack proper evaluation - existing benchmarks use surrogate signals like code similarity or LLM judges that can't properly measure task correctness, and are limited in size and based on artificial sources rather than real GIS workflows.

Method: Created GISAgentBench with 349 multi-step GIS tasks curated from GIS Stack Exchange questions, instantiated on real public data across six geographic areas. Each task includes executable reference trajectory and exact ground truth output file for strict, tolerance-aware output matching evaluation.

Result: Evaluation of six LLM models shows realistic GIS workflows remain challenging - best agent completes only 32.7% of tasks under strict tolerance-aware scoring, though most produce outputs close to ground truth. Current models struggle with complex spatial analysis workflows.

Conclusion: Real-world GIS workflow automation remains difficult for current LLM agents, highlighting the need for better benchmarks with ground truth outputs and the complexity gap between artificial tasks and real GIS analysis requirements.

Abstract: Geographic Information System (GIS) professionals rely on multi-step spatial analysis workflows to support decision-making in urban planning, disaster response, and environmental monitoring. The process is tedious, time-consuming, and error-prone. While recent large language model (LLM) agents equipped with external tools have the potential to automate geospatial analysis, their ability to perform realistic GIS workflows remains largely unexplored. Existing GIS agent benchmarking datasets are mostly drawn from textbooks, tutorials, or LLM-generated seeds and remain limited in size and trajectory depth. More importantly, none provides ground truth outputs. They therefore rely on surrogate signals such as code similarity, trajectory matching, or LLM and VLM judges, which can conflate workflow resemblance with task correctness. To address this gap, we introduce GISAgentBench, a benchmark of 349 multi-step GIS tasks curated from GIS Stack Exchange and instantiated on real public data across six selected geographic areas of interest. Each task ships with an executable reference trajectory and an exact ground truth output file, enabling strict, deterministic, tolerance-aware output matching beyond LLM judging. Evaluations of six LLM models reveal that realistic GIS workflows remain challenging: the best agent completes only 32.7% of tasks under strict tolerance-aware scoring, although most models produce outputs that are close to the ground truth.

</details>


### [121] [LongCat Sparse Attention: Taming the Lightning via Streaming-aware Hierarchical Cross-Layer Indexing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01662)
*Wen Zan,Jiaqi Zhang,Jianchao Tan,Hong Liu,Cunguang Wang,Xiang Li,Duyue Ma,Guanyu Wu,Yifan Lu,Fengcun Li,Yerui Sun,Peng Pei,Yuchen Xie,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LSA (LongCat Sparse Attention) is a hardware-algorithm co-designed framework that optimizes sparse attention for efficient long-context modeling through three strategies: streaming-aware indexing, cross-layer indexing, and hierarchical indexing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) has limitations in practical deployment due to expensive O(L²) scoring overhead and hardware-inefficient, discontinuous memory-access patterns from its Lightning Indexer outputs, creating system-level bottlenecks for long-context modeling.

Method: LSA introduces three complementary strategies: 1) Streaming-Aware Indexing - converts scattered KV entries into hardware-aligned contiguous layouts for coalesced HBM access; 2) Cross-Layer Indexing - reuses indexing results across consecutive layers with cross-layer distillation; 3) Hierarchical Indexing - uses coarse-to-fine scoring to progressively narrow candidate sets.

Result: LSA achieves performance on par with full attention across scaling experiments (69B-A3B to 560B-A27B models) on general-purpose and long-context benchmarks, supports native training with up to 1M token contexts, and enables LongCat-2.0 (1.6T-A48B) development. LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B) is open-sourced.

Conclusion: LSA effectively addresses the system bottlenecks of DSA through hardware-algorithm co-design, enabling efficient long-context modeling at scale while maintaining full attention performance, advancing sparse attention deployment in practical systems.

Abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) enables efficient long-context modeling through its Lightning Indexer. However, practical deployment remains constrained by the indexer's expensive $O(L^2)$ scoring overhead and the hardware-inefficient, discontinuous memory-access patterns induced by its outputs. To address these system-level bottlenecks, we introduce LongCat Sparse Attention (LSA), a hardware-algorithm co-designed framework comprising three complementary and orthogonal strategies: (1) Streaming-Aware Indexing, which selectively converts scattered KV entries into hardware-aligned contiguous layouts to enable coalesced HBM access; (2) Cross-Layer Indexing, which amortizes indexing overhead by reusing the results produced by a single layer across consecutive layers, supported by cross-layer distillation; and (3) Hierarchical Indexing, which adopts a coarse-to-fine scoring scheme to progressively narrow the candidate set for each query, thereby substantially reducing indexing computation. Extensive scaling experiments, ranging from 69B-A3B to 560B-A27B models, demonstrate that LSA consistently achieves performance on par with full attention across both general-purpose and long-context benchmarks. Moreover, LSA supports native training with context lengths of up to one million tokens and underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 (1.6T-A48B). To facilitate further research, we also introduce and open-source LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B), which integrates LSA into LongCat-Flash-Lite and incorporates an updated long-context training corpus.

</details>


### [122] [Allocation Before Ranking: Decoupled Token Compression for OmniLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01665)
*Zhenghui Guo,Yilin Yang,Yuanbin Man,Miao Yin,Weidong Shi,Rabimba Karanjai,Omprakash Gnawali,Chengming Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Macer is a training-free token compression method for multimodal LLMs that separates audio and video budget allocation from token ranking, addressing the bias in traditional top-K compression that favors audio tokens over video tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current token compression methods in OmniLLMs treat multimodal compression as a single saliency-ranking problem where all tokens compete equally. This approach has a fundamental flaw: the same attention score determines both modality allocation (how much capacity each modality gets) and token selection within modalities. Since audio tokens typically receive higher attention scores, they consume most of the retention budget before video tokens can compete, leading to suboptimal video token retention.

Method: Macer uses a two-stage approach: 1) First assigns explicit budgets for audio and video tokens separately (allocation-before-ranking principle), 2) Then performs allocation-normalized ranking within each modality using modality-specific shallow layers. This training-free compressor separates modality allocation from token selection, ensuring fair competition between audio and video tokens while maintaining efficiency.

Result: At 25% retention rate, Macer preserves 98.7% of full-token performance on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 97.3% on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, the 25% setting achieves performance comparable to OmniZip at 45% retention while using lower FLOPs. On OmniVinci-9B, the allocation-before-ranking principle improves over shared top-K ranking by up to 12.9 points across various benchmarks including audio-grounded, audio-video joint, visual-dominant, and video-centric tasks.

Conclusion: Token compression in multimodal LLMs should not be treated as a single saliency-ranking problem. By separating modality budget allocation from within-modality token selection, Macer provides a more effective approach that significantly reduces token costs while preserving accuracy across diverse multimodal tasks, outperforming traditional shared top-K compression methods.

Abstract: Token compression in OmniLLMs is typically posed as a single saliency-ranking problem: score each multimodal token, keep the top-K. We argue this abstraction is mis-specified. The same attention score simultaneously decides two things: how much retained capacity each modality receives, and which tokens within a modality are kept. A shared top-K rule therefore inherits this audio-favoring allocation prior, spending retained capacity on audio before video tokens have a chance to compete. We propose Macer, a training-free compressor that first assigns explicit audio and video budgets, then performs allocation-normalized ranking within each modality at modality-specific shallow layers. Macer significantly reduces token cost while preserving accuracy across audio-grounded, audio--video joint, visual-dominant, and video-centric benchmarks. At 25 % retention, Macer preserves 98.7 % of full-token performance on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 97.3 % on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, this 25 % setting reaches OmniZip-level performance at 45 % retention while using lower FLOPs. On OmniVinci-9B, the same allocation-before-ranking principle improves over shared top-K ranking by up to 12.9 points.

</details>


### [123] [TCPO: Turn-Level Credit Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01667)
*Sicong Liao,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TCPO introduces turn-level credit assignment for verifier-guided multi-turn RL, converting verifier scores to proper credit through reference-based comparisons, improving performance across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current verifier-guided RL provides dense feedback through scores but lacks proper credit assignment - scores measure current output quality while credit should measure how each turn affects the refinement trajectory, creating a mismatch that limits learning efficiency.

Method: TCPO frames credit assignment as score-to-credit conversion using three reference-based comparison techniques: retrospective credit (immediate progress/regression), hindsight delayed credit (non-improving turns with later payoff), and selective fixed-history counterfactual estimation (refining high-surprisal turns under same history).

Result: TCPO improves or matches strongest baselines across model scales (Qwen3-4B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B), task domains (math reasoning, code generation, AppWorld agent), and verifier types. Achieves best/tied-best best-turn Pass@8, reduces turns to success, and improves multi-turn agent performance.

Conclusion: Score-to-credit conversion is essential for verifier-guided multi-turn policy optimization, and TCPO's turn-level credit assignment effectively addresses the mismatch between verifier scores and proper credit assignment, leading to improved RL performance across diverse applications.

Abstract: Verifier-guided reinforcement learning has become a powerful paradigm for improving LLM reasoning.
