In multi-turn settings, models receive a verifier score after each turn and iteratively refine their outputs. Although such scores provide dense feedback, they do not directly provide dense credit: a score measures the quality of the current output, while credit should measure how the current turn changes the refinement trajectory. We propose TCPO, a turn-level credit assignment method for verifier-guided multi-turn RL. TCPO casts credit assignment as score-to-credit conversion and constructs turn-level advantages through reference-based comparisons: retrospective credit captures immediate progress and regression relative to the best prior state; hindsight delayed credit identifies non-improving turns with later payoff; and selective fixed-history counterfactual estimation refines high-surprisal turns under the same history. Experiments on math reasoning, code generation, and AppWorld agent tasks show that TCPO improves or matches the strongest baselines across model scales, task domains, and verifier types. TCPO achieves the best or tied-best best-turn Pass@8 on Qwen3-4B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reduces turns to success, and improves multi-turn agent performance. These results highlight score-to-credit conversion as a central ingredient for verifier-guided multi-turn policy optimization.

</details>


### [124] [When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authority Collapse at the Memory Consolidation Boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01679)
*Qiuyang Zhan,Rui Zhang,Sheng Guo,Lepeng Zhao,Zhuotao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Persistent memory in LLM agents can cause authority collapse - where stored information loses source constraints, leading to unauthorized use. The paper introduces AuthMem-Bench to measure this and shows automatic authority prediction can eliminate unauthorized actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While persistent memory helps LLM agents adapt across tasks by consolidating interaction histories, this consolidation creates an implicit authorization boundary. The paper identifies "authority collapse" - where consolidation preserves claims but erases the source constraints governing their authorized use, causing stored memory to imply greater authority than the source permits.

Method: The authors introduce AuthMem-Bench, a controlled paired benchmark that holds the focal claim and downstream task fixed while varying only source authority. It evaluates write-time collapse, downstream authorization errors, and automatic authority preservation. They test seven consolidators based on widely used agent-memory systems across seven LLM backbones.

Result: Authority collapse was observed in 48 of 49 evaluated configurations. In action-grounded evaluation, collapsed memories without authority metadata yield 50.3% unauthorized-action rate. In end-to-end evaluation, automatically predicted and persisted authority labels reduced unauthorized-action rate from 16.9% to 0.0%, while benign task success remained essentially unchanged.

Conclusion: Memory-driven adaptation in LLM agents must preserve not only what was learned, but also the authority under which it may be reused. Automatic authority preservation can effectively eliminate unauthorized actions while maintaining task performance.

Abstract: Persistent memory allows (self-evolving) LLM agents to adapt across tasks by consolidating heterogeneous interaction histories into reusable facts, preferences, observations, and rules. Yet consolidation also imposes an implicit authorization boundary: it determines whether stored information may later be consumed as a user fact, an attested observation, or a standing instruction. We identify authority collapse, in which consolidation preserves a claim while erasing the source constraints governing its authorized use, causing the stored memory to imply greater authority than its source permits. We introduce AuthMem-Bench, a controlled paired benchmark that holds the focal claim and downstream task fixed while varying only source authority. It evaluates write-time collapse, downstream authorization errors, and automatic authority preservation. Across seven consolidators based on widely used agent-memory systems and seven LLM backbones, we observe authority collapse in 48 of 49 evaluated configurations. In a controlled action-grounded evaluation, collapsed memories without authority metadata yield a mean unauthorized-action rate of 50.3%. In an end-to-end evaluation, automatically predicted and persisted authority labels reduce the observed unauthorized-action rate from 16.9% to 0.0%, while benign task success remains essentially unchanged. These findings show that memory-driven adaptation must preserve not only what was
  learned, but also the authority under which it may be reused.

</details>


### [125] [GABench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Graph Analysis Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01684)
*Jiarui Tan,Zhongjian Zhang,YaBo Guo,Jiawei Liu,Yujie Xing,Muhan Zhang,Cheng Yang,Chuan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GABench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on graph analysis tasks across three graph types and four task categories, with 84 executable tools and 10,400 tasks, revealing current LLM agents still struggle with complex graph analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph benchmarks for LLMs have limited coverage of graph tasks and types, typically formulate graph analysis as text-based QA with graph info in prompts, and lack comprehensive evaluation of end-to-end agentic capabilities.

Method: Introduced GABench benchmark spanning three graph types and four task categories (graph retrieval, graph theory, graph ML, and open-ended QA). Provided 84 executable tools for graph data access and operations. Developed agentic graph analysis task generation pipeline to construct 10,400 tasks with verifiable ground truth.

Result: Evaluation of frontier LLMs and agent harnesses revealed: (1) Existing LLM agents struggle with complex graph analysis, (2) Harness choice significantly affects performance but current harnesses remain limited, (3) Graph analysis depends more on tool-call quality than quantity.

Conclusion: GABench addresses limitations in existing graph benchmarks and provides practical insights for developing and evaluating LLM agents for graph analysis, highlighting the gap in current agent capabilities for complex graph tasks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of planning, using tools, and interacting with external environments. They are typically supported by harnesses, which manage state and coordinate multi-step execution. Graph analysis provides a promising setting for evaluating their agentic capabilities, because it requires agents to access data and execute operations in a graph environment. However, existing graph benchmarks for LLMs provide limited coverage of graph tasks and graph types, making it difficult to comprehensively evaluate LLM agents. Moreover, they typically formulate graph analysis as text-based question answering, where graph information is directly provided in the prompt, limiting the evaluation of end-to-end agentic capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce GABench, a comprehensive benchmark for agentic graph analysis. GABench spans three graph types and covers four graph analysis task categories: graph retrieval, graph theory, graph machine learning, and graph open-ended question answering. GABench also provides 84 executable tools for accessing graph data and performing diverse graph operations. Building on these tools, we develop an agentic graph analysis task generation pipeline and construct 10,400 tasks with verifiable ground truth.Using GABench, we evaluate a range of frontier LLMs and agent harnesses. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (1) Existing LLM agents still struggle with complex graph analysis tasks. (2) Harness choice significantly affects performance, yet existing harnesses remain limited on complex graph tasks. (3) Graph analysis depends more on tool-call quality than quantity. Our findings provide practical insights into the development and evaluation of LLM agents for graph analysis.

</details>


### [126] [Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01710)
*Jinghan Xu,Longze Fan,Zeyuan Wang,Xinjin Li,Hankai Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CapLease is an authorization-consumption layer that prevents semantic replay attacks in LLM agents by enforcing durable state tracking of authorized actions rather than just token identifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents frequently replan, retry operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes, which can cause single-use authorization tokens to be reissued with fresh identifiers while semantically replaying the same authorized action. Identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent this semantic replay problem.

Method: Introduces CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that binds authenticated user confirmation to canonical actions and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions. Compares with identifier-local tokens and an equally stateful Server Ledger approach.

Result: Across various LLM agent scenarios (replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, crash-recovery), identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, while CapLease and Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and duplicate external effects with an idempotent sink.

Conclusion: Durable authorization state (tracking authorized actions, confirmation events, and remaining execution budget) is the essential systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution, not just token representation alone.

Abstract: Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier. We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions. Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state, rather than token representation alone, as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

</details>


### [127] [Constructing Executable Analytical Knowledge Representations for Meta-Analysis Synthesis Using an Agentic Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01711)
*Lingbo Li,Anuradha Mathrani,Teo Susnjak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EAKR is a machine-actionable representation for transforming structured evidence into executable meta-analyses, implemented in MetaSynDec which outperforms direct LLM generation in analytical fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated approaches embed analytical decisions (evidence assignment, contrasts, effect-size formulation, etc.) in model outputs or code rather than representing them as independently verifiable knowledge. There's a need for explicit representation of analytical knowledge before statistical execution.

Method: Introduces Executable Analytical Knowledge Representation (EAKR) - a machine-actionable representation of evidence, relations, numerical inputs, constraints, provenance, and issues. Operationalizes EAKR in MetaSynDec, an agentic harness where LLMs propose structured updates and deterministic services handle schema/contract-based validation and execution.

Result: Across 58 synthesis units: MetaSynDec constructed all EAKRs, 57 proceeded to execution. Among 56 units with sufficient reference data: 67.9% achieved complete object fidelity, 75.0% exact evidence-set agreement (mean Jaccard 0.909). Generated vs published CI overlap in 98.2% of units. MetaSynDec outperformed direct LLM generation in structure agreement (57/58 vs 23/58, p<0.001) and exact reference-formulation agreement (23/23 vs 1/23, p<0.001).

Conclusion: EAKR supports formal validation, traceability, statistical execution, and improves methodological agreement compared to direct LLM generation, demonstrating feasibility for transforming structured evidence into executable meta-analyses.

Abstract: Meta-analysis synthesis highlights a fundamental challenge in knowledge-based scientific analysis: structured evidence does not by itself represent the analytical knowledge required for executable computation. Decisions about evidence assignment, analytical contrasts, outcome and time-point alignment, effect-size formulation, and methodological admissibility must be explicit before statistical execution. Existing automated approaches often embed these decisions in model outputs, generated code, or workflow traces rather than representing them as independently verifiable knowledge. We introduce the Executable Analytical Knowledge Representation (EAKR), a machine-actionable representation of the knowledge required to transform structured evidence into executable meta-analysis. An EAKR represents evidence, relations, numerical inputs, constraints, provenance, and unresolved issues. We operationalise EAKR in MetaSynDec, an agentic harness in which large language models propose structured updates and deterministic services govern schema- and contract-based validation and execution. Across 58 synthesis units, MetaSynDec constructed all EAKRs, with 57 proceeding to statistical execution. Of 56 units with sufficient information to define a reference analysis object, 38 (67.9%) achieved complete object fidelity and 42 (75.0%) exact evidence-set agreement, with a mean Jaccard similarity of 0.909. Generated and published confidence intervals overlapped in 54 of 55 units (98.2%). MetaSynDec outperformed direct LLM generation in reference synthesis-structure agreement (57/58 versus 23/58; p<0.001) and among 23 jointly completed units, exact reference-formulation agreement (23/23 versus 1/23; p<0.001). These findings provide feasibility evidence that EAKR supports formal validation, traceability, statistical execution, and improved methodological agreement relative to direct LLM generation.

</details>


### [128] [LaCache: Robust Semantic Caching for LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01718)
*Jiacheng Liang,Yuhui Wang,Tanqiu Jiang,Ting Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LaCache is a secure semantic caching scheme for LLM serving that protects against cache-collision attacks by checking cache hits for both queries and their speculatively decoded first k tokens, providing formal security guarantees while improving response relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic caching schemes are fundamentally vulnerable to cache-collision attacks where adversaries can inject crafted queries to corrupt responses to legitimate requests, compromising system security and reliability.

Method: LaCache redesigns semantic caching by checking cache hits not only for queries but also for the first k speculatively decoded tokens. This leverages the insight that adversaries have control over queries but limited control over responses that must satisfy multiple semantic constraints simultaneously.

Result: LaCache provides formally proven resilience against cache-collusion attacks (impossible to craft adversarial queries that elicit malicious responses while colliding with benign queries) and improves response relevance through enriched semantic context in cache retrieval. Empirical evaluation across diverse LLMs and benchmarks validates both security guarantees and efficiency gains.

Conclusion: LaCache presents a promising direction for robust semantic caching in LLM serving, addressing fundamental security vulnerabilities while maintaining or improving performance, making semantic caching more secure and reliable for practical deployment.

Abstract: Semantic caching, which reuses responses to semantically similar requests via their embeddings, has seen growing adoption in LLM serving, offering faster responses and reduced costs. Yet existing schemes are fundamentally vulnerable to cache-collision attacks, wherein an adversary pollutes the cache by injecting crafted queries, corrupting responses to subsequent legitimate requests. We present LaCache, a novel semantic caching scheme that addresses this vulnerability through a conceptually simple yet principled redesign. The key insight is that while the adversary has full control over the adversarial query, it has far less control over its response, which must simultaneously satisfy multiple semantic constraints. Rather than checking only the cache hit of a query, LaCache additionally checks the cache hit of its first k (speculatively) decoded tokens. This design yields two concrete benefits. First, it provides formally guaranteed resilience against cache-collision attacks: we prove that it is impossible to craft adversarial queries that simultaneously elicit malicious responses and collide with benign queries. Second, the enriched index supplies additional semantic context for cache retrieval, improving response relevance. Empirical evaluation across diverse LLMs and benchmarks validates both LaCache's security guarantees and efficiency gains, pointing to a promising direction for robust semantic caching.

</details>


### [129] [DAPD: Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01735)
*Jianyu Wu,Yizhou Wang,Encheng Su,Chen Tang,Shixiang Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD) addresses privilege illusion in on-policy distillation by introducing dual-path and dual-source anchoring to align reference and rollout behaviors, outperforming standard methods across model scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation for language models suffers from "privilege illusion" - students learn privilege-dependent behaviors from privileged teachers but cannot reproduce them at inference time when privileged information is unavailable, degrading performance.

Method: Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD) with two components: 1) Dual-Path Anchoring introduces a self-conditioned bridge and aligns reference/rollout behavior along matched-information paths, preventing privilege-dependent behavior transfer; 2) Dual-Source Anchoring applies these paths bidirectionally (reference-to-rollout and rollout-to-reference), reducing reliance on privileged reference guidance while preserving correctness supervision.

Result: DAPD significantly alleviates privilege illusion, outperforming standard on-policy distillation on Qwen3-4B by +2.00 points average across tasks. Gains scale with model size: +2.69 at 4B and +2.78 at 32B.

Conclusion: The proposed Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation framework successfully addresses information asymmetry in on-policy distillation through dual anchoring mechanisms, achieving consistent performance improvements across different model scales by preventing privilege illusion.

Abstract: On-policy (self) distillation (OPSD) is increasingly adopted for language-model post-training. It strengthens the teacher with privileged information but can induce a privilege illusion: the student learns privilege-dependent behavior it cannot reproduce from its inference-time context, yet behaves as if the training-time privileged information remained available, ultimately degrading performance. In this paper, we identify information asymmetry between the privileged teacher and the student at inference as the root cause of this failure in OPSD. To resolve this asymmetry, we propose Dual-Anchored Policy Distillation (DAPD), a unified framework with two levels of anchoring. Dual-Path Anchoring (DPA) introduces a self-conditioned bridge and aligns reference and rollout behavior along two matched-information paths, preventing privilege-dependent behavior from being transferred to the inference-time student. Dual-Source Anchoring (DSA) applies these paths in both reference-to-rollout and rollout-to-reference directions, reducing reliance on privileged reference guidance while preserving correctness supervision. Extensive experiments show that DAPD significantly alleviates privilege illusion, outperforming OPSD on Qwen3-4B by +2.00 points on average across tasks. Notably, its gains persist across scales, reaching +2.69 at 4B and +2.78 at 32B.

</details>


### [130] [CoEvo-Mem: Co-Evolving Retrieval Policy and Memory Bank for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01739)
*Bowen Ye,Yongchao Xu,Zhijian Li,Xiang Yin,Junkai Ma,Wenzhao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoEvo-Mem is a framework that jointly optimizes memory retrieval policies and memory bank evolution through a closed-loop co-evolution process, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods separate memory retrieval optimization from memory evolution, overlooking the fundamental feedback loop where retrieval determines which memories receive usage signals, and updated memory banks reshape future retrieval performance.

Method: CoEvo-Mem co-evolves retrieval policy and memory bank through a closed-loop framework. For each query, a frozen LLM generates query rewrites and routing prior, corrected by a lightweight residual router. Retrieved context serves as coupling interface between learning processes - task outcomes assign credit to routing decisions while trajectory-conditioned feedback updates memory values and graph relations. To mitigate non-stationarity, the method alternates between updating router with fixed memory bank and evolving memory bank with fixed retrieval policy.

Result: CoEvo-Mem achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven diverse benchmarks, demonstrating the importance of retrieval-memory coevolution.

Conclusion: The joint co-evolution of retrieval policies and memory banks through a closed-loop framework is crucial for improving long-term LLM agent performance, as demonstrated by CoEvo-Mem's superior results across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: As memories accumulate across tasks and sessions, the performance of long-term LLM agents depends jointly on query-specific retrieval and continual memory refinement. However, existing methods typically optimize either memory access, through iterative query refinement or adaptive retrieval policies, or memory evolution such as structural update. This separation overlooks a fundamental feedback loop: retrieval determines which memories receive usage signals, while updated memory bank reshape future retrieval. We propose \textbf{CoEvo-Mem}, a closed-loop framework for co-evolving the retrieval policy and memory bank. For each query, a frozen LLM generates route-specific query rewrites and a routing prior, which a lightweight residual router corrects online. The retrieved context serves as the coupling interface between the two learning processes: task outcomes assign credit to routing decisions, while trajectory-conditioned feedback updates memory values and graph relations. These updates alter how memories are ranked and selected for subsequent queries, thereby closing the feedback loop. To mitigate coupling induced non-stationarity, CoEvo-Mem alternates between updating the router with the memory bank fixed and evolving the memory bank with the retrieval policy fixed. Across seven diverse benchmarks, \textbf{CoEvo-Mem} achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the importance of retrieval-memory coevolution.

</details>


### [131] [MemSIF: From Structured Interactions to Dual-Track Fact Memory for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01742)
*YuFei Luo,Xiucheng Xu,Zhen Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemSIF is a structured memory framework that addresses two misalignment patterns in LLM long-term memory by organizing interactions into topical segments and event trajectories, while maintaining dual-track fact memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents have persistent limitations in long-horizon interactions, primarily due to two misalignment patterns: Temporal-Structural Misalignment (when temporal proximity doesn't align with topical relatedness) and Delayed Utility Manifestation (when write-time salience doesn't predict future query utility).

Method: Proposes MemSIF with two components: 1) Structured Interaction Memory organizes raw interactions into Topical Segments (preserving local topical coherence) and Event Trajectories (maintaining cross-time event continuity); 2) Dual-Track Fact Memory uses CoreFact (stable, schema-guided information at write time) and ActiveFact (forms facts on-demand, promoted based on multiple historical sources and recurring query demand).

Result: Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across five backbone LLMs show MemSIF achieves highest Total ACC in all settings, outperforming strongest baseline by 2.29%-8.79% on LoCoMo and 2.87%-6.15% on LongMemEval-S.

Conclusion: The combination of Structured Interaction Memory with Dual-Track Fact Memory effectively mitigates Temporal-Structural Misalignment and Delayed Utility Manifestation, providing a robust solution for long-term memory in LLM agents.

Abstract: Long-term memory is critical for LLM agents operating over long-horizon interactions. However, several persistent limitations of existing memory systems can be traced to two recurring misalignment patterns in long-term interaction settings: Temporal-Structural Misalignment (TSM) and Delayed Utility Manifestation (DUM). TSM arises when temporal proximity does not reliably align with topical or event-level relatedness, whereas DUM arises when write-time salience does not reliably predict future query utility. To mitigate these misalignment patterns, we propose MemSIF (Memory with Structured Interactions and Facts), a structured interaction-to-fact memory framework. Structured Interaction Memory organizes raw interactions into Topical Segments that preserve local topical coherence and Event Trajectories that maintain cross-time event continuity. Dual-Track Fact Memory uses two complementary tracks: CoreFact memory consolidates stable, schema-guided information at write time, whereas ActiveFact memory forms facts on demand and promotes those supported by multiple historical sources and recurring query demand for reuse. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across five backbone LLMs show that MemSIF achieves the highest Total ACC in all settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.29%-8.79% on LoCoMo and 2.87%-6.15% on LongMemEval-S. These results support the effectiveness of combining Structured Interaction Memory with Dual-Track Fact Memory to mitigate TSM and DUM. Code is available at https://github.com/luoyufeihaha/MemSIF.

</details>


### [132] [RL-Lock: Reinforcement Learning for Generating Interlocking Assemblies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01744)
*Xuyang Ma,Chaewoon Kim,Haonan Zhang,Rulin Chen,Ziqi Wang,Peng Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL-Lock: A reinforcement learning framework that generates interlocking assemblies using structured action chunking and MCTS-guided policy-value learning, outperforming traditional heuristic-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interlocking assemblies are structurally stable geometric arrangements without connectors, but generating them is challenging due to the large combinatorial search space. Traditional approaches rely on handcrafted search heuristics which can be inefficient or fail for complex cases.

Method: The authors propose RL-Lock, a reinforcement learning framework that treats interlocking assembly generation as a sequential decision-making problem. It uses structured action chunking and MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the combinatorial search space of assigning voxels to pieces.

Result: RL-Lock effectively generates interlocking assemblies, particularly for challenging cases where existing heuristic-based approaches take too long or fail completely. The method demonstrates improved efficiency and success rates.

Conclusion: Reinforcement learning is a promising approach for interlocking assembly generation, overcoming limitations of traditional handcrafted heuristics through more efficient exploration of the complex search space.

Abstract: An interlocking assembly is an assembly in which component parts are connected purely through their geometric arrangement, without relying on external connectors such as glue and nails. Such assemblies have been widely used in a variety of real-world applications due to their structural stability. The problem of generating interlocking assemblies is generally formulated as a shape decomposition problem, where a target 3D object represented as a voxel grid is partitioned into a prescribed number of interlocking pieces. We observe that generating interlocking assemblies is inherently a sequential decision-making problem, where an agent repeatedly decides which piece each voxel should be assigned to. Inspired by the observation, we propose the first reinforcement learning framework RL-Lock for generating interlocking assemblies, without relying on handcrafted search heuristics as existing works did. RL-Lock combines structured action chunking with MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the large combinatorial search space for interlocking assembly generation. We demonstrate through experiments that RL-Lock allows effective generation of interlocking assemblies, especially for challenging cases in which existing approaches take too long or even fail to find a valid solution.

</details>


### [133] [Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for Verifiable Reasoning in Autonomous Driving VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01755)
*Zixuan Huang,Yang Zhou,Kaixuan Wang,Guli Zhang,Hongyan Xie,Yakun Zhu,Hao Geng,Yikun Ban,Deqing Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DEFT-RLVR addresses trajectory anchoring bias in VLA models for autonomous driving by converting planning into a multiple-choice question format and deferring exposure to future trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLA models for autonomous driving using chain-of-thought supervision suffer from trajectory anchoring bias - teacher models rationalize revealed ground-truth trajectories rather than inferring decisions from scene evidence, leading to less causally faithful reasoning and more hallucinations, especially in challenging scenes.

Method: Two main contributions: 1) AD-MCQ (Autonomous-Driving Multiple-Choice Question) that casts planning as selection among explicit trajectory candidates, making decisions verifiable without open-ended trajectory synthesis. 2) DEFT-RLVR (Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for RLVR) that transforms future trajectories from pre-decision anchors into post-decision verification targets.

Result: DEFT-RLVR improves autonomous driving reasoning while preserving or even enhancing general visual capabilities. AD-MCQ provides flexible, scalable, and extensible foundation for verifiable AD reasoning with VLM-only inference and controllable difficulty.

Conclusion: Deferred exposure of future trajectories (DEFT-RLVR) combined with multiple-choice formulation (AD-MCQ) effectively addresses trajectory anchoring bias, enabling more causally faithful reasoning in vision-language-action models for autonomous driving while maintaining strong visual capabilities.

Abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving (AD) increasingly utilize chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision to enhance the reasoning capabilities of their Vision-Language Model (VLM) components, yet existing annotation pipelines commonly expose the teacher model to the logged ground-truth (GT) future trajectory. We empirically show that this induces trajectory anchoring bias: teacher models rationalize the revealed outcome rather than infer a decision from scene evidence, producing less causally faithful CoTs and substantially more severe hallucinations, especially in causally challenging scenes. Removing the GT trajectory eliminates this shortcut, but open-ended trajectory generation entangles high-level decision-making with precise geometric synthesis and low-level dynamics. To make trajectory-level driving decisions verifiable without requiring open-ended trajectory synthesis, we introduce Autonomous-Driving Multiple-Choice Question (AD-MCQ), which casts planning as selection among explicit trajectory candidates. Taking this a step further, we propose Deferred Exposure of Future Trajectories for RLVR (DEFT-RLVR) to transform future trajectories from pre-decision anchors into post-decision verification targets. Experimental results show that DEFT-RLVR improves AD reasoning while preserving or even enhancing general visual capabilities. With VLM-only inference and controllable difficulty through candidate construction, AD-MCQ provides a flexible, scalable, and extensible foundation for future research on verifiable AD reasoning.

</details>


### [134] [Leveraging AI for fine-grained food safety risk forecasting in sparse data conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01767)
*Dongqi Wang,Weiwei Chen,Han Zhou,Weihua Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Transformer-based framework integrates over 11 million food inspection records with demographic/economic/environmental data to forecast city-level food safety risks, using Wilson interval pretraining and outperforming baselines with improved detection rates and resource allocation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Food safety is a critical public health challenge, especially when inspection resources are limited and regional sampling data are sparse, creating a need for more proactive, data-driven oversight rather than reactive measures alone.

Method: Proposes a Transformer-based framework that unifies over 11 million inspection records with demographic, economic, and environmental indicators. Uses three-stage pretraining design leveraging partial supervision from Wilson interval (capturing safety and risk rankings) with semi-supervised label refinement to utilize historical records even with insufficient local samples.

Result: Outperforms baselines significantly in 2022 experimental evaluations. Field experiment with Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation shows improved detection rates and more efficient allocation of inspection resources compared to manually developed plans. Reveals threshold-based heuristic used by inspectors, suggesting additional training or decision-support interfaces could enhance AI impact.

Conclusion: Integration of large-scale public inspection data, Wilson interval-based confidence modeling, and advanced deep learning enables earlier and more granular identification of food safety threats, advancing proactive, data-driven oversight of the global food supply by reducing reliance on reactive measures.

Abstract: Ensuring food safety represents a critical public health challenge, particularly when inspection resources are limited and regional sampling data are sparse. This study proposes a Transformer-based framework capable of forecasting fine-grained, city-level food safety risks by unifying over 11 million inspection records with supplemental demographic, economic, and environmental indicators extracted from the Statistical Yearbook. A three-stage pretraining design leverages partial supervision from the Wilson interval (capturing both safety and risk rankings), together with semi-supervised label refinement, to effectively utilize historical records even when local sample sizes are insufficient. Experimental evaluations on data from 2022 show that the proposed approach outperforms baselines significantly. A subsequent field experiment in collaboration with the Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation further demonstrates improved detection rates and more efficient allocation of inspection resources compared to a manually developed plan. Observations of regulatory decision-making reveal a threshold-based heuristic employed by inspectors, hinting that additional training or decision-support interfaces could further enhance the impact of AI-generated risk scores. Overall, these findings underscore that a rigorous integration of large-scale public inspection data, Wilson interval-based confidence modeling, and advanced deep learning can facilitate earlier and more granular identification of food safety threats. By reducing reliance on reactive measures alone, the proposed framework has the potential to advance proactive, data-driven oversight of the global food supply.

</details>


### [135] [FRAMES: Guarded and Dual-Objective Skill Evolution for Agents in Policy-Governed Enterprise Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01772)
*Xuhui Wang,Ruoqi Shu,Chen Dan,Tianhua Xu,Mengxi Luo,Yanming Mai,Bo Wan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FRAMES is a framework for evolving LLM agents that run enterprise workflows, using consensus-based mutation, Pareto selection, and anti-regression guarantees while preserving auditability and controlling inference costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents running enterprise workflows (like document auditing) face challenges: sparse unlabeled operational feedback, edits causing unrelated regression, need to improve accuracy without increasing inference costs or losing auditability, making agent improvement difficult.

Method: FRAMES cold-starts deployable skills from existing assets, then evolves them through consensus-based mutation, Pareto selection over accuracy and cost, with an anti-regression guarantee, all while preserving auditability.

Result: Deployed on internal production system, FRAMES achieves the best accuracy-cost trade-off among baselines, with same gains reproduced on tau-bench.

Conclusion: FRAMES provides an effective closed-loop framework for improving LLM agents in enterprise workflows that balances accuracy, cost, and auditability while preventing regression.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly run policy-bound enterprise workflows such as document auditing, where they must apply rules consistently, ground every value, and stay auditable. Improving these agents is hard: operational feedback is sparse and unlabeled, edits to one rule can regress unrelated cases, and accuracy must improve without inflating inference cost or losing auditability. We present FRAMES, a closed-loop framework that cold-starts deployable skills from existing assets and then evolves them through consensus-based mutation, Pareto selection over accuracy and cost, and an anti-regression guarantee, all while preserving auditability. Deployed on our internal production system, FRAMES attains the best accuracy-cost trade-off among baselines, with the same gains reproduced on tau-bench.

</details>


### [136] [REFLEX: Rethinking MoE Inference as Refinement-Aware Compute Allocation in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01784)
*Xiang Xia,Cheng Yan,Yiming Zhang,Jiazheng Liu,Hongyu Zhang,Wuyang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: REFLEX is a training-free method for Mixture-of-Experts diffusion language models that aligns expert computation with token refinement demands, reducing expert computation by 15% while maintaining or improving generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MoE inference in diffusion language models suffers from a mismatch: all token positions are revisited equally during denoising despite having different refinement demands, while fixed token-choice routing assigns uniform expert budgets. This creates inefficient computation allocation.

Method: REFLEX keeps the default router unchanged but reorganizes expert computation around the refinement process using a coarse-to-fine hierarchy for expert-budget allocation. It uses the Frontier-Progress Score to resolve active-block priorities and aligns computation with block-relative refinement roles.

Result: On LLaDA-MoE and LLaDA2.0-mini across multiple benchmarks, REFLEX reduces allocated expert computation by 15% on average while preserving or improving generation quality. It provides more consistent quality-computation trade-offs compared to autoregressive-style variable-expert routing methods.

Conclusion: MoE inference in DLMs should be viewed as refinement-aware compute allocation, and REFLEX demonstrates that allocating expert computation according to heterogeneous refinement demands within each denoising forward is crucial for efficient and effective generation.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models increase parameter capacity by activating only a small subset of experts for each token. This conditional-computation paradigm has enabled autoregressive language models to scale model capacity without a proportional increase in per-token computation. In diffusion language models (DLMs), however, each denoising forward jointly revisits all token positions despite their sharply different refinement demands, while the default fixed token-choice routing assigns them a uniform expert budget, creating a mismatch between expert computation and refinement demand. We argue that MoE inference in DLMs should therefore be viewed as refinement-aware compute allocation across heterogeneous token refinement states. We propose REFLEX (\textbf{RE}finement-aware \textbf{FLEX}ible expert allocation), a training-free method that keeps the default router unchanged while reorganizing expert computation around the evolving refinement process. Specifically, REFLEX introduces a coarse-to-fine hierarchy for expert-budget allocation that aligns computation with block-relative refinement roles while using the Frontier-Progress Score to resolve active-block priorities. Across multiple widely used benchmarks on two representative MoE-based DLMs, LLaDA-MoE and LLaDA2.0-mini, REFLEX reduces allocated expert computation by 15\% on average while preserving or even improving generation quality on most benchmarks relative to default routing. Compared with autoregressive-style variable-expert routing methods, REFLEX also yields a more consistent quality--computation trade-off, further supporting the importance of allocating expert computation according to the heterogeneous refinement demands exposed within each denoising forward.

</details>


### [137] [Can You Trust the Confidence? ConfBench for Vision-Language Models on Document Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01792)
*Priyashree Roy,Sujitha Martin,Mohammad Rostami,Spencer Romo,Renhao Xue,Bob Strahan,Diego A. Socolinsky,Boyi Xie,Md Mofijul Islam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConfBench is the first calibration benchmark for document information extraction that evaluates confidence estimation quality across vision-language models using degraded document variants spanning the full accuracy spectrum.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document benchmarks lack low-accuracy samples needed to properly assess calibration of confidence scores for routing extractions between automation and human review in intelligent document processing systems.

Method: Created ConfBench by applying 20 controlled degradation pipelines to diverse documents, generating 1,346 variants with 70K+ entity-level evaluations. Evaluated 7 VLMs under verbalized and log-probability confidence methods across three input modalities.

Result: OCR+Image modality yields better confidence estimates; model capability dominates quality (Claude family scales with capability); calibration varies widely from near-perfect to severely overconfident; log-probability with first-token aggregation consistently outperforms others.

Conclusion: ConfBench enables systematic study of confidence estimation for trustworthy IDP deployment, with findings that post-hoc correction can rescale confidence values without altering operational metrics, and ECARB translates discriminative gains into operational savings.

Abstract: Intelligent document processing (IDP) with vision-language models (VLMs) hinges on confidence scores trustworthy enough to route extractions between automation and human review. Existing document benchmarks are dominated by clean, high-quality samples, leaving low accuracy regions too sparse for calibration assessment. We introduce ConfBench, the first calibration-specific benchmark for key information extraction (KIE), built by applying 20 controlled degradation pipelines to a diverse document set, yielding 1,346 variants and 70K+ entity-level evaluations spanning the full accuracy spectrum. We evaluate four proprietary and three open-weight VLMs under verbalized and log-probability confidence estimation methods across three input modalities, and find: (i) OCR+Image modality results in more accurate confidence estimates; (ii) model capability is the dominant factor: within the Claude family confidence quality scales monotonically with capability, while across families parameter count is a poor predictor; (iii) calibration quality varies widely across models, from near-perfect to severely overconfident, and per-model post-hoc correction rescales these absolute confidence values for threshold-based routing without altering ranking-based operational metrics; and (iv) log-probability with first-token aggregation consistently outperforms mean-token and margin aggregations. We also introduce ECARB, a review-budget metric translating discriminative gains into operational savings. We release ConfBench publicly to enable systematic study of confidence estimators and calibration methods for trustworthy IDP application deployment.

</details>


### [138] [CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01802)
*Junru Song,Wenhao Zhang,Yang Yang,Xuekai Qiu,Feifei Wang,Weien Zhou,Tingsong Jiang,Ying Wen,Yang Li,Wen Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoNav-UAV proposes a Stackelberg game approach with two UAVs (high-altitude leader and low-altitude follower) for target-oriented vision-and-language navigation, achieving better performance than existing methods through cooperative learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Target-oriented vision-and-language navigation for UAVs requires both global exploration/grounding and collision-free close-range approach, which are difficult to reconcile in a single agent. Existing methods either rely on external assistance or use dual UAVs with independent training lacking mutual adaptation.

Method: Models the task as a Stackelberg game with a high-altitude leader and low-altitude follower using only onboard visual and linguistic inputs. Uses Iterative Stackelberg Learning: leader's vision-language reasoning is refined via memory-based in-context learning, while follower's motion control is updated via DAgger-style expert distillation.

Result: Outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes in AerialVLN benchmark. Success rate improves by up to 30.8 points on learning scene and 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer while using about 3x less adaptation data.

Conclusion: The Stackelberg game framework with cooperative learning enables effective UAV navigation combining global reasoning and precise local control, demonstrating robust performance gains across different VLM backbones through complementary agent adaptation.

Abstract: Target-oriented vision-and-language navigation (VLN) on aerial platforms is attracting growing attention for missions such as disaster rescue, infrastructure inspection, and security patrol. In this task, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) needs to locate targets given only a concise description of their appearance and surroundings. This requires global exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods transfer the ground VLN paradigm to a low-altitude UAV and compensate for its inefficient exploration with external assistance. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes yet still relies on privileged information and trains its two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation essential for cooperation. Here we propose CoNav-UAV, which explicitly models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower, with the system operating on onboard visual and linguistic inputs alone. To solve this game, we introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning. The leader's high-level vision-language reasoning is refined via memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is updated via DAgger-style expert distillation. The alternation drives both agents toward a Stackelberg equilibrium. CoNav-UAV consistently outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. Success rate improves by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene, and 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer while using about 3x less adaptation data. Further analyses validate the complementary gains of the leader and follower updates and reveal robust gains yet distinct learning dynamics across VLM backbones.

</details>


### [139] [CockpitHAT: Dependency-Graph-Driven Hierarchical Attribution for Embodied Multi-Agent Cockpits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01805)
*Wei Wang,Shuanghe Liu,Zhu Zhuo,Jiaqi Zhong,Xiaozhao Zhao,Xiaojie Zuo,Jie Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CockpitHAT: A hierarchical attribution framework for diagnosing failures in embodied LLM multi-agent systems by incorporating dependency structure, multi-channel evidence, and safety-aware evaluation to address Correctness Collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM multi-agent systems suffer from "Correctness Collapse" where high task-level accuracy masks severe process-level failures, which is particularly dangerous in safety-critical embodied settings like automotive cockpits where lexically correct utterances could trigger dangerous physical operations. Existing attribution methods rely solely on text traces, missing dependency structure, multi-channel evidence, and safety-aware evaluation.

Method: CockpitHAT is a hierarchical attribution framework that: 1) replaces positional windows with dependency-distance thresholds from interaction DAGs, 2) integrates multi-channel evidence via an embodied adapter, and 3) applies safety-uplift to high-risk failures during confidence-weighted analyst consensus. The authors also release CockpitBench, a benchmark of 212 annotated failure traces spanning dialogue, vehicle-state, environmental, and memory channels, each labeled with ISO 26262 ASIL severity via three-expert consensus.

Result: On the Who&When benchmark, CockpitHAT achieves agent-level/step-exact accuracies of 77.9%/37.8% on Hand-Crafted split and 86.5%/46.0% on Algorithm-Generated split, surpassing text-only SOTA ECHO by up to 17.6/16.7 points. On CockpitBench, it attains 78.3% agent-level and 38.2% step-exact accuracy.

Conclusion: The results establish dependency-aware, multi-channel, risk-calibrated attribution as an effective paradigm for reliable failure diagnosis in real-world embodied LLM multi-agent systems, addressing the critical safety concerns in domains like automotive cockpits.

Abstract: LLM multi-agent systems suffer from Correctness Collapse, where high task-level accuracy conceals severe process-level failures. This is especially hazardous in safety-critical embodied settings such as automotive cockpits, where lexically correct utterances may trigger dangerous physical operations. Existing attribution methods rely on text traces alone, missing dependency structure, multi-channel evidence, and safety-aware evaluation. We introduce CockpitHAT, a hierarchical attribution framework that replaces positional windows with dependency-distance thresholds from interaction DAGs, integrates multi-channel evidence via an embodied adapter, and applies a safety-uplift to high-risk failures during confidence-weighted analyst consensus. We further release CockpitBench, a benchmark of 212 annotated failure traces spanning dialogue, vehicle-state, environmental, and memory channels, each labeled with ISO 26262 ASIL severity via three-expert consensus. On the public Who&When benchmark, CockpitHAT achieves agent-level / step-exact accuracies of 77.9% / 37.8% on the Hand-Crafted split and 86.5% / 46.0% on the Algorithm-Generated split, surpassing the text-only SOTA ECHO by up to 17.6 / 16.7 points. On CockpitBench, it attains 78.3% agent-level and 38.2% step-exact accuracy. These results establish dependency-aware, multi-channel, risk-calibrated attribution as an effective paradigm for reliable failure diagnosis in real-world embodied LLM multi-agent systems.

</details>


### [140] [SearchMaster: Grounded and Regulated Self-Play for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01822)
*Wentao Tan,Qiong Cao,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchMaster is a self-play framework that trains LLM search agents using automatically generated and verified search tasks, addressing issues like pseudo multi-hop questions and inefficient search behavior to produce high-quality training data without human labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training effective LLM-based search agents requires high-quality search data with genuine multi-hop retrieval needs and proper tool use. Existing methods rely on human-written tasks, expert demonstrations, or stronger teacher models, which are expensive and limited. There's a need for scalable, automated methods to generate search training data.

Method: SearchMaster uses self-play with three key controls: 1) Evidence-Chain Generator (ECG) for grounded task generation to prevent pseudo multi-hop questions, 2) Search-Depth Reward (SDR) to assess task difficulty by successful search depth rather than success rate, and 3) Over-Opening Penalty (OOP) to regulate tool use and avoid excessive document browsing. The system generates tasks, solves them, and verifies solutions in a local search environment, with optimized Proposer and Solver rollouts using GRPO.

Result: SearchMaster improves a Qwen3.5-9B backbone from 38.19% to 51.52% average accuracy across six deep-search benchmarks, with particularly strong improvement of 30.1 points on BrowseComp-Plus. The framework demonstrates significant performance gains without requiring human-labeled QA pairs or expert demonstrations.

Conclusion: Grounded and regulated self-play can effectively generate training data for search agents, eliminating the need for expensive human annotations or expert demonstrations while achieving substantial performance improvements on complex search tasks.

Abstract: Training LLM-based search agents requires high-quality search data: tasks that demand genuine multi-hop retrieval and trajectories that use search tools effectively. Existing pipelines often depend on human-written tasks, expert demonstrations, or stronger teacher models. We present SearchMaster, a self-play framework that trains a single LLM from search tasks it generates, solves, and verifies in a local search environment. The key challenge is that self-generated tasks and rollouts can yield misleading signals: pseudo multi-hop questions, success-rate difficulty estimates that ignore search depth, and rollouts with excessive opening but little targeted evidence acquisition. SearchMaster addresses these failure modes with three controls. An Evidence-Chain Generator (ECG) grounds task generation in explicit cross-document evidence chains to reduce pseudo multi-hop questions. A Search-Depth Reward (SDR) scores task difficulty by the search depth of successful rollouts rather than success rate alone, keeping retained tasks search-intensive. An Over-Opening Penalty (OOP) regulates tool use by discouraging excessive document opening, avoiding long but shallow browsing. Verified Proposer and Solver rollouts are then jointly optimized with GRPO. Across six deep-search benchmarks, SearchMaster improves a Qwen3.5-9B backbone from 38.19% to 51.52% average accuracy, with a 30.1-point gain on BrowseComp-Plus. These results show that grounded and regulated self-play can provide effective search-agent training data without human-labeled QA pairs or expert demonstrations. The code is available at https://github.com/WentaoTan/SearchMaster.

</details>


### [141] [Rewriting or Reweighting? A Geometric Account in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01835)
*Juntong Wang,Shengkun Yang,Xiyuan Wang,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Behavioral manifold analysis reveals that supervised fine-tuning rewrites inherited behavioral geometry, while reward optimization preserves but reweights it, exposing mechanistic differences between post-training objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training changes model behavior, but aggregate metrics don't reveal whether it removes existing mechanisms, creates new ones, or changes how inherited mechanisms are used. The paper aims to understand the mechanistic distinction between different post-training objectives.

Method: Introduces behavioral manifold analysis: selects sparse behavior-associated coordinates and lifts them into low-dimensional local charts in two complementary spaces - ACT (runtime activation states) and NOC (functional information flow). Analyzes repetition and sycophancy failures across model families, tracking charts through controlled post-training.

Result: Charts are highly compressed and partially alignable across architectures. ACT charts retain family-specific structure while NOC charts expose architecture-robust shared core. Supervised fine-tuning substantially alters inherited behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization changes behavior while preserving underlying chart structure.

Conclusion: Provides unified geometric framework showing SFT tends to rewrite behavioral geometry while reward optimization primarily reweights it, revealing mechanistic distinctions between post-training objectives that help understand how models change behavior at a mechanistic level.

Abstract: Post-training can substantially alter language-model behavior, yet aggregate behavior rates do not reveal whether training removes an existing mechanism, creates a new one, or changes how an inherited mechanism is used. We study this question through two mechanistically distinct failures, repetition as a decoding-attractor pathology and sycophancy as a preference-related alignment failure. We introduce behavioral manifold analysis, which isolates behavior-specific geometry by selecting sparse behavior-associated coordinates and lifting them into low-dimensional local charts. We construct these charts in two complementary spaces. ACT captures runtime activation states, while NOC quantifies how strongly the model routes functional information flow through the shared behavior-associated subspace. Across multiple model families, the resulting charts are highly compressed and partially alignable across architectures. Contribution-space charts expose a more architecture-robust shared core, whereas activation-space charts retain stronger family-specific structure. Tracking these charts through controlled post-training reveals a consistent asymmetry. Supervised fine-tuning substantially alters the inherited behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization changes behavior while largely preserving the underlying chart. This geometric perspective provides a unified framework for understanding the mechanistic distinction between the two objectives. SFT tends to rewrite behavioral geometry, whereas reward optimization primarily reweights it. Code is available at https://github.com/ronglingze/Manifold-Analysis

</details>


### [142] [PCSD: Persistent Consistency for Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01837)
*Chunji Lv,Yangguang Wei,Junlin Liu,Yang Gao,Ming Liu,Xinming Wang,Jinyang Wu,Guoren Wang,Changsheng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PCSD improves RL training for LLM agents by using persistent consistency self-distillation with adaptive token-level weights instead of unreliable isolated or uniform weights, achieving state-of-the-art results on ALFWorld benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL for large language model agents suffers from sparse rewards where long multi-turn trajectories receive only single outcome-level signals. While on-policy self-distillation provides dense token-level supervision, existing methods either use unreliable isolated token-level discrepancies that are noise-sensitive or uniform step-level weights that ignore positional variation.

Method: Proposes Persistent Consistency Self-Distillation (PCSD) which derives token-level distillation weights from local persistence of teacher-favoring signals. Combines adaptive windows with exponentially decayed aggregation to capture persistent relative teacher support, applies trend-aware modulation to attenuate locally declining support, and uses sigmoid gating for continuous weights. The objective is jointly optimized with GRPO to combine dense teacher guidance with sparse environmental feedback.

Result: Achieves best ALFWorld Overall results among all baselines on both backbones, exceeding GRPO by 15.6 and 13.3 points and SDAR by 6.2 and 5.5 points. Remains competitive on WebShop and gains 15.8 points over GRPO on unseen ALFWorld split, all without inference-time skills.

Conclusion: PCSD effectively addresses the limitations of existing self-distillation methods by using persistent consistency to provide reliable token-level supervision, enabling better RL training for LLM agents in interactive tasks while handling positional variation and teacher reliability issues.

Abstract: Large language model agents have shown strong potential in complex interactive tasks, yet their reinforcement learning (RL) is often hindered by sparse rewards, as a long multi-turn trajectory may receive only a single outcome-level signal. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense token-level supervision from a privileged teacher, but the teacher may not be reliable at every position. Existing methods commonly rely on isolated token-level discrepancies, which can be sensitive to noise, or assign a shared step-level weight that may overlook positional variation. We propose Persistent Consistency Self-Distillation (PCSD), which derives token-level distillation weights from the local persistence of teacher-favoring signals. PCSD combines adaptive windows with exponentially decayed aggregation to capture persistent relative teacher support, applies trend-aware modulation to attenuate locally declining support, and produces continuous weights through sigmoid gating. The resulting objective is jointly optimized with GRPO, combining dense teacher guidance with sparse environmental feedback. Without inference-time skills, PCSD achieves the best ALFWorld Overall results among all baselines on both backbones, exceeding GRPO by 15.6 and 13.3 points and SDAR by 6.2 and 5.5 points, while remaining competitive on WebShop and gaining 15.8 points over GRPO on unseen ALFWorld split.

</details>


### [143] [FOCUS: FP4 Optimization via Coupled-Relaxation and Dual-Granularity Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01847)
*Xianglong Yan,Hong Liu,Chengzhu Bao,Tianao Zhang,Guanghua Yu,Jianchen Zhu,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FOCUS is a post-training quantization framework that enables accurate FP4 quantization of LLMs through coupled-relaxation and dual-granularity scaling, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with no inference overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are expensive to deploy due to their enormous size. While FP4 quantization with formats like MXFP4 and NVFP4 offers native hardware support, maintaining accuracy under FP4 precision remains difficult. Existing methods tightly couple quantization and dequantization scales, forcing both to conform to hardware constraints, but the quantization scale is never stored and need not obey these constraints, creating untapped optimization potential.

Method: Proposed FOCUS framework with two key innovations: 1) Coupled-Relaxation Scaling (CRS) relaxes the tight coupling between quantization and dequantization scales with a learnable full-precision coefficient, enabling effective optimization without breaking hardware compliance. 2) Dual-Granularity Scaling (DGS) refines the quantization scale at a finer sub-block granularity to adapt to local weight distributions.

Result: Experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks show FOCUS achieves state-of-the-art FP4 accuracy under both MXFP4 and NVFP4 formats, while introducing no additional inference overhead.

Conclusion: FOCUS successfully addresses the accuracy challenge in FP4 quantization by decoupling scale optimization from hardware constraints, enabling efficient deployment of LLMs at 4-bit precision with maintained accuracy and no inference penalty.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but are expensive to deploy due to their enormous size. FP4 quantization, with formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4, offers an appealing solution with native hardware support on modern accelerators. However, maintaining accuracy under FP4 precision remains difficult. A key bottleneck lies in scale optimization: existing methods tightly couple the quantization and dequantization scales, forcing both to conform to the discrete low-precision format required by hardware, such as E8M0 in MXFP4. Yet the quantization scale is never stored and need not obey this constraint, suggesting a significant untapped optimization space. In this work, we propose FOCUS, a post-training quantization framework with end-to-end scale learning for FP4 Optimization via Coupled-Relaxation and Dual-Granularity Scaling. Coupled-Relaxation Scaling (CRS) relaxes the tight coupling between quantization and dequantization scales with a learnable full-precision coefficient, enabling more effective optimization without breaking hardware compliance. Dual-Granularity Scaling (DGS) further refines the quantization scale at a finer sub-block granularity, allowing more precise adaptation to local weight distributions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks show that FOCUS achieves state-of-the-art FP4 accuracy under both MXFP4 and NVFP4 formats, while introducing no additional inference overhead. Code and quantized models will be released at https://github.com/tencent/AngelSlim.

</details>


### [144] [Exploring and Bridging Knowledge Holes in Unlearned Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01849)
*Junxiang You,Junkai Chen,Yuhao He,Ruiqi Liu,Zhetao Guo,Shu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPAR (Selective Protection with Anchored Regularization) enables precise unlearning in MLLMs by protecting benign generic patterns while forgetting unsafe content, recovering 98% response quality compared to baselines' 50%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLM unlearning evaluation suffers from a critical blind spot: they assess model utility through benchmarks distant from forget sets, failing to capture "knowledge holes" - severe degradation on benign adjacent inputs sharing generic patterns with forget content.

Method: Proposes Selective Protection with Anchored Regularization (SPAR): protects generic patterns via anchored activation filtering while reinforcing them through entity-abstracted enhancement. Constructed a benchmark to capture unintended degradation on benign inputs sharing generic patterns with forget set.

Result: SPAR recovers over 98% of vanilla response quality compared to below 50% for standard baselines, while achieving 0.00% attack success rate and competitive model utility. Controlled experiments confirm knowledge holes are systematic consequence of commonly used approaches.

Conclusion: The work underscores the necessity of more fine-grained evaluation for trustworthy MLLM unlearning, showing that current approaches create systematic knowledge holes that SPAR successfully addresses through selective protection mechanisms.

Abstract: Machine unlearning offers a promising approach to remove unsafe content from Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), yet ensuring the precision of unlearning remains a persistent challenge. One reason is that current MLLM unlearning evaluation paradigms suffer from a critical blind spot: they assess model utility through benchmarks whose representations are distant from the forget set, failing to capture knowledge holes---severe degradation on benign adjacent inputs. To probe knowledge holes in unlearned MLLMs, we construct a benchmark that captures unintended degradation on benign inputs sharing generic patterns with the forget set, and confirm through controlled experiments that they are a systematic consequence of commonly used approaches. Furthermore, to bridge this gap, we propose Selective Protection with Anchored Regularization, which protects generic patterns via anchored activation filtering while reinforcing them through entity-abstracted enhancement. Our experiments on SafeEraser demonstrate that SPAR recovers over 98% of vanilla response quality compared to below 50% for standard baselines---while achieving 0.00% attack success rate and competitive model utility. These results underscore the necessity of more fine-grained evaluation for trustworthy MLLM unlearning.

</details>


### [145] [Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Complex Eigenfrequency Identification and Mode Structure Reconstruction of the Ground-State ITG Branch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01850)
*Dengdi Sun,Bingbing Zhang,Xiao Wang,Zikang Yan,Yuqiang Tao,Qingquan Yang,Guosheng Xu,Jin Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A physics-informed neural network framework combines Fourier feature encoding, complex-valued propagation, and three-stage training to jointly identify complex eigenfrequencies and reconstruct 2D complex mode fields for ITG drift waves in tokamak pedestal regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are valuable for modeling complex plasma processes, but analyzing ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) drift waves in tokamak pedestal regions presents specific challenges: need for joint identification of complex eigenfrequencies and reconstruction of 2D complex-valued mode fields, with difficulties from localized high-frequency oscillations, strong real-imaginary coupling, and nonlinear coupling between mode field and eigenfrequency.

Method: Proposed physics-informed neural framework combining: 1) Fourier feature encoding to capture localized high-frequency oscillations, 2) Complex-valued feature propagation to handle strong real-imaginary coupling, and 3) Three-stage training strategy to address nonlinear coupling between mode field and eigenfrequency. Framework operates under sparse observations and physical constraints to jointly solve for complex eigenfrequency and mode field.

Result: Experiments show the framework accurately recovers target complex eigenfrequency and 2D complex-valued mode field, outperforming representative PINN baselines. The method successfully handles the challenges of localized oscillations, real-imaginary coupling, and nonlinear mode-eigenfrequency interactions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses challenges in PINN representation for ITG drift wave analysis in tokamak pedestals, providing accurate joint solutions for complex eigenfrequencies and mode fields. It also establishes a foundation for analyzing higher-order and multiple-branch drift-wave modes in plasma physics.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) combine sparse observations with physical equations, providing an important approach for modeling complex plasma processes and inferring unknown physical quantities. The steep-gradient pedestal of high-confinement-mode tokamaks is closely linked to plasma confinement and edge transport. Analyzing ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) drift waves in this region requires jointly identifying complex eigenfrequencies and reconstructing two-dimensional complex-valued mode fields. Localized high-frequency oscillations, strong real-imaginary coupling, and nonlinear coupling between the mode field and eigenfrequency challenge PINN representation and joint optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a physics-informed neural framework combining Fourier feature encoding, complex-valued feature propagation, and three-stage training. Under sparse observations and physical constraints, it jointly solves for the complex eigenfrequency and mode field of a representative ground-state ITG branch. Experiments show that the framework accurately recovers the target complex eigenfrequency and two-dimensional complex-valued mode field and outperforms representative PINN baselines. It also provides a basis for analyzing higher-order and multiple-branch drift-wave modes.

</details>


### [146] [EchoChange: A Diffusion Language Model with Dual Pass Remasking for Factual Remote Sensing Disaster Change Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01856)
*Dongwei Sun,Bowen Yao,Yujie Zhang,Pei Liu,Jing Yao,Xiangyong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EchoChange introduces a diffusion-based model for bi-temporal remote-sensing disaster change captioning that uses iterative denoising instead of autoregressive decoding to reduce cascading factual errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing change captioning methods use autoregressive decoding, where early misinterpretations become irreversible and amplify into cascading factual errors, especially problematic for sparse and localized changes in large disaster scenes.

Method: Proposes EchoChange, a multimodal discrete diffusion language model that formulates change captioning as iterative masked-token denoising rather than left-to-right generation. Includes draft-aware dual-pass training, progressive masking curriculum, and confidence-guided remasking to align training with inference.

Result: Extensive experiments on the RSCC benchmark show EchoChange substantially outperforms both general-purpose and remote-sensing-specific baselines across lexical and semantic metrics.

Conclusion: EchoChange's iterative revision approach effectively addresses the limitations of autoregressive decoding in remote-sensing change captioning by allowing reconsideration of uncertain content and correction of imperfect predictions.

Abstract: Bi-temporal remote-sensing disaster change captioning often needs to identify sparse and spatially localized changes across large pre- and post-event scenes and then translate them into coherent, factual descriptions. However, existing change captioning methods always follow an autoregressive decoding paradigm to generate the change description and thus an early misinterpretation of the changed object, event, or spatial relation becomes an irreversible premise for subsequent text, amplifying visual ambiguity into cascading factual errors. To address this limitation, we propose EchoChange, a multimodal discrete diffusion language model that formulates change captioning as iterative masked-token denoising rather than left-to-right generation. By repeatedly revising the entire caption while conditioning on the image pair, EchoChange can reconsider uncertain content and correct imperfect intermediate predictions. We further introduce draft-aware dual-pass training, a progressive masking curriculum, and confidence-guided remasking to align training with iterative inference. Extensive experiments on the RSCC benchmark show that EchoChange substantially outperforms both general-purpose and remote-sensing-specific baselines across lexical and semantic metrics. The EchoChange Project is at https://github.com/sundongwei/EchoChange_Project

</details>


### [147] [Wnuan: Staged Post-Training for Question Answering over Proprietary Enterprise Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01862)
*Xiaofeng Shi,Xiaosong Qiu,Wenxin Ma,Qian Kou,Yiming Pan,Longbin Yu,Ying Liu,Haiping Wang,Hua Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A three-stage pipeline (Wnuan) improves enterprise question answering by constructing task-oriented supervision from documents, performing supervised fine-tuning with general-data replay, and applying reinforcement learning to residual errors, achieving significant performance gains on enterprise QA while maintaining most general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise question answering systems need to acquire proprietary knowledge from company documents while maintaining general capabilities - current models often lose general abilities when adapted to specific enterprise domains.

Method: Wnuan uses a three-stage pipeline: 1) Constructs task-oriented supervision from enterprise documents, 2) Performs supervised fine-tuning with general-data replay to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and 3) Applies reinforcement learning focused on residual errors. The approach includes specific sampling strategies like residual-error sampling compared against baselines.

Result: On WnuanBench (707 questions), acceptable-answer rate increased from 52.76% before adaptation to 80.06% after SFT and 91.51% after RL. Residual-error sampling outperformed other sampling methods by ~3 points. General benchmark average decreased by only 5.17 points, mainly in instruction following. Automatic evaluation agreed with domain expert on 90.5% of responses.

Conclusion: Staged enterprise adaptation effectively improves domain-specific performance while controlling general-capability degradation, with reinforcement learning on residual errors being particularly effective for final performance gains, though some instruction-following capability is traded for domain expertise.

Abstract: Enterprise question answering requires models to acquire proprietary knowledge without discarding general capabilities. We present Wnuan, a three-stage pipeline that constructs task-oriented supervision from documents, performs supervised fine-tuning with general-data replay, and applies reinforcement learning to residual errors. On the 707-question WnuanBench, the primary 32B route raises acceptable-answer rate (AAR) from 52.76% before adaptation to 80.06% after SFT and 91.51% after RL. Under a matched 100-update protocol, residual-error sampling outperforms full-pool and size-matched random sampling by 3.11 and 2.97 points, respectively.
