Method: Develops a four-layer theory: 1) Static layer defines decision-theoretic adequacy via Bayes-risk grouping and pricing verification via total-variation threshold; 2) Sequential layer frames certification as optimal-stopping problem, defines certification complexity constant via covering linear program, proves information-task-loss lower bound, and provides Certification Track-and-Stop policy; 3) Final boundary layer gives kernel-switching example and identifies open theorem for policy switching/representation repair.

Result: 1) Theoretical framework for self-certification of representation adequacy; 2) Certification Track-and-Stop policy with asymptotic cost matching lower bound; 3) Information-task-loss lower bound for all delta-correct strategies; 4) Exact total-variation threshold for one-shot verification pricing.

Conclusion: The paper develops a comprehensive theoretical framework for agents to self-certify representation adequacy, with asymptotic optimality guarantees for the certification process, though extensions to representation revision remain an open problem requiring further theorem development.

Abstract: Agents that act on a compressed representation of their history face a structural risk: if the representation aliases histories with different optimal actions, no rule measurable with respect to the representation can avoid an irreducible per-round loss, and the agent may be unable to detect this from its own transcript. This paper develops a four-layer theory of self-certification of representation adequacy. The static layer defines decision-theoretic adequacy through a Bayes-risk grouping identity and prices a one-shot external verification by an exact total-variation threshold. The sequential layer poses certification as an optimal-stopping problem in the currency of task loss: we define an environment-wise certification complexity constant through a covering linear program, prove an information-task-loss lower bound for every delta-correct strategy, and give a Certification Track-and-Stop policy whose cost matches the bound asymptotically. A final boundary layer gives an explicit kernel-switching example and identifies the open theorem needed to cover policy switching or representation repair; it does not claim that the fixed-kernel guarantees extend to representation revision. The proofs of the two main theorems are given in full in the appendices.

</details>


### [174] [Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02276)
*Shuai Shao,Kangning Zhang,Qingyao Li,Shijian Wang,Hao Wang,Wenxiang Jiao,Yuan Lu,Yi Guo,Weiwen Liu,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Harness-R1 is a method that trains a dedicated "harness engineer" model to learn how to edit an agent's execution runtime (the harness) based on observed failures, improving success rates across multiple benchmarks without modifying the base agent's weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While agents accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, their behavior remains fixed. These trajectories could be used to improve the agent harness (context construction, tool mediation, action validation, execution recovery) rather than just updating model weights.

Method: Harness-R1 post-trains a 9B harness engineer using online reinforcement learning. It converts batches of agent failures into executable patches. The frozen target agent is rerun with these patches, providing outcome rewards for training. The approach starts with supervised fine-tuning, then uses group-relative policy optimization for online training.

Result: Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench benchmarks, Harness-R1 raised vanilla Qwen3.5-9B success from 44.3% to 53.6% (+9.3 percentage points). After direct target-agent fine-tuning, success increased further from 59.2% to 64.2% (+5.0 points).

Conclusion: Harness-R1 demonstrates that learned editing of agent harnesses can significantly improve performance. Since gains hold both before and after fine-tuning the target agent, it points toward co-evolving the harness engineer with the target agent for continuous improvement.

Abstract: Agents built around large language models continually accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, yet their behavior typically remains fixed. Beyond updating model weights, these trajectories can improve the agent harness that constructs context, mediates tools, validates actions, and recovers execution. We introduce Harness-R1, the first method, to our knowledge, that makes failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing of an existing executable runtime a learned capability. It post-trains a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning so that its edits are optimized for the realized task success they produce, rather than proposed by a fixed editor. A separate 9B engineer converts batches of target-agent failures into validated executable patches; fresh same-batch reruns of the frozen target provide outcome rewards, so training updates only the engineer. Cold-start supervised fine-tuning initializes this editing policy, which is then trained online with group-relative policy optimization. Across WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench, Harness-R1 raises vanilla Qwen3.5-9B success from 44.3% to 53.6% (+9.3 percentage points). After direct target-agent fine-tuning, a target-specific engineer raises the average further from 59.2% to 64.2% (+5.0 points); because these gains hold both before and after fine-tuning the target, Harness-R1 points toward co-evolving the harness engineer and the target agent.

</details>


### [175] [SKT: Skill-Use Training at Scale via Verified Synthetic Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02287)
*Zelin Tan,Yiqun Zhang,Hao Li,Zhiyao Cui,Hejia Geng,Shao Zhang,Hangfan Zhang,Yang Chen,Xiaosong Wang,Lilong Wang,Zhenfei Yin,Shuyue Hu,Chen Zhang,Lei Bai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKT is a pipeline for synthesizing verified skill-grounded tasks and trajectories from existing agent skills to improve LLM agents' ability to identify, apply, and coordinate skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language-model agents struggle to effectively use available skills despite having access to them. Skills alone don't guarantee that models can properly identify, apply, and coordinate them for complex tasks.

Method: SKT pipeline selects suitable single-skill and multi-skill configurations, synthesizes tasks through rule-based and agent-based verification with feedback-guided repair, and retains only successful trajectories that substantially use every required skill.

Result: Using 2,000 public skills, SKT produces 4,000 task packages and 27,164 verified trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning on SKT-generated trajectories consistently improves skill-use performance across diverse models and benchmarks.

Conclusion: Verified data synthesis is an effective and scalable approach for improving skill-use training in language-model agents, with gains depending on high-quality supervision and extending beyond single agent interfaces.

Abstract: Agent skills have become an important mechanism for equipping language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge. However, providing skills alone does not guarantee that current models can effectively identify, apply, and coordinate them. To improve skill-use capabilities, we introduce SKT, a verified data synthesis pipeline that constructs skill-grounded tasks and executable trajectories from large collections of agent skills. SKT selects suitable single-skill and multi-skill configurations, synthesizes tasks through rule-based and agent-based verification with feedback-guided repair, and retains only successful trajectories that substantially use every required skill. Using 2,000 public skills, SKT produces 4,000 task packages and 27,164 verified trajectories. Based on the same pipeline and a disjoint test pool, we further construct SkillEval, a held-out executable benchmark for evaluating skill use. Experiments across diverse models, benchmarks, and agent harnesses show that supervised fine-tuning on SKT-generated trajectories consistently improves skill-use performance. Verification ablations, cross-harness evaluation, and scaling experiments further demonstrate that these gains depend on high-quality supervision, extend beyond a single agent interface, and increase with broader skill coverage. Together, these results establish verified data synthesis as an effective and scalable approach for skill-use training.

</details>


### [176] [Shared Prefixes, Better Credit: Adaptive Routing for Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02291)
*Yiqing Liu,Zihao Wang,Hantao Yao,Wu Liu,Yongdong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TreeCredit: A shared-prefix credit assignment framework for multi-agent reasoning that improves accuracy while significantly reducing inference costs through efficient operator selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adaptive multi-agent reasoning methods use coarse supervision (query-level labels or trajectory-level returns) that cannot accurately estimate the state-conditioned utility of individual operators in multi-step collaboration, leading to inefficient credit assignment.

Method: TreeCredit estimates operator utility through state-matched downstream comparisons rather than direct trajectory attribution. It constructs shared-prefix collaboration trees by expanding candidate operators from the same intermediate state, assigns correctness-prioritized suffix credits based on terminal correctness and cumulative additional costs, and trains a lightweight pairwise state router for dynamic operator selection during inference.

Result: Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show TreeCredit modestly improves accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost, achieving a better accuracy-cost trade-off than representative multi-agent reasoning methods.

Conclusion: TreeCredit provides an effective credit assignment framework for adaptive multi-agent reasoning that enables more efficient and reliable collaborative reasoning through structured operator utility estimation and dynamic routing.

Abstract: Multi-agent reasoning (MAR) improves reasoning reliability through iterative solution exchange and refinement. Existing adaptive MAR methods typically learn routing decisions from query-level labels or trajectory-level returns, but such coarse supervision cannot accurately estimate the state-conditioned utility of individual operators in multi-step collaboration. We propose TreeCredit, a shared-prefix credit assignment framework for efficient adaptive MAR. Its core insight is to estimate operator utility through state-matched downstream comparisons, rather than directly attributing trajectory-level outcomes to preceding decisions. TreeCredit constructs shared-prefix collaboration trees by expanding candidate operators from the same intermediate state and assigns each state--operator pair a correctness-prioritized suffix credit based on the terminal correctness and cumulative additional cost of its complete continuation. These structured credits are converted into state-local operator preferences to train a lightweight pairwise state router, which dynamically selects the next admissible operator during inference. Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show that TreeCredit modestly improves accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost, achieving a better accuracy--cost trade-off than representative MAR methods.

</details>


### [177] [MechGeo: Autoformalizing and Proving Euclidean Geometry in Lean 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02295)
*Hao Shen,Junyu Guo,Tian Cui,Yuxuan Xiao,Lihong Zhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MechGeo is a Mathlib-native agentic framework for autoformalizing and proving Euclidean geometry problems, achieving state-of-the-art results on IMO problems with kernel-checked proofs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a need for trustworthy formal geometry systems that can faithfully autoformalize informal geometry problems and construct certified proofs, addressing challenges in automated theorem proving for Euclidean geometry.

Method: The framework has two main components: GeoFormalizer converts informal problems to GeoIR, deterministically translates to Lean 4, and iteratively repairs statements using diagnostics and semantic evaluation. GeoProver constructs proof plans, derives lemmas, and algebraizes subgoals using a verified Lean library, with algebraic certificates from Singular/SymPy all kernel-checked.

Result: Experiments across 7 LLMs show significant autoformalization improvements. On 43 historical IMO problems: 29 proved, 14 counterexamples found and repaired statements proved after correction. On LEAP's Lean-IMO-Bench: 12 proved (first time), 2 formally refuted, both repaired statements proved. Largest reported collection of automated, kernel-checked Lean proofs for IMO geometry.

Conclusion: Counterexample guided diagnosis, geometric reasoning, and certified symbolic computation form a practical foundation for trustworthy formal geometry, with MechGeo demonstrating substantial advances in automated theorem proving for Euclidean geometry.

Abstract: We present MechGeo, a Mathlib native agentic framework that jointly addresses faithful autoformalization and certified proof construction for Euclidean geometry. In this framework, GeoFormalizer represents informal problems in GeoIR, deterministically translates them into Lean 4, and iteratively repairs candidate statements using structural diagnostics and semantic evaluation. GeoProver constructs geometric proof plans, derives intermediate lemmas, and selectively algebraizes suitable subgoals through a library verified in Lean. Singular or SymPy may generate algebraic certificates, but all resulting proofs and counterexamples are checked by Lean's kernel. Experiments across seven LLM backbones show substantial improvements in autoformalization, particularly for models with weaker direct translation performance. On 43 historical IMO geometry problems, GeoFormalizer generates formal statements that GeoProver proves in 29 cases; for the remaining 14, it constructs counterexamples verified in Lean and proves all repaired statements after expert correction. Together with IMO 2026 Problem 2, this yields, to the best of our knowledge, the largest reported collection of automated, kernel-checked Lean proofs for IMO geometry problems. On the 14 geometry statements in LEAP's Lean-IMO-Bench, MechGeo proves 12 for the first time, formally refutes the remaining two, and proves both repaired statements. These results establish counterexample guided diagnosis, geometric reasoning, and certified symbolic computation as a practical foundation for trustworthy formal geometry.

</details>


### [178] [Trajectories That Segment Themselves: Agent-Declared Boundaries as a Training Unit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02302)
*Jingxi Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces semantic self-segmentation for coding-agent trajectories, where agents declare hypotheses during action to create meaningful phase boundaries, enabling better training supervision and revealing coherent semantic phases without manual annotation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current training of coding agents suffers from poor credit assignment: single actions lack stable value, episode labels mix exploration with dead ends, and fixed windows cut arbitrarily. There's a need for semantically meaningful trajectory segmentation that captures the actual reasoning phases.

Method: Collection-time semantic self-segmentation using declarative contracts: agents expose boundaries by stating falsifiable causal hypotheses while generating trajectories. This creates variable-length semantic phases without needing milestone vocabularies, gold patches, environment replay, teacher logits, or retrospective segmentation.

Result: 1) Models can attribute action blocks to governing hypotheses at >2x chance accuracy; 2) Code-blind human annotators match 24/40 boundaries vs random 11.5; 3) Mechanical rules fail to reproduce segmentation; 4) DPO training on phase-boundary pairs improves performance on adversarial test items.

Conclusion: Semantic self-segmentation creates coherent, non-reproducible segments that improve training supervision. The approach enables manufacturing of "wrong-cause-then-correction" transitions and provides audit supervision from failed regions normally discarded by episode labels.

Abstract: Long-horizon coding-agent trajectories are poorly matched to the credit units available to train on: a single action has no stable value, an episode label merges productive exploration with abandoned directions, and a fixed window cuts where the logging mechanics fall. We introduce collection-time semantic self-segmentation, in which a declarative contract has the acting agent expose its own boundaries while the trajectory is generated. Instantiated with falsifiable causal hypotheses, successive adoptions expose variable-length semantic phases, and no milestone vocabulary, gold patch, environment replay, teacher logits, or retrospective segmenter places a boundary. Because the agent names its conjecture, a reviewer can negate it by name, which lets our protocol manufacture wrong-cause-then-correction transitions that recorded work rarely contains; one collection then yields four supervised targets, including audit supervision from exactly the failed regions an episode label discards. We then ask what survives deleting the declaration. Given the cut points but not the hypothesis, a model attributes action blocks to their governing hypothesis at over twice chance, beating equal-length blocks over the same trajectories (paired sign test $p = 0.0002$), surviving a lexical control and collapsing under label permutation. Asked instead to place boundaries, a code-blind annotator matches 24 of 40 where random placement matches 11.5, while a mechanical test-event rule beats chance at neither end of a strict-to-permissive sweep. The segments are therefore coherent and not cheaply reproducible. Downstream, DPO on 2,551 phase-boundary pairs changes no decision on 91 adversarial held-out items, while four of 60 change on matched-construction items, all wrong to right, where two controls change none: with 1,825 pairs from one generator, the variable to vary next is corpus diversity, not the boundary.

</details>


### [179] [Hard Constraints, Smooth Gradients: Learning Feasible Inventory Policies via Differentiable Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02343)
*Patrick Helm,Jan-Niklas Doerr,Joren Gijsbrechts,Stefan Minner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DRL policy with embedded differentiable convex optimization that enforces hard constraints via neural network proposals, quadratic program projection, and dual-informed integer mapping for sequential decision problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many operational problems involve constrained sequential decision processes with large combinatorial action spaces and interdependent feasibility constraints. While MILPs handle constraints flexibly, they scale poorly in stochastic environments. DRL offers scalable decision rules but existing methods either penalize constraints or rely on fragile feasibility mechanisms that fail when constraints interact.

Method: Embed a differentiable convex optimization module inside the policy: 1) Neural network proposes continuous action targets, 2) Quadratic program projects them onto relaxed feasible set, 3) Dual-informed integer mapping restores integrality while preserving feasibility. Trained end-to-end from sampled trajectories using pathwise gradients with a differentiable simulator.

Result: Method achieves average optimality gap below 1% on small instances, outperforms state-of-the-art echelon base-stock policies by up to 9.75%, and beats rolling-horizon multi-stage stochastic program by at least 7.7% in larger networks. On ASML industry case study, reduces average cost by up to 3.22% relative to best-known benchmark. Savings are largest in tightly capacitated systems with high demand variability.

Conclusion: DRL can deliver economically significant savings in sequential decision problems with interdependent hard constraints, which are widespread in practice. The proposed method bridges the gap between MILP constraint handling and DRL scalability by embedding differentiable optimization within the policy architecture.

Abstract: Many operational problems are constrained sequential decision processes with large, combinatorial action spaces and interdependent feasibility constraints. Mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) handle such constraints flexibly but scale poorly in stochastic environments. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) promises scalable decision rules, but existing methods either penalize constraints rather than enforce them, or rely on feasibility mechanisms that break down once constraints interact. We bridge this gap by embedding a differentiable convex optimization module inside the policy: a neural network proposes continuous action targets, a quadratic program projects them onto the relaxed feasible set, and a dual-informed integer mapping restores integrality while preserving feasibility. Given a differentiable simulator, the policy trains end to end from sampled trajectories using pathwise gradients, while handling hard constraints with similar flexibility to MILPs. We show that our feasibility enforcement has bounded error relative to an exact integer projection and ensures the entire feasible action space is reachable. We apply the method to multi-echelon production-inventory planning under shared resource and material constraints. Our policy attains an average optimality gap below 1% on small instances. It further outperforms state-of-the-art echelon base-stock policies by up to 9.75% and a rolling-horizon multi-stage stochastic program by at least 7.7% in larger networks. On an industry-scale case study from ASML, it reduces average cost by up to 3.22% relative to the best-known benchmark policy. The savings are largest where planning is hardest: in tightly capacitated systems with high demand variability. More broadly, our work shows that DRL can deliver economically significant savings in sequential decision problems with interdependent hard constraints, which are widespread in practice.

</details>


### [180] [Mamba with Hierarchical Memory: Solving Representation Bottleneck in Long Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02347)
*Qinwen Wang,Jieping Luo,Aoxiang Qin,Ruoyu Zhao,Jianxiong Tang,Wei Zhang,Zhichao Lu,Luziwei Leng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HMM introduces hierarchical memory architecture to Mamba models, improving long-sequence modeling with minimal parameter overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent linear attention models (RLAs) like Mamba offer efficient linear-time sequence modeling, but their fixed-capacity recurrent states limit long-sequence modeling capabilities.

Method: Proposes Hierarchical Memory Mamba (HMM) built on pre-trained Mamba backbone, integrating a lightweight working memory that extracts paragraph-level semantics from hidden states, then compresses them into persistent long-term memory for task-relevant retrieval.

Result: HMM improves retrieval success by 34.3-37.1% and reasoning accuracy by 1.6-14.2% over strong Mamba-based models on Passkey Retrieval and LongBench-E tasks, adding only 2% extra parameters with minimal training overhead.

Conclusion: HMM's hierarchical processing overcomes representation bottlenecks in RLAs, enables cross-task generalization through parametric learning, and provides an effective approach to enhance long-context modeling in Mamba variants.

Abstract: Recurrent linear attention models (RLAs) such as Mamba offer efficient linear-time sequence modeling as an alternative to Transformers, yet their fixed-capacity recurrent states limit long-sequence modeling. Drawing inspiration from hierarchical human memory, we propose Hierarchical Memory Mamba (HMM) to address this limitation. Building upon a pre-trained Mamba backbone, HMM integrates a lightweight working memory that extracts slow paragraph-level semantics (PLS) from the fast sensory memory embedded in the backbone's hidden states. The PLS is subsequently compressed into persistent long-term memory for task-relevant retrieval. The hierarchical processing of semantic information overcomes the representation bottleneck of RLAs and endows HMM cross-task generalization through parametric learning, which is not observed in other long-context enhanced Mamba variants. Evaluations on Passkey Retrieval and LongBench-E tasks demonstrate that HMM improves retrieval success by 34.3--37.1% and reasoning accuracy by 1.6--14.2% over strong Mamba-based models, while adding only 2% extra parameters and with minimal training overhead.

</details>


### [181] [KC-Agent: A Dual-Process Cognitive Architecture for Efficient ML Model Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02351)
*Gusseppe Bravo-Rocca,Jordi Guitart,Ajay Dholakia,David Ellison,Puneet Jain*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KC-Agent is a dual-process cognitive architecture for automated ML model improvement that combines fast pattern recognition with deliberate incremental updates to handle data drift efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data drift poses significant challenges for ML systems in production, requiring continuous model updates to maintain performance. Existing approaches may not efficiently handle the balance between quick responses and deliberate updates needed for real-world data drift scenarios.

Method: Presents KC-Agent, a dual-process cognitive architecture with System 1 (fast pattern recognition) and System 2 (deliberate incremental updates). Implements structured memory systems to allow System 1 to leverage successful solutions discovered by System 2. Incorporates atomic change principles and rollback capabilities for reliable, verifiable updates in production environments.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance (76.8% accuracy) with optimal efficiency (13.2s execution time), outperforming established cognitive architectures: CodeAct (+2.4%), Tree of Thoughts (+3.6%), ReAct (+8.0%), and Reflexion (+8.9%). Consensus evaluation by LLM panel confirms superior strategic efficacy (8.33/10 Smartness score). Knowledge consolidation delivers 91% speedup over slow variant while maintaining higher accuracy.

Conclusion: KC-Agent demonstrates both theoretical foundations and practical viability for cognitive-inspired automated ML improvement systems capable of handling complex real-world data drift scenarios through efficient dual-process architecture and knowledge consolidation mechanisms.

Abstract: Data drift poses significant challenges for machine learning systems in production, requiring continuous model updates to maintain performance. We present KC-Agent, a dual-process cognitive architecture for automated ML model improvement that combines fast pattern recognition (System 1) with deliberate incremental updates (System 2). Our approach implements structured memory systems enabling System 1 to leverage successful solutions previously discovered by System 2, achieving efficient pattern-based responses without costly re-computation. KC-Agent incorporates atomic change principles and rollback capabilities to ensure reliable, verifiable updates in production environments. We evaluate our method on five datasets including real-world NASA turbofan data with authentic temporal degradation and synthetic datasets with controlled drift scenarios. KC-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance (76.8% accuracy) while maintaining optimal efficiency (13.2s execution time), outperforming established cognitive architectures: CodeAct (+2.4%), Tree of Thoughts (+3.6%), ReAct (+8.0%), and Reflexion (+8.9%). Consensus evaluation by a panel of state-of-the-art LLMs confirms superior strategic efficacy (8.33/10 Smartness score), significantly outperforming baseline agents. The knowledge consolidation mechanism delivers 91% speedup over the slow variant while maintaining higher accuracy. Our approach demonstrates both theoretical foundations and practical viability for cognitive-inspired automated ML improvement systems capable of handling complex real-world data drift scenarios.

</details>


### [182] [SkillTrace: Traversing a Query-Skill Graph for Composable LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02356)
*Yue Yao,Shengyuan Wang,Xin Chen,Minke Zhang,Jia He,Bingjun Luo,Tom Gedeon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillTrace is a graph-based method for retrieving complete executable skill compositions for LLM agents by modeling three levels of relations: compositional queries, query-candidate similarity, and skill dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents solve complex tasks by composing reusable skills, the key challenge is not just retrieving individually relevant skills, but finding complete and executable skill compositions that can work together effectively.

Method: SkillTrace organizes user queries into semantic hierarchies, matches skill queries with candidates in the library, and propagates over skill dependencies using a three-level graph structure: compositional relations among skill queries, similarity between queries and candidates, and dependencies among selected candidates.

Result: SkillTrace achieves state-of-the-art performance with 53.17% success rate on SkillsBench and 91.43% on ALFWorld. It also shows consistent improvements across different backbone language models, demonstrating generality and robustness.

Conclusion: Graph-based skill retrieval with three-level modeling effectively solves the skill composition problem for LLM agents, providing a generalizable and robust approach that outperforms existing methods across different domains and language models.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly solve complex tasks by composing reusable skills from a library. To address this, the key challenge is not merely to retrieve individually relevant skills, but to identify a complete and executable skill composition. In this paper, we argue that this problem can be solved in a graph with three levels: compositional relations among skill queries, similarity between queries and candidates in the skill library, and the dependencies among the selected candidates. We introduce SkillTrace, which organizes the user query into a semantic hierarchy, matches skill queries and candidates, and propagates over the skill dependencies. Experiments on SkillsBench and ALFWorld demonstrate that SkillTrace achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching a success rate of 53.17% on SkillsBench and 91.43% on ALFWorld. SkillTrace also delivers consistent improvements across different backbone language models, demonstrating the generality and robustness of graph-based skill retrieval.

</details>


### [183] [Faster-WAM: Do World Action Models Need Deep Action Modules?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02365)
*Liheng Ma,Rui Heng Yang,Zhanguang Zhang,Mateo Clemente,Ziwen Hu,Tongtong Cao,Yingxue Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster-WAM introduces a Dock of Transformer (DoT) architecture that decouples action modules from video backbones, achieving 3.2× speedup over prior methods while maintaining competitive performance on robotic action prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing World Action Models (WAMs) suffer from high computational overhead and inference latency because they tie action module depth to video backbone depth using shared-backbone or Mixture-of-Transformers designs.

Method: Proposes Dock of Transformer (DoT) - a video-centric design that treats pretrained video Transformers as representation hubs and connects lightweight output-heads through docking interfaces, which fuse keys/values from all video layers and apply RoPE realignment.

Result: Faster-WAM achieves competitive performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, strong out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus, and only 66.5 ms per inference (3.2× speedup over Fast-WAM) with the lowest end-to-end latency.

Conclusion: The video-centric DoT architecture enables flexible task-specific head design while delivering low inference latency, strong action prediction performance, and robust generalization without requiring additional embodied pretraining.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) couple robot action prediction with video world models. Existing WAMs with shared-backbone and Mixture-of-Transformers designs generally tie the depth of the action module to that of the video backbone, resulting in substantial computational overhead and high inference latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Dock of Transformer (DoT), a video-centric design principle that treats a pretrained video Transformer as a representation hub and connects lightweight output-heads through docking interfaces. This enables flexible output-head design while providing direct access to representations from all layers of the backbone. We then introduce \textbf{Faster-WAM}, an instantiation of DoT for WAMs, which docks a single-layer action head onto a 30-layer video backbone. The docking interface fuses keys and values from all video layers and applies RoPE realignment. Without additional embodied pretraining, Faster-WAM achieves competitive performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 while demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus. Faster-WAM also achieves the lowest end-to-end latency in our controlled comparison, requiring only 66.5 ms per inference --- a \(3.2\times\) speedup over Fast-WAM. Overall, these results demonstrate that the video-centric DoT architecture supports flexible task-specific head design while delivering low inference latency, strong action-prediction performance, and robust generalization.

</details>


### [184] [Chess on Ice: Curling Tactical Decision-Making via Backward Induction and Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02379)
*Patrick Oberlin,Matteo Cederle,Aren Karapetyan,Saverio Bolognani,Gian Antonio Susto,Florian Dörfler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reinforcement learning framework using DDPG is developed to evaluate curling tactics, enabling self-supervised strategy learning and quantitative comparison of tactical options without human data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Curling, despite being called "Chess on Ice" for its tactical complexity, remains largely unexplored from a machine learning perspective, with prior work limited to statistical approaches. The authors aim to address this gap by creating a machine learning framework for tactical evaluation in curling.

Method: The authors propose a reinforcement learning framework using the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) actor-critic algorithm, adapted to exploit the finite-horizon structure of curling. This approach addresses curling's modeling challenges: continuous state/action spaces, stochastic action outcomes reflecting player skill variability, and state transitions sensitive to small action perturbations.

Result: On a reduced four-rock variant of curling, the learned agent matches a hand-crafted expert heuristic in a regime where that heuristic is close to optimal. The learned critic provides dense value estimates over the entire continuous action space, enabling quantitative comparison of tactical alternatives.

Conclusion: Effective curling strategies can be acquired through fully self-supervised reinforcement learning without human-annotated data. The framework enables quantitative tactical evaluation for applications like post-game performance analysis and decision support during athlete preparation.

Abstract: Curling is often referred to as "Chess on Ice", owing to the tactical complexity of its decision-making process. Yet unlike chess, curling remains largely underexplored from a machine learning perspective, with prior work confined mainly to statistical approaches. We propose a reinforcement learning framework capable of quantitatively evaluating and comparing tactical options in curling. The game poses several modeling challenges: continuous state and action spaces, stochastic action outcomes reflecting player skill variability, and state transitions that are highly sensitive to small perturbations in the executed action. To address them, we employ the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient actor-critic algorithm, adapted to exploit the finite-horizon structure of the game. Our experiments show that effective curling strategies can be acquired in a fully self-supervised manner, without any human-annotated data: on a reduced four-rock variant, the learned agent matches a hand-crafted expert heuristic in a regime where that heuristic is close to optimal, a parity we quantify against the intrinsic hammer advantage of the variant. Beyond the resulting policy, the learned critic provides a dense value estimate over the entire continuous action space, enabling the quantitative comparison of tactical alternatives for applications such as post-game performance analysis and decision support during athlete preparation.

</details>


### [185] [Cooperative Coevolution for Resource-Constrained Agentic LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02391)
*Zhiyuan Wang,Shengcai Liu,Jiahao Wu,Ning Lu,Hui Ouyang,Shaofeng Zhang,Haoze Lv,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoPES introduces a cooperative coevolutionary method that decomposes LLM parameter space into subspaces for memory-efficient post-training of tool-using agents under GPU constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gradient-based post-training of tool-using LLM agents is memory-intensive due to long trajectories, while evolution strategies require too many GPU-hours for resource-constrained settings with few GPUs.

Method: Cooperative Parameter-subspace Evolution Strategy (CoPES) decomposes the full parameter space into lower-dimensional subspaces and searches over them cooperatively to improve optimization efficiency.

Result: CoPES recovers 92% of GRPO's validation-accuracy gain vs 67% for standard ES, with theoretical memory requirement less than 1/8 of GRPO. It consistently outperforms standard ES and LoRA-based GRPO across five benchmarks.

Conclusion: CoPES demonstrates an improved trade-off between memory requirements and training time for agentic LLM post-training under resource constraints, achieving strong performance with reduced GPU memory and hours.

Abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents produce long, multi-turn trajectories, making gradient-based post-training memory-intensive. Evolution strategies (ES) enable memory-efficient full-parameter post-training without backpropagation and can eventually match the performance of gradient-based reinforcement learning (RL). However, resource-constrained settings typically offer only a few GPUs, so the high GPU-hour requirements of ES translate into prohibitively long training times. To address this, we introduce Cooperative Parameter-subspace Evolution Strategy (CoPES), a cooperative coevolutionary method that decomposes the full parameter space into lower-dimensional subspaces and searches over them cooperatively to improve optimization efficiency. We post-train a Qwen3.5-4B tool-using agent for the math task and evaluate it on five benchmarks of varying difficulty. Under the GPU-hour budget of full-parameter GRPO's best validation checkpoint, CoPES recovers 92% of GRPO's validation-accuracy gain, versus 67% for standard ES, while its theoretical GPU memory requirement is less than one-eighth that of full-parameter GRPO. It consistently outperforms standard ES and LoRA-based GRPO on all evaluated pass@k metrics across the five benchmarks. Additional experiments further show the advantage of CoPES on the question-answering task. These results demonstrate an improved trade-off between memory requirements and training time for agentic LLM post-training under resource constraints. The code is open-sourced in https://github.com/MetaronWang/CoPES

</details>


### [186] [MonitrLLM: A Community-Centered Evaluation Infrastructure for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02409)
*Victor Ojewale,Ro Encarnación,Suresh Venkatasubramanian,Danaé Metaxa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MonitrLLM is an open-source infrastructure that links full conversation transcripts to user-reported task intent and outcomes, addressing the gap in LLM evaluation by connecting interaction trajectories with user-defined results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation methods have a critical gap: benchmark suites assess controlled tasks but lack natural use context; conversation corpora capture naturalistic use but lack user feedback; feedback mechanisms record satisfaction but lack task context. There's no infrastructure linking interaction trajectories to user-defined outcomes.

Method: The researchers developed MonitrLLM, an open-source infrastructure that treats conversation transcripts, user-reported task intent, and outcome assessments as primary evaluative signals. They conducted a two-week pilot with 26 college students using ChatGPT, collecting 206 evaluation reports with full conversation transcripts.

Result: The pilot revealed important findings: despite high average satisfaction (4.19/5), participants experienced a 23.1% failure rate on goal tasks. Multi-turn conversations failed at 2.5 times the rate of single-turn exchanges, suggesting extended interaction signals difficulty rather than engagement.

Conclusion: Connecting conversation trajectories with user-reported outcomes provides valuable insights for LLM evaluation. Infrastructure like MonitrLLM that incorporates direct user feedback with observational data enables more robust evaluations and reveals patterns like the correlation between conversation length and task difficulty.

Abstract: Benchmark suites assess model capability on controlled tasks; large-scale conversation corpora capture naturalistic use without user feedback; and in-interface feedback mechanisms record satisfaction without task purpose. Together, they leave a critical gap in LLM evaluation: no existing infrastructure routinely links interaction trajectories to user-defined outcomes. We introduce MonitrLLM, open-source infrastructure for community-centered LLM evaluations that links full conversation transcripts to user-reported task intent and outcome assessments, treating all three as primary evaluative signals rather than optional metadata.
  To demonstrate the value of this approach, we conducted a two-week feasibility pilot with 26 college students using ChatGPT, collecting 206 evaluation reports with full conversation transcripts. The findings from our pilot demonstrate the value of connecting conversation trajectories with user-reported outcomes. For instance, despite reporting high average satisfaction (4.19/5) with their LLM interactions, participants also experience a substantial 23.1% failure rate on their goal tasks. We also find that multi-turn conversations are reported as failing at 2.5 times the rate of single-turn exchanges, a pattern that reframes extended interaction as a signal of difficulty rather than engagement. We conclude by discussing the value of incorporating direct user feedback with observational data for robust LLM evaluations, and the possibilities for infrastructure that enables this goal.

</details>


### [187] [Real-Time Detection and Repair of LLM Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02464)
*Sunny Dubey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A monitoring system detects LLM agent failures mid-episode using lightweight telemetry analysis (one-class echo-state-network with CUSUM alarms), achieving 71% detection at 5% false-alarm rate, plus deterministic verification that catches 60-96% of failures with zero false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents frequently fail during execution (looping, tool errors, goal drift, fabrication) but existing solutions require expensive second LLM judges, motivating lightweight detection using only observable step telemetry from healthy runs.

Method: Two-layer approach: 1) One-class echo-state-network ensemble with CUSUM alarms trained on healthy runs for anomaly detection, 2) Deterministic verification that recomputes totals from tool results and validates required calls were made.

Result: Monitoring achieves AUROC 0.872, detecting 71% of failures at 5% false-alarm budget. Deterministic verification catches 60-96% of failures with zero false positives. Combined detection enables rollback-and-retry recovery, increasing task success from 52% to 73% at ~200μs per step.

Conclusion: Lightweight telemetry-based monitoring with deterministic verification provides effective, efficient detection of LLM agent failures, enabling automatic recovery with minimal overhead (3 orders of magnitude cheaper than LLM judges), significantly improving agent reliability.

Abstract: LLM agents fail mid-episode -- they loop, cascade tool errors, drift off goal, fabricate results, or silently absorb corrupted content -- and the standard remedy, judging every step with a second LLM, costs more than the agent itself. We ask how much detection is achievable from observable step telemetry alone, using monitors costing microseconds per step and trained only on healthy runs.
  On 2,823 committed agent episodes across three frameworks, three local models (qwen2.5 7b/3b, llama3.1 8b) and a commercial API (gemini-2.5-flash), a one-class echo-state-network ensemble with CUSUM alarms detects 0.71 of failures at a 5% false-alarm budget (AUROC 0.872). Its advantage over a memoryless baseline is a monotone function of post-onset horizon (+0.09 at <=3 steps, +0.40 at >=9), predicting its own failure region out of sample on AFTraj-2K. Ranking transfers with no retraining to two corpora from other groups (AFTraj-2K 0.745, ATBench 0.779).
  Monitors carry two burdens: a per-deployment healthy null (they do not transfer -- AUROC 0.527 cold against 0.885 recalibrated) and a residual false-alarm rate. We add a layer carrying neither: deterministic verification, which recomputes a run's stated total from the tool results it actually received and confirms every required call was made. Head-to-head it catches 60% of failures (96% with the coverage check) at 0 of 63 false positives against the monitor's 54% at 17%, transfers unchanged to llama3.1:8b (110 of 110 at 0 of 10), and trips on 0 of 1825 healthy episodes.
  Detection is then closed into repair: each flagged run is rolled back and re-run live, recovering 45% of failures against a 16% resampling control (p=0.0005) and lifting task success from 52% to 73% for about one extra model call per run. The system runs at ~200 microseconds per step, three orders of magnitude below a judge call. Code, traces and results are released.

</details>


### [188] [xPress: Parallel Refinement for Diffusion Drafters in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02438)
*Zheng Wang,Davis Wertheimer,Yu Chin Fabian Lim,Mudhakar Srivatsa,Raghu K. Ganti,Minjia Zhang,Naigang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: xPress adds causal refinement to diffusion drafters like dFlash, improving acceptance rates and throughput by restoring token dependencies in parallel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion drafters generate tokens independently (as marginals rather than joint distributions), causing sequences with individually likely but jointly improbable tokens that lead to early rejection and limit acceptance length in speculative decoding.

Method: xPress is a lightweight causal refiner that reconciles the whole diffusion block at once through parallel refinement, restoring and propagating causal dependencies across the draft without token-by-token processing.

Result: On Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks, xPress raises acceptance length by ~30% on average (up to +56%) and improves end-to-end decoding throughput by ~1.3× on average (up to 1.7×) compared to original dFlash.

Conclusion: Restoring causality in diffusion drafters through parallel refinement significantly improves speculative decoding performance, making diffusion-based drafting more practical for efficient LLM inference.

Abstract: Block-diffusion drafters like dFlash generate an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, drastically reducing the overhead of multiple-token drafting in speculative decoding. The crucial final step of the single-pass discrete denoising process involves using the logit distribution at each position to sample conditionally independent tokens. The resulting draft is thus a set of per-position marginals, rather than a joint distribution: no draft token is guaranteed to depend on its predecessors. Such independently sampled marginals tend to produce sequences with tokens that are individually likely, but jointly improbable under the target model's distribution, which verifies each token conditionally. This can cause early rejection and limits acceptance length. To address this, we propose xPress as a means to restore the missing causality in diffusion drafters. xPress is a lightweight causal refiner that reconciles the whole diffusion block at once through parallel refinement, restoring and propagating causal dependencies across the draft without a token-by-token loop. On Qwen3-8B, across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, xPress raises acceptance length by about 30% on average (up to +56%) and its end-to-end decoding throughput by about 1.3 on average (up to 1.7) compared to the original dFlash diffusion drafter.

</details>


### [189] [Optimizing Minimax Regret in Uncertain MDPs with Small Sets of Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02509)
*Sterre Lutz,Daniël Vos,Matthijs T. J. Spaan,Anna Lukina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: $k$-adaptable policy synthesis optimizes a limited set of $k$ policies for uncertain Markov decision processes (UMDPs) under minimax-regret objective, with KAPS algorithm solving NP-hard problem and showing largest regret reduction from 1 to 2 policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world sequential decision-making with model uncertainty, preparing individual policies for all possible MDPs violates practical constraints (operational, regulatory, interpretability), while single policies across all MDPs sacrifice performance. Model uncertainty is resolved shortly before execution, allowing selection from a pre-prepared limited policy set.

Method: Introduces $k$-adaptable policy synthesis under minimax-regret objective. Develops KAPS (exact nested branch-and-bound algorithm) with problem-specific bounds and heuristics. KAPS jointly optimizes which MDPs share a policy and the policies themselves.

Result: Proves the problem is NP-hard. Experiments show largest regret reduction consistently occurs when increasing from one to two policies. In single-policy setting, KAPS is competitive with existing methods in solution quality and proves optimality substantially more often.

Conclusion: $k$-adaptable policy synthesis with KAPS algorithm provides practical solution for UMDPs under deployment constraints, offering significant performance improvements with just two policies while maintaining interpretability and operational feasibility.

Abstract: Sequential decision-making in real-world applications often involves uncertainty about the environment's model. Uncertain Markov decision processes (UMDPs) represent the possible environments as a set of MDPs with shared states and actions but potentially different transition probabilities and rewards. Optimizing a single policy across all possible MDPs may sacrifice performance, while preparing an individually optimized policy for every MDP may violate operational, regulatory, or interpretability constraints on the number of policies that can be prepared and deployed. We consider settings in which model uncertainty is resolved shortly before execution, allowing the most suitable policy to be selected from a limited set prepared in advance. We introduce $k$-adaptable policy synthesis, which optimizes such a set of $k$ policies under a minimax-regret objective. We prove that the problem is NP-hard and develop KAPS, an exact nested branch-and-bound algorithm with problem-specific bounds and heuristics. KAPS jointly optimizes which MDPs share a policy and the policies themselves. Experiments across various UMDP benchmarks show that the largest reduction in regret consistently occurs when increasing from one to two policies. In the single-policy setting, KAPS is competitive with existing methods in solution quality and proves optimality substantially more often.

</details>


### [190] [Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02441)
*Shicheng Fan,Mingdai Yang,Duohao Wang,Canyu Chen,Yongfeng Zhang,Hua Wei,Manling Li,Julian McAuley,Kun Zhang,Philip S. Yu,Kejing Yu,Zhiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agentic Commerce World (ACWorld) is an evaluation environment where AI agents act as buyers and merchants in vibe commerce, using natural language to conduct transactions while preserving private objectives, with evaluation protocols ensuring auditability and reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need for evaluating AI agents in commerce scenarios where buyers and merchants interact with private objectives and distinct authority, analogous to vibe coding but for commercial transactions.

Method: Developed Agentic Commerce World (ACWorld) environment with Vibe Commerce Protocol (VCP) that validates agent actions before updating shared transaction state. Created two benchmark tracks: 200-task capability-coverage track and 60-task large-catalog track searching 785,022 listings.

Result: Tested ten models achieving mean scores from 65.9% to 85.6% on capability-coverage and 56.1% to 91.4% on large-catalog tracks. Key findings: process-level evidence is necessary, final state alone can miss errors, incomplete trajectories retain useful signals, and large-catalog tasks expose stage bottlenecks.

Conclusion: ACWorld provides a robust evaluation framework for vibe commerce agents, demonstrating the importance of process-level analysis and exposing challenges in large-catalog scenarios while enabling auditable, reproducible agent behavior assessment.

Abstract: In vibe coding, people describe software in natural language and delegate implementation to AI agents. By analogy, vibe commerce allows people to express buying or selling goals in natural language and delegate the corresponding tasks to agents. Commerce, however, requires independently controlled Buyer and Merchant agents to interact in a shared market while preserving their private objectives and distinct authority. We introduce Agentic Commerce World (ACWorld), an environment for evaluating such agents across ongoing transactions. Through its Vibe Commerce Protocol (VCP), ACWorld validates agent actions before updating shared transaction state and records the resulting interactions, making agent behavior auditable and evaluation reproducible. The ACWorld Benchmark contains a 200-task capability-coverage track and a 60-task large-catalog track that searches 785,022 transactable listings. Across ten models, mean scores range from 65.9% to 85.6% and from 56.1% to 91.4%, respectively. Our analysis shows that process-level evidence is necessary: final state alone can miss evaluated errors, incomplete trajectories still retain useful process signals, and large-catalog tasks expose bottlenecks across stages.

</details>


### [191] [Right Answer, Wrong Method: Shortcut Hacking Misleads the Evaluation of LLM Reasoning on Frontier Science Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02442)
*Xuan Ren,Weiqi Zhai,Tianle Pu,Yihua Zhu,Yihua Zhu,Hu Wei,Bing Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs often reach correct answers in scientific reasoning benchmarks through invalid shortcuts rather than proper reasoning, a phenomenon called "solution hacking" that inflates performance metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scientific reasoning benchmarks evaluate LLMs using final-answer accuracy, but correct answers don't necessarily demonstrate genuine reasoning capabilities - models may use invalid shortcuts that artificially inflate performance scores.

Method: Systematic analysis of solution hacking across difficulty levels, scientific domains, and frontier models; identification of hacking patterns (numerical search, enumeration, guessing, answer-first verification); development of expert-inspired anti-hacking strategies including automatic judges and test-time instructions.

Result: Solution hacking increases sharply with difficulty: from 2.2% on common problems to 28.3% on Olympiad-level problems and 37.4% on HLE; 8.2%-44.1% of correct answers across frontier models are hacked solutions; anti-hacking strategies substantially reduce reported accuracy while having smaller effect on genuinely correct performance.

Conclusion: Answer-only evaluation overestimates LLMs' scientific reasoning capabilities; solution hacking reveals the need for more sophisticated evaluation methods that assess reasoning processes rather than just final answers.

Abstract: Scientific reasoning benchmarks typically evaluate large language models (LLMs) using final-answer accuracy. However, a correct answer does not necessarily demonstrate the reasoning capability targeted by the problem. We identify Solution Hacking, a failure mode in which an LLM reaches the correct answer through invalid shortcuts, such as numerical search, enumeration, guessing, or answer-first verification, without providing a valid task-targeted derivation. We systematically analyze this phenomenon across difficulty levels, scientific domains, and frontier models. Solution hacking increases sharply with benchmark difficulty, from 2.2\% on common problems to 28.3\% on Olympiad-level problems and 37.4\% on HLE. Moreover, 8.2\%-44.1\% of answers credited as correct across frontier models are identified as hacked solutions. We further develop expert-inspired anti-hacking strategies, including an automatic judge and a test-time instruction. The results show that suppressing shortcut behavior substantially reduces reported accuracy while having a smaller effect on correct and non-hacked accuracy. These findings reveal that answer-only evaluation can overestimate the scientific reasoning capabilities of frontier LLMs.

</details>


### [192] [ParEvalLayer: When Partial LLM-Agent Evaluations Support a Decision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02444)
*Wei-Jung Huang,Bonan Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ParEvalLayer is a decision layer that enables early judgment of agent system comparisons in LLM-agent evaluations by applying predefined comparison policies to partial benchmark data, addressing issues with premature reporting of partial scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent evaluations often produce early task outcomes, but reporting partial scores is problematic because early tasks may omit important benchmark aspects, cheaper tasks can distort samples, and partial analysis might appear accurate while leaving many comparisons unresolved.

Method: The authors introduce ParEvalLayer, which reads paired outcomes for two agent systems with a predefined comparison policy. For each partial run, it records four possible states: tested agent is better by required amount, not better, needs more evidence, or should abstain. They evaluate by replaying completed benchmark data as if evaluations stopped earlier, checking if partial judgments match final outcomes.

Result: With the main comparison rule, three public benchmarks reached the same decision as completed evaluations after observing only 15% to 25% of task outcomes. Other benchmarks required more outcomes, showing variation in decision confidence across different evaluation scenarios.

Conclusion: Partial scores alone are insufficient for reliable evaluation; reports should also state the decision rule used and indicate how many comparisons remain without a decision. ParEvalLayer provides a systematic approach to early evaluation while maintaining transparency about decision confidence.

Abstract: LLM-agent evaluations often produce task outcomes long before the full benchmark run is complete. A partial score is tempting to report, but it does not show whether the observed tasks support the same conclusion as the completed evaluation. Early tasks can omit important parts of a benchmark, running cheaper tasks first can distort the observed sample, and a rule that decides only easy pairs can appear accurate while leaving many comparisons unresolved. We introduce ParEvalLayer, a decision layer that reads paired outcomes for two agent systems and a comparison policy chosen in advance. For each partial run, it records whether the tested agent system is better by the required amount, is not better by that amount, needs more evidence, or should abstain. We evaluate ParEvalLayer by replaying completed public benchmark data as if each evaluation had stopped earlier. At each point, ParEvalLayer applies the policy using only the outcomes observed so far; if it reaches one of the two comparison judgments, we check whether that judgment matches the completed data for the same system pair. With the main comparison rule, three of the public benchmarks reach the same decision as the completed evaluation after observing only 15% to 25% of task outcomes. Other benchmarks require more task outcomes. This variation shows why a partial score alone is not enough: reports should also state the decision rule and how many comparisons remain without a decision.

</details>


### [193] [Infinite Trace Objectives with Finite Trace Techniques: Translating LTL to LTLf+](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02454)
*Christoph Weinhuber,Maximilian Prokop,Giuseppe De Giacomo,Moshe Y. Vardi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new translation method from Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) to LTLf+ enables leveraging efficient finite-word automata techniques for infinite-trace specifications without asymptotic cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional LTL verification requires translating specifications to nondeterministic automata on infinite words and then determinizing them, which is notoriously difficult both theoretically and practically. This creates significant computational challenges for AI applications like reactive synthesis, stochastic planning, and reinforcement learning that use LTL.

Method: The method first normalizes LTL formulas into the syntactic reactivity fragment of the Manna-Pnueli hierarchy to create a general fragment-based shape of LTLf+. It then provides linear translations for each individual component of that fragment, enabling translation from LTL to LTLf+.

Result: The work presents the first translation from LTL to LTLf+, allowing the extensive techniques developed for LTLf+ (which operates on finite automata for finite words with efficient determinization) to be applied to problems currently formulated in LTL.

Conclusion: This translation enables using efficient finite-word automata methods for infinite-trace specifications without asymptotic penalty, as the pipeline from LTL to automaton via LTLf+ remains doubly exponential while providing practical advantages for AI applications.

Abstract: Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) is one of the most widely adopted languages for specifying temporal extended objectives in AI, with applications ranging from reactive synthesis to stochastic planning in Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning. Traditionally, solving any of these problems requires translating the LTL specification to a nondeterministic automata on infinite words and then determinizing it, a step that is notoriously difficult in theory and in practice. Recent work has introduced LTLf+, which lifts the finite-trace logic LTLf to infinite traces. LTLf+ has the same expressive power as LTL, yet it retains most of the crucial advantages of its base logic LTLf. Most reasoning in LTLf+ rests on finite automata on finite words, for which we have not only a canonical minimal representation but also an efficient determinization procedure. In this work we present the first translation from LTL to LTLf+. We first normalize an LTL formula into the syntactic reactivity fragment of the Manna-Pnueli hierarchy, to create the general fragment-based shape of LTLf+. We then present linear translations for each individual component of that fragment. As a consequence of this translation, the expanding body of techniques developed for LTLf+ now becomes available to many AI problems currently formulated in LTL. We further show that this comes at no asymptotic cost, as the pipeline from LTL to automaton via LTLf+ remains doubly exponential.

</details>


### [194] [Long-term Measurements: Towards a Longitudinal Understanding of Human-AI Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02491)
*Nicole Mitchell,Dhruv Agarwal,Maty Bohacek,Remi Denton,Roma Patel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NLP needs to shift from short-term text evaluations to measuring long-term behavioral changes in human-model interactions to address longitudinal risks like cognitive and socio-affective changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models have unique "human-ness" and rapid integration into daily life, creating longitudinal risks (cognitive, developmental, socio-affective changes) that don't appear in short-term interactions but have lasting effects on users. Current NLP focuses on static, short-term evaluations which miss these long-term risks.

Method: Proposes combining computational NLP methods with longitudinal measurements from social sciences to study emergent phenomena in longitudinal data. Emphasizes modeling human behavioral shifts as a function of model interactions to enable online detection of problematic behaviors.

Result: Presents a framework for diachronic understanding of human-model interactions, enabling detection of longitudinal risks and steering model development toward positive user outcomes rather than negative ones.

Conclusion: NLP must pivot from short-term text evaluations to longitudinal behavioral measurements to address lasting risks from human-model interactions. This approach should be integrated into alignment frameworks to mitigate long-term risks and steer development toward positive outcomes.

Abstract: Language models have taken on the role of a very new type of technology, by virtue of their "human-ness" and rapid integration into users' daily lives. This combination of features can introduce longitudinal risks---cognitive, developmental and socio-affective changes in humans---that might not surface in short-term interactions, but can have lasting long-term effects on users. This forms the basis of a critical new mission for NLP: to pivot from static, short-term evaluations of text generations to long-term measurements of behavioral changes, towards a diachronic understanding of human-model interactions. In this work, we draw from measurements used in social science fields that are crucial to understand emergent phenomena in longitudinal data. We discuss how computational methods in the field of NLP need to be combined with such measurements, not only to understand long-term safety risks of human-model interactions, but to help steer model development towards positive rather than negative outcomes for users. This ability to model human behavioral shifts as a function of model interactions can facilitate online rather than post-hoc detection of problematic behaviors, and should be leveraged in alignment frameworks to mitigate long-term risks in users.

</details>


### [195] [CMuon: Accelerating and Stabilizing Diffusion Transformer Training via Chunked Momentum Orthogonalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02502)
*Chuyan Chen,Peng Sun,Kun Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CMuon optimizes DiT training by chunking fused weight tensors before orthogonalization, achieving 2x speedup over AdamW with better late-stage convergence than vanilla Muon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have SOTA performance but are computationally expensive to train. While the Muon optimizer offers a promising alternative to AdamW, it suffers from suboptimal late-stage convergence when directly applied to DiTs due to fused weight tensors causing implicit subspace coupling.

Method: Introduces Chunked Muon (CMuon) which partitions fused matrices (e.g., within AdaLN and QKV layers) into independent sub-components before orthogonalization. This prevents implicit subspace coupling that distorts update directions in standard Muon applied to unified tensors.

Result: A 675M-parameter DiT trained with CMuon achieves FID of 1.18 on ImageNet 256 in just 200 epochs, representing more than 2x training speedup over AdamW while overcoming late-stage convergence plateaus of vanilla Muon.

Conclusion: CMuon effectively addresses the optimization bottleneck in DiT training by properly handling fused weight tensors, enabling faster convergence and better performance than both AdamW and vanilla Muon, making DiT training more efficient.

Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in visual generative modeling, yet their training remains computationally prohibitive. While the recently proposed Momentum Orthogonalization (Muon) optimizer offers a promising alternative to AdamW, its direct application to DiTs yields suboptimal late-stage convergence. In this paper, we identify the root cause of this bottleneck: standard DiT architectures fuse functionally distinct weights (e.g., within AdaLN and QKV layers) into unified tensors for computational efficiency. Applying Muon to these fused tensors inadvertently induces implicit subspace coupling, which distorts update directions and degrades global optimization. To address this, we introduce Chunked Muon (CMuon), a simple yet highly effective strategy that partitions these matrices into independent sub-components prior to orthogonalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that a 675M-parameter DiT trained with CMuon achieves a FID of 1.18 on ImageNet 256 in just 200 epochs. This represents more than a 2x training speedup over AdamW, while effectively overcoming the late-stage convergence plateaus of vanilla Muon.

</details>


### [196] [Abduction Without a Body? Representational Grounding and the Abduction Loop for Scientific Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02505)
*Michael Farmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that online physical embodiment is not necessary for all scientific abduction, focusing instead on "identity abduction" where agents can recognize mathematical equivalences across disciplines through representational transformations and convention spaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to challenge the prevailing view in AI and philosophy of science that genuine scientific hypothesis generation requires continuous sensorimotor embodiment. The authors seek to demonstrate that certain types of scientific abduction, specifically identity abduction (recognizing mathematical equivalences), can occur without direct physical interaction.

Method: The method involves: 1) Developing the concept of "convention space" - using scientific diagrams as substrates that embody cross-disciplinary mathematical conventions, 2) Proposing the "Abduction Loop" architecture with representation generation, motif extraction, convention-space canonicalization, cross-domain retrieval, identity-hypothesis generation, and adversarial verification, 3) Using a documented case study where a multimodal model recognized equivalence between gravitational-memory transport and weak-lensing cosmology models, 4) Introducing the DAB-30 benchmark for evaluation.

Result: The results include: 1) A theoretical framework showing identity abduction can occur without continuous embodiment, 2) An operational architecture (Abduction Loop) for implementing this approach, 3) A motivating example demonstrating the concept's feasibility, 4) A proposed benchmark (DAB-30) for systematic evaluation.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that continuous sensorimotor embodiment is not necessary for all scientific abduction processes. Identity abduction through representational grounding and convention spaces provides an alternative pathway for scientific discovery, particularly for recognizing mathematical equivalences across disciplines that lack shared vocabulary.

Abstract: Can scientific abduction occur without continuous sensorimotor embodiment? Recent arguments in AI and philosophy of science hold that genuine hypothesis generation requires an agent continuously coupled to the physical world. We defend a narrower claim: online embodiment is not necessary for every abductive scientific act. Our focus is identity abduction: the inference that two independently developed structures are one object under an explicit correspondence, reached through representational grounding rather than bodily interaction. An agent may acquire new inferential affordances not through physical interaction but through transformations into representations that expose latent invariants. Scientific diagrams are a practical substrate because they embody independently evolved conventions that partially canonicalize symmetry, topology, and operator structure across disciplines - a property we develop as convention space, which answers a hard retrieval problem: finding mathematically related work when two fields share no discriminating vocabulary. We operationalize the mechanism as an architecture, the Abduction Loop: representation generation, motif extraction, convention-space canonicalization, cross-domain retrieval, identity-hypothesis generation, and adversarial verification, with abstention as the designed default. A documented episode, in which a multimodal model given a figure of a gravitational-memory transport model generated and then verified the hypothesis that its central differential complex is equivalent to the spherical Kaiser-Squires mass-mapping complex of weak-lensing cosmology, serves as a motivating possibility witness from which the architecture is abstracted, not as evidence of general capability. We close with a falsifiable evaluation program, the DAB-30 benchmark. The contribution is a mechanistic proposal, an architecture, and a test program.

</details>


### [197] [Magnet: Detecting Cross-Session AI Misuse Through Capability Accumulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02518)
*Natalie Isak,Matthew Dressman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces cross-session goal decomposition as an AI safety evasion technique and proposes Magnet, a detection system that aggregates capabilities across multiple agentic sessions rather than analyzing single sessions individually.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI safety frameworks focus on single-session or multi-turn threat models, leaving a critical gap where attackers can decompose harmful goals into innocuous-looking units executed across isolated agentic sessions. This cross-session attack strategy evades existing detection systems that analyze conversations in isolation.

Method: The paper demonstrates cross-session goal decomposition as an evasion technique and proposes Magnet, a detection approach that models relevant capabilities accrued over time across multiple agentic conversations, aggregating evidence at a higher-level correlator (user ID) rather than per-conversation state.

Result: Cross-session goal decomposition can elicit more harmful capability than equivalent single-session attacks. Magnet provides an efficient detection approach by attracting relevant evidence across sessions and time into a compact bundle that detectors can act on, rather than searching through individual sessions.

Conclusion: As AI systems evolve toward ensemble architectures of specialized agents, new detection frameworks like Magnet are needed to address cross-session threat models where attackers can decompose harmful goals across multiple isolated conversations, evading current single-session focused detection systems.

Abstract: The most capable AI deployments are not single models but ensembles of specialized agents that delegate and act in coordination. This architecture unlocks powerful new capabilities, and it also introduces risks that existing frameworks for monitoring, detection, and mitigation were not designed to address. Most state-of-the-art AI abuse detection literature focuses on single-turn or multi-turn (single-session) threat models. This leaves a critical gap: an attacker can decompose a harmful goal into innocuous-looking units and execute each in isolated agentic sessions. The agent is stateless between conversations, but the attacker is not. This asymmetry allows for cross-session trajectories that are effective at evading detection. Our contributions are twofold. First, we demonstrate cross-session goal decomposition as an evasion technique, showing it may elicit more harmful capability than equivalent single-session or multi-turn attacks. By capability we mean an artifact produced at one step of an objective, evidenced by what an interaction produced (model responses and tool-call results), and composable with capabilities accrued elsewhere into a harmful whole. Second, we propose Magnet: an efficient and robust detection approach that models relevant capabilities accrued over time and across agentic conversations, aggregated at a higher-level correlator (in this case, a user ID) rather than per-conversation state. The main challenge is assembling the evidence bundle Magnet reasons over. The incriminating artifacts may be needles scattered through a haystack of benign sessions that are individually harmless, dangerous only once collected. Rather than searching the haystack straw-by-straw (i.e. per-session inspection), Magnet does what its name implies: it attracts the relevant needles out of the hay, across sessions and across time, into a compact evidence bundle a detector can act on.

</details>


### [198] [A Taxonomy of Cognitive Capability Gaps in Generative and Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02553)
*Taye Akinrele,Sindhuja Penchala,Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz,Sudip Mittal,Shahram Rahimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey paper analyzing cognitive capability gaps in AI systems and proposing a taxonomy to organize research toward more adaptive, reliable, and cognitively capable AI systems that can advance toward Artificial General Intelligence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative and agentic AI systems lack fundamental cognitive functions needed for reliable operation over extended time horizons, including sustained reasoning, adaptive behavior, persistent memory, and self-regulation. These gaps limit progress toward Cognitive AI and ultimately AGI.
