Motivation: To develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for predicting asphalt concrete splitting strength (ST) to support data-driven mixture design in pavement engineering, addressing the need for accurate prediction and understanding of influencing factors.

Method: Established database of 296 samples with 14 input variables (asphalt properties, aggregate gradation, fiber characteristics). Developed six ML models: TabPFN, ANN, SVR, RF, XGBoost, LightGBM. Performed hyperparameter optimization using NSGA-II for five models, used default TabPFN. Applied SHAP analysis for interpretability.

Result: All six models achieved satisfactory predictive performance. TabPFN delivered best overall results on testing set: RMSE 0.28, MAE 0.21, MAPE 18.01%, MAD 0.14, R² 0.88, composite score 0.91. SHAP identified 9 dominant variables accounting for 92.0% of contribution (Ag9.5, FT, Ag4.75, AC, Du most influential). Quantified favorable parameter ranges for improved ST.

Conclusion: The interpretable ML framework successfully predicts asphalt concrete splitting strength and identifies key influencing parameters. The developed GUI platform with prediction and SHAP-based explanation enhances accessibility and practical applicability for mixture design optimization in pavement engineering.

Abstract: This paper presents an interpretable machine-learning framework for predicting the splitting strength (ST) of asphalt concrete and supporting data-driven mixture design. A database consisting of 296 samples was established, and 14 input variables related to asphalt properties, aggregate gradation, and fiber characteristics were selected for modeling. Six machine-learning models, namely TabPFN, ANN, SVR, RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM, were developed and compared. Hyperparameter optimization was performed for five models using NSGA-II, while TabPFN was directly applied with its default configuration. The results show that all six models achieved satisfactory predictive capability, whereas TabPFN delivered the best overall performance on the testing set, with the lowest RMSE of 0.28, MAE of 0.21, MAPE of 18.01%, MAD of 0.14, the highest R^2 of 0.88, and the highest composite score of 0.91. SHAP analysis further revealed that nine dominant variables accounted for 92.0% of the total average contribution, among which Ag9.5, FT, Ag4.75, AC, and Du were the most influential. In addition, favorable parameter ranges for improving ST were quantified, such as Ag9.5 < 66.8%, Ag4.75 < 45.0%, AC < 5.4 wt.%, AV < 3.6%, and Du > 134.7 cm. Finally, a GUI platform integrating prediction and SHAP-based explanation was developed to improve the accessibility and practical applicability of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [248] [One-Sided Quantile Coupling for Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00978)
*Jin-Young Kim,So-Yoon Cho,Hyun-Gyoon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QC-FM proposes a lightweight one-sided coupling for Flow Matching that samples only data batches and constructs paired sources directly using quantile mapping along random orthogonal directions, avoiding quadratic-cost assignment problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing structured couplings for Flow Matching rely on mini-batch transport or assignment procedures with quadratic cost growth in batch size, limiting scalability and efficiency.

Method: Quantile Coupling Flow Matching (QC-FM) samples only data batches, projects data ranks along random orthogonal directions, maps them to Gaussian quantiles, and completes latent codes in orthogonal complements via conditional Gaussian sampling - all with linear cost.

Result: QC-FM improves FID by up to 12.9% over Baseline under matched training budgets, outperforms OT-CFM on CIFAR-10, CelebA, FFHQ, and ImageNet-64, and eliminates irreducible regression variance along selected slices while maintaining straight ideal flows.

Conclusion: Preserving projected rank structure provides a simple, scalable way to inject useful geometric bias into FM couplings without solving expensive mini-batch transport problems, offering better performance and efficiency.

Abstract: Flow Matching trains continuous-time generative models by regressing the velocity field of a probability path between a simple source distribution and a target data distribution. The coupling that pairs source and target samples strongly affects optimization and sample quality, but structured couplings typically rely on mini-batch transport or assignment procedures whose cost grows at least quadratically in batch size. We propose Quantile Coupling Flow Matching (QC-FM), a lightweight one-sided coupling: rather than matching two pre-sampled batches, it samples only the data batch and constructs each paired source directly. Data ranks projected along a small number of random orthogonal directions are mapped to Gaussian quantiles, and the latent code is completed in the orthogonal complement by conditional Gaussian sampling. The construction is one-dimensional per slice, so the coupling requires no pairwise cost matrix and no assignment to solve. We show that, for each drawn frame, this coupling eliminates the irreducible regression variance along every selected slice and makes the ideal flow exactly straight there, while leaving the sampling prior unchanged: generation still starts from the standard Gaussian, and the training source deviates from it only through the copula of the slice codes, whose transport cost we bound. For training, we apply QC to an anchor subset and complete the remaining source slots with exact Gaussian samples, retaining the QC bias while preserving an explicit signal from the Baseline coupling. Across CIFAR-10, CelebA, FFHQ, and ImageNet-64, QC-FM improves over the Baseline under matched training budgets, reducing FID by up to 12.9%, and outperforms OT-CFM on all four datasets. These results suggest that preserving projected rank structure is a simple and scalable way to inject useful geometric bias into FM couplings without solving a mini-batch transport problem.

</details>


### [249] [Beyond Gene Reconstruction: Learning Cell Representations through Complementary Transcriptomic Views](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00985)
*Jiaqi Xiong,Yuntao hu,Yu Zheng,Yifei Shi,Xinyue Guo,Jiaxin Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a contrastive pretraining framework for single-cell transcriptomic data that learns cell representations through complementary views, addressing limitations of standard reconstruction-based methods that don't optimize for whole-cell representations needed for downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current foundation models for single-cell transcriptomic data are primarily pretrained by reconstructing masked expression values, which encourages learning gene dependencies but doesn't directly optimize whole-cell representations that are essential for many downstream tasks like cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network inference.

Method: The authors propose a contrastive pretraining framework with three key adaptations: 1) Co-expression-guided gene partitioning to construct two complementary views of each cell, 2) Expression-aware contrast-set construction that creates hard negatives by permuting expression values while keeping gene identities unchanged to prevent shortcut learning, and 3) Competence-gated contrastive onset using a controller to determine how the contrastive objective is applied.

Result: Experiments on cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network (GRN) inference show competitive transfer performance. In the six-network GRN evaluation, their method achieves the highest mean AUROC and AUPRC point estimates among compared variants, though the highest-scoring variant differs across individual networks.

Conclusion: Complementary-view contrastive learning represents an effective direction for single-cell pretraining that goes beyond traditional gene reconstruction objectives, providing better whole-cell representations for downstream biological tasks.

Abstract: The rapid growth of single-cell transcriptomic data has enabled the development of foundation models pretrained primarily by reconstructing masked expression values. This objective encourages these models to learn gene dependencies but does not directly optimize whole-cell representations, which are essential for many downstream tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a contrastive pretraining framework that learns cell representations through complementary transcriptomic views. Since standard contrastive learning is not readily applicable to single-cell pretraining, we introduce specific adaptations along three dimensions --- co-expression-guided gene partitioning, expression-aware contrast-set construction, and competence-gated contrastive onset. Specifically, we first construct two complementary views of each cell by partitioning its genes according to their co-expression structure. Then, to prevent the model from using gene-set identity as a shortcut, we construct hard negatives by permuting expression values while keeping gene identities unchanged. Finally, we introduce a competence-aware controller to determine how the contrastive objective is applied. Experiments on cell-type annotation and gene regulatory network inference demonstrate competitive transfer under the evaluated protocols. In the six-network GRN evaluation, our method records the highest mean AUROC and AUPRC point estimates among the compared variants, while the highest-scoring variant differs across individual networks. These results establish complementary-view contrastive learning as an effective direction for single-cell pretraining beyond gene reconstruction.

</details>


### [250] [Who Belongs in the Eval Set? A Capability-Taxonomy-Driven Pipeline for Curating Regression Eval Sets in Agent-Extensibility Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01004)
*Tezan Sahu,Aritra Das,Pankaj Mittal,Sudipta Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A pipeline for curating regression test sets in agent-extensible platforms by projecting customer queries onto a capability taxonomy, using a hybrid classifier and quality rater to maintain minimal query sets with maximal capability coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Platform teams face a regression-economics paradox: each new customer provides domain-specific evaluation sets, but platform regression sets have limited query capacity due to release cadence constraints. Existing solutions only address customer-side evaluation or treat benchmarks as fixed pools, not streaming inputs.

Method: A three-component pipeline: 1) Hybrid classifier using deterministic specification extraction and LLM semantic inference to map queries to capability taxonomy, 2) Invocation Quality (IQ) rater scoring how thoroughly queries exercise capabilities, 3) Conservative consolidator comparing incoming queries against regression sets via rule-based decision cascade with options to admit, drop, swap, or flag for human review.

Result: A taxonomy-agnostic mechanism for regression eval-set curation that maintains minimal query sets capturing maximal spread of capability signatures (distinct capability combinations), applied to Microsoft 365 Copilot's declarative agents with custom actions.

Conclusion: The pipeline addresses the industrial platform-side curation problem by treating regression sets as living collections that evolve with incoming customer evaluation streams, enabling taxonomy evolution based on pipeline evidence while maintaining query economy.

Abstract: Platform teams hosting agent-extensibility surfaces face a regression-economics paradox: every onboarding customer ships an evaluation set tuned to their domain, but the platform's regression set must live under a hard query-count ceiling bounded by release cadence. To our knowledge, no published industrial pipeline addresses this platform-side curation problem: existing evaluation frameworks are customer-side, and benchmark-compression work treats benchmarks as fixed pools rather than streams of incoming sets. We describe a capability-taxonomy-driven curation pipeline applied to declarative agents with custom actions in Microsoft 365 Copilot. It takes an agent specification and a customer's eval set as input, projects each query into a platform-owned capability taxonomy, and outputs per-query decisions (admit, drop, swap, or human review), under the philosophy that a healthy regression set is the minimal set of queries capturing the maximal spread of capability signatures -- distinct combinations of capabilities a query exercises together. Three components instantiate this: a classifier producing per-(query, capability) verdicts via a hybrid of deterministic specification-based extraction and large-language-model (LLM) semantic inference; an Invocation Quality (IQ) rater scoring how thoroughly a query exercises each capability, so a new query sharing a signature with an existing entry can still be recognized as a better test and displace it; and a consolidator comparing incoming queries against the regression set on coverage and quality through a rule-based decision cascade, backed by a conservative curator that only suggests evictions. The mechanism is taxonomy-agnostic and applies to any regression eval-set curation problem with a typed capability taxonomy, including taxonomies that evolve in response to the very evidence the pipeline surfaces.

</details>


### [251] [Hierarchical Solomonoff Induction: An Unbounded Machine Learning Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01005)
*Nathan Young*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hierarchical Solomonoff Induction (HSI) extends Solomonoff Induction to handle dataset conditioning via exchangeability theory, maintaining optimal prediction guarantees in the limit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solomonoff Induction is ideal for unbounded sequence prediction but doesn't naturally model extrapolation from training datasets like LLMs do. The paper aims to create a theoretical framework that bridges this gap while maintaining ideal properties.

Method: Apply de Finetti's theorem on exchangeable distributions to Solomonoff Induction to create HSI, which maintains a hyperprior over all Solomonoff priors that can be conditioned on observed sequences. Extend Wood et al.'s proof about universal mixtures to show equivalence between HSI and SolInd.

Result: Prove HSI=SolInd and establish that HSI's excess error compared to true generator is bounded by generator's complexity in hyperprior, analogous to SolInd's Kolmogorov complexity bound. This forces HSI's average excess error to converge to 0 with dataset growth.

Conclusion: HSI provides an ideal unbounded model of sequence prediction given a dataset, analogous to how SolInd provides ideal prediction over individual sequences, bridging the gap between theoretical foundations and practical dataset-based learning.

Abstract: Solomonoff Induction, or SolInd, provides an ideal unbounded model of a priori sequence prediction but cannot naturally describe extrapolation from a given training dataset, as performed by Large Language Models. We apply de Finetti's theorem on exchangeable distributions to SolInd to produce what we call Hierarchical Solomonoff Induction, or HSI, which maintains a hyperprior over all Solomonoff priors that can be conditioned on previously observed sequences.
  We extend Wood et al.'s proof that universal mixtures of semimeasures are equivalent to SolInd to show that universal mixtures of these mixtures are also equivalent, proving that HSI=SolInd. We also prove that HSI's excess error on any distribution, compared to its true generator, is bounded by that generator's complexity in the hyperprior. This result is directly comparable to SolInd's prediction error being bounded by the Kolmogorov complexity of the sequence being predicted, and forces HSI's average excess error to converge to 0 as a dataset grows, leading to optimal prediction in the limit. We claim that HSI is an ideal unbounded model of sequence prediction given a dataset in the same way that SolInd is ideal over individual sequences.

</details>


### [252] [Fused Bayesian Flow Networks for Dual-Target Molecular Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01007)
*Jingyuan Zhou,Shikui Tu,Lei Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FusedBFN is a fused Bayesian flow network for dual-target 3D molecular design that formulates generation as distribution fusion and uses product-of-experts to incorporate dual-target information throughout the generative process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dual-target drug design aims to generate 3D molecules that simultaneously interact with two target proteins for polypharmacology against complex diseases. Existing approaches have limitations: they either focus on sequence generation or introduce predictive drift terms in diffusion models, which prevents full integration of both targets' feature information.

Method: FusedBFN formulates dual-target generation as distribution fusion in a unified continuous parameter space using a product-of-experts formulation. It employs a pretrained target-aware BFN model as shared backbone to address data scarcity. The method also introduces chemically aware prior-based alignment and prior-free pocket alignment strategies to construct aligned dual-target contexts.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that FusedBFN generates molecules with strong binding affinity toward dual targets while maintaining favorable molecular properties.

Conclusion: FusedBFN provides an effective approach for dual-target molecular design by fully integrating feature information from both targets throughout the generative process, addressing limitations of existing methods and overcoming data scarcity challenges.

Abstract: Dual-target drug design aims to generate 3D molecules that can simultaneously interact with two target proteins, offering a promising route for discovering polypharmacological compounds against complex diseases. While recent generative models have shown encouraging performance in single-target drug design, existing dual-target approaches either focus on sequence generation or introduce an additional predictive drift term into the diffusion-based generative trajectory, which limits their ability to fully integrate feature information from both targets. We propose FusedBFN, a fused Bayesian flow network (BFN) for dual-target molecular design. FusedBFN formulates dual-target generation as distribution fusion in a unified continuous parameter space and employs a product-of-experts formulation to incorporate dual-target information throughout the generative process. To address the scarcity of dual-target structural data, we leverage a pretrained target-aware BFN model as the shared backbone. We further introduce a chemically aware prior-based alignment method and a prior-free pocket alignment strategy to construct aligned dual-target contexts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FusedBFN generates molecules with strong binding affinity toward dual targets while maintaining favorable molecular properties.

</details>


### [253] [Caliber: Cross-Architecture Extraction-Cost Control for Score-Returning APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01023)
*Chi Wang,Hanwen Wang,Yu Xia,Zihan Wang,Guangdong Bai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Caliber: A defense against model extraction attacks that adds calibrated Gaussian noise to logits to degrade surrogate model training while maintaining utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To defend against model extraction attacks where attackers query APIs to train surrogate models via knowledge distillation. Need a practical defense that provides provable guarantees while maintaining utility.

Method: Output perturbation defense adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise to internal logits. Noise selection framed as calibration: balancing degradation of supervision signal for surrogate training vs. query cost to recover clean logits. Noise variance normalized by squared median top-two logit margin.

Result: Establishes monotone agreement degradation (unique noise scale for target agreement) and per-input recovery cost (closed-form minimax lower bound). Across 30+ model-dataset combos, achieves 0.6-1.4% mean absolute relative error in calibration. End-to-end experiments confirm surrogate performance tracks configured degradation.

Conclusion: Caliber provides effective, calibrated defense against model extraction with provable guarantees on degradation and recovery costs, maintaining practical utility across diverse models and datasets.

Abstract: We present Caliber, an output-perturbation defense against model extraction that formulates noise selection as a calibration problem: how much the defense degrades the supervision signal used to train a surrogate, and the provable per-input query cost of recovering the clean logits. To defend against an attacker that uses returned scores for knowledge distillation, Caliber adds independent and identically distributed Gaussian noise to the internal logits. We establish two properties of the resulting perturbed predictions. Monotone agreement degradation: When the clean logits have a unique maximizer, agreement with the clean prediction decreases strictly with the noise scale, so every target in $(1/K,1)$ corresponds to a unique positive scale; task accuracy is bounded by computable lower and upper envelopes. Per-input recovery cost: We derive a closed-form minimax lower bound on the repeated queries needed to recover the clean logits for a fixed input. Caliber normalizes noise variance by the squared median top-two logit margin and fits the resulting noise-utility relationship with a logistic curve, either per model or shared within a task. Across more than thirty model-dataset combinations, per-model calibration achieves mean absolute relative errors of 0.6-1.4%. End-to-end experiments show that surrogate performance generally tracks the configured degradation, while fixed-input averaging follows the expected variance reduction.

</details>


### [254] [The Fourth Quadrant: A Stylized View of Benign Misfitting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01032)
*Gireeja Ranade,Anant Sahai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear regression exhibits "benign misfitting" where predictors must fit training data worse than zero predictor to generalize well, with SGD achieving this optimal trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding the gap between training error (observable) and test error (what matters) in linear regression, especially when predictors that generalize well must have worse training fit than zero predictor.

Method: Analyzes linear regression with squared error in a deterministic single-spike model. Considers predictors in the span of training vectors, focusing on training sizes where generalization requires misfitting training data worse than zero predictor.

Result: Identifies "benign misfitting" regime where best span predictor begins to generalize when n ≫ d/γ², while interpolation requires n ≫ d/γ. One-pass SGD with large constant learning rate achieves small test error matching best span predictor.

Conclusion: There exists a regime where predictors must fit training data poorly to generalize well, and SGD naturally achieves this optimal trade-off. The nuisance component causing training misfit also controls adversarial sensitivity.

Abstract: Training error is what we can observe on a training set; test error is the quantity we actually care about. We study linear regression with squared-error in a deterministic $(d+1)$-dimensional single-spike model. Each stylized training vector has the same informative spike coordinate, of amplitude $\sqrtγ$ with $γ>1$. The remaining directions are nuisance, and the nuisance components of distinct training vectors all have equal norm and are mutually orthogonal. The training labels are all $1$. Fresh test points are drawn from $\vec{x}_{\rm test} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vec{0},\operatorname{diag}(γ,1,\ldots,1))$, with the noise-free test labels being the normalized spike coordinate $x_{\rm test}[1]/\sqrtγ$. We focus on linear predictors in the span of the training vectors, the class naturally reached by zero-initialized linear gradient methods.
  We exhibit a range of training-set sizes $n$ in which every span predictor that generalizes well must fit the training data \emph{worse} than the zero predictor. We call this regime \emph{benign misfitting}, or the fourth quadrant. The best span predictor begins to generalize when $n\gg d/γ^2$, while interpolation does not generalize until the later threshold $n\gg d/γ$. In the window $d/γ^2 \ll n \ll d/γ$, useful prediction within the linear span lies beyond interpolation: predictions on the training points overshoot the labels. We show that one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD), with a large constant learning rate, reaches small test error throughout this window---matching the best span predictor up to a logarithmic factor. We also verify directly that it indeed has \emph{large} empirical training error (despite the descent premise in its name). Finally, we show that the unavoidable nuisance component responsible for the training misfit also controls the predictor's adversarial sensitivity.

</details>


### [255] [Characterizing Bias in Post-Bandit Inference under Index Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01069)
*Lisu Wang,Yilun Chen,Jiaqi Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes bias in post-bandit sample means caused by adaptive sampling, characterizes bias for stable index algorithms like UCB1, reveals a regret-bias trade-off, and develops a novel empirical fluid approximation method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bandit algorithms generate data used for downstream statistical inference, but their adaptive sampling introduces biases in post-bandit sample means that need characterization and understanding.

Method: Analysis of stable index algorithms (including UCB1 and generalizations) using sharp leading-order expressions for sample-mean bias and expected Z-statistics, with a novel empirical fluid approximation of sampling dynamics.

Result: Reveals bias originates from an algorithmic property called effective exploration rate; shows UCB1 bias decays slowly at 1/√log T; demonstrates regret-bias trade-off where more exploration reduces bias but increases regret.

Conclusion: The paper provides a systematic characterization of bias in post-bandit inference, uncovers fundamental trade-offs between exploration and bias reduction, and offers new analytical tools for understanding adaptive sampling effects.

Abstract: Bandit algorithms generate data for downstream inference, but adaptive sampling biases post-bandit sample means. We analyze this bias for stable index algorithms, including UCB1 and its generalizations, and derive sharp leading-order expressions for the sample-mean bias and expected $Z$-statistic. Our characterization reveals the algorithmic origin of bias through a key index-function-dependent quantity, which we term effective exploration rate. For example, under UCB1, the effective exploration rate is of order $\sqrt{\log T}$, and the standardized bias of any arm (that is not uniquely optimal) decays at the extremely slow rate $1/\sqrt{\log T}$. We also show how the choice of the index function affects both regret and bias, which reveals a regret-bias trade-off: more exploratory algorithm reduces bias but increases regret. Our sharp characterization for bias uses a novel empirical fluid approximation of the algorithm's sampling dynamics, which may be of independent interest.

</details>


### [256] [Logit-Origin Centering for Singleton Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01074)
*Mayank Sharma,Rohit Kumar Mourya,Pratik Mazumder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PLOC is a lightweight streaming test-time adaptation method for tabular data that shifts logit space without weight updates, outperforming batch-based approaches in strict streaming regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test-time adaptation methods for tabular data degrade in strict streaming regimes where examples arrive one at a time, because batch-level statistics become unavailable or poorly estimated at batch size of one.

Method: Proposes Prequential Logit-Origin Centering (PLOC) - keeps source model frozen and shifts logit space at each step using only a single running number (mean of past logits), with no labels, prior estimation, or weight updates.

Result: PLOC significantly outperforms strong tabular and entropy-based baselines across five tabular benchmarks, three architectures (MLP, FT-Transformer, TabTransformer), and five independent source checkpoints.

Conclusion: Singleton tabular FTTA is a distinct identifiability problem requiring specialized approaches, and PLOC's lightweight logit-space shifting effectively addresses streaming test-time adaptation for tabular data.

Abstract: Tabular data is used extensively in many real-world use cases. Deep learning models have been developed to deal with tabular data, but generally perform poorly when the test data distribution differs from that of the training data. Researchers have proposed test-time adaptation approaches to deal with this problem. The fully test-time adaptation (FTTA) setting involves adapting deployed classifiers to shifted target distributions using only unlabeled test data. Leading FTTA methods inherit a batch-dependent approach from computer vision literature. This paper demonstrates for the first time that such approaches degrade sharply in strict streaming regimes where examples arrive and must be classified one at a time. This occurs because at a batch size of one, batch-level statistics become unavailable or poorly estimated. We argue that singleton tabular FTTA is not merely a small-batch variant of ordinary FTTA, but a distinct identifiability problem where only the location of the model's score stream remains directly observable. To address this, we propose Prequential Logit-Origin Centering (PLOC), a lightweight approach that keeps the source model frozen and shifts the logit space at each step. PLOC stores only a single running number (the mean of past logits), requires no labels, estimates no priors, and bypasses weight updates entirely. A deferred variant applies a static shift that preserves the source ranking, and thus the AUROC, exactly. Evaluated across five tabular benchmarks, three architectures (MLP, FT-Transformer, and TabTransformer), and five independent source checkpoints, PLOC significantly outperforms strong tabular and entropy-based baselines.

</details>


### [257] [Breaking Diversity Collapse in Spiking Pseudo-Ensembles for Efficient OOD Detection in Remote Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01090)
*Srinivas Anumasa,Rushi Shah,Qiran Zou,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Efficient spiking pseudo-ensemble for OOD detection with diversity-promoting training to reduce computational costs while maintaining ensemble uncertainty benefits


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for resource-constrained remote-sensing systems, but reliable out-of-distribution detection remains challenging. Traditional deep ensembles provide strong predictive uncertainty but require multiple complete models and backbone evaluations, making them computationally expensive.

Method: Propose an efficient spiking pseudo-ensemble that attaches multiple lightweight classification heads to a frozen SNN backbone. Introduce an "agree-disagree" objective that preserves correct predictions on clean in-distribution samples while encouraging diversity on structured transformations of the same inputs, providing diversity-promoting training without needing external OOD data.

Result: Experiments with Spikformer and ResNet19-SNN on EuroSAT show consistent improvements over conventional pseudo-ensembles. Using three backbones with five heads each matches or improves upon a five-model deep ensemble on UCM and AID datasets, while requiring approximately 38% fewer parameters and 40% fewer backbone evaluations.

Conclusion: Explicit diversity promotion can recover useful ensemble-style uncertainty at substantially lower deployment cost, making SNNs more practical for resource-constrained remote-sensing applications requiring reliable OOD detection.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained remote-sensing systems, but reliable out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains challenging. Deep ensembles provide strong predictive uncertainty, yet require multiple complete models and backbone evaluations. We propose an efficient spiking pseudo-ensemble that attaches multiple lightweight classification heads to a frozen SNN backbone. Naively training these heads with cross-entropy can lead to diversity collapse, where independently parameterized heads may produce correlated predictions. To address this, we introduce an agree--disagree objective that preserves correct predictions on clean in-distribution samples while encouraging diversity on structured, uncertainty-inducing transformations of the same inputs. This provides a diversity-promoting training signal without requiring external OOD data. Experiments with Spikformer and ResNet19-SNN on EuroSAT demonstrate consistent improvements over conventionally trained pseudo-ensembles. Using three backbones with five heads each matches or improves upon a five-model deep ensemble on UCM and AID, while requiring approximately 38% fewer parameters and 40% fewer backbone evaluations. These results show that explicit diversity promotion can recover useful ensemble-style uncertainty at substantially lower deployment cost.

</details>


### [258] [Factorized AdaBoost.MH Achieves the Same Convergence Rate as AdaBoost.MH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01091)
*Xin Zou,Jingyuan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Factorized AdaBoost.MH achieves the same convergence rate as AdaBoost.MH up to a universal constant factor, removing previous dimension-dependent slowdown.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Factorized AdaBoost.MH uses a more structured factorization that achieves better practical performance but had unclear convergence guarantees with previous bounds suggesting dimension-dependent slowdown.

Method: The authors analyze the combinatorial step of factorized boosting, proving new bounds on the minimax quantity $\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}$ governing the factorized edge. They derive explicit formulas for constants $C_q$ depending on whether $q$ is 1, even ≥2, or odd ≥2.

Result: Proved $\max\{1/n,C_K\}\le\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}\le C_{\min\{n,K\}}$ with $C_q$ constants that approach 1/3 asymptotically, showing $\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}=Θ(1)$ uniformly over $n$ and $K$.

Conclusion: Factorized AdaBoost.MH achieves the same boosting-type convergence rate as AdaBoost.MH up to a universal constant factor, eliminating the previously suggested additional dependence on dimensions $n$ or $K$ in the number of boosting rounds.

Abstract: AdaBoost.MH reduces multi-class classification to a collection of binary subproblems and enjoys the classical boosting-type convergence guarantee under a weak learning condition. A more structured variant, Factorized AdaBoost.MH, uses base classifiers of the form $\mathbf{h}(x)=α\mathbf{v} \bm{\varphi}(x)$, where a single binary classifier $\bm{\varphi}$ is shared across all classes and the label dependence is carried by a vote vector $\mathbf{v} \in\{\pm1\}^K$. This factorization is algorithmically attractive and achieves better performance in practice, but its convergence depends on whether one can always choose a vote vector with sufficiently large induced binary weight mass. Previous work resolved this question with a lower bound $\max\{1/n,1/\sqrt{2K}\}$, which still leaves a dimension-dependent slowdown relative to the original AdaBoost.MH analysis. In this paper, we sharpen this combinatorial step. For the minimax quantity $\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}$ governing the factorized edge, we prove $\max\{1/n,C_K\}\le\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}\le C_{\min\{n,K\}}$, where $C_q=1$ for $q=1$, $C_q=q/(3q-4)$ for even $q\ge2$, and $C_q=(q+1)/(3q-1)$ for odd $q\ge2$. Since $C_q\downarrow 1/3$, our bounds show that $\mathfrak{W}_{n,K}=Θ(1)$ uniformly over $n$ and $K$. Consequently, Factorized AdaBoost.MH achieves the same boosting-type convergence rate as AdaBoost.MH up to a universal constant factor, removing the previously suggested additional dependence on $n$ or $K$ in the number of boosting rounds.

</details>


### [259] [FL-OA: A Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning Framework with Outsourced Auditing for Intelligent Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01095)
*Hongliang Zhang,Zhongyuan Yu,Fenghua Xu,Teng Hu,Jian Meng,Jiguo Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FL-OA: A Byzantine-robust federated learning framework using outsourced auditing with third-party data, gradient ascent adjustments, and parameter importance indicators to overcome limitations of existing defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current federated learning defenses against Byzantine attacks have strong assumptions (malicious devices <50%, server needs matching root dataset) and limited effectiveness due to ignoring benign update divergence and high-dimensional comparison challenges.

Method: FL-OA introduces outsourced auditing where server collaborates with third-party organization holding additional root dataset, adds gradient ascent step and correction term during local training to reduce benign update divergence, and uses parameter importance indicators to extract critical parameters for auditing.

Result: Extensive experiments show FL-OA outperforms existing defense methods against Byzantine attacks, with detailed theoretical analysis supporting the approach.

Conclusion: FL-OA provides an effective Byzantine-robust federated learning framework that eliminates strong assumptions of prior methods and addresses key limitations through outsourced auditing and specialized training techniques.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple intelligent devices to collaboratively train a high-accuracy model without sharing raw data. However, due to its distributed nature, FL is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks. Existing defense methods rely on strong assumptions, such as the proportion of malicious devices not exceeding 50\%, or the server having an additional root dataset that matches the training task. Moreover, they show limited efficacy as they overlook $(i)$ the divergence among benign updates and $(ii)$ the curse of dimensionality involved in comparing two high-dimensional updates. To solve these concerns, we propose FL-OA, a Byzantine-robust federated learning framework utilizing outsourced auditing. In FL-OA, the server collaborates with third-party organization that holds an additional root dataset to perform outsourced auditing, thereby enabling the server to achieve robust aggregation without strong assumptions. Additionally, FL-OA introduces a gradient ascent step and a correction term during local training to mitigate the divergence among benign updates, and designs a parameter importance indicator to extract critical parameters for auditing, alleviating the curse of dimensionality. We further provide a detailed theoretical analysis of FL-OA. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FL-OA outperforms existing defense methods against Byzantine attacks.

</details>


### [260] [When Do Surrogate Updates Improve Decisions? A Local Theory of Trajectory-Wise Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01130)
*Yuyang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes the mismatch between trajectory-based training (using surrogate losses) and downstream task evaluation, providing theoretical conditions for when trajectory training transfers to improved decision utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many models are trained using trajectory losses but evaluated on downstream task rewards, creating a mismatch where reducing surrogate losses doesn't necessarily improve actual decision-making utility.

Method: Theoretical analysis separating learnability (surrogate risk reduction) and decision utility (decision risk reduction). Develops transfer bounds, gradient alignment conditions, calibration-based regret bounds, and trade-offs across update spaces.

Result: Four main theoretical results: 1) Transfer bounds separating gradient misalignment and curvature effects, 2) Conditions for universal first-order transfer, 3) Calibration gap bounds decision regret, 4) Approximation-calibration trade-off. Experimental validation in gridworld and LLM post-training.

Conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical framework for understanding when trajectory training transfers to improved decision utility, with practical implications for model training and trajectory selection strategies.

Abstract: A broad range of models face the mismatch where they are updated through trajectory losses but are evaluated by downstream task reward. Here, a trajectory is a training instance that induces a surrogate loss whose reduction might not track the model's decision utility update. Theoretically, we ask when one step of trajectory training reduces both population surrogate loss and decision risk, and how transfer accumulates along repeated updates. To formalize this, we first fix a checkpoint and a restricted update space, and define the reductions in population surrogate risk and decision risk induced by a trajectory as its learnability and decision utility, respectively. On this basis, our theory yields four main results. First, a one-step transfer bound separates their discrepancy into first-order gradient misalignment after nonnegative calibration and second-order curvature; and a pathwise extension accumulates the same terms over repeated updates. Second, when the accessible surrogate gradient is nonzero, universal first-order transfer over every accessible direction holds exactly when the accessible surrogate and decision gradients are positively collinear. Third, the calibration gap bounds the decision regret of learnability-based trajectory selection, while a candidate-difference refinement tightens this guarantee by retaining only directions that affect pairwise rankings. Finally, we establish an approximation--calibration trade-off across nested update spaces. Controlled gridworld and LLM post-training experiments yield results consistent with our predictions.

</details>


### [261] [Policy Optimality Measurement for Multi-Vehicle Decision-Making: From Extrinsic Indicators to Intrinsic Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01133)
*Ye Han,Lijun Zhang,Dejian Meng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel information-theoretic framework that uses MCTS as an oracle to diagnose MARL policies in autonomous driving, providing granular semantic analysis of policy quality beyond traditional extrinsic metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional MARL evaluation in autonomous driving relies on extrinsic statistical indicators (reward curves, success rates) that mask intrinsic policy degradation and algorithmic blind spots, creating a black-box evaluation problem.

Method: Uses fully converged Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) as an asymptotic oracle to establish theoretical ground-truth baseline distribution. Formulates a bounded policy optimality score (M_opt) using forward KL divergence to penalize fatal collaborative omissions, and semantically decouples this metric into lateral and longitudinal dimensions for granular analysis.

Result: The framework exposes hidden directional biases, identifies temporal average-policy traps, and transforms heuristic hyperparameter tuning into visually trackable trajectory optimization when applied to state-of-the-art MARL architectures and exploration mechanisms.

Conclusion: This information-theoretic diagnostic framework establishes a rigorous, model-agnostic standard for benchmarking intrinsic multi-agent policy quality in autonomous driving, moving beyond black-box extrinsic evaluations.

Abstract: Evaluating Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policies in autonomous driving fundamentally relies on extrinsic statistical indicators (e.g., reward curves and success rates), which often mask intrinsic policy degradation and algorithmic blind spots. To break this black-box evaluation, this letter proposes a novel information-theoretic diagnostic framework. By leveraging a fully converged Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) as an asymptotic oracle, we establish a theoretical ground-truth baseline distribution. We formulate a bounded policy optimality score ($\mathcal{M}_{opt}$) using the forward KL divergence to rigorously penalize fatal collaborative omissions. Crucially, we semantically decouple this metric into lateral and longitudinal dimensions, creating a granular "semantic microscope". Extensive spatial and temporal diagnostics on state-of-the-art MARL architectures and exploration mechanisms demonstrate that our framework conclusively exposes hidden directional biases, identifies temporal average-policy traps, and transforms heuristic hyperparameter tuning into a visually trackable trajectory optimization. This framework establishes a rigorous, model-agnostic standard for benchmarking intrinsic multi-agent policy quality.

</details>


### [262] [EulerLoRA: Rank-Driven Jump Dynamics for Calibrated Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01142)
*Srinivas Anumasa,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EulerLoRA extends LoRA for uncertainty estimation by generating multiple predictive trajectories via sampling structured variations along rank-one components, achieving comparable performance to LoRA ensembles with significantly fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LoRA produces deterministic models without predictive uncertainty estimation capabilities, which is important for reliable deployment in real-world applications where uncertainty quantification is needed.

Method: EulerLoRA introduces stochasticity by sampling structured variations along the rank-one components of shared low-rank adapters while preserving the deterministic LoRA transformation in expectation, enabling multiple predictive trajectories from a small number of shared adapters.

Result: EulerLoRA achieves comparable or improved performance relative to LoRA-Ensemble baselines on vision transformers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and HAM10000 datasets with out-of-distribution detection on SVHN, while using 69% fewer trainable parameters (3M vs 10M).

Conclusion: Useful predictive diversity can be obtained from a small number of shared adapters, demonstrating that EulerLoRA provides an efficient approach for uncertainty estimation while maintaining parameter efficiency compared to ensemble methods.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning, but standard LoRA produces a single deterministic model and does not directly support predictive uncertainty estimation. We introduce EulerLoRA, a stochastic extension of LoRA that generates multiple predictive trajectories by sampling structured variations along the rank-one components of shared low-rank adapters, while preserving the deterministic LoRA transformation in expectation. We evaluate EulerLoRA with vision transformers on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and HAM10000, together with out-of-distribution detection on SVHN. Across these benchmarks, EulerLoRA achieves comparable or improved performance relative to strong LoRA-Ensemble baselines. Using two rank-20 adapters, EulerLoRA requires approximately 3 million trainable adapter parameters, compared with about 10 million for a rank-8, 16-adapter LoRA-Ensemble, corresponding to roughly 69% fewer trainable parameters. These results show that useful predictive diversity can be obtained from a small number of shared adapters.

</details>


### [263] [Differentiable Lifting for Topological Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01160)
*Jorge Luiz Franco,Gabriel Duarte,Alexander Nikitin,Moacir Ponti,Diego Mesquita,Amauri H. Souza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ∂lift (DiffLift) is an end-to-end framework for learning optimal graph liftings to higher-order structures (hypergraphs, cellular/simplicial complexes) to improve Topological Neural Networks performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Topological Neural Networks (TNNs) rely on higher-order structures like cycles and cliques to enhance message-passing neural networks, but these structures are typically identified a priori through unsupervised graph lifting operations. The choice of lifting method is crucial and significantly impacts TNN performance on downstream tasks, creating a need for a more adaptive approach.

Method: The proposed ∂lift (DiffLift) framework learns graph liftings in an end-to-end fashion by leveraging learned vertex-level latent representations to identify and parameterize distributions over candidate higher-order cells for inclusion. This creates a scalable model that can be integrated into any TNN architecture.

Result: ∂lift outperforms existing lifting methods on multiple benchmarks for graph and node classification across different TNN architectures. The approach achieves gains of up to 45% over static liftings, including both connectivity- and feature-based methods.

Conclusion: End-to-end learning of graph liftings through ∂lift provides a more effective approach than static lifting methods, significantly boosting TNN performance by adaptively discovering optimal higher-order structures tailored to specific tasks.

Abstract: Topological neural networks (TNNs) enable leveraging high-order structures on graphs (e.g., cycles and cliques) to boost the expressive power of message-passing neural networks. In turn, however, these structures are typically identified a priori through an unsupervised graph lifting operation. Notwithstanding, this choice is crucial and may have a drastic impact on a TNN's performance on downstream tasks. To circumvent this issue, we propose $\partial$lift (DiffLift), a general framework for learning graph liftings to hypergraphs and cellular- and simplicial complexes in an end-to-end fashion. In particular, our approach leverages learned vertex-level latent representations to identify and parameterize distributions over candidate higher-order cells for inclusion. This results in a scalable model which can be readily integrated into any TNN. Our experiments show that $\partial$lift outperforms existing lifting methods on multiple benchmarks for graph and node classification across different TNN architectures. Notably, our approach leads to gains of up to 45% over static liftings, including both connectivity- and feature-based ones.

</details>


### [264] [Interpretable Machine Learning for Traffic Congestion Prediction: Unveiling the Impact of Different COVID-19 Periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01180)
*Dan Zhu,Chi Sin Ng,Litian Xie,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops traffic congestion prediction models for Alameda County, CA during COVID-19 periods using machine learning with feature selection, finding Bi-LSTM performs best and interpreting how COVID-19 variables affected congestion patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The COVID-19 pandemic altered travel behavior and increased complexity in traffic congestion prediction, creating a need for models that can handle these changes and understand pandemic-related factors' impacts on congestion.

Method: Used Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation for feature selection; trained and optimized multiple models (SVR, MLR, RNN, LSTM); employed adaptive parameter selection for LSTM due to hyperparameter sensitivity; evaluated using Normalized RMSE; used Integrated Gradients for Bi-LSTM interpretation and SHAP for SVR interpretation.

Result: Bidirectional LSTM consistently performed best across all periods (pre-lockdown, lockdown, post-lockdown) by capturing temporal dependence in both directions; new COVID-19 cases had negative effects on congestion during lockdown/post-lockdown; post-pandemic hospitalization reduced congestion while higher fuel prices increased congestion due to shift to private vehicles.

Conclusion: Bi-LSTM is effective for traffic prediction during pandemic disruptions, and COVID-19 variables significantly impacted travel behavior - with risk awareness and restrictions reducing congestion, while economic factors like fuel prices paradoxically increased congestion through private vehicle shifts.

Abstract: Traffic congestion prediction is essential for congestion mitigation, but the COVID-19 pandemic and related control measures altered travel behavior and increased prediction complexity. This study predicts congestion in Alameda County, California, during pre-lockdown, lockdown, and post-lockdown periods. Weather, seasonality, and COVID-19 variables are incorporated, and Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation is used to select important features and reduce overfitting. Support vector regression, multiple linear regression, recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory networks are trained and optimized. Because LSTM is more sensitive to hyperparameter settings, an adaptive parameter selection approach is used, while SVR and RNN are manually tuned. Performance is evaluated using Normalized Root Mean Square Error. Bidirectional LSTM consistently performs best across all periods because it captures temporal dependence in both directions. Integrated Gradients is used to interpret Bi-LSTM predictions, and SHapley Additive exPlanations is applied to SVR. New COVID-19 cases have a mainly negative effect on congestion during lockdown and post-lockdown, likely due to greater risk awareness, voluntary travel reduction, and compliance with mobility restrictions. In the post-pandemic period, higher hospitalization reduces travel and congestion, while higher fuel prices do not prevent a shift toward private vehicles and therefore increase congestion.

</details>


### [265] [SAFE-Merge: Data-Free Continual Model Merging with General Knowledge Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01184)
*Zihuan Qiu,Zhiyang Liao,Chiyuan He,Yi Xu,Fanman Meng,Linfeng Xu,Qingbo Wu,Hongliang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAFE-Merge is a data-free continual model merging framework that protects both pretrained general knowledge and previously acquired tasks by selectively retaining safe parameter updates and recovering lost task information through masked low-rank recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual model merging methods focus on suppressing interference among downstream tasks but overlook the erosion of pretrained general knowledge. This erosion degrades generalization to held-out distributions and weakens the foundation for future task acquisition, creating a safety gap in data-free continual merging.

Method: SAFE-Merge uses a two-step approach: 1) Risk-aware sparse masking that selects parameter updates carrying task-specific information while posing low risk to general knowledge, and 2) Masked low-rank recovery that compensates for lost task information using only retained parameter updates while leaving masked parameters unchanged. The combined update is then fused into the backbone without additional inference cost.

Result: Across vision and language benchmarks, SAFE-Merge consistently achieves the best H-score. On longer CLIP task sequences, it substantially improves H-score over NUFILT while also achieving the highest accuracy.

Conclusion: SAFE-Merge effectively addresses the safety gap in data-free continual model merging by protecting both pretrained general knowledge and task-specific information, leading to superior performance across diverse benchmarks and task sequences.

Abstract: Data-free continual model merging must incorporate a stream of specialized models while retaining both pretrained general knowledge and previously acquired tasks, without access to task data. Existing methods mainly merge task updates by suppressing interference among downstream tasks; while this protects previously acquired tasks, it overlooks the safety of the pretrained knowledge itself, whose erosion degrades generalization to held-out distributions and weakens the foundation for future task acquisition. We propose SAFE-Merge, a simple data-free continual-merging framework that first decides which parameter updates are safe to retain, and then recovers the task information lost through masking. Specifically, to ensure safety, risk-aware sparse masking selects parameter updates that carry task-specific information while posing low risk to general knowledge. Masked low-rank recovery then compensates for the lost task information using only the same retained parameter updates, while leaving all masked-out parameters strictly unchanged. Finally, the combined update is fused into the backbone, incurring no additional inference cost. Across vision and language benchmarks, SAFE-Merge consistently achieves the best H-score. On longer CLIP task sequences, it substantially improves H-score over NUFILT while also achieving the highest accuracy.

</details>


### [266] [ReBRAC-v2: The Return of the King](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01205)
*Denis Tarasov,Robert K. Katzschmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReBRAC-v2 modernizes traditional behavior-regularized actor-critic with exact-likelihood normalizing flows, mixed regularization objectives, classification-based residual critics, and multi-sample inference, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple offline RL benchmarks with a single shared configuration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper questions whether progress in offline RL needs complex generative policies and specialized value-guidance mechanisms, or can instead come from systematically modernizing conventional behavior-regularized actor-critic methods while preserving algorithmic simplicity.

Method: Introduces ReBRAC-v2 which: 1) Uses exact-likelihood normalizing flow as RL actor, 2) Combines likelihood, MSE, and MAE behavior regularization, 3) Integrates classification-based residual critic, 4) Employs staged optimization, 5) Uses multi-sample test-time action selection. The configuration was developed via ~600 Bayesian proposals on six OGBench tasks and then fixed for all experiments.

Result: Achieves 74.8 average across ten state-based OGBench categories (vs 52.3 next-best), ranks first in eight categories. Also obtains strongest averages on D4RL AntMaze (90.2) and Adroit (33.6) without structural changes. Ablations show sensitivity to mixed cloning objectives, staged training, flow capacity, and multi-sample inference.

Conclusion: Disciplined, transferable engineering can achieve state-of-the-art aggregate performance in offline RL without abandoning minimalist foundations, demonstrating that systematic modernization of conventional approaches can compete with more complex specialized methods.

Abstract: Recent offline reinforcement learning methods increasingly rely on expressive generative policies and specialized value-guidance mechanisms. We ask whether comparable progress can instead come from systematically modernizing a conventional behavior-regularized actor-critic while preserving its algorithmic simplicity. We introduce ReBRAC-v2, which directly trains an exact-likelihood normalizing flow as the RL actor, combines likelihood, MSE, and MAE behavior regularization, and integrates a classification-based residual critic, staged optimization, and multi-sample test-time action selection. Rather than tuning this recipe separately for every task, we develop a single shared configuration via roughly 600 Bayesian proposals on six challenging OGBench tasks, freeze all structural and optimization choices, and adapt only two behavior-regularization coefficients over a 16-point grid. Across ten common state-based OGBench categories, ReBRAC-v2 averages 74.8 compared to 52.3 for the next-best aggregate result and ranks first in eight categories. The same recipe, without structural changes, obtains the strongest averages in our comparisons on D4RL AntMaze (90.2) and Adroit (33.6). Fixed-recipe ablations show the largest sensitivity to the selected mixed cloning objective, staged training, sufficient flow capacity, and multi-sample inference, while showing that several smaller choices depend on the values of other hyperparameters. These results show that disciplined, transferable engineering can achieve state-of-the-art aggregate performance without abandoning a minimalist offline RL foundation.

</details>


### [267] [AdaHAT: Adaptive Hard Attention to the Task in Task-Incremental Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01252)
*Pengxiang Wang,Hongbo Bo,Jun Hong,Weiru Liu,Kedian Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AdaHAT extends HAT with adaptive attention to better balance stability-plasticity trade-off in long task sequences, alleviating network capacity problems in continual learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Architecture-based approaches for catastrophic forgetting in task-incremental learning face network capacity problems in long task sequences - as more tasks are learned, more parameters become static to prevent forgetting, reducing plasticity for new tasks.

Method: Proposed Adaptive Hard Attention to the Task (AdaHAT) with adaptive attention mechanism that allows adaptive updates to static parameters by considering both importance to previous tasks and current network capacity. Developed new neural network architecture extending HAT.

Result: Experimental results on multiple datasets show AdaHAT achieves better average performance across tasks than baselines including HAT, especially on long task sequences, demonstrating effective balancing of stability-plasticity trade-off.

Conclusion: AdaHAT successfully addresses network capacity problems in long task sequences by adaptive parameter updates, improving task-incremental learning performance while alleviating catastrophic forgetting.

Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a major problem in task-incremental learning, where neural networks tend to overwrite previously learned knowledge when trained on new tasks. A number of architecture-based approaches have been proposed to address this problem. However, the architecture-based approaches suffer from another problem related to network capacity when the networks learn long task sequences: As a network is trained on an increasing number of new tasks in a long task sequence, a growing proportion of active parameters becomes static to prevent forgetting of previously learned knowledge. In this paper, we propose Adaptive Hard Attention to the Task (AdaHAT) with an adaptive attention mechanism which allows adaptive updates to static parameters by taking into account the information about previous tasks on both the importance of these parameters to previous tasks and the current network capacity. Based on this idea, we develop a new neural network architecture incorporating our proposed AdaHAT mechanism. AdaHAT extends an existing architecture-based approach, Hard Attention to the Task (HAT), to better support task-incremental learning over long task sequences. We conduct experiments on a number of datasets and compare AdaHAT with task-incremental learning baselines including HAT. Our experimental results show that AdaHAT achieves better average performance across tasks than these baselines, especially on long task sequences, demonstrating the benefits from balancing the trade-off between stability and plasticity of a network when learning such sequences of tasks, alleviating the network capacity problem. Our code is available at pengxiang-wang.com/projects/continual-learning-arena.

</details>


### [268] [Distill What the Student Can See: Fisher-Projected On-Policy Distillation for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01263)
*Leyan Xue,Feng Xiong,Mingjun Ma,Changqing Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FP-OPD improves vision-language model distillation by projecting teacher corrections onto the student's local capacity constraints, addressing the mismatch between full teacher distributions and compact student capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard On-Policy Distillation (OPD) assumes the complete teacher distribution is appropriate for all student capacities, but in vision-language reasoning, teacher corrections often depend on visual distinctions that compact students cannot represent. This leads to inefficient distillation as students can't fully realize prescribed distribution shifts.

Method: Fisher-Projected On-Policy Distillation (FP-OPD) estimates the student's local visual tangent space using continuous visual perturbations, then projects the teacher-student log-probability gap onto this space under the student's Fisher metric. This creates a capacity-aware target optimized with full-vocabulary reverse KL on student trajectories.

Result: In 8B-to-2B distillation, FP-OPD improves all seven evaluated multimodal benchmarks, raising average score by 2.77 points over pretrained student and by 1.60 points over standard OPD.

Conclusion: Locally realizable teacher corrections provide a more effective target for distilling compact vision-language models, addressing the capacity mismatch issue that limits standard distillation methods.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) samples trajectories from the current student policy and minimizes token-level divergence between student and teacher next-token distributions at prefixes along those trajectories. This aligns the distillation states with the student's own generation distribution. However, it still assumes that the complete teacher distribution is an appropriate target across student capacities. In vision--language reasoning, teacher corrections can depend on visual distinctions that a compact student cannot represent. Our target-scaling study shows that, as the target approaches the complete teacher distribution, the student realizes less of the prescribed shift and obtains worse downstream performance. We therefore propose \emph{Fisher-Projected On-Policy Distillation} (FP-OPD), which distills only locally realizable teacher corrections. FP-OPD uses continuous visual perturbations to estimate the student's local visual tangent space and projects the centered teacher--student log-probability gap onto this space under the student's Fisher metric. The resulting capacity-aware target is optimized with full-vocabulary reverse KL on student trajectories, retaining the standard OPD framework. In 8B-to-2B distillation, FP-OPD improves all seven evaluated multimodal benchmarks. It raises the average score by 2.77 points over the pretrained student and by 1.60 points over standard OPD. These results demonstrate that locally realizable teacher corrections provide a more effective target for distilling compact vision--language models.

</details>


### [269] [Riemannian Attention Mechanisms for Transformers: A Theoretical Framework and Architecture Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01283)
*Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Riemannian geometry into Transformer attention mechanisms, replacing Euclidean inner products with learned per-token Riemannian metrics to address representational rank collapse, while maintaining computational feasibility through low-rank approximations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the fundamental limitation of standard Transformer architectures where Euclidean inner product attention causes representational rank to decay doubly exponentially with depth, as proven by Dong et al. (2021), which severely limits the expressive power of deep Transformer models.

Method: The method involves: (1) replacing flat Euclidean metrics with learned per-token Riemannian metrics, (2) proving Riemannian attention scores with heterogeneous metrics are non-Gram and cannot be factorized as QK^T, (3) using low-rank metric factors to make geometric operations tractable via Woodbury identity (O(d*r) and O(d*r^2) complexity), and (4) proposing the Fiber Bundle Transformer architecture with geodesic distance attention and metric-preconditioned feed-forward updates.

Result: Theoretical results show: (1) Riemannian attention with heterogeneous metrics cannot be factorized as QK^T (non-Gram property), (2) low-rank approximations make Riemannian attention feasible at billion-parameter scale with negligible overhead, and (3) complete architecture specification for the Fiber Bundle Transformer is provided with formal predictions about geometric architectures.

Conclusion: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for Riemannian attention as a structural solution to rank collapse in Transformers and provides a complete architectural framework, but leaves empirical validation as future work while identifying the central open problem of proving whether heterogeneous Riemannian metrics prevent the rank collapse caused by row-stochastic attention matrices.

Abstract: All Transformer-based large language models compute attention via the Euclidean inner product, an architectural choice that Dong et al. (2021) proved causes representational rank to decay doubly exponentially with depth in pure self-attention stacks. We develop a theoretical framework that targets this structural limitation at the mathematical level by replacing the flat Euclidean metric with learned per-token Riemannian metrics. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We prove that Riemannian attention scores with heterogeneous per-token metrics are non-Gram---they cannot be factorized as QK^T with factorization dimension O(d). We are explicit that this is a structural observation, not a proof of rank preservation. (2) We establish that low-rank metric factors render all geometric operations tractable: geodesic distance in O(d*r) per token and metric inversion in O(d*r^2) via the Woodbury identity---both far below the O(d^3) cost of a general matrix---making Riemannian attention feasible at billion-parameter scale with negligible overhead. (3) We present the Fiber Bundle Transformer, a complete architecture specification in which each token position carries its own Riemannian metric, attention is geodesic distance computation, feed-forward updates use metric-preconditioned steps, and the connection carries explicit curvature and torsion proxies. We derive formal predictions about correctly implemented geometric architectures and identify the central open problem: proving or disproving that heterogeneous Riemannian metrics prevent the rank collapse that row-stochastic attention matrices otherwise cause. This paper presents theoretical analysis and architectural design; empirical validation is the subject of future work.

</details>


### [270] [Training nGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01284)
*Ilya Loshchilov,Boris Ginsburg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Normalized Transformer (nGPT) with hyperspherical constraints achieves 2x training efficiency, reaching same validation loss with half the tokens compared to unnormalized models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve training efficiency of large language models by constraining them to hyperspherical representations, potentially reducing training time and computational costs.

Method: Proposes a practical training recipe for nGPT including: Logit Gradient Preconditioning, Logarithmic Learning Rate Decay, GatedAdamW, angular update control, and optional exploration mechanisms. Applied to hybrid Mamba-2--Transformer Mixture-of-Experts models.

Result: 14B-parameter nGPT model reaches same validation loss as unnormalized model with approximately half the training tokens. Recipe scales effectively up to 14B total parameters.

Conclusion: Normalized Transformer training recipe enables significantly more efficient training of large language models, offering potential for faster iteration and reduced computational requirements in model development.

Abstract: The normalized Transformer (nGPT) realizes hyperspherical representation learning by constraining model parameter vectors and activation vectors to the unit hypersphere. In this paper, we describe a practical training recipe for nGPT and evaluate it on modern hybrid Mamba-2--Transformer Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The recipe introduces Logit Gradient Preconditioning, Logarithmic Learning Rate Decay, GatedAdamW, angular update control, and optional exploration mechanisms. Compared with an unnormalized model of the same hybrid MoE architecture trained with AdamW, the 14B-total-parameter nGPT model reaches the same validation loss using approximately half as many training tokens. The recipe scales across the models considered, which contain up to 14B total parameters.

</details>


### [271] [Stop When Memory Suffices: Evidence-Conditioned Progressive Execution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01285)
*Yidan Lin,Kaixiang Wang,Jiong Lou,Jie Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Router-Mem is a memory system for LLMs that balances answer quality with low latency by using evidence-conditioned progressive execution, with early termination when sufficient evidence is found and deeper analysis when needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory systems for LLMs face a trade-off: compressed systems lose important dependencies while comprehensive systems have high latency and cost. There's a need for a memory system that achieves strong answer quality while maintaining low online latency.

Method: Router-Mem uses evidence-conditioned progressive execution with three key components: 1) shared low-cost retrieval prefix for evidence gathering, 2) lightweight sufficiency router that predicts if context supports early termination (single-token decision at inference), 3) when evidence is insufficient, reuses retrieval hits to expand memory blocks for deeper analysis and aggregation. It's trained with evidence-level supervision and rationale-conditioned representation distillation.

Result: On AMA-Bench and BEAM datasets, Router-Mem achieves 55.17% and 38.77% scores while reducing average inference time by 27.3% and 25.5% compared with full memory execution approaches.

Conclusion: Router-Mem successfully demonstrates that it's possible to achieve strong answer quality while maintaining low online latency in LLM memory systems through evidence-conditioned progressive execution with early termination capabilities.

Abstract: The continued development of LLMs toward persistent and adaptive intelligence increasingly requires long-term memory mechanisms that preserve and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems either compress and structure histories for efficient access or perform deep research over broader trajectories. The former lowers online cost but may omit temporal, causal, or cross-step dependencies, while the latter improves evidence coverage at substantial latency and inference cost. This raises a key question: can a memory system achieve strong answer quality while maintaining low online latency? We introduce Router-Mem, an evidence-conditioned progressive execution framework for long-horizon agent memory. Router-Mem first applies a shared low-cost retrieval prefix to obtain evidence. A lightweight sufficiency router then predicts whether the context supports early termination, which enable a single-token decision at inference time. It is trained with evidence-level supervision and rationale-conditioned representation distillation. When evidence is insufficient, Router-Mem reuses retrieval hits to expand memory blocks and perform deeper analysis and aggregation. Experiments on AMA-Bench and BEAM show that Router-Mem achieves 55.17\% and 38.77\% score while reducing average inference time by 27.3\% and 25.5\% compared with full memory execution.

</details>


### [272] [FedChronos: Federated Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Privacy-Preserving Commodity Price Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01290)
*Amit Sharma,Nitin Auluck,Akramul Azim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedChronos enables federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of time-series foundation models using LoRA adapters, achieving improved forecasting accuracy with privacy guarantees in distributed settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series foundation models show strong forecasting capabilities but can't be adapted to institutionally fragmented settings where data cannot be centralized due to regulatory, competitive, or sovereignty constraints.

Method: Applies Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to Chronos-T5 backbone and trains across distributed clients using FedAvg and FedProx, transmitting only lightweight adapter weights (384KB per round), with differential privacy as implicit regularization.

Result: Best configuration (ε=5) reduces MAPE by 31% over zero-shot and 26% over traditional baselines on Indian agricultural commodity price data, while providing differential privacy guarantees.

Conclusion: Privacy and accuracy can be complementary rather than competing objectives in federated TSFM fine-tuning, with compact models suitable for edge AI deployments.

Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos have demonstrated strong forecasting capabilities across domains, yet adapting them to institutionally fragmented settings, where data cannot be centralized due to regulatory, competitive, or sovereignty constraints, remains unexplored. We introduce FedChronos, a framework for federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of an already pre-trained TSFM, a setting that existing federated time-series work has not addressed, since prior methods either pre-train from scratch or align prototypes rather than adapt a fixed backbone. Our approach applies Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to the Chronos-T5 backbone and trains across distributed clients using FedAvg and FedProx, transmitting only lightweight adapter weights (384~KB per round, an 86$\times$ reduction over full-model exchange). We evaluate FedChronos on daily commodity prices from 15 Indian agricultural markets across 9 states, a naturally non-IID federated setting, and find that naïve LoRA fine-tuning overfits substantially on small per-client datasets, dropping below zero-shot performance. We further observe that differential privacy (DP) noise can act as implicit regularization and counteract this overfitting: in our experiments the strongest configuration ($\varepsilon = 5$) reduces mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) by 31% over zero-shot and 26% over the best traditional baseline, while bounding each round's information leakage via per-round $(\varepsilon, δ)$-differential privacy. Because the model is compact and the updates are small, the approach also suits edge AI deployments where both the network link and the client device are constrained. Overall, our findings suggest that privacy and accuracy can be complementary rather than competing objectives in federated TSFM fine-tuning.

</details>


### [273] [AlphaG-OPD: Reliability-Gated Sibling Counterfactuals for On-Policy Distillation in Symbolic Alpha Factor Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01303)
*Yaoyu Su*

Main category: cs.LG
