TL;DR: The paper provides sharp, dimension-free characterizations for local root anti-concentration in online optimization of piecewise-Lipschitz functions, removing previous √N losses and offering verifiable criteria for dependent coefficient laws.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the one-dimensional local root anti-concentration questions posed by Balcan, Pegden, and Sharma in the context of online optimization of piecewise-Lipschitz functions, aiming to provide sharp characterizations without dimension-dependent losses.

Method: Uses section-averaged projective incidence speed analysis for homogeneous feature curves, develops conditional and joint coefficient-space area formulas, employs a two-chart certificate for verification, and applies projective incidence theorem and rigid translation techniques.

Result: For cube-supported coefficients, shows worst-case interval-hitting constant equals A times section-averaged projective incidence speed (equivalent to projective Lipschitz constant up to universal constants). For monic degree-d polynomials, proves interval-hitting constant is finite iff ordered real-root laws have bounded densities with sharp factor-d comparison. Achieves expected regret bounds for graph-learning applications.

Conclusion: The paper provides complete, sharp characterizations of local root anti-concentration that are dimension-free, removes previous √N losses, and offers verifiable criteria applicable even to dependent and singular coefficient laws, with practical applications in graph learning.

Abstract: This paper answers the one-dimensional local root anti-concentration questions posed by Balcan, Pegden, and Sharma in the context of online optimization of piecewise-Lipschitz functions. For a homogeneous feature curve and coefficients whose density relative to the uniform law on a symmetric convex body $K$ is bounded by $A$, we show that the worst-case interval-hitting constant equals $A$ times a section-averaged projective incidence speed. For cube-supported coefficients, this speed is equivalent, up to universal constants, to the projective Lipschitz constant. This yields a sharp, dimension-free characterization and removes the previous $\sqrt N$ loss. For monic degree-$d$ polynomials under arbitrary coefficient laws, we prove that the interval-hitting constant is finite if and only if the ordered real-root laws have bounded densities, with a factor-$d$ comparison that is sharp. Conditional and joint coefficient-space area formulas, together with a two-chart certificate, make this criterion verifiable for dependent and singular coefficient laws. We also give two graph-learning applications that complete the transition-to-regret chain. A cost-sensitive Gaussian-RBF harmonic classifier uses the projective incidence theorem and achieves expected regret $\widetilde O((An^2D e^{BD}/\ell+1)\sqrt T)$. A common-offset polynomial-kernel model uses rigid translation of the ordered roots and achieves $\widetilde O((qn^2κ+1)\sqrt T)$ regret, even when the induced coefficient law is singular in the ambient coefficient space.

</details>


### [298] [Progressive Agent Skill Generation via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01678)
*Junhao Shen,Zhanqiu Zhang,Yiwen Guo,Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Skill-α is a reinforcement learning method that treats skill generation as a sequential editing process, using rollback rewards to evaluate individual edits by comparing downstream task performance with original vs edited skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill generation methods rely on heuristics or pipeline approaches that need customization for different evidence sources. Learning-based approaches offer more unified modeling but lack natural supervision signals for skills, as skill value can only be determined by whether they improve downstream task performance.

Method: Skill-α formulates skill generation as a sequential editing process that decomposes skill construction into individually evaluable edits. It introduces a novel rollback reward that evaluates each edit by comparing downstream execution under the original and edited skills on an anchored query, using reinforcement learning for progressive skill generation.

Result: Skill-α generates more effective skills than heuristic or pipeline methods in both document-to-skill and experience-to-skill settings. With GPT-4o worker, it improves average downstream success rates by 3.3 points on CL-Bench and 6.7 points on tau2-bench over the strongest baseline. Ablations confirm the importance of rollback reward and progressive generation.

Conclusion: The proposed Skill-α method successfully addresses the supervision challenge in learning-based skill generation through sequential editing with rollback rewards, demonstrating significant performance improvements over existing approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Existing skill generation methods largely rely on heuristics or pipeline-style consolidation, which must be specially designed for different evidence sources. In contrast, learning-based approaches offer a more unified way to model skill generation across heterogeneous sources. However, learning-based skill generation remains challenging because skills lack a natural supervision signal based on relevance or correctness; their value can largely be determined only by whether they improve the behavior of the agent on downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose Skill-$α$, a reinforcement learning method for progressively generating high-quality agent skills. Specifically, we formulate skill generation as a sequential editing process that decomposes skill construction into individually evaluable edits, and introduce a novel rollback reward that evaluates each edit by comparing downstream execution under the original and edited skills on an anchored query. Extensive experiments show that Skill-$α$ generates more effective skills than methods based on heuristics or pipelines in both document-to-skill and experience-to-skill settings. Under the main GPT-4o worker, Skill-$α$ improves average downstream success rates over the strongest skill-generation baseline by 3.3 points on CL-Bench and 6.7 points on tau2-bench. Further ablations validate the importance of rollback reward and progressive generation.

</details>


### [299] [Beckmann Transport Models: From Autonomous Flows to One-Step Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01692)
*Lee Cheuk-Kit,Florentin Coeurdoux,Peter Potaptchik,Yilun Du,Michael Samuel Albergo,Eric Vanden-Eijnden*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces an autonomous flow matching method using time-independent velocity fields to exactly map between distributions when the target is singular (lower-dimensional manifold). It shows the one-step generative map solves a conservation equation that can be learned directly from samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a unified framework for flow matching that handles singular target distributions (supported on lower-dimensional manifolds) and establishes connections between various existing methods like Poisson-flow generative models and equilibrium matching.

Method: Proposes autonomous flows - flow matching with time-independent velocity fields that exactly map between distributions when the target is singular. Shows that the one-step generative map solves a conservation equation that can be learned directly from samples.

Result: Provides a unifying framework that recovers existing methods like Poisson-flow generative models and equilibrium matching. Demonstrates effectiveness on ImageNet 256x256 and corrects inconsistencies in existing methods.

Conclusion: Autonomous flows and one-step maps offer a principled approach to flow matching for singular distributions, providing a unifying framework with connections to transportation theory and practical effectiveness on large-scale image generation tasks.

Abstract: We propose an instantiation of flow matching that relies on a time-independent velocity field (an \emph{autonomous flow}) to exactly map between two distributions, so long as the target is singular, i.e.\ supported on a lower-dimensional data manifold. We also show that the one-step generative map associated with this flow is the unique solution of a simple conservation equation, which can be used to learn the map directly from samples. These autonomous flows and maps give a dynamical meaning to the flux constraint of Beckmann's transportation problem. Their construction provides a unifying framework that recovers, for instance, the closed-form Poisson-flow generative model and equilibrium matching with a quadratic flow-matching regression loss. We illustrate how this theory corrects inconsistencies in existing methods and demonstrate the effectiveness of the autonomous flow and the one-step map on ImageNet 256x256.

</details>


### [300] [Beyond On-Policy Exploration: Integrating External Policy Rollouts for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01717)
*Wonseok Lee,Jimyeong Kim,Jungmin Ko,Wonjong Rhee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ERILS integrates external high-reward rollouts with on-policy rollouts in dLLM reinforcement learning using length control and separate reward processing to address training instability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy reinforcement learning for diffusion LLMs suffers when target model produces few successful rollouts, limiting training progress due to insufficient positive rewards.

Method: ERILS (External Rollout Integration with Length Control and Source-Specific Processing) controls external rollout lengths and processes on-policy/external rewards separately to avoid training instability.

Result: ERILS improves multi-sample performance across Sudoku, Countdown, and MATH500 tasks, achieving 98.4% best-of-4 accuracy on Sudoku vs. 40.3% baseline, while maintaining ~90% single-completion accuracy across token lengths.

Conclusion: Rollout construction and reward processing are crucial design dimensions for integrating external rollouts in dLLM reinforcement learning, with ERILS demonstrating effectiveness through controlled length and source-specific processing.

Abstract: Recent reinforcement learning methods for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) commonly rely on on-policy rollouts generated by the target dLLM itself. When successful on-policy rollouts are scarce, however, on-policy training may receive little positive reward and make only limited progress. To mitigate this problem, we explore incorporating higher-reward rollouts generated by a stronger external policy alongside on-policy rollouts from the target dLLM. However, directly incorporating these external rollouts introduces two practical challenges: differences in rollout length and instability when jointly processing rewards from on-policy and external rollouts. To address these challenges, we propose External Rollout Integration with Length Control and Source-Specific Processing (ERILS), which controls external-rollout length and processes the rewards of on-policy and external rollouts separately. Experiments on Sudoku, Countdown, and MATH500 under zero-shot evaluation show that ERILS improves multi-sample performance across all three tasks, with the largest gains on Sudoku. On Sudoku, ERILS achieves 98.4% best-of-4 completion accuracy, compared with 40.3% for the strongest baseline. ERILS also maintains approximately 90% deterministic single-completion accuracy on Sudoku across generation lengths of 128, 256, and 512 tokens. Our component analysis further shows that length-controlled external rollouts are more effective than uncontrolled external rollouts, and that source-specific reward processing avoids the training collapse observed with joint reward processing. These results show that rollout construction and reward processing are important design dimensions when integrating external rollouts into dLLM reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [301] [LLM-Guided Retrieval for Prediction of Molecular Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01734)
*Betty Xiong,Jan-Christian Huetter,Gabriele Scalia,Tommaso Biancalani,Sepideh Maleki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM-Guided Retrieval (LGR) uses large language models to select relevant neighbor drugs for predicting transcriptomic responses, outperforming baselines in drug-cell perturbation prediction tasks, especially for unseen cell-line generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exhaustive profiling of all drug-cell combinations is infeasible, and current methods for predicting transcriptomic responses to small-molecule perturbations across cell lines need improvement, particularly for zero-shot scenarios where drugs or cell lines are unseen during training.

Method: Frames perturbation prediction as retrieve-and-aggregate: uses LLM to rank candidate neighbor drugs (limited to those profiled in target cell line), then aggregates their observed expression deltas with a fixed mean aggregator to predict responses for unmeasured drug-cell combinations.

Result: LGR consistently outperforms drug mean, ChemCPA, and chemistry-based kNN baselines on Tahoe-100M dataset, with strongest gains in unseen cell-line generalization (higher correlation, lower error). Improves directional accuracy of gene regulation across all settings.

Conclusion: Retrieval quality is more important than predictor complexity for zero-shot molecular perturbation prediction. LLMs serve as effective constrained retrieval modules, providing useful biological priors for predicting drug effects across cell lines.

Abstract: Predicting transcriptomic responses to small-molecule perturbations across cell lines is central to drug discovery, but exhaustive profiling of drug-cell combinations is infeasible. We frame molecular perturbation prediction as retrieve-and-aggregate: approximate an unmeasured drug's response in a cell line by aggregating measured responses of a small set of biologically related compounds. We propose LLM-Guided Retrieval (LGR), where a large language model (LLM) ranks candidate neighbor drugs (restricted to those profiled in the target cell line); after which a fixed mean aggregator combines their observed expression deltas to form the prediction. We evaluate on the Tahoe-100M single-cell perturbation atlas under unseen-drug, unseen-cell-line, and open-world regimes. LGR consistently improves over drug mean, ChemCPA, and chemistry-based kNN baselines, with the strongest gains for unseen cell-line generalization, where it achieves higher correlation and lower error than mean baselines. Across settings, LGR improves directional (sign) accuracy of gene regulation, indicating better recovery of biologically meaningful perturbation effects even when magnitude-based metrics are similar. These results suggest that retrieval quality, rather than predictor complexity, is a key driver of zero-shot molecular perturbation prediction, and that LLMs can provide a useful biological prior when used as constrained retrieval modules.

</details>


### [302] [Disagree to Accelerate: Closing the Loop on Diffusion Feature Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01740)
*Yanchao Li,Jiaqing Xie,Ben Gao,Wanhao Liu,Yanbo Wang,T. Y. Tsui,Jinfei Liu,Yuqiang Li,Tianfan Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RACER introduces a training-free closed-loop controller that dynamically adjusts trust in feature forecasts during diffusion sampling acceleration, using forecast disagreement as a cheap reliability signal to improve sample quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current training-free feature forecasting methods for diffusion sampling acceleration use open-loop caches that trust forecasts equally at all skipped steps, but forecast error varies sharply across steps. This fixed trust breaks down with aggressive acceleration, highlighting the need for dynamic reliability assessment.

Method: RACER uses forecast disagreement as a cheap runtime signal of reliability (no extra denoiser evaluation). It has two responses: 1) continuously shrinks uncertain forecasts toward last computed features using deterministic error bounds, and 2) at riskiest steps, refreshes the feature and skips a later scheduled evaluation to repay computational cost.

Result: RACER improves quality over strongest open-loop baselines across SD3.5-Large, FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo on DrawBench, VBench, and COCO. On SD3.5, it samples faster at equal quality. RACER also generalizes across forecasting designs and recovers quality lost on simpler forecasting methods.

Conclusion: Reliable diffusion acceleration depends not only on better forecasting but also on how forecasts are used. RACER's closed-loop control with dynamic trust adjustment provides significant quality improvements without extra computational cost.

Abstract: Training-free feature forecasting accelerates diffusion sampling by predicting features at skipped denoising steps. Recent work has mainly focused on designing stronger forecasters. Yet forecast error varies sharply across steps, and open-loop caches trust the forecast in full at every skipped step. This fixed trust is what breaks as acceleration turns aggressive. The missing question is not only how to forecast better, but when and how much to trust a forecast. We show that reliability can be observed from the cache itself. Two forecasts agree where the feature trajectory is smooth, and they diverge where prediction turns hard. Their disagreement is a cheap runtime signal, and it costs no extra denoiser evaluation. Based on this signal, we introduce RACER, a training-free closed-loop controller with two responses. It continuously shrinks uncertain forecasts toward the last computed feature. At the riskiest steps, RACER refreshes the feature and repays the added evaluation by skipping a later scheduled one. We derive a deterministic error bound for the shrinkage and empirically evaluate its validity and tightness across acceleration regimes. At the same number of denoiser evaluations, RACER improves the strongest open-loop baseline across SD3.5-Large, FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo on DrawBench, VBench, and COCO. On SD3.5, we further show that RACER samples faster at equal quality. RACER generalizes across forecasting designs as well. For example, it recovers much of the quality lost on a Taylor base. These results show that reliable diffusion acceleration also depends on how forecasts are used. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/RACER

</details>


### [303] [Toward Plasticity-Preserving KL Regularization for Capability Retention in LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01743)
*Li Wang,Xiaodong Lu,Xiaohan Wang,Jiajun Chai,Wei Lin,Tianhao Peng,Guojun Yin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoKL is a conditional KL regularization method for RL-based LLM post-training that preserves base model capabilities while learning new tasks by only constraining the distribution of correct responses, avoiding limitations of standard full-policy KL regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard full-policy KL regularization in RL-based LLM post-training unnecessarily constrains the entire response distribution, potentially restricting exploration and target-task learning, while trying to mitigate forgetting of existing capabilities.

Method: Proposes Correctness-Conditioned KL Regularization (CoKL) that narrows preservation constraints from full output distribution to only correctness-conditioned response distributions, using forward KL divergence with a practical finite-group training objective.

Result: CoKL achieves better balance between target-task improvement and prior-capability retention than existing regularization methods in multi-solution environments and continual post-training across multiple model scales, and avoids the optimal correctness gap limitation of full-policy KL.

Conclusion: Conditional regularization focusing only on correct responses provides a more precise preservation mechanism for RL-based LLM post-training, enabling better target-task learning while retaining existing capabilities without unnecessary constraints.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central paradigm for large language model (LLM) post-training, but optimization toward new objectives can degrade capabilities already present in the base model. KL regularization is widely used to mitigate such forgetting by constraining policy drift toward a reference model. However, standard full-policy KL regularization constrains the entire response distribution and may unnecessarily restrict exploration and target-task learning. This raises a natural question: can a more precise constraint preserve existing capabilities while minimizing interference with learning new tasks? To this end, we propose \underline{Co}rrectness-Conditioned \underline{KL} Regularization (CoKL), a conditional regularization framework that narrows the preservation constraint from the full output distribution to correctness-conditioned response distributions. We instantiate CoKL with forward KL divergence and derive a practical finite-group training objective for RL-based LLM post-training. At the population level, CoKL decouples the total probability assigned to correct responses from their correctness-conditioned distribution, thereby regularizing the relative probability allocation among reference-supported correct responses without directly anchoring incorrect outputs or total correctness mass. We further show that full-policy forward and reverse KL regularization induce a strict optimal correctness gap when the reference policy is imperfect, whereas CoKL avoids this limitation. Experiments in controlled multi-solution environments and continual post-training settings across multiple model scales demonstrate that CoKL achieves a more favorable balance between target-task improvement and prior-capability retention than existing regularization methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lumina04/CoKL.

</details>


### [304] [Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Radio Resource Management under Coupled Finite-Horizon Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01745)
*Yeonseo Jeong,Wonhyeok Ko,Sungweon Hong,Songnam Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HeLyMARL is a Lyapunov-embedded heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that jointly manages wireless network operations under hard energy and handover constraints through virtual queues and drift-plus-penalty decomposition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Managing dense wireless networks requires simultaneous optimization of user association, scheduling, BS activation, and handover control under strict finite-horizon energy and handover budgets. Traditional MARL approaches struggle with finite-horizon constraints and the nonlinear proportional fairness utility that lacks principled per-slot decomposition.

Method: HeLyMARL uses Lyapunov-embedded heterogeneous MARL with drift-plus-penalty decomposition and virtual queues. It internalizes constraint pressures into a unified per-slot reward, converting the constrained finite-horizon problem into an unconstrained MARL problem. The virtual queues regulate cumulative budget consumption at every partial horizon within episodes.

Result: HeLyMARL outperforms conventional MARL, Lyapunov-based methods, and constrained MARL benchmarks. It's the only method that sustains throughput-fairness balance with uninterrupted service throughout the horizon without premature budget exhaustion. Virtual queues provide pacing guarantees that Lagrangian relaxation cannot achieve.

Conclusion: HeLyMARL successfully resolves the tension between BS-side energy management and user-side handover regulation in dense wireless networks by embedding constraint satisfaction directly into the MARL framework through virtual queues, enabling effective distributed sequential control under hard budget constraints.

Abstract: Maximizing throughput under proportional fairness in dense wireless networks requires jointly managing user association, scheduling, base station (BS) activation, and handover control under hard finite-horizon energy and handover budgets, which induces a fundamental tension between BS-side energy management and user-side handover regulation. While multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a natural framework for such distributed sequential control, its application here faces two difficulties: finite-horizon budget constraints cannot be evaluated at each time slot, and the nonlinear proportional fairness utility admits no principled per-slot decomposition. We propose HeLyMARL, a Lyapunov-embedded heterogeneous MARL framework that resolves both via drift-plus-penalty decomposition with virtual queues. The energy and handover constraint pressures are internalized directly into a unified per-slot reward, converting the constrained finite-horizon problem into an unconstrained MARL problem. Comparison against two Lagrangian-based alternatives reveals a timescale separation: Lagrangian relaxation regulates constraints only across training episodes, whereas the virtual queues of HeLyMARL bound cumulative budget consumption at every partial horizon within an episode, a pacing guarantee beyond the reach of greedy Lyapunov-based control. Simulations show that HeLyMARL is the only method that sustains the throughput-fairness balance together with uninterrupted service throughout the horizon, outperforming conventional MARL, Lyapunov-based, and constrained MARL benchmarks without premature budget exhaustion.

</details>


### [305] [Multi-Source Dynamic Graph Learning for Compound-Flood Forecasting in Managed Coastal Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01775)
*Liangjun You,Min Wu,Orlando Woods,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an anchored forecasting framework that selectively integrates multi-station information with bounded residual corrections to improve prediction of sustained high-water plateaus for flood early warning while maintaining local forecast stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current compound flooding forecasting models have limitations: they can capture temporal dependencies with low average errors but may poorly reproduce prolonged high-water plateaus critical for flood early warning. Single-site records don't fully represent high-water dynamics, while unconstrained fusion of cross-site signals can degrade local forecast stability.

Method: Develops an anchored forecasting framework that incorporates cross-site information through state- and lead-dependent bounded residual corrections. Uses a multi-source regime representation from hydrometeorological and operational observations to adaptively calibrate inter-site relationships and correction scales, preserving local temporal forecast as a stable anchor.

Result: The approach improves prediction reliability of sustained high-water plateaus while maintaining high accuracy during routine hydrological conditions. Experiments show that selectively integrating multi-station dynamic conditions enhances forecasting performance beyond conventional global error statistics.

Conclusion: The anchored forecasting framework effectively integrates cross-site information to improve prediction of high-water characteristics relevant to flood early warning, supporting better water-management decision support by maintaining forecast stability while enhancing event-scale prediction capabilities.

Abstract: Compound flooding in managed coastal systems is influenced by hydrological conditions and water-management activity observed across multiple monitoring stations. Current forecasting models can capture temporal dependencies with low average errors, but global error metrics may conceal poor reproduction of prolonged high-water plateaus that are relevant to flood early warning. Because hydrometeorological and operational signals are distributed across heterogeneous gages, single-site records do not fully represent high-water dynamics. Nevertheless, unconstrained fusion of cross-site signals can degrade the stability of local temporal forecasts. This work proposes an anchored forecasting framework that incorporates cross-site information through state- and lead-dependent bounded residual corrections. A multi-source regime representation constructed from hydrometeorological and operational observations adaptively calibrates inter-site relationships and correction scales, enabling targeted cross-site adjustment while preserving the local temporal forecast as a stable anchor. Beyond conventional global error statistics, we evaluate event-scale high-water characteristics through the temporal alignment of forecasted and observed high-water processes. Experiments demonstrate that selectively integrating multi-station dynamic conditions improves the prediction reliability of sustained high-water plateaus while maintaining high accuracy during routine hydrological conditions, supporting flood early warning and water-management decision support.

</details>


### [306] [ReFP-AD: Rectified Flow Preconditioning for Energy-Based Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01793)
*Camile Lendering,Erkut Akdag,Joaquín Figueira,Egor Bondarev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReFP-AD introduces a geometric reparameterization method using optimal transport-coupled rectified flow to stabilize Energy-Based Models for unified anomaly detection in high-dimensional token spaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified anomaly detection requires modeling heterogeneous normal data without access to anomalies. While foundation models like DINOv2 provide rich representations, leveraging these for density estimation is challenging due to anisotropy and cross-dimensional correlations in high-dimensional token spaces, which degrades MCMC sampling in Energy-Based Models.

Method: ReFP-AD learns a geometric reparameterization via optimal transport-coupled rectified flow that maps high-dimensional embeddings into a well-conditioned latent space. This preconditioning enables stable persistent contrastive divergence with preconditioned SGLD. Anomaly scores are derived from gradient norms of the learned energy landscape.

Result: Achieves 98.6%/97.9% Image/Pixel AUROC on MVTec-AD and 97.3%/99.0% on VisA, outperforming prior unified EBM baselines by up to +10.8% in Image AUROC. Ablation shows geometric reparameterization is critical for finite-step MCMC and accurate anomaly localization.

Conclusion: Geometric reparameterization via rectified flow preconditioning effectively addresses the instability of EBMs in high-dimensional token spaces, enabling stable training and superior anomaly detection performance in unified settings.

Abstract: Unified anomaly detection requires modeling highly heterogeneous normal data without access to anomalous samples. While foundation models like DINOv2 provide rich token representations, leveraging these spaces for explicit density estimation remains challenging. Energy-Based Models (EBMs) offer a principled formulation, but their training in high-dimensional token spaces is unstable due to anisotropy and strong cross-dimensional correlations, which degrades finite-step Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. We identify this instability as fundamentally geometric and introduce ReFP-AD (Rectified Flow Preconditioning for Anomaly Detection), which learns a geometric reparameterization that maps high-dimensional embeddings into a well-conditioned latent space via an optimal transport (OT)-coupled rectified flow. This preconditioning enables stable persistent contrastive divergence with preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) in full-dimensional token spaces. Anomaly scores are then derived from the learned energy landscape using gradient norms. Under a strict unified protocol on the MVTec-AD and VisA datasets, ReFP-AD achieves 98.6%/97.9% Image/Pixel AUROC on MVTec-AD and 97.3%/99.0% on VisA, outperforming prior unified EBM baselines by up to +10.8% in Image AUROC. Ablation experiments demonstrate that geometric reparameterization is critical for finite-step MCMC and accurate anomaly localization in high-dimensional token spaces. Code is available at https://github.com/CLendering/ReFP-AD

</details>


### [307] [LEAP: Lean Environment-Feedback via Adaptive Pruning for Code RL in GPU Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01804)
*Tankun Li,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LEAP is a scalable RL framework for low-level systems programming that uses adaptive pruning to focus computational resources on complex tasks, avoiding wasted effort on simple or catastrophic cases while enabling efficient multi-turn learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current critic-free RL frameworks for code generation face severe challenges when applied to low-level systems programming (like CUDA kernels): binary pass/fail rewards cause signal sparsity, multi-turn feedback suffers from prohibitive compilation latencies, and reward dilution occurs across trajectories, making the problem computationally inefficient.

Method: LEAP introduces Difficulty-Conditioned Pruning (DCP) - a dynamic gating mechanism that adaptively cuts off simple and overly catastrophic tasks from multi-turn expansion, focusing compilation and hardware exploration only on high-value complex tasks. It also uses Rank-Based Reward formulation that derives scale-free relative advantages from pairwise tournament outcomes within GRPO rollout groups to penalize token inefficiency on simple prompts while maximizing learning gradients on challenging distributions.

Result: Empirical evaluations show LEAP achieves superior first-turn proficiency and robust multi-turn debugging resilience while converging faster than unpruned multi-turn baselines.

Conclusion: LEAP establishes a practical paradigm for low-level code reinforcement learning by solving the computational inefficiency problems of existing methods through adaptive task pruning and rank-based rewards, making RL feasible for hardware accelerator alignment in systems programming.

Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) via reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced code generation capabilities. To bypass the heavy memory footprint of critic networks, current state-of-the-art frameworks leverage critic-free paradigms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) tied to rule-based verification sandboxes. However, applying these frameworks to low-level systems programming, such as CUDA kernel generation-presents severe challenges: binary pass/fail rewards introduce severe signal sparsity, while multi-turn environmental feedback loops suffer from prohibitive compilation latencies and reward dilution across trajectories. In this work, we introduce LEAP (Lean Environment-Feedback via Adaptive Pruning), a scalable and computationally efficient multi-turn RL framework optimized for low-level hardware accelerator alignment. LEAP features Difficulty-Conditioned Pruning (DCP), a dynamic gating mechanism that adaptively cuts off simple and overly catastrophic tasks from multi-turn expansion, focusing resource-heavy compilation and hardware exploration exclusively on high-value, complex tasks. To fully operationalize these paths without manual hyperparameter engineering, we propose a Rank-Based Reward formulation. By deriving scale-free relative advantages from pairwise tournament outcomes within the GRPO rollout group, our method inherently penalizes token inefficiency on simple prompts while maximizing learning gradients on challenging distributions. Empirical evaluations show that LEAP achieves superior first-turn proficiency and robust multi-turn debugging resilience while converging faster than unpruned multi-turn baselines, establishing a practical paradigm for low-level code RL.

</details>


### [308] [Predictive Maintenance: Deep Learning-Based Remaining Useful Life Prediction for Combat Aircraft Engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01819)
*Fatih Ürgen,Doğay Altınel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning model for predicting remaining useful life of combat aircraft engines achieves high accuracy on NASA datasets and enables reliable predictive maintenance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve combat aircraft operational readiness and reduce unplanned maintenance costs by accurately estimating remaining useful life, as traditional maintenance is insufficient for dynamic mission profiles.

Method: Developed a deep learning-based predictive maintenance model that autonomously extracts features from multivariate sensor data, using sequential blocks created via sliding windows (50-step for FD001, 30-step for FD004 datasets). Model architecture superiority validated against RF, CNN-LSTM, and BiLSTM baselines.

Result: On FD001 dataset: R-squared of 0.8901, RMSE of 13.28, NASA risk score of 320.34. On multi-regime FD004: RMSE of 15.71. Maintenance protocol achieved 0.9973 AUC at critical 30-cycle threshold. A decision-support simulator validates protocol under aggressive combat flight profiles.

Conclusion: The proposed deep learning model effectively extracts temporal degradation features and provides accurate RUL estimation, enabling reliable predictive maintenance for combat aircraft engines with high operational reliability, validated through simulation.

Abstract: To improve the operational readiness of combat aircraft engines and reduce unplanned maintenance costs, accurately estimating the remaining useful life (RUL) is critical. Traditional maintenance often proves insufficient under dynamic mission profiles. In this study, a deep learning-based predictive maintenance model capable of autonomously extracting features from multivariate sensor data was developed. Using the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 and FD004 datasets, data were converted into sequential blocks via 50- and 30-step sliding windows, respectively. The model's architectural superiority in autonomously extracting temporal degradation features was validated against RF, CNN-LSTM, and BiLSTM baselines. On FD001, it achieved an R-squared (R2) of 0.8901, a 13.28 RMSE, and a 320.34 NASA risk score, demonstrating generalizability on the multi-regime FD004 dataset with a 15.71 RMSE. The proposed maintenance protocol achieved a 0.9973 AUC at the critical 30-cycle threshold, ensuring high reliability. Additionally, a decision-support simulator has been developed to validate this protocol under aggressive combat flight profiles.

</details>


### [309] [tFUSOperator: Operator Learning for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01839)
*Minjee Seo,Haris Ghafoor,Minju Seol,Seonaeng Cho,Kyungho Yoon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: tFUSOperator is a neural operator for fast acoustic field prediction in transcranial focused ultrasound that maps free-field pressure, skull anatomy, and treatment parameters to intracranial field distribution, running 56,000× faster than numerical simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate intracranial acoustic field estimation is essential for tFUS, but numerical solvers are computationally expensive for digital twins requiring repeated simulations. Existing deep learning surrogates lack mechanisms reflecting how acoustic energy propagates through skull anatomy.

Method: Proposes tFUSOperator, a coordinate-aware neural operator that treats tFUS simulation as an operator learning problem, mapping free-field pressure, skull anatomy, and treatment parameters to intracranial field within a shared physical coordinate frame.

Result: Achieves ~90% Dice on seen skulls and ~72% Dice on unseen skulls for acoustic focus localization, performs nearly as well from MR as from CT input, and runs 5.6×10⁴ times faster than numerical simulation.

Conclusion: tFUSOperator enables fast, radiation-free patient-specific tFUS treatment planning and represents the first operator-based formulation for tFUS field prediction, offering practical digital twins for safe tFUS applications.

Abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) requires accurate estimation of the intracranial acoustic field, which is distorted by skull-induced aberrations. Numerical solvers are accurate but computationally expensive for digital twins, where the field must be re-estimated repeatedly as treatment conditions change. Existing deep-learning surrogates are fast but typically use voxel-to-voxel regression on a fixed grid, with no mechanism reflecting how acoustic energy propagates through the skull. We instead cast tFUS simulation as an operator learning problem and propose tFUSOperator, a coordinate-aware neural operator that maps the free-field pressure, skull anatomy, and treatment parameters to the intracranial field within a shared physical coordinate frame. To our knowledge, this is the first operator-based formulation of tFUS field prediction. On both seen and unseen skulls, the model localizes the acoustic focus accurately-reaching about 90% and 72% Dice, respectively-and it performs nearly as well from magnetic resonance (MR) as from computed tomography (CT) input while running $5.6 \times 10^4$ times faster than numerical simulation. These results suggest a fast, radiation-free route to safe and practical digital twins for patient-specific tFUS treatment. The code is available at: https://github.com/CMME-Lab/tFUSOperator.git.

</details>


### [310] [WorldDynCache: Risk-Controlled Latent Dynamics Approximation for Diffusion World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01845)
*Leyang Chen,Junyi Wu,Shaoqiu Zhang,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WorldDynCache is a risk-controlled latent dynamics approximation framework that speeds up diffusion world models by predicting when cached latent features can be reused, achieving up to 4.92x speedup while maintaining generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing caching methods for diffusion world models are slow due to repeated transformer evaluations. Current approaches that reuse cached features have limitations: they can miss approximation-induced latent transition defects that accumulate over time, and they don't adapt to phase- or condition-dependent changes in latent evolution direction.

Method: The proposed WorldDynCache framework has two key components: 1) A lightweight latent-transition risk estimator that tracks accumulated future impact of approximation defects and calibrates predictions against counterfactual defects observed at exact anchors. 2) A condition- and phase-aware lifted latent surrogate that approximates latent evolution without extra transformer evaluations.

Result: On HunyuanVoyager-13B, WorldDynCache achieves 4.92 times speedup, and on Aether-5B, it achieves 2.15 times speedup. It attains the best generation quality among compared caching methods across multiple metrics: WorldScore, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

Conclusion: WorldDynCache successfully addresses the limitations of existing caching methods by introducing risk-controlled latent dynamics approximation, enabling significant inference speedups while maintaining or improving generation quality in diffusion world models.

Abstract: Diffusion world models generate high-quality futures, but re- peated transformer evaluations make inference prohibitively slow. Existing caches reuse intermediate features, selectively update tokens, or reuse and extrapolate denoising outputs ac- cording to local drift or short native-space histories. These criteria can miss both approximation-induced latent transition defects that accumulate across skipped steps and phase- or condition-dependent changes in the direction of latent evo- lution. We propose WorldDynCache, a risk-controlled latent dynamics approximation framework with two core compo- nents. First, a lightweight latent-transition risk estimator tracks the accumulated future impact of approximation defects and calibrates its predictions against counterfactual defects ob- served at exact anchors. Second, a condition- and phase- aware lifted latent surrogate approximates latent evolution without extra transformer evaluations. On HunyuanVoyager- 13B and Aether-5B, WorldDynCache achieves 4.92 times and 2.15 times speedups, respectively, while attaining the best gen- eration quality among the compared caching methods across WorldScore, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

</details>


### [311] [Beyond Magnitude and Shape: A Direction-Aware Loss for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01857)
*Seunghan Lee,Jaehoon Lee,Jun Seo,Junhyeok Kang,Sangjun Han,Sungdong Yoo,Minjae Kim,Tae Yoon Lim,Dongwan Kang,Hwanil Choi,Soonyoung Lee,Wonbin Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CosDir is a direction-aware loss function that improves forecasting of series direction (up/down moves) through cosine similarity alignment, addressing MSE's failure on small moves while maintaining magnitude accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most forecasting losses optimize point magnitude or shape/frequency structure, but none explicitly target direction of change (up/down moves), which is crucial for decision-driven applications like risk management and financial forecasting. MSE-trained forecasters fail on direction of small moves.

Method: Propose CosDir - a scale-invariant, direction-aware loss that aligns difference vectors of prediction and target via cosine similarity. CosDir maintains directional gradient on small moves where MSE lacks signal. Also propose CosDir-UW extension that makes the mixing ratio between directional and magnitude terms adaptive by learning it during training.

Result: Over 100K experiments show the method consistently and significantly improves directional accuracy while preserving magnitude accuracy. It outperforms various loss functions. CosDir is lightweight, plug-in term that attaches to any backbone without architectural modification.

Conclusion: The CosDir loss function effectively addresses the critical need for direction-aware forecasting in practical applications, providing a simple yet powerful solution that maintains both directional and magnitude accuracy.

Abstract: The direction of change --- whether a series will move up or down --- is often as important as its exact value in decisiondriven applications such as risk management and financial forecasting. However, most forecasting losses optimize either point magnitude or shape and frequency structure, and none explicitly targets the direction of change. In this paper, we find that MSE-trained forecasters fail on the direction of small moves. To address this, we propose CosDir, a simple yet effective direction-aware loss that aligns the difference vectors of the prediction and the target via cosine similarity. Being scale-invariant, CosDir keeps a directional gradient on small moves, re-injecting learning signal exactly where MSE neglects it. CosDir is a lightweight, plug-in term that attaches to any backbone without architectural modification. Since the best ratio for mixing the directional and magnitude terms differs across datasets, we further propose CosDir-UW, an extension that makes this ratio adaptive by learning it during training, matching a per-dataset tuned weight with no hyperparameter. We conduct over 100K experiments, demonstrating that our method consistently and significantly improves directional accuracy while preserving magnitude accuracy, and that it outperforms various loss functions. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/cosdir.

</details>


### [312] [LAB-Tab: LLM-Augmented Bayesian Network Adaptation for Few-Shot Tabular Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01879)
*Zijian Shen,Taijie Chen,Bin Zhou,Ziyang Jiang,Jintao Ke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LAB-Tab is an LLM-augmented Bayesian network adaptation framework for few-shot tabular data generation that combines source data with limited target samples using LLM-guided structural expansion and PPO-based edge calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When target-domain data are scarce but collecting complete samples is costly, existing few-shot tabular generators either overfit to sparse target statistics or preserve irrelevant source-domain dependencies. There's a need for better methods that leverage both source data and limited target samples while adapting to target-specific patterns.

Method: LAB-Tab first fits a Bayesian network from source data, then uses an LLM to propose plausible target-domain BN edges absent from the source graph. A PPO policy then calibrates edges in the augmented BN through edge-level actions (keep, weaken, strengthen, flip, deactivate), trained with rewards combining distributional alignment, downstream utility, and preservation of target-relevant dependencies.

Result: Across six source-target distribution-shift scenarios from US Census (ACS) prediction tasks, LAB-Tab achieves best performance at 10% target-data budget, leads four of six individual scenarios, and reduces macro Overall score by 33.8% relative to strongest baseline, while obtaining best macro JSD, WAPE, and UtilityGap with competitive feature-label preservation.

Conclusion: LAB-Tab effectively addresses few-shot tabular generation by combining source domain knowledge with limited target data through LLM-augmented structural expansion and reinforcement learning-based calibration, outperforming existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics.

Abstract: Tabular data generation supports analysis and decision-making when target-domain data are scarce, yet collecting complete target samples is often costly. A practical but underexplored setting provides only a few target records together with richer source data from a related domain. Existing few-shot tabular generators often either fit sparse target statistics directly, which can overfit incidental patterns, or reuse source-domain generators, which may preserve dependencies that no longer hold in the target domain. To address this problem, we propose LAB-Tab, an LLM-augmented Bayesian network (BN) adaptation framework for source-aware few-shot tabular generation. LAB-Tab first fits a BN from source data and then uses an LLM to propose plausible target-domain BN edges that are absent from the source BN graph. This step converts semantic and weak statistical evidence into explicit structural hypotheses, thereby expanding the editable edge space beyond the source-fitted graph. Because the proposed edges may be noisy and interact with existing dependencies, a PPO policy calibrates edges in the augmented BN through edge-level actions, including keep, weaken, strengthen, flip, and deactivate. The PPO policy is trained with a reward that combines distributional alignment, downstream utility, and preservation of target-relevant dependencies. The adapted BN is then sampled to synthesize target-domain tables. Across six source--target distribution-shift scenarios built from three US Census (ACS) prediction tasks, LAB-Tab achieves the best performance at the 10% target-data budget, leads four of the six individual scenarios, and reduces the macro Overall score by 33.8% relative to the strongest baseline. It also obtains the best macro JSD, WAPE, and UtilityGap while maintaining competitive feature--label preservation.

</details>


### [313] [CARE: A Cascaded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01885)
*Zemin Chao,Qianhui Xu,Jianhe Cen,Guangzhi Ge,Xiao Chen,Hoangzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CARE: A model-agnostic cascaded inference framework that speeds up anomaly detection by using a lightweight pre-filter to route only uncertain samples to complex models, achieving 2.7-4.8× speedup while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models for time series anomaly detection have high inference overhead, but anomalies are scarce while most data points are normal patterns. Current uniform inference strategies across all data points are inefficient.

Method: CARE integrates a Lightweight Pre-filter Model (LPM) with existing Complex Detection Models (CDM). LPM uses Residual MLP AutoEncoder and Normality-Conditioned Gating to filter high-confidence normal samples. Includes Structure Attention module to capture channel-wise anomaly contributions and confidence-guided selective routing objective.

Result: CARE effectively isolates high-confidence normal samples, achieving 2.7× to 4.8× inference speedup compared to state-of-the-art approaches across eight real-world benchmarks while maintaining competitive detection quality.

Conclusion: The CARE framework successfully addresses the inference bottleneck in anomaly detection by using cascaded inference to reduce unnecessary computations on normal samples, achieving significant speedups without sacrificing detection performance.

Abstract: While deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in time series anomaly detection, their complex architectures incur substantial inference overhead. Existing methods typically apply a uniform inference strategy across all data points, which is inefficient given that anomalies are inherently scarce and the vast majority of temporal data consists of predictable normal patterns. To mitigate this bottleneck, we propose CARE, a model-agnostic cascaded inference framework that integrates a Lightweight Pre-filter Model (LPM) with an existing high-capacity Complex Detection Model (CDM). The LPM rapidly filters high-confidence normal samples using a Residual MLP AutoEncoder and a Normality-Conditioned Gating mechanism. Crucially, we introduce a Structure Attention module to explicitly capture channel-wise anomaly contributions, and optimize the gating network via a confidence-guided selective routing objective that learns reliable routing decisions to reduce unnecessary CDM invocations. Extensive experiments across eight real-world benchmarks demonstrate that CARE effectively isolates high-confidence normal samples. By routing only uncertain samples to the CDM, our framework achieves $2.7\times$ to $4.8\times$ inference speedup compared to the most accurate SOTA approaches, while still maintaining competitive detection quality.

</details>


### [314] [Understanding and Correcting Low-Frequency Bias in EEG Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01898)
*Junjie Yu,Zihan Deng,Jianyu Zhang,Junrong Mu,Jiahui An,Wenxiao Ma,Ziling Lu,Yue Wang,Yan Zhu,Kexin Lou,Quanying Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FAME introduces frequency-balanced masked autoencoding for EEG data, addressing the low-frequency bias in existing EEG foundation models by balancing reconstruction across EEG frequency bands, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 24 out of 41 downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EEG foundation models show persistent low-frequency bias in learned representations that persists regardless of dataset scale, model capacity, or pretraining objectives, limiting downstream task performance. This bias stems from EEG's 1/f^α spectral structure interacting with neural networks' tendency to preferentially learn low-frequency components.

Method: FAME (Frequency-balanced Masked Autoencoding framework) reconstructs time-frequency activity in predefined EEG bands from masked EEG inputs. It independently standardizes reconstruction targets within each frequency band and assigns equal weight to all band-specific losses, balancing supervision across the entire EEG spectrum.

Result: FAME learns more spectrally balanced representations and achieves state-of-the-art performance on 24 out of 41 downstream tasks in the OmniEEG-Bench evaluation framework. It demonstrates that balanced spectral supervision is crucial for learning transferable EEG representations.

Conclusion: Balanced spectral supervision is essential for learning effective EEG representations. FAME successfully addresses the low-frequency bias problem in EEG foundation models through frequency-balanced masked autoencoding, leading to superior downstream task performance across diverse EEG applications.

Abstract: Increasing EEG pretraining data scale or model capacity does not consistently improve downstream performance. We identify a persistent low-frequency bias in representations learned by diverse EEG foundation models, which remains across dataset scales, model capacities, and pretraining objectives. Our analysis links this bias to the interaction between EEG's $1/f^α$-like spectral structure and neural networks' tendency to preferentially learn low-frequency components. In masked autoencoders, the $\ell_2$ reconstruction objective further amplifies this imbalance: under comparable relative reconstruction errors, high-power low-frequency components contribute disproportionately to the loss. To address this issue, we introduce FAME, a frequency-balanced masked autoencoding framework that reconstructs time--frequency activity in predefined EEG bands from masked EEG inputs. FAME independently standardizes the reconstruction targets within each band and assigns equal weight to all band-specific losses, thereby balancing supervision across the EEG spectrum. Evaluated on 41 downstream tasks in OmniEEG-Bench, FAME learns more spectrally balanced representations and achieves state-of-the-art performance on 24 of them. These results underscore the importance of balanced spectral supervision for learning transferable EEG representations.

</details>


### [315] [Finite-Time Analysis of Discounted Exponential-Utility Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01917)
*Ankur Naskar,Vivek T A,Aditya Kumar,Gugan Thoppe,Prashanth L. A*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First finite-time convergence guarantees (Õ(1/√n)) for two model-free algorithms in discounted exponential-utility RL, using parameter-free stepsizes under asynchronous Markovian sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work on discounted exponential utility for risk-sensitive sequential decision-making only provided asymptotic convergence results. The nonlinear structure of exponential utility complicates reinforcement learning, and there was a need for finite-time convergence guarantees for practical applications.

Method: Established finite-time convergence rates for two existing algorithms: 1) For the simpler one-timescale method, overcame operator mismatch using boundedness, monotonicity, and homogeneity properties to obtain local pseudo-contraction, then used Moreau-envelope-based Lyapunov function and Polyak-Ruppert averaging. 2) For the two-timescale method, controlled tracking error on the faster timescale.

Result: Achieved finite-time convergence rates of Õ(1/√n) for both algorithms under asynchronous Markovian sampling with parameter-free stepsize choices. This represents the first finite-time guarantees for model-free discounted exponential-utility reinforcement learning.

Conclusion: The paper successfully provides the first finite-time convergence analysis for model-free discounted exponential-utility RL, addressing a significant gap in previous asymptotic-only results and enabling more practical application of risk-sensitive sequential decision-making methods.

Abstract: Discounted exponential utility provides a principled criterion for risk-sensitive sequential decision-making, but its nonlinear structure complicates reinforcement learning. A recent work \citep{thoppe2026reinforcement} addressed this difficulty by introducing a Bellman-compatible surrogate and two model-free fixed-point algorithms for optimizing it over stationary policies. However, their main convergence results are asymptotic. In this work, we establish finite-time rates of $\tilde{O} (1/\sqrt{n})$ for the aforementioned two algorithms under asynchronous Markovian sampling, where $n$ is the iteration index and $\tilde{O}$ hides logarithmic expressions. Importantly, we employ parameter-free choices for the stepsize parameter to derive these rate results. For the algorithmically simpler one-timescale method, the main challenge is that its update equation is not directly aligned with the contraction geometry of its underlying power-law operator. We overcome this mismatch by exploiting the boundedness, monotonicity, and homogeneity of the operator to obtain a local pseudo-contraction property for the relative-error dynamics. We then use a Moreau-envelope-based Lyapunov function and Polyak--Ruppert averaging to obtain the stated convergence rate with parameter-free stepsizes. For the two-timescale method, the main challenge is to control a tracking error on the faster timescale. These results provide the first finite-time guarantees for model-free discounted exponential-utility reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [316] [HarnessCompass: Guiding Automatic Harness Evolution toward Generalizable and Effective Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01918)
*Luan Zhang,Ruochen Zhou,Dandan Song,Zhengyu Chen,Yuhang Tian,Jun Yang,Huipeng Ma,Chenhao Li,Guangyuan Feng,Xudong Li,Yizhou Jin,Yan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HarnessCompass is a novel automatic harness evolution framework that uses constrained evolution, proactive feedback, and component-wise optimization to improve agent performance without overfitting to evolution tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic harness evolution methods suffer from three main problems: they overfit to evolution tasks, rely only on trajectory-derived signals, and optimize harness components jointly causing interference. These limitations prevent the creation of generalizable harnesses that perform well on new tasks and environments.

Method: HarnessCompass introduces three key techniques: 1) Constrained evolution that enforces global constraints to allow only task-agnostic harness changes, 2) Proactive first-person feedback from agents about harness usage to complement trajectory data, and 3) Component-wise optimization that decouples and optimizes different harness components separately before consolidation to reduce interference.

Result: On SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.4, HarnessCompass improved Pass@1 from 54% to 66% in just 5 evolution iterations, outperforming existing methods (AHE) in both effectiveness and evolution efficiency. The evolved harness also demonstrated strong generalization to held-out tasks and other models.

Conclusion: HarnessCompass addresses key limitations of previous automatic harness evolution methods by preventing overfitting, enriching evolution signals, and reducing component interference, resulting in more generalizable and efficient harness evolution for LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Harness design plays a critical role in agent performance by shaping how large language models (LLMs) perceive, reason over, and act within executable environments. Recent work has proposed automatic harness evolution, which iteratively improves the harness from agent--environment interactions. However, existing methods often overfit to the evolution tasks, rely exclusively on trajectory-derived signals, and optimize harness components jointly, causing interference across components. We propose HarnessCompass, a novel automatic harness evolution framework built around constrained evolution, proactive feedback, and component-wise optimization. HarnessCompass first enforces global constraints on evolution, restricting modifications to task-agnostic harness changes that generalize beyond the evolution tasks. It then augments trajectory-derived evidence with proactive first-person feedback from the agent about harness usage, yielding richer signals for evolution. Finally, it decouples the optimization of different harness components before consolidating them into a unified harness, reducing cross-component interference while preserving component synergy. On SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.4, HarnessCompass improves Pass@1 from 54\% to 66\% in only 5 evolution iterations, outperforming AHE in both effectiveness and evolution efficiency. In addition, the evolved harness transfers effectively to held-out tasks and other models, demonstrating substantially stronger generalization than prior automatic harness evolution methods.

</details>


### [317] [ChaosProbe: A Neurochaotic Lens on Frozen Transformer Input-Embedding Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01968)
*Kunal Kumar Pant,Nithin Nagaraj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deterministic neurochaos-inspired method called ChaosProbe creates response-based fingerprints of frozen transformer embedding spaces using chaotic trajectories to analyze model structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers are typically evaluated by their performance on tasks, but their frozen input-embedding spaces can be examined through deterministic probes before contextual computation, offering a different perspective on model structure.

Method: ChaosProbe applies chaotic trajectory-based transformations to prompt-level embedding matrices, measuring Firing Rate and Entropy channel responses with complementary representation-level measures to produce fixed-length signatures for each model.

Result: In a study with 80 prompts and 4 pretrained models (GPT-2, DistilGPT2, BERT-base-uncased, RoBERTa-base), correlation and similarity metrics successfully recovered model family relationships, with paired bootstrap resampling supporting the stability of these findings.

Conclusion: The results provide a proof-of-concept that deterministic neurochaotic response signatures can reveal broad structure among frozen transformer input-embedding spaces, offering a new approach to model analysis beyond traditional performance metrics.

Abstract: Transformer models are most often understood through what they do: their benchmark performance, generation quality, or behavior on downstream tasks. Yet frozen transformer input-embedding spaces may also be examined through their responses to a controlled deterministic probe before contextual computation or task-specific adaptation. Guided by this response-based view, we introduce \emph{ChaosProbe}, a deterministic neurochaos-inspired method for constructing response-based fingerprints of frozen transformer input-embedding spaces. For each prompt-level embedding matrix, ChaosProbe applies a chaotic trajectory-based transformation and summarizes its Firing Rate and Entropy channel responses with complementary representation-level measures, producing a fixed-length signature for each model. In a bounded proof-of-concept study of $80$ neutral prompts and four pretrained models---GPT-2, DistilGPT2, BERT-base-uncased, and RoBERTa-base---Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, and cosine similarity each recover all four same-family nearest-neighbor assignments and both expected mutual family pairs. Euclidean distance recovers three of the four assignments and one of the two mutual family pairs. Paired bootstrap resampling supports the stability of the Pearson and Spearman pairings over the observed prompt set, and signature-validity checks show that constant or collapsed responses do not dominate the reported fingerprints. These results provide a cohort-dependent proof of concept that deterministic neurochaotic response signatures can expose broad structure among frozen transformer input-embedding spaces.

</details>


### [318] [AOS: Adaptive Optimizer Switching via Training-State Signals for Faster Convergence and Better Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01997)
*Alok Kumar Pandey,Umang Chaturvedi,Aatish Rana,Gopi Krishna Nedanuri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AOS-R is a rule-based adaptive optimizer switching system that monitors gradient-space signals to automatically switch between AdamW, SGD-M, and Lion during different training phases, achieving faster convergence and better accuracy than individual optimizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single optimizers are suboptimal for different phases of deep network training: adaptive methods handle early noisy gradients well but overshoot flat minima, while SGD with momentum generalizes better in late phases but converges slowly initially. There's a need for an adaptive system that can leverage the strengths of different optimizers at appropriate times.

Method: AOS-R uses a lightweight controller that monitors six online gradient-space signals: gradient noise scale (GNS), Hutchinson curvature trace, loss stagnation, update stability ratio, gradient stability index (GSI), and loss improvement ratio (LIR). Based on these signals, it switches among AdamW, SGD-M, and Lion. The system includes state-preserving momentum transfer and a 400-step learning-rate bridge to prevent accuracy degradation during transitions.

Result: On CIFAR-100/WRN-28x10, AOS-R achieves 78% top-1 accuracy in 81 epochs, which is 26% fewer epochs than AdamW (109), 43% fewer than SGD-M (143), and 16% fewer than Lion (96). Across eight model-dataset benchmarks, AOS-R achieves best accuracy on 6 of 8 combinations with mean +0.4 percentage point gain and 0.80x convergence speedup over AdamW using a single shared hyperparameter configuration.

Conclusion: AOS-R demonstrates that adaptive optimizer switching based on gradient-space signals can effectively leverage the complementary strengths of different optimizers, achieving both faster convergence and better final accuracy than using any single optimizer alone, while maintaining simplicity with a shared hyperparameter setup.

Abstract: Single-optimizer training is a poor fit for the distinct phases of deep network optimization: adaptive methods handle noisy early gradients well but overshoot flat minima, while SGD with momentum generalizes better in the late phase but converges slowly early on.
  We introduce AOS-R (Adaptive Optimizer Switching, Rule-Based), a lightweight controller that monitors six online gradient-space signals -- gradient noise scale (GNS), Hutchinson curvature trace, loss stagnation, update stability ratio, gradient stability index (GSI), and loss improvement ratio (LIR) -- and switches among AdamW, SGD-M, and Lion as the optimization landscape evolves. State-preserving momentum transfer and a 400-step learning-rate bridge prevent accuracy degradation at every transition point.
  On CIFAR-100/WRN-28x10, AOS-R reaches 78% top-1 in 81 epochs -- 26% fewer than AdamW (109), 43% fewer than SGD-M (143), and 16% fewer than Lion (96). Across eight model-dataset benchmarks, AOS-R achieves best accuracy on 6 of 8 combinations with a mean +0.4 pp gain and 0.80x convergence speedup over AdamW under a single shared hyperparameter configuration.

</details>


### [319] [Scikit-fingerprints: Python library for scikit-learn compatible molecular fingerprints and chemoinformatics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02027)
*Jakub Adamczyk,Adam Staniszewski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: scikit-fingerprints is a Python library that bridges the gap between molecular fingerprinting tools (RDKit) and the scikit-learn ecosystem, providing a unified interface for molecular machine learning workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current open-source molecular fingerprinting frameworks (like RDKit) are not compatible with the scikit-learn ecosystem, creating fragmentation in molecular machine learning workflows and limiting reuse of mature machine learning tooling.

Method: Developed a comprehensive Python library that wraps RDKit functionality with scikit-learn compatible interfaces, providing molecular fingerprints, filters, similarity/distance measures, applicability domain estimation, and data splitting strategies under a unified API.

Result: Created scikit-fingerprints - a fully scikit-learn compatible library that enables seamless integration of molecular fingerprinting with the wider Python ML ecosystem, supporting composable workflows from SMILES strings to deployable models.

Conclusion: The library addresses compatibility issues in molecular machine learning, making workflows faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy through unified interfaces, computational efficiency, and extensibility while maintaining familiarity for chemoinformatics users.

Abstract: We present scikit-fingerprints, a comprehensive, fully scikit-learn compatible library for molecular machine learning in Python, based on RDKit. Molecular fingerprints and related functionalities are workhorses of chemoinformatics, yet the widely used open-source frameworks are not compatible with the wider Python machine learning ecosystem based on scikit-learn conventions. scikit-fingerprints closes this gap, bringing molecular fingerprints, molecular filters, similarity and distance measures, applicability domain estimation, data splitting strategies, and more under a single, familiar interface. Scikit-learn compatibility means that an entire chemoinformatics workflow, from a raw SMILES string to a deployable model, can be assembled from composable building blocks and can reuse the mature tooling of the surrounding ecosystem. The underlying RDKit code makes it familiar and extensible for custom chemoinformatics use cases. We put a strong focus on unified interfaces, ease of use, computational efficiency, customization, and extensibility. scikit-fingerprints makes molecular machine learning faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy.

</details>


### [320] [DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02032)
*Yixiao Qian,Song Chen,Pengkai Wang,Jiaxu Liu,Shengze Cai,Chao Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DART proposes a hybrid architecture that combines Mamba-2's state space models with attention mechanisms by decoding token-conditioned keys and values from recurrent states, enabling efficient attention over compressed memories while maintaining language modeling quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current architectures (Transformers with attention memories vs recurrent models with compact states) are typically separate or interleaved at layer level. The paper explores whether a shared memory representation can support both recurrent compression and attention-style retrieval, addressing the observation that Mamba-2 decodes values but not keys from its compressed state.

Method: Proposes DART (Decoded Attention over Recurrent sTates), which retains Mamba-2 chunked scan states as chunk state memories, decodes token-conditioned keys and values from these memories, performs state-memory attention (SMA) over the resulting KV pairs, and combines this with native Mamba-2 output via gated residual connection. Uses practical training techniques reusing Mamba-2 chunked scan and implementing SMA as FlashAttention-style computation.

Result: DART achieves 75% inference cache savings compared to matched attention baseline (with S=256 chunk size, N=128 state size). Substantially improves associative recall and retrieval over Mamba-2 while preserving general language-modeling quality.

Conclusion: DART successfully demonstrates that a shared memory representation can support both recurrent compression and attention-style retrieval, providing an efficient hybrid architecture that combines the benefits of state space models and attention mechanisms for improved performance and reduced memory requirements.

Abstract: Modern language models are built primarily from Transformers, recurrent models, and their hybrid architectures. Transformers rely on token-level attention memories, while recurrent models such as state space models (SSMs) and linear attention maintain compact recurrent states. These architectures are typically instantiated separately or interleaved at the layer level, leaving open whether a shared memory representation can support both recurrent compression and attention-style retrieval. We study this question through the state space duality (SSD) view of Mamba-2, where the SSM state can be interpreted as a compressed associative key--value (KV) cache. We observe that Mamba-2 decodes token-conditioned values from this state but does not decode token-conditioned keys. Based on this observation, we propose DART (Decoded Attention over Recurrent sTates), which retains the chunk state contributions produced by the Mamba-2 chunked scan as chunk state memories, decodes token-conditioned keys and values from these memories, and performs state-memory attention (SMA) over the resulting KV pairs. The retrieved output is then combined with the native Mamba-2 output through a gated residual connection. DART supports practical training by reusing the Mamba-2 chunked scan and implementing SMA as a FlashAttention-style computation. Our analysis and experiments show that DART substantially reduces the length-dependent inference cache compared with a matched attention baseline (e.g., $75\%$ savings when the chunk size is $S=256$ and the state size is $N=128$). Compared with Mamba-2, DART substantially improves associative recall and retrieval while preserving general language-modeling quality.

</details>


### [321] [Upper-Expectile Multi-Step Q-Learning for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02034)
*Abdelghani Ghanem,Mounir Ghogho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Expectile n-step Q-learning (ENQ) uses asymmetric expectile loss to accelerate reward propagation while reducing pessimistic bias from suboptimal logged actions, achieving competitive performance with Long-Horizon Q-learning with simpler hyperparameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-step returns help propagate rewards faster in off-policy RL but create pessimistic bias by coupling each decision evaluation with suboptimal logged actions that follow it, with bias growing with horizon length.

Method: ENQ replaces symmetric n-step TD loss with asymmetric expectile loss on action-value error, using expectile level τ as the only additional hyperparameter beyond standard n-step TD. The method maintains γ^n-contraction properties.

Result: Under deterministic dynamics, ENQ bias vanishes at optimal Q* for in-support pairs; under stochastic dynamics, bias has horizon-independent noise bounds. With τ=0.8, ENQ matches LQL performance on 27 tasks, achieves higher training throughput, and benefits more from ensemble scaling.

Conclusion: ENQ provides an effective alternative to existing long-horizon methods with simpler hyperparameter tuning, better computational efficiency, and strong ensemble scalability, making it practical for complex manipulation and navigation tasks.

Abstract: Multi-step returns accelerate reward propagation in off-policy reinforcement learning, but couple the evaluation of each decision to the suboptimal logged actions that follow it, inducing a pessimistic bias that grows with the horizon. We propose Expectile $n$-step Q-learning (ENQ), which replaces the symmetric $n$-step temporal-difference (TD) loss with an asymmetric expectile loss on the action-value error, with expectile level $τ$ as the only method-specific hyperparameter added beyond $n$-step TD. We prove that the ENQ operator is a $γ^{n}$-contraction.
