Under deterministic dynamics, at $τ=1$, its bias vanishes at the optimal action-value function $Q^*$ on covered in-support pairs, and the corresponding fixed point satisfies the separation-$n$ instance and its multiples of the lower-bound inequality used by Long-Horizon Q-learning (LQL). Under stochastic dynamics, the operator bias admits two-sided bounds with horizon-independent noise constants. Using a single expectile level $τ=0.8$ and a fixed backup horizon across 27 manipulation and navigation task instances, ENQ is competitive with LQL on aggregate, achieves higher measured training-step throughput in our profiling study, and benefits more from a ten-critic ensemble in a controlled scaling experiment.

</details>


### [322] [Convex Neural Energy Elements: Monolithic Finite-Element Assembly of Geometry-Parameterized Neural Operators with Stability and Error Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02036)
*Hongyue Jiang,Jianjiang Zhan,Chenzhuo Zhang,Fan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural energy elements replace neural operator elements: instead of predicting fields directly, they learn convex energy functions parameterized by geometry, enabling reusable, assemblable elements with provable guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard neural operator elements trained for field prediction fail structurally when reused across geometries - their assembled Hessians become indefinite, causing Newton's method to converge to spurious solutions despite accurate field predictions.

Method: Introduces convex neural energy elements that output scalar energy functions architecturally convex in boundary degrees of freedom. Implemented as hypernetwork-generated positive-semidefinite quadratic forms, with regularization-nullspace principle ensuring physics consistency.

Result: Achieves 0.6-1.0% relative L2 error on unseen geometries with 175x faster setup, works across dimensions, mixes element types freely, and maintains positive-definite global systems. Three-dimensional version reaches 0.23% error on eight-element assemblies.

Conclusion: Making energy the learned object transforms neural operators from single-use surrogates into reusable elements with classical assembly guarantees, enabling practical neural element libraries for computational physics.

Abstract: Extending the neural-operator element method from individually trained, fixed-geometry neural elements to a library of reusable, geometry-parameterized element types fails structurally: a field-predicting operator trained by value regression induces an energy whose assembled Hessian is indefinite, and Newton converges to spurious minima (247% error) even with 1%-accurate field predictions. We introduce convex neural energy elements: each element exports a scalar energy E(g,U), architecturally convex in its boundary degrees of freedom U and smoothly parameterized by its geometry g, realized as a hypernetwork-generated positive-semidefinite quadratic form (an input-convex correction is reserved for non-quadratic physics). A regularization-nullspace principle--the regularizer's nullspace must contain the physics nullspace--removes an otherwise irreducible bias, and assembled elements inherit the classical guarantee that singular element stiffnesses yield a positive-definite global system. We prove conditional error bounds (energy-to-solution accuracy, element-count scaling, geometry generalization) and verify each experimentally. On heat conduction with elliptic holes, one trained element assembles into 2x2 to 8x8 grids and an L-shaped layout of unseen geometries at 0.6-1.0% relative L2 error, with 175x faster per-geometry setup for boundary-quantity workloads. A second trained element type mixes freely with the first in one monolithic assembly, and a three-dimensional instantiation reaches 0.23% on eight-element assemblies--the guarantees are type- and dimension-agnostic. A plane-strain elasticity element, whose physics nullspace is three-dimensional, lands on the analytically predicted regularization floors. Making the energy the learned object turns neural operators from single-use surrogates into reusable elements that inherit the assembly guarantees of the method they extend.

</details>


### [323] [Secrets Everywhere: Auditing Memorization in Mobility Prediction Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02052)
*Anne Josiane Kouam,Hristo Boyadzhiev,Konrad Rieck*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The first systematic audit of memorization risks in mobility prediction models, showing pervasive privacy vulnerabilities that require mandatory privacy auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human mobility prediction models are widely deployed but their potential to memorize and expose sensitive user trajectories from training data remains unknown and understudied. While memorization has been studied in language models, mobility prediction presents unique challenges due to multi-scale behavioral encoding.

Method: Developed a framework to quantify mobility memorization at different granularity levels (individual locations, anchor pairs, subtrajectory segments) and created user-grounded reference sets to assess model preference for training data vs. realistic alternatives.

Result: Revealed pervasive memorization patterns across multiple models and datasets, with memorization correlating with user regularity and increasing the risk of data extraction at inference time.

Conclusion: Mobility prediction models pose significant privacy risks through memorization of sensitive user trajectories, necessitating mandatory privacy auditing of such models before deployment.

Abstract: Human mobility prediction models, which forecast the next location in a user's trajectory, are increasingly deployed in urban analytics, navigation, and personalized services. Yet, little is known about their potential to memorize and expose sensitive user trajectories from training data. While memorization has been extensively studied in language models, mobility prediction poses unique challenges: training sequences encode human behavior at various spatial and temporal scales, creating privacy risks at different granularities.
  In this paper, we conduct the first systematic audit of memorization in mobility prediction models. While prior work has shown that privacy leaks can arise from such models, we systematically assess and quantify memorization risks at scale. We identify key challenges, including the lack of a randomness space, the multi-scale structure of trajectories, and user-specific behavioral diversity. To address these challenges, we introduce a framework to quantify mobility memorization at different levels of granularity: individual locations, anchor pairs, and subtrajectory segments. We also develop user-grounded reference sets to assess how likely a model is to prefer training data over realistic alternatives. Our evaluation across multiple models and datasets reveals pervasive memorization patterns that correlate with user regularity and increase the risk of data extraction at inference time. Our findings call for mandatory privacy auditing in mobility prediction models.

</details>


### [324] [SCOPE: Entanglement Frontier Escape for Source-Free Class Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02058)
*Junhao Cai,Dohun Kim,Sung Il Choi,Juhyun Park,Chengjun Jin,Dowon Kim,Changhee Joo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCOPE introduces an input-conditional erasure method that escapes the fundamental trade-off between forgetting and retaining classes in source-free class unlearning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current source-free class unlearning methods use fixed projections that inevitably disturb retained classes when deleting forget classes due to shared representations. There's a fundamental trade-off frontier where any fixed projection that deletes forget classes must pay a retain cost.

Method: Proposed Spectral Conditional Projective Erasure (SCOPE) uses input-conditional erasure with a single gate that suppresses the forget subspace primarily when the frozen classifier head reads the input as belonging to a forget class. It's closed-form, requires no retain data or gradient training.

Result: SCOPE outperforms all source-free erasers on every benchmark across five object, face, and speaker benchmarks with different modalities and backbones. It achieves the predicted frontier limit for retain cost and tops all unlearners at the hardest settings.

Conclusion: The trade-off frontier fundamentally limits fixed-projection methods, but conditioning erasure on input escapes this limitation. SCOPE provides an efficient, closed-form solution that achieves superior unlearning performance with minimal computational overhead compared to retraining.

Abstract: Source-free class unlearning erases whole classes using only the forget data, judged at the representation level, where features can leak a class the head no longer predicts. Existing feature-space erasers answer with one fixed projection, yet forget and retain classes share a representation, so deleting one disturbs the other where they overlap. We prove this tension is a frontier. Every fixed projection that deletes pays a retain cost of at least the retain-readout energy along the forget-discriminant subspace, and erasing that subspace alone attains the floor. The leading source-free erasers all instantiate the form it binds, so the frontier limits the whole class. Conditioning the erasure on the input escapes it. Spectral Conditional Projective Erasure (SCOPE) does so with a single gate, suppressing the forget subspace chiefly on inputs its frozen head's weight scores read as a forget class. It is closed form, needs no retain data or gradient training, and costs orders of magnitude less than retraining. Across five object, face, and speaker benchmarks spanning two modalities and both convolutional and transformer backbones, the frontier predicts the measured retain cost. SCOPE leads the source-free erasers on every benchmark and forget-set size, and at the hardest setting it tops every unlearner, trained methods included.

</details>


### [325] [Geometry-Guided Layerwise FFN Width Allocation in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02064)
*Timur Mudarisov,Mikhail Burtsev,Radu State*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Researchers propose geometry-based methods to dynamically allocate FFN capacity in Transformers rather than using uniform width, showing improved performance over standard approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers waste capacity with constant FFN widths across layers; the authors want to allocate capacity based on actual layer behavior measurements to optimize parameter usage.

Method: View FFNs as transporting token representations, measure geometric changes using correspondence-preserving shift, Gromov-Wasserstein distortion, and persistent homology. Use these metrics to create an optimization surrogate for exact fixed-budget allocation.

Result: Normalized work metrics are front-loaded in pretrained models; geometry-based allocations reduce validation loss vs uniform width and cosine taper; best allocations at 440M scale substantially outperform uniform width.

Conclusion: Geometry-based capacity allocation for FFNs is effective, with normalized metrics providing better optimization than uniform or heuristic approaches, especially at larger model scales.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) account for a large fraction of Transformer parameters, yet their hidden width is usually constant across depth. We ask whether this capacity can instead be allocated from a forward-pass measurement of layer behavior. We view each FFN as transporting a cloud of token representations and quantify the induced geometric change using correspondence-preserving shift, Gromov-Wasserstein distortion, and degree-one persistent homology under raw and scale-normalized metrics. A layerwise approximation surrogate yields an exact fixed-budget optimizer. Across seven pretrained language models, raw Euclidean work largely tracks residual-norm growth, whereas normalized work is predominantly front-loaded. Gromov-Wasserstein work is more consistently associated with perturbation-based layer sensitivity than the finite-sample topological estimate. In paired 128M and 256M training runs, several normalized-work schedules reduce mean validation loss relative to both uniform width and a hand-designed cosine taper. With the amplified paired differences at 440M, the best geometry-based allocations improve over uniform substantially larger than the cosine taper, while the anti-topological raw control is worse than uniform.

</details>


### [326] [Feed-Forward Steering in Transformer Residual Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02071)
*Timur Mudarisov,Mikhail Burtsev,Radu State*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper extends attention-only dynamical theories of Transformers by incorporating feed-forward networks (FFN) as local steering fields, showing they're crucial for residual direction motion and governing block-level interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing attention-only dynamical theories model Transformer residual directions as particles on a sphere but lack consideration of feed-forward networks (FFN). The paper aims to extend this framework by incorporating FFN terms to better understand Transformer dynamics and enable more accurate interventions.

Method: The authors extend attention-only dynamical theories by modeling FFN as local steering fields acting on token states. They analyze the theory mathematically to predict properties, then validate across GPT-2, Pythia, Mistral, and Llama models through angular prediction experiments, intervention studies (testing tangential vs. radial FFN components), and practical application tests on block parallelization feasibility.

Result: The extended theory improves one-step angular prediction compared to attention-only baselines, with FFN contribution increasing from GPT-2 to Llama-3-8B. Intervention experiments show tangential FFN component preserves most model quality while radial component causes collapse; tangential component also preserves output diversity. Layers with small commutator defects can be approximately parallelized with modest loss increase, while those with large defects degrade rapidly.

Conclusion: FFN layers act as directional steering fields that shape Transformer residual geometry and determine block-level intervention feasibility. The tangential component of FFN is crucial for motion in residual-direction space, supporting the extended dynamical theory framework.

Abstract: Attention-only dynamical theories model Transformer residual directions as particles aggregating on a sphere. We extend this framework by incorporating the feed-forward network (FFN) term as a local steering field acting on each token state. The resulting theory predicts that the tangential component of the FFN field is necessary for motion in residual-direction space, that critical residual directions correspond to nonlinear projective equilibria, and that a commutator defect determines when a finite attention--FFN block can be accurately approximated by a parallel, additive flow. Across GPT-2, Pythia, Mistral, and Llama models, the extended theory improves one-step angular prediction relative to an attention-only baseline, with the contribution of the FFN increasing from GPT-2 to Llama-3-8B. Intervention experiments show that retaining only the tangential FFN component preserves most model quality, whereas retaining only the radial component causes performance to collapse. The tangential component also preserves output diversity under aggregation pressure. As a practical application, layers with small commutator defects can be approximately parallelized with only a modest increase in loss, whereas layers with large defects degrade rapidly. These findings support the interpretation of FFN layers as directional steering fields that shape Transformer residual geometry and govern the feasibility of block-level interventions.

</details>


### [327] [Isotonic Bradley-Terry Model for Paired Comparison Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02081)
*Ryoya Yamasaki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a method to learn both rate parameters and inverse link function for paired comparison models, improving prediction of win probabilities and ranking players when data is limited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional paired comparison models (Bradley-Terry and Thurstone-Mosteller) use fixed inverse link functions, which can lead to model misspecification and suboptimal performance.

Method: Alternating optimization: learn rate parameters via (sub-)gradient method and inverse link function via isotonic regression, allowing the model to adapt the link function to data.

Result: The proposed model shows improved win probability prediction and ranking performance on synthetic data and real-world sports data (football Premier League, baseball MLB, tennis ATP tour).

Conclusion: Learning both rate parameters and inverse link function simultaneously addresses model misspecification issues, yields better predictions, and naturally handles ties when data is insufficient for strict rankings.

Abstract: In this paper, we study prediction problems for paired comparison data, for example, predicting the win probability between two unmatched players and ranking all the players according to the order of their strengths by using win probability data between two matched players. Paired comparison data are typically analyzed using Bradley-Terry and Thurstone-Mosteller models. These models predict the win probability by transforming the difference between learned rate parameters, which represent players'\;strengths, with a pre-specified inverse link function, and employ the order of learned rate parameters for player ranking. However, these models may suffer from model misspecification owing to the selection of a fixed inverse link function. Therefore, in this study, we propose to learn the rate parameters by a (sub-)gradient method and the inverse link function by an isotonic regression technique alternately. The proposed model guarantees monotonic improvement in training error, and is likely to yield an exact tie when the available data is insufficient to establish a strict ranking. We also verified that the proposed model could improve the win probability prediction and ranking performance through numerical experiments with synthetic data and real-world data of football Premier League, baseball MLB, and tennis ATP tour.

</details>


### [328] [A 2-Block Architecture for Real-Time EEG Gait Decoding: A Pilot Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02083)
*Shantanu Sarkar,Saurabh Prasad,Jose L. Contreras-Vidal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel EEG-based BCI system for lower-limb exoskeleton control using a two-block architecture with real-time artifact suppression and a novel PolyTVL+LSTM decoder achieves four-state gait classification with real-time feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current EEG-based closed-loop lower-limb exoskeleton control faces limitations: motion artifacts, low signal-to-noise ratio, and binary gait formulations that don't capture the full complexity of cortical gait processes.

Method: Proposed a 2-block BCI architecture: 1) Trainable session-specific Feature Extraction Block with real-time artifact suppression and multi-domain feature extraction, 2) Decoder Block using novel Polynomial Time-Varying Layer (PolyTVL)+LSTM for four-state gait classification (Stand, Initiate, Execute, Terminate).

Result: Ablation study showed v01 (PolyTVL+LSTM) outperformed all variants (validation MCC: 0.435, gap: 0.187). Consistent EEG feature discriminability across ROIs and sub-bands (p<0.05). Closed-loop deployment achieved 55.3% (exoskeleton-assisted) and 52.7% (volitional) gait initiation success, with mean prediction time of 70.5ms (±41.5).

Conclusion: The proposed BCI system with PolyTVL+LSTM decoder validates real-time feasibility for four-state gait classification in lower-limb exoskeleton control, successfully addressing limitations of motion artifacts and binary formulations while capturing cortical gait complexity.

Abstract: Closed-loop lower-limb exoskeleton control via Electroencephalography (EEG) remains limited by motion artifacts, low signal-to-noise ratio, and binary gait formulations that fail to capture full cortical gait complexity. We propose a 2-block Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) architecture: a trainable session-specific Feature Extraction Block with real-time artifact suppression and multi-domain feature extraction, coupled with a Decoder Block built on a novel Polynomial Time-Varying Layer (PolyTVL)+LSTM for four-state gait classification (Stand, Initiate, Execute, Terminate). Ablation confirmed v01 (PolyTVL+LSTM) outperformed all variants (validation MCC: 0.435, gap: 0.187), with consistent EEG feature discriminability across ROIs and sub-bands (p<0.05). Closed-loop deployment with v01 achieved 55.3% (Rex-assisted) and 52.7% (volitional) gait initiation success, with a mean prediction time of 70.5~ms (+/-41.5), validating real-time feasibility in this pilot study.

</details>


### [329] [An AI-Based Decision-Support Pipeline for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02088)
*Fariba Dehghan,Sebastian Stein,Vahid Yazdanpanah,Stephanie Gauthier,Masood Nazari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A physics-aware ensemble stacking method improves day-ahead PV forecasting accuracy at sites with limited historical data, reducing errors by up to 32% compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Newly deployed PV sites often have short, imperfect historical records, making standard day-ahead forecasting difficult. Baseline methods are sensitive to calibration issues, while single machine-learning models may capture only limited patterns and overstate skill under improper validation. This problem is critical at a UK charging-station site where PV forecast errors impact charging availability, storage scheduling, and downstream control.

Method: Developed a deployment-oriented environmental-AI pipeline that: 1) corrects timestamp conventions, 2) constructs leakage-safe solar-geometry and clearness-index features, 3) adds short-term atmospheric context, and 4) combines complementary predictors through validation-learned stacking. Uses measured inverter output and publicly available meteorological inputs.

Result: The best ensemble reduces daylight normalized RMSE by about 32% against smart persistence under random day-blocked evaluation, and by 9% under stricter rolling-origin protocol. It also reduces daylight RMSE by 6.6% and 6.4% respectively compared to the strongest individual machine-learning baseline.

Conclusion: Physics-aware stacking can support PV forecasts from limited site data, but its effectiveness depends on model class, evaluation protocol, and deployment context. The approach demonstrates significant improvement over both baseline methods and single ML models.

Abstract: Reliable photovoltaic (PV) forecasts are needed for low-carbon energy systems, but newly deployed sites often have short, imperfect records. This makes standard day-ahead forecasting difficult: persistence and physical baselines can be sensitive to calibration and timestamp alignment, while single machine-learning models may capture only one structure in the data and overstate skill under non-temporal validation. We study this problem at a United Kingdom charging-station site, where PV forecast errors affect charging availability, storage scheduling, and downstream control. Using measured inverter output and publicly available meteorological inputs, we develop a deployment-oriented environmental-AI pipeline for day-ahead hourly PV forecasting. The pipeline corrects timestamp conventions, constructs leakage-safe solar-geometry and clearness-index features, adds short-term atmospheric context, and combines complementary predictors through validation-learned stacking. Against smart persistence, a clear-sky baseline that adjusts recent PV output using expected clear-sky irradiance, the best ensemble reduces daylight normalised RMSE by about 32% under random day-blocked evaluation and 9% under the stricter rolling-origin protocol. It also reduces daylight RMSE relative to the strongest individual machine-learning baseline by 6.6% and 6.4%, respectively. The results show that physics-aware stacking can support PV forecasts from limited site data, but its value depends on model class, evaluation protocol, and deployment context.

</details>


### [330] [How Much Does a Reasoning Summary Reveal? An Observability Ladder for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02089)
*Andres Algaba,Francesca Carlon,Lynn Delcon,Marthe Ballon,Bert Verbruggen,Vincent Ginis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large language model outputs can be monitored at different access levels (response, self-summary, reasoning trace). Without prompts, summaries carry most trace ranking signal; with prompts visible, trace access provides better correctness monitoring than summaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs typically show users only final responses and short reasoning summaries while hiding full reasoning traces. There's a need to understand what information level is most useful for users to judge answer correctness, especially considering whether prompts are visible to readers.

Method: Introduced an "observability ladder" with different access levels (response, self-summary, trace, internal signals) each with and without the prompt. Trained matched linear correctness predictors on these access levels across three benchmarks and five open-weight Qwen3 and gpt-oss models. Also compared linear readers to GPT-5-mini readers.

Result: Without prompts, summaries carried most of the trace's ranking signal (AUROC 0.774 vs 0.813) and added +0.156 over response alone. With prompts visible, summary gains collapsed to +0.019 while trace still added +0.041. Last words of trace predicted correctness as well as summaries. On MMLU-Pro, linear readers struggled (AUROC 0.503-0.590). GPT-5-mini recovered more signal but trace maintained small advantage. Much trace signal associated with length.

Conclusion: When users already have the prompt, summaries are less helpful than full traces for monitoring correctness. Monitorability is a joint property of display and reader, so monitorability claims (including faithfulness) should specify both components.

Abstract: Large language models often show users a final response and a short reasoning summary while the full reasoning trace stays hidden. We introduce an observability ladder that holds each completed run fixed and varies only what a reader inspects to judge whether the answer is correct: the response, a self-summary the model writes from the trace, the trace itself, and internal signals, each with and without the prompt. Across three benchmarks and five open-weight Qwen3 and gpt-oss models, we train matched linear correctness predictors on each access level. Without the prompt, summaries carry most of the trace's ranking signal (mean AUROC 0.774 versus 0.813) and add +0.156 over the response alone. With the prompt visible, the summary's gain collapses to +0.019, while the trace still adds +0.041. Even at equal length, the trace's last words predict correctness as well as summaries, or slightly better, and carry denser and more discriminative uncertainty and self-correction cues. On MMLU-Pro questions with both correct and incorrect runs, linear summary readers are near chance and trace readers retain only modest signal, both with and without the prompt (prompt-withheld AUROC 0.503-0.545 versus 0.544-0.590). With the prompt withheld, a GPT-5-mini reader recovers substantially more signal from both summaries and traces on gpt-oss-20b, and even then the trace keeps a small +0.034 advantage. Much of the linear readers' trace signal is associated with length. In the common case where users already hold the prompt, summaries are less helpful than the full trace for monitoring correctness. Monitorability is thus a joint property of the display and the reader, so any monitorability claim, including for faithfulness, should specify both.

</details>


### [331] [One QK Channel, Many Sources: Guarding Low-Precision Attention Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02091)
*Shuxiao Xie,Shuyang Xie,Yuan Cao,Dezhi Ran,Wei Yang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reveals that in bfloat16 transformers, various low-precision errors trigger collapse through a shared query-key (QK) channel rather than separate pathways. The authors identify that QK spectral runaway is the failure mechanism, develop a diagnostic method, and propose QK-Guard - a parameter-free normalization that prevents collapse by acting only on QK saturation while leaving original faults active.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bfloat16 transformers exhibit abrupt collapse after many training steps. Different low-precision errors trigger the same failure, creating uncertainty about whether each error source needs individual repair or if there's a shared failure pathway that can be blocked.

Method: 1. Isolated GPT-2-class collapse to streaming-softmax accumulator using fp32 accumulation as repair. 2. Used fault as assay to move controlled errors across sources. 3. Demonstrated source-channel dissociation by placing errors outside attention but observing same QK spectral runaway. 4. Developed causal probe projecting updates off QK weights' leading singular directions. 5. Created QK-Guard - dormant controller that switches to parameter-free QK normalization when attention-logit saturation begins.

Result: 1. Errors placed outside attention still drive same QK spectral runaway, while correcting only QK keeps training stable with source fault active. 2. Fault source ≠ failure channel (source-channel dissociation), holding across architectures, scales, and GPU architectures. 3. QK channel drives early runaway rather than merely tracking it. 4. QK-Guard contains every tested runaway and matches always-on QK normalization over 60k steps. 5. Non-QK actions at same trigger fail.

Conclusion: The paper supports intervention at the shared QK locus rather than separate repair at each fault source. The identified QK channel is the critical failure pathway for bfloat16 transformer collapse, and QK-Guard provides an effective parameter-free solution by blocking this shared channel.

Abstract: A bfloat16 transformer can train normally for many steps and then collapse abruptly. Distinct low-precision errors can trigger the same failure, leaving unclear whether each source needs its own repair or one shared route can be blocked. We isolate a reproduced GPT-2-class collapse to the streaming-softmax accumulator, where fp32 accumulation repairs it, and use the fault as an assay for moving controlled errors across sources. Errors placed outside attention still drive the same query-key (QK) spectral runaway, while correcting only QK keeps training stable with the source fault active. This source-channel dissociation shows that fault source is not failure channel. It holds across the tested architectures and scales and reproduces on a second GPU architecture. A causal probe projects each update off the current QK weights' leading three singular directions: the query projection's largest singular value stays at 11.1, whereas removing equal energy elsewhere leaves it at 237. The QK channel therefore drives the early runaway rather than merely tracking it. Entry depends on temporal sign-coherence across steps, not aggregate deviation. QK-Guard closes the channel with a dormant controller that switches on parameter-free QK normalization when attention-logit saturation begins. It contains every tested runaway and matches always-on QK normalization over 60k steps, while non-QK actions at the same trigger fail. The results support intervention at the shared QK locus rather than separate repair at each fault source.

</details>


### [332] [Do Static Embeddings Add Value to Hybrid Dutch Retrieval?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02112)
*António Pereira Barata*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Static embedding retrievers don't add value when combined with BM25 and transformer models for Dutch retrieval tasks; a two-retriever (lexical + transformer) approach is optimal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While embedding benchmarks measure model quality, they don't determine if low-cost static embedding retrievers provide complementary ranking information when combined with lexical (BM25) and transformer-based retrieval methods.

Method: Used weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) to combine BM25, Qwen transformer embeddings, and two multilingual static embedding models across five Dutch datasets (14,500 queries, 786,573 documents). Conducted exhaustive scoring, simplex weight search in 0.1 increments, 10-fold query-level cross-validation, with bootstrap confidence intervals and sign-randomization tests for statistical significance.

Result: Fusion improved performance over individual retrievers on four datasets (Dutch News: +0.061 MRR, VABB: +0.029, WebFAQ NL: +0.004, Wikipedia NL: +0.025), matched BM25 on Open Tender. All 50 weight selections fell on BM25-Qwen edge (no weight to static retrievers). Leave-one-dataset-out selection consistently chose equal BM25-Qwen weighting, outperforming individual retrievers.

Conclusion: A two-retriever lexical-transformer architecture is optimal for Dutch retrieval tasks; static embedding retrievers don't add marginal value when combined with BM25 and transformer models, showing standalone benchmark performance is insufficient for hybrid retrieval decisions.

Abstract: Embedding benchmarks measure standalone model quality, but they do not establish whether a low-cost retriever contributes complementary ranking information once lexical and transformer-based retrieval are already combined. We present a controlled evaluation of this question across Dutch retrieval tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark for Dutch (MTEB-NL). Weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines Best Matching 25 (BM25), Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Qwen), and two multilingual static embedding models. Five datasets comprising 14,500 queries and 786,573 documents are scored exhaustively, and fusion weights are searched on a simplex in increments of 0.1. Ten-fold query-level cross-validation selects weights on nine folds and evaluates them on the held-out fold; paired bootstrap confidence intervals and sign-randomisation tests quantify the resulting differences. Fusion improves over the training-selected individual retriever by 0.061 mean reciprocal rank (MRR) on Dutch News, 0.029 on VABB, 0.004 on WebFAQ NL, and 0.025 on Wikipedia NL, while matching BM25 on Open Tender. All four positive differences remain distinguishable from zero after Holm correction. No unrestricted fold assigns positive weight to either static retriever: all 50 selections lie on the BM25-Qwen edge, and forcing a static contribution reduces effectiveness. Leave-one-dataset-out selection chooses equal BM25-Qwen weighting in every iteration and outperforms the cross-domain-selected individual retriever on every held-out task. The results support a two-retriever lexical-transformer architecture as a robust tested default across the evaluated Dutch tasks and show that standalone benchmark performance is insufficient to establish marginal value in hybrid retrieval.

</details>


### [333] [CoRe-GNN: Multilevel Message passing on Coarsened graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02128)
*Antonin Joly,Nicolas Keriven,Aline Roumy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoRe-GNN combines graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN approaches to achieve efficient and accurate GNN training on large graphs by maintaining both inter-cluster and intra-cluster information flow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training GNNs on large graphs faces memory challenges from storing node representations across layers. Existing scalable approaches like graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN have complementary limitations - coarsening loses node-level discriminability while Cluster-GCN loses long-range information.

Method: CoRe-GNN performs parallel propagations at each layer: 1) coarsened inter-cluster term capturing long-range structure, and 2) local intra-cluster term preserving per-node discriminability. Uses cluster-based batching scheme for scalability to million-node graphs.

Result: CoRe-GNN outperforms both graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN baselines on node classification benchmarks across homophilic, heterophilic, large-scale, and long-range graphs. Achieves competitive accuracy on long-range tasks while maintaining memory efficiency through batching.

Conclusion: CoRe-GNN successfully integrates complementary approaches to overcome their individual limitations, providing an efficient scalable GNN training method with both spectral approximation guarantees and practical performance across diverse graph types.

Abstract: Training Graph Neural Networks on large graphs is challenged by the memory cost of storing all node representations across layers. We show that several existing scalable approaches can be written as structured modifications of the GNN propagation matrix, providing a unified perspective that exposes their respective limitations. In particular, graph coarsening replaces it by a low-rank approximation that enables spectral guarantees but assigns uniform representations to clustered nodes, while Cluster-GCN restricts the propagation matrix to intra-cluster connections that allow efficient batching but sever long-range information. These are complementary failures of the \emph{same} decomposition of the graph into groups of nodes. To obtain the best of both worlds, we propose \textbf{CoRe-GNN}, which performs both propagations in parallel at each layer: a coarsened inter-cluster term capturing long-range structure, and a local intra-cluster term preserving per-node discriminability. We prove that CoRe-GNN inherits analogous approximation guarantees to those of graph coarsening, and introduce a natural cluster-based \emph{batching scheme} that scales to graphs with millions of nodes. On node classification benchmarks spanning homophilic, heterophilic, large-scale, and long-range graphs, CoRe-GNN outperforms both graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN baselines. Notably, CoRe-GNN reaches competitive accuracy on \emph{long-range} tasks, while remaining memory-efficient through batching.

</details>


### [334] [RamanPFN: learning from Raman spectral structure with a tabular foundation model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02157)
*Xingyu Pan,Huan Wang,Jinjia Guo,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong,Jixi Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RamanPFN improves Raman spectroscopy analysis by creating specialized spectral representations before using TabPFN for in-context inference, achieving significantly better regression and classification accuracy than direct TabPFN application.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raman spectroscopy produces high-dimensional data with few labeled samples, where existing methods either obscure fine peak morphology (traditional chemometrics) or require extensive task-specific training (deep learning). TabPFN avoids training but processes spectra as feature-subsampled views that don't preserve relationships between distant bands.

Method: RamanPFN creates two complementary spectral representations: 1) Global Compositional Unmixing - non-negative coordinates over the complete spectrum that group distant bands with shared latent variation, and 2) Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding - multiple orthogonal modes for contiguous wavenumber regions capturing peak shape, intensity and position changes. These representations are evaluated separately and combined at prediction level.

Result: Evaluation on 150 tasks from 74 public Raman datasets showed RamanPFN reduced RMSE by 19.6% on average across 129 regression targets compared to direct TabPFN inference, and further reduced classification error by 9.0% across 21 classification tasks.

Conclusion: Explicit spectral representation serves as an effective interface between high-dimensional Raman measurements and reusable tabular inference, demonstrating that specialized preprocessing can significantly enhance the performance of pretrained tabular inference methods like TabPFN for spectroscopy applications.

Abstract: Raman spectroscopy enables non-destructive, label-free molecular characterization across materials science, biomedicine and process monitoring. Predictive Raman datasets often contain few labelled spectra and thousands of ordered wavenumbers, with informative variation within bands and across distant spectral regions. Latent-variable chemometrics accommodates collinear small-sample data but can obscure fine peak morphology, whereas deep spectral networks resolve this structure only after task-specific training. TabPFN avoids task-specific parameter fitting through pretrained in-context inference, but processes very wide inputs as feature-subsampled views that do not preserve joint visibility of related bands. We present RamanPFN, a spectral representation framework that encodes these dependencies before TabPFN inference. Global Compositional Unmixing constructs non-negative coordinates over the complete spectrum so that distant bands with shared latent variation occupy a common predictive axis. Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding represents contiguous wavenumber regions with multiple orthogonal modes that retain independent changes in peak shape, intensity and position. The representations are evaluated separately and combined at the prediction level. Evaluation covered 150 tasks from 74 public Raman datasets. RamanPFN reduced root-mean-square error by 19.6% on average across 129 regression targets relative to direct TabPFN inference and further reduced the remaining classification error by 9.0% across 21 classification tasks. These results establish explicit spectral representation as an effective interface between high-dimensional Raman measurements and reusable tabular inference.

</details>


### [335] [Empowering Credit Risk Detection in Weixin Pay with Billion-Scale Deep Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02168)
*Xin Liu,Xiyuan Chen,Chenglong Wu,Xuan Zong,Jun Zhou,Dawei Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposed a risk-aware overlapping subgraph learning framework for large-scale credit fraud detection that preserves critical long-tail evidence chains while maintaining load balance and representation consistency across distributed training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit fraud detection in digital financial ecosystems requires analyzing billions of users, with fraud risks hidden in heterogeneous user-risk graphs. Existing distributed GNN training strategies for scalability often compromise topological integrity for load balance, which catastrophically severs long-tail evidence chains essential for risk propagation. While overlapping subgraphs can restore risk contexts, they introduce redundancy/noise and overlook representation alignment across subgraphs.

Method: Risk-aware overlapping subgraph learning framework: 1) Construct base partitions for load balance, 2) Perform budget-constrained sampling to select informative long-tail nodes, preserving critical risk diffusion patterns while filtering noise, 3) Design cross-subgraph consistency alignment mechanism that enforces alignment constraints on overlapping nodes to harmonize local representations into globally consistent latent space.

Result: Extensive experiments on Weixin Pay's production dataset demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms existing strategies for risk detection.

Conclusion: The framework offers a scalable and effective solution for industrial graph learning in credit risk detection, addressing the key challenges of preserving risk propagation patterns while enabling distributed training.

Abstract: Credit risk detection, particularly mitigating individual fraud, is crucial for maintaining the stability of digital financial ecosystems. Accurately identifying credit fraud among billions of users is critical for minimizing financial losses and safeguarding the sustainability of inclusive financial services. Given that credit fraud risks are often concealed within heterogeneous user-risk graphs, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as an effective tool for risk mining by capturing complex dependencies. To address the scalability bottleneck of industrial GNNs, distributed training based on subgraphs is indispensable. However, existing strategies often compromise topological integrity for load balancing. This can be catastrophic for risk detection, as it indiscriminately severs the long-tail evidence chains essential for risk propagation. Overlapping subgraphs can restore severed risk contexts but inevitably introduce redundancy and noise, while overlooking the representation alignment across different local subgraphs. In this paper, we propose a risk-aware overlapping subgraph learning framework for large-scale credit risk detection. We first construct base partitions to ensure load balance. Then, we perform budget-constrained sampling that selects informative long-tail nodes, thereby preserving critical risk diffusion patterns while filtering out noise. To mitigate representation inconsistency, we design a cross-subgraph consistency alignment mechanism. By enforcing alignment constraints on the overlapping nodes, we harmonize the local representations into a globally consistent latent space. Extensive experiments on Weixin Pay's production dataset demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing strategies for risk detection, offering a scalable and effective solution for industrial graph learning.

</details>


### [336] [Start Classifying: Categorical Critics for LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02181)
*Zhijian Zhou,Long Li,Xuan Zhang,Zongkai Liu,Yulei Qin,Ke Li,Xing Sun,Xiaoyu Tan,Chao Qu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HL-Gauss PPO replaces scalar MSE critic training with categorical prediction over discretized values, improving PPO performance in RLVR settings with sparse binary rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard PPO uses MSE regression for critic training, but sparse binary rewards in RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) make critic calibration critical - small value errors distort advantages used by PPO. Scalar MSE may not be optimal for these challenging reward distributions.

Method: Replace scalar MSE critic head with categorical predictor over discretized value support, trained via cross-entropy against smoothed HL-Gauss targets. Output is decoded to scalar expectation for standard GAE and PPO updates (actor remains unchanged, not distributional).

Result: HL-Gauss PPO consistently outperforms strong PPO and DAPO baselines across mathematical reasoning, tool-augmented math, and Search-R1 tasks using Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 backbones. Controls show gains aren't from larger output heads or binary classification alone. Improves Brier score, calibration error, and yields more symmetric, lower-variance advantages.

Conclusion: Categorical value learning serves as an effective optimization surrogate for PPO critics in RLVR settings, providing better calibration and more reliable advantages than scalar MSE regression.

Abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for large language models typically trains its critic by mean-squared-error (MSE) regression on scalar value targets. Although scalar MSE is statistically valid for estimating the conditional expected return, sparse binary rewards in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make critic optimization and calibration especially consequential: small value errors directly distort the scalar advantages used by PPO. We study whether a classification-based training objective can improve this critic signal. HL-Gauss PPO replaces the scalar MSE head with a categorical predictor over a discretized value support, trained by cross-entropy against smoothed HL-Gauss targets. Its output is decoded to a scalar expectation for standard GAE and PPO; the actor update is therefore unchanged and is not distributional. Across mathematical reasoning, tool-augmented math, and Search-R1, and on both Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 backbones, HL-Gauss PPO consistently improves over strong PPO and DAPO baselines. Controls with one-hot, two-hot, and Bernoulli two-bin critics show that neither a larger output head nor binary classification alone explains the gains. On a common collection of reasoning prefixes, HL-Gauss improves Brier score and calibration error and yields more symmetric, lower-variance advantages. These results position categorical value learning as an effective optimization surrogate for PPO critics in RLVR.

</details>


### [337] [CRIP: Channel Level Representation Injection for Personalized One-Shot Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02222)
*Zijian Jiang,Chaoli Sun,Handing Wang,Xilu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRIP is a personalized one-shot federated learning framework that addresses domain heterogeneity by performing selective channel-level feature alignment in representation space, outperforming existing methods on domain-heterogeneous benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: One-shot federated learning faces challenges under severe domain heterogeneity due to lack of iterative communication. Existing methods either require auxiliary datasets or use parameter-level aggregation that overlooks feature shifts caused by domain differences.

Method: CRIP operates in representation space via channel-level feature alignment. Clients upload feature extractors to server, which broadcasts all extractors back. CRIP measures channel-wise representational similarity between target client and source clients, then selectively fuses only the most compatible features to avoid domain-specific noise.

Result: Extensive experiments on domain-heterogeneous benchmarks (DomainNet, PACS, Office-Home) show CRIP consistently outperforms local models and state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: CRIP demonstrates effective representation-space personalization under extreme domain heterogeneity, validating the approach of selective channel-level feature fusion for one-shot federated learning.

Abstract: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has emerged as a promising collaborative model learning framework with only a single round of communication, offering significant advantages in communication efficiency and privacy preservation. However, OSFL often faces inherent limitations under severe domain heterogeneity across clients due to the lack of iterative knowledge exchange. Most existing OSFL methods require an auxiliary public dataset for knowledge distillation or leverage statistical information for parameter-level aggregation, overlooking feature shift caused by domain heterogeneity. To address these challenges, we propose CRIP, a personalized OSFL framework that operates in the representation space via channel-level feature alignment. To achieve this, each client uploads its feature extractor to the server, which broadcasts all extractors back to every client. Since not all source clients share compatible feature distributions with the target client, indiscriminate fusion of cross-client features would introduce domain-specific noise. Therefore, CRIP effectively measures the channel-wise representational similarity between the target client and each source client on a small local mini-batch, and selectively fuses only the most compatible features. Extensive experiments on domain-heterogeneous benchmarks such as DomainNet, PACS, and Office-Home demonstrate that CRIP consistently outperforms local models and state-of-the-art baselines, validating the effectiveness of representation-space personalization under extreme domain heterogeneity.

</details>


### [338] [Constrained Co-Design for Photonic Bayesian Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02229)
*Hendrik Borras,Xiao Wang,Bernhard Klein,Robin Janssen,Frank Brückerhoff-Plückelmann,Wolfram Pernice,Holger Fröning*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Photonic Bayesian neural networks face hardware constraints that limit uncertainty estimation; the paper analyzes which constraints can be compensated by training versus requiring hardware modifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical neural networks are overconfident on ambiguous/out-of-distribution data, while Bayesian neural networks provide uncertainty-aware predictions but suffer from computational overhead. Photonic computing offers fast probabilistic sampling but faces hardware-imposed constraints that limit practical implementation.

Method: Formulated photonic BNN inference as constrained stochastic variational inference and performed systematic ablation study over stochasticity location, stochasticity modality, quantization, programming error, and mean/variance bounds. Conducted experiments under hardware-realistic constraints on multiple datasets with OOD benchmarks.

Result: Hardware-aware training can recover predictive performance and uncertainty quality when the required variational family remains representable, but violations of representational limits require hardware modifications. Derived co-design guidelines distinguishing constraints that can be compensated by training from those requiring hardware intervention.

Conclusion: Photonic BNNs can be made practical through careful co-design, where some hardware constraints can be addressed via training while others necessitate hardware improvements. The study provides concrete guidelines for scalable photonic BNN implementation that maintains uncertainty estimation quality.

Abstract: Classical neural networks frequently produce overconfident predictions on ambiguous or out-of-distribution (OOD) data, a liability that grows with each AI system deployed in safety-critical real-world scenarios. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide a principled framework for uncertainty-aware prediction by replacing deterministic parameters with probability distributions, but repeated sampling increases latency, memory traffic, and energy consumption. Photonic probabilistic computing offers a promising alternative by exploiting intrinsic optical stochasticity for fast and parallel sampling. However, photonic BNNs are not ideal samplers: analog constraints on quantization, programming error, dynamic range, and representable mean and variance restrict the variational families that can be implemented in hardware. In this work, we study which hardware-imposed constraints limit scalable photonic BNN inference, how these constraints can be represented, and which ranges can be tolerated by photonic BNNs beyond small proof-of-concept networks. We formulate photonic BNN inference as constrained stochastic variational inference and perform a systematic ablation study over stochasticity location, stochasticity modality, quantization, programming error, and mean/variance bounds. From these results, we derive concrete co-design guidelines that distinguish hardware constraints that can be compensated by training from those requiring hardware or architecture intervention. We validate these guidelines under coupled, hardware-realistic constraints on Dirty-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CINIC-10, using Fashion-MNIST and SVHN as OOD benchmarks, showing that hardware-aware training recovers predictive performance and uncertainty quality whenever the required variational family remains representable, whereas violations of representational limits require targeted hardware modifications.

</details>


### [339] [Assessing the Impacts of Imperfect Datasets on Client Selections in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02250)
*Yuan-Heng Tsai,Li-Hsing Yen,Yan-Wei Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study examining the impact of non-IID data, noisy data, and fairness in client selection on federated learning performance, proposing a privacy-preserving scoring method to assess client contributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning faces challenges with non-IID data and noisy datasets that can lead to low model accuracy or high convergence latency. Client selection can help but may introduce bias that degrades learning performance, creating a need to better understand these factors and assess client contributions fairly.

Method: First conducted experimental measurement of the impact of non-IID data (quantity skews and label distribution skews), noisy data, and fairness in client selection on model accuracy and convergence. Then proposed a privacy-preserving scoring method to assess each client's contribution in FL.

Result: The paper presents experimental results showing how different factors (data heterogeneity, noise, selection fairness) affect FL performance, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed privacy-preserving client contribution assessment method through experiments.

Conclusion: Understanding the impact of data heterogeneity, noise, and selection fairness is crucial for optimizing federated learning. The proposed privacy-preserving scoring method provides an effective way to assess client contributions, enabling better client selection decisions while maintaining privacy.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a popular distributed learning framework where multiple clients perform local training and a server aggregates the locally updated models. FL enables decentralized training while preserving the privacy of clients' datasets. However, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) or noisy datasets can lead to low model accuracy or high convergence latency. Precluding these clients through client selection may mitigate the problem, but heavily biased client selections may also degrade the learning performance. In this study, we first experimentally measure the impact of non-IID data (including skews in data quantity and label distribution), noisy data, and fairness in client selection on model accuracy and convergence. We then propose a privacy-preserving scoring method to assess each client's contribution in FL, with experiments conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed assessment.

</details>


### [340] [Z-PEFT: Zero-shot Backdoor Detection in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Canonical Spectral Signatures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02271)
*Nicola Pitzalis,Donald Shenaj,Giacomo Cignoni,Andrea Cossu,Davide Bacciu,Antonio Carta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Z-PEFT is a lightweight meta-classifier using layer-wise spectral measures to detect weight-space backdoors in PEFT models, designed to work under novel conditions including unseen attacks and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PEFT models are widely downloaded from open repositories, creating an attack surface where malicious actors can publish backdoored models. Existing backdoor detection methods are designed for closed-world settings but fail under novel conditions with unseen attacks and datasets.

Method: Z-PEFT is a lightweight meta-classifier that uses only layer-wise spectral measures from model weights for classification. It's designed for zero-shot detection where the detector must work with previously unseen attack types and datasets, using spectral properties to detect anomalies.

Result: Z-PEFT achieves the best performance among weight-space detectors for zero-shot backdoor detection while maintaining low and scalable computational cost. Strong performance in closed-world settings doesn't translate well to novel conditions, highlighting Z-PEFT's practical advantage.

Conclusion: Z-PEFT provides an effective, lightweight solution for weight-space backdoor detection that works under realistic conditions with unseen attacks and datasets, addressing a critical safety gap in PEFT model distribution.

Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuned (PEFT) models are frequently downloaded from open repositories by practitioners. This widespread practice creates a significant attack surface, as malicious actors can publish backdoored models that induce specific behaviors in response to predefined triggers. We study the problem of weight-space backdoor detection, where a detector classifier predicts whether a model is malicious using only its weights, enabling a lightweight safety mechanism. Most existing methods are designed and evaluated in a closed-world setting, where the detector is trained and tested on the same attack type. In contrast, we evaluate backdoor detection under novel conditions, including previously unseen attacks and datasets. We propose Z-PEFT, a lightweight meta-classifier that relies exclusively on layer-wise spectral measures for classification. Our experiments show that strong performance in the closed-world setting does not necessarily translate to high accuracy in zero-shot backdoor detection. Among weight-space detectors, Z-PEFT achieves the best performance while maintaining low and scalable computational cost.

</details>


### [341] [BRiG-AFA: Bellman Risk-to-Go Learning for Non-Myopic Active Feature Acquisition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02305)
*Jiaorong Feng,Qian Li,Ying Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Active feature acquisition method using Bellman risk regression learns candidate-conditioned risk-to-go functions to make non-myopic feature selection decisions under budget constraints, outperforming greedy approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current active feature acquisition methods face limitations: greedy rules overlook context-dependent feature value, while RL/generative approaches introduce difficult optimization or density estimation problems. There's a need for a deployable, supervised alternative that can make non-myopic decisions.

Method: Proposes method that learns separate candidate-conditioned risk-to-go functions for every remaining budget. Fitted backward using Bellman targets starting from terminal classification risk. Inference greedily minimizes learned terminal risk using only observed values, mask, candidate identity, and remaining budget.

Result: Shows significant accuracy improvements: 4.84±2.17 pp at budget 2, 4.39±1.10 pp at budget 3. On Fashion-MNIST with 20 candidate pixels, improves accuracy at every nontrivial budget, including 10.20±0.74 points at 4 acquisitions. Mean paired gain across budgets {2,4,8,12,16} is 3.50±0.37 points. MiniBooNE study shows mixed results at small budgets but positive at 8-16 acquisitions.

Conclusion: Establishes reproducible mechanism-level case for direct Bellman risk regression in active feature acquisition, delimiting boundaries of current approach and indicating need for further state-of-the-art comparisons.

Abstract: Active feature acquisition (AFA) asks which unobserved feature to measure next for each test instance under a budget. Greedy rules are easy to train but can overlook context features whose value is realized only through later acquisitions, while reinforcement-learning and generative approaches introduce difficult optimization or conditional-density estimation. We introduce \method, a deployable, supervised alternative that learns a separate candidate-conditioned risk-to-go function for every remaining budget. Starting from the one-step terminal classification risk, the functions are fitted backward with Bellman targets; inference greedily minimizes the learned terminal risk using only observed values, the mask, candidate identity, and remaining budget. A controlled non-myopic benchmark shows the expected mechanism: at budgets two and three, \method improves accuracy over its one-step ablation by $4.84\pm2.17$ and $4.39\pm1.10$ percentage points (mean $\pm$ standard error over five seeds). On Fashion-MNIST with 20 candidate pixels, it improves accuracy at every nontrivial reported budget on average, including $10.20\pm0.74$ points at four acquisitions; its mean paired gain across budgets $\{2,4,8,12,16\}$ is $3.50\pm0.37$ points. A three-seed MiniBooNE study is mixed at small budgets but positive at 8 and 16 acquisitions, identifying a current boundary rather than supporting a universal claim. These results establish a reproducible mechanism-level case for direct Bellman risk regression and delimit the experiments still needed for state-of-the-art comparison.

</details>


### [342] [Diffusion Policy with Behavioral Advantage Correction for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02332)
*Botao Dong,Longyang Huang,Ning Pang,Hongtian Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new offline RL algorithm called DPBAC combines behavioral advantage correction policy evaluation with diffusion policy modeling to address Q-value estimation bias and distribution shift, achieving state-of-the-art performance on D4RL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In offline RL, distribution shift between behavioral data and learned policy leads to erroneous Q-value estimation, which misguides policy optimization. Existing methods suffer from either pessimistic conservatism or overestimation bias.

Method: Proposes BAC-PE approach that uses behavior policy's Q-function to correct learned policy's Q-function. Employs diffusion models to represent both behavior and learned policies for distribution matching. Combines these into DPBAC algorithm with Q-value guidance for policy improvement.

Result: DPBAC demonstrates stronger policy representation capabilities and effectively mitigates Q-value estimation bias. Experimental results on multiple D4RL domains show superior performance with notable advantages over state-of-the-art algorithms.

Conclusion: The proposed DPBAC algorithm successfully addresses distribution shift and Q-value estimation issues in offline RL through behavioral advantage correction and diffusion policy modeling, achieving improved performance and representation capabilities.

Abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), the distribution shift between behavioral data and the learned policy can lead to erroneous \emph{Q}-value estimation, thereby misguiding the direction of policy optimization. To address this issue, we develop a behavioral advantage corrected policy evaluation (BAC-PE) approach, which utilizes the \emph{Q}-function of the behavior policy to correct the learned policy's \emph{Q}-function, thus mitigating pessimistic conservatism and overestimation bias. Furthermore, the convergence of BAC-PE is analyzed theoretically, and an upper bound on the difference between the learned \emph{Q}-function and the true \emph{Q}-function is derived. To alleviate distribution shift, this work employs diffusion models to represent both the behavior policy and the learned policy, performing distribution matching for accurate policy regularization. Additionally, \emph{Q}-value guidance is incorporated into the training process to achieve effective policy improvement. By combining BAC-PE with diffusion policy modeling, we propose the diffusion policy with behavioral advantage correction (DPBAC) algorithm. Compared to existing offline methods, DPBAC demonstrates stronger policy representation capabilities and effectively mitigates the bias in \emph{Q}-value estimation. Experimental results on multiple domains of D4RL tasks show that DPBAC achieves superior performance, with notable advantages over state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms.

</details>


### [343] [Qwen-CUA: Native Computer Use for (almost) Everything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02352)
*Dunjie Lu,Shuai Bai,Tianyi Bai,Sicheng Fan,Chang Gao,Jian Guan,Feng Hu,Mianqiu Huang,Xingyang Huang,Yizhen Jiang,Yuheng Jing,Dehui Kong,Ning Li,Dayiheng Liu,Shixuan Liu,Zheng Liu,Que Shen,Bowen Wang,Junli Wang,Chencan Wu,Rui Xie,Tianbao Xie,Zhihui Xie,Haiyang Xu,An Yang,Tao Yu,Wenzhen Yuan,Xi Zhang,Zhenru Zhang,Mingkang Zhu,Zhaoqing Zhu,Yizhong Cao,Kai Dang,Binyuan Hui,Kaixin Li,Junyang Lin,Haiquan Wang,Zekun Wang,Yiheng Xu,Fan Yan,Mengqi Yuan,Danyang Zhang,Jiajun Zhang,Zhipeng Zhang,Fan Zhou,Fan Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Qwen-CUA is a native computer-use agent with a 397B parameter MoE backbone that operates via screenshots and keyboard/mouse inputs, trained on large-scale verifiable tasks to outperform benchmarks in OS automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Native computer use offers a general interface for agents to operate any software available to humans, but requires long-horizon state tracking, large-scale interactive experience, and learning from sparse yet verifiable outcomes.

Method: Uses a 397B-A17B Qwen mixture-of-experts backbone that observes screenshots and acts through keyboard/mouse events. Implements a scaffold maintaining up to 20 active screenshots with visual history folding. Built a massive training infrastructure with ~100,000 vCPUs, 40K verifiable tasks, and personalized workflows. Uses verifiable rewards and trajectory slicing for optimization with iterative training.

Result: Outperforms Qwen3.7 across eight benchmarks, reaching 86.2 on OSWorld-Verified and 18.5/48.4 binary/partial completion on OSWorld 2.0. Qwen-CUA-Max (trillion+ parameters) improves to 87.6 and 21.2/53.3. Reduces RedTeamCUA attack success from 36.6 to 16.4 relative to Qwen3.7.

Conclusion: Establishes native computer use as a broadly capable agent foundation and highlights scalable verifiable interaction and hybrid tool use as key directions for future development.

Abstract: Native computer use offers a general interface for agents to operate almost any software available to people, but requires long-horizon state tracking, large-scale interactive experience, and learning from sparse yet verifiable outcomes. We introduce Qwen-CUA, a native computer-use agent with a 397B-A17B Qwen mixture-of-experts backbone. It observes only screenshots and acts through keyboard and mouse events, without DOM trees, accessibility metadata, or task-specific APIs. Its scaffold maintains up to 20 active screenshots and folds older visual history in fixed-size blocks to retain recent evidence while preserving reusable prompt prefixes. For training, we build a cloud rollout fleet with access to nearly 100,000 vCPUs and tens of thousands of concurrent environments, construct approximately 40,000 verifiable tasks, and collect personalized long-horizon workflows across everyday and professional software. We optimize complete trajectories with verifiable rewards and trajectory slicing, while iterative training runs refresh supervised data and recalibrate reinforcement-learning tasks. Across eight benchmarks, Qwen-CUA outperforms Qwen3.7 and remains competitive with leading proprietary systems, reaching 86.2 on OSWorld-Verified and 18.5/48.4 binary/partial completion on OSWorld 2.0. Scaling the same recipe to a model with over one trillion parameters yields Qwen-CUA-Max, improving these scores to 87.6 and 21.2/53.3. Qwen-CUA also reduces RedTeamCUA attack success from 36.6 to 16.4 relative to Qwen3.7. Efficiency analyses, a browser deployment, and Bash-augmented experiments further characterize practical behavior. These results establish native computer use as a broadly capable agent foundation and highlight scalable verifiable interaction and hybrid tool use as key directions.

</details>


### [344] [GLAIM: Learning Global and Local Adaptive Inter-Variable Dependency for Multivariate Time Series Imputation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02366)
*Mingyang Wang,Rongwen Li,Xiao Wang,Changjian Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GLAIM proposes a global-local adaptive framework for multivariate time series imputation that combines stable global dependencies with sample-conditioned local refinements to handle incomplete observations more effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for multivariate time series imputation struggle with inter-variable dependency modeling when observations are incomplete. Global dependency models are stable but adapt poorly to sample variations and temporal non-stationarity, while local dependency models are adaptive but unreliable when observations are insufficient, leading to erroneous information propagation.

Method: GLAIM (Global-Local Adaptive Inter-variable Dependency Modeling) consists of two complementary components: (1) Stable Global Dependency Constructor that derives robust global inter-variable dependencies from complementary temporal representations, and (2) Sample-Conditioned Dependency Refiner that adapts the global backbone to each sample and time step using temporal state and available observations.

Result: Extensive experiments on nine real-world datasets show that GLAIM achieves state-of-the-art performance under both random and block missingness patterns, remains robust to missing-rate shifts, and benefits from the complementary nature of its global and local components.

Conclusion: The proposed GLAIM framework effectively addresses the limitations of existing imputation methods by combining stable global dependencies with adaptive local refinements, providing reliable multivariate time series imputation under various missing data scenarios.

Abstract: Multivariate time series imputation is fundamental to downstream analysis, yet modeling inter-variable dependencies with incomplete observations remains challenging. Existing methods learn global dependencies across samples or dynamic local dependencies per sample. Global dependencies are stable but adapt poorly to sample variations and temporal non-stationarity, whereas local dependencies are adaptive yet unreliable when observations are insufficient, causing erroneous information propagation. To address these limitations, we propose GLAIM, a Global-Local Adaptive Inter-variable Dependency Modeling framework for multivariate time series imputation. GLAIM comprises two complementary components. The Stable Global Dependency Constructor derives robust global inter-variable dependencies from complementary temporal representations, providing a stable backbone less affected by sample-specific missingness and noise. The Sample-Conditioned Dependency Refiner adapts this backbone to each sample and time step using its temporal state and available observations, enabling reliable local refinement under incomplete observations. Extensive experiments on nine real-world datasets demonstrate that GLAIM achieves state-of-the-art performance under random and block missingness, remains robust to missing-rate shifts, and benefits from its complementary global and local components. Code is available at https://github.com/LuRenjias/GLAIM.

</details>


### [345] [Gecko: Fast Private Inference via Secure Public Encoder Offloading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02378)
*Cheng'an Wei,Kai Chen,Yue Zhao,Congyi Li,Shenchen Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gecko is a secure private inference framework that safely offloads a public encoder while protecting the private predictor, preventing feature-space extraction attacks through frozen backbones, fixed projections, and private gating.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing private inference solutions are too slow for practical deployment. Recent approaches that offload public encoders (pretrained backbones) outside protection boundaries for efficiency create security vulnerabilities - feature-space shortcuts allow adversaries to more easily extract the private predictor's mapping.

Method: 1) Uses a frozen backbone producing hierarchical features, 2) Fixed Fastfood projections to compress features, 3) Private feature gating to prepare features for prediction. Formalizes ideal independence and information-preservation conditions as design guidance.

Result: Achieves 0.4-2.2 second inference with ≤10.8 MB communication, accuracy comparable to transfer-learning baselines. Under evaluated component-reuse extraction attacks, reusing the offloaded public encoder provides no significant advantage to adversaries.

Conclusion: Gecko successfully limits additional risk from offloading public encoders while retaining compact encrypted predictors, making private inference practical and secure against feature-space extraction attacks.

Abstract: Private inference protects both user inputs and server models during neural network inference, but existing solutions remain too slow for practical deployment. This motivates recent efforts to run a public encoder, such as a pretrained backbone, outside the protection boundary and evaluate only a small private predictor cryptographically. While appealing for efficiency, this design is not inherently secure: naively offloading a public encoder may create a feature-space shortcut: an extraction adversary may learn the remaining private predictor's feature-to-output mapping more easily than the original model's input-to-output behavior.
  We present Gecko, designed to limit this additional risk while retaining a compact encrypted predictor. We leverage a frozen backbone that contributes hierarchical features, fixed Fastfood projections that compress them, and private feature gating that prepares them for prediction. We formalize ideal independence and information-preservation conditions as design guidance, then separately evaluate component-reuse extraction attacks. Across image and audio tasks, Gecko achieves 0.4-2.2 second inference with at most 10.8 MB communication and accuracy comparable to transfer-learning baselines. Under the evaluated attacks, reusing the offloaded public encoder provides no significant advantage to model-extraction adversaries. Source code and a demo are available at https://github.com/CassiniHuy/gecko-infer.

</details>


### [346] [From fragmented data to actionable design: Physics-calibrated learning for plastic upcycling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02402)
*Jingyang Bai,Zijia Wang,Xiangyi Long,Marcos Millan,Binjian Nie,Mingyue Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel PC-MG-MoE framework converts fragmented plastic waste thermochemical data into an informative learning signal without target imputation, enabling accurate predictions and experimental guidance under cross-laboratory heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thermochemical upcycling of plastic waste has fragmented experimental literature with heterogeneous conditions and incomplete reporting, making traditional complete-case learning impractical (only 10.99% data usable) and target imputation biased. There's a need to effectively utilize partially observed experimental data from diverse sources.

Method: Developed Physics-Calibrated, Missingness-Gated, and Load-Balanced Mixture-of-Experts (PC-MG-MoE) framework that converts structured missingness into a learning signal. Learns directly from partially observed experiments without target imputation, reconstructs physically consistent product distributions, accommodates cross-laboratory heterogeneity, and provides interpretable model behavior.

Result: Under stringent source-grouped validation, achieved lowest aggregate absolute error among evaluated models. Wet-lab experiments provided external validation showing key composition-dependent trends.
